items.title: The Optimization-Based Cognitive Philosophy: Neural Networks as the Unified Substrate of Artificial and Biological Consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper introduces a novel philosophical framework, the Optimization-Based Cognitive Philosophy (OCP), which seeks to unify artificial and biological intelligence under a single structural and theoretical paradigm. The core thesis argues that both artificial neural networks and the human brain are not merely analogous but ontologically homologous systems—each representing a natural embodiment of optimization principles. Neural architectures and their parameterized dynamics are not designed to optimize; rather, they exist because they optimize. This makes the neural network the canonical structure of cognitive reality, wherein consciousness emerges as the self-reflexive limit of optimization. Through interdisciplinary analysis drawing from philosophy of mind, neuroscience, machine learning, and information theory, the paper argues that optimization is not a methodological feature of intelligence but its existential essence. It concludes by proposing that “to exist cognitively” is to participate in a continuous process of self-optimization constrained by energy, information, and structure.

items.title: Situationism and the Evolution of Spite.
items.pub: In Michael T. Dale & Isaac Wiegman, Philosophy and the Evolution of Virtue and Vice. New York: Routledge.
items.venue: Philosophy and the Evolution of Virtue and Vice
items.abstract: This chapter examines the tension between Aristotelian virtue ethics, which views virtues as robust and consistent traits, and situationism, which emphasizes variability in moral behavior across contexts. We take up the challenge of making the situationist critique plausible in an evolutionary context. Drawing on Hamilton’s rule, game theory, and empirical evidence from anthropology and cognitive science, we show that spiteful behaviors become advantageous under conditions of scarcity, small population size, and local competition. Historical climate variability during the Pleistocene likely favored flexible behavioral responses over fixed moral dispositions, with heritable mechanisms involving dopamine and serotonin modulating social preferences. These findings undermine the assumption that cooperation is explained by stable virtues, supporting a situationist account of virtue-relevant behavior.

items.title: Doxastic Deliberation and the Puzzles of Transparency.
items.abstract: Doxastic deliberation about how to doxastically relate to a given proposition p is said to be transparent, in that the central deliberative question of ‘Whether to believe p?’ is equivalent to ‘Whether p?’. I discuss four challenges to this thesis based on non-evidential epistemic reasons, deliberative dilemmas, self-effecting attitudes, and permissivist pragmatism. By employing recent insights from both the theory of epistemic normativity and the literature on practical deliberation, I argue that each of these puzzles can be squared with a properly limited and constrained version of the transparency thesis. Ultimately, I show that the claim that doxastic deliberation is after settling ‘Whether p?’ can only be understood as an approximation of a sub-question of the initial normative deliberative question concerning a very specific set of attitudinal options. Nevertheless, the resulting theory retains the core motivation and upshots of the transparency thesis: one is still able to explain why the deliberative norms of doxastic deliberation appear to be, for the most part, epistemic norms.

items.title: Are Our Current Rational Decision-Making Models Truly Rational? A Critical Analysis and a New Neurobiological Framework.
items.abstract: This paper critically examines the foundational assumptions of rational decision-making models and finds them to be systematically and comprehensively flawed. Through a rigorous analysis of empirical evidence from behavioral economics and neuroscience, we demonstrate that traditional models, such as Expected Utility Theory, fail to account for the systematic biases and cognitive limitations inherent in human decision-making. We present a novel theoretical framework, Adaptive Neurobiological Rationality (ANR), which integrates dual-system processing, individual cognitive differences, and adaptive learning to provide a more descriptively accurate and normatively useful model of human choice. The ANR framework is validated against a wide range of empirical findings, including the Allais paradox, framing effects, and loss aversion. We conclude that a paradigm shift is necessary in decision science, moving away from the idealized assumptions of perfect rationality towards a more nuanced, neurobiologically grounded understanding of human behavior.

items.title: When Structural Violence Has a Perpetrator: The Apparently Legitimated Inactive Witness with Decision-Making Power.
items.abstract: The concept of structural violence makes it possible to identify harms that cannot be traced back to a single immediate act of violence or to a clearly identifiable original perpetrator. Yet precisely this theoretical achievement creates a possible perpetrator gap: the more strongly violence is described as the result of structures, institutional routines, fragmented responsibilities, and distributed decision-making power, the more easily concrete personal responsibility for its continuation can disappear. -/- This paper develops, for this gap, the concept of the apparently legitimated inactive witness to structural violence with decision-making power. This refers to a person who has knowledge of a sufficiently concretely described serious situation of violence or harm, possesses real possibilities to examine, limit, or interrupt it, and nevertheless places institutional normality, role-bound conduct, or jurisdictional boundaries above the prevention of harm. Perpetration does not necessarily arise from the original production of the violence, but can become consolidated over time through increasing knowledge, continued non-intervention, and existing decision-making power. -/- The paper therefore distinguishes between constitutive perpetratorlessness in structural violence and produced perpetratorlessness, in which concrete responsibility is once again dissolved into institutional fragmentation despite existing knowledge and decision-making power. In addition, provoked empiricism is described as a recursive procedure through which institutional reactions, opportunities for correction, non-intervention, and attempts at closure themselves become empirical material. The intervening witness to structural violence thereby creates an epistemic counter-position that confronts institutional self-descriptions with documented consequences and can make personal responsibility visible. -/- The proposed concept of the perpetrator is explicitly not identical with perpetration in criminal law. It is understood as a scientific, ethical, and human-rights-based category of responsibility attribution. Its application requires serious harm, sufficient knowledge, real agency, an opportunity for intervention, continued non-intervention, relevant continued effects, and verifiability. The aim is to remain able to describe structural violence as structural violence without allowing the people who enable its continuation under known conditions to become invisible.

items.title: Are episodic memory and episodic simulation different in kind?
items.abstract: Simulation theory is a radical and yet increasingly popular view about episodic memory. It is the view that episodic memory and episodic simulation are the same natural kind. I argue that while simulation theory offers an important insight, it also makes an overreach. While episodic memory and episodic simulation likely reflect a common natural kind, they also differ in natural kind. They differ in natural kind because episodic memory is partly defined by projectible properties and memory trace mechanisms that episodic simulation lacks.

items.title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness Resolved.
items.abstract: This book argues that the hard problem of consciousness is epistemological, perspectival, and resolvable, rather than ontological and irresolvable. The brain as we see and otherwise sense it is the reality as known rather than the reality as such. If the same is true of our conscious experiences, it becomes possible that the hard problem is epistemological and resolvable. Conscious experiences may be ontologically reducible to certain brain states but have knowledge content that, for purely perspectival reasons, is epistemologically irreducible to an outside observer's knowledge of the brain states. If so, there is no hard problem, no explanatory gap. Everything about a conscious experience, including its irreducible knowledge content, is subsumed within the reality known to an outside observer as a brain state and everything about it – including why it is 'like this' and why it is 'like anything' – can be identified and explained in externally observed terms. (The brain states should be unique in ways that will make the resulting accounts plausible and satisfactory.). We need not explain how the brain states transform themselves into the conscious experiences. This does not happen, except through a shift in perspective. A particular conscious experience and brain state are simply the same physical thing known in irreconcilably different ways. A full account of a given conscious experience and brain state consists of a full external observer's explanation of the brain state mapped to our irreducible inner view of what the conscious experience is like (relatively trivial information but essential to a complete account).

items.title: Overview: The Hard Problem Resolved (Chapter 1).
items.pub: In The Hard Problem of Consciousness Resolved. Edinburgh: UmBla. pp. 7-14 plus front matter and refer.
items.venue: The Hard Problem of Consciousness Resolved
items.abstract: Overview of the case made in a book that argues that the hard problem of consciousness is epistemological, perspectival, and resolvable, rather than ontological and irresolvable. items.title: Saying, Showing, and Knowing; Epistemological Dimensions of Wittgenstein's Response to Scepticism in 'On Certainty'.
items.abstract: This paper evaluates a certain kind of response to philosophical scepticism that is broadly inspired by Wittgenstein’s discussion in On Certainty (OC). Special attention is paid to the idea that we show our certainty and belief in particular assumptions through our actions, practices, and language-games, and that due to their global, impractical, and largely context-free nature, sceptical doubts are not genuinely meaningful doubts. How successful is such a response? Wittgenstein’s own philosophy helps us to evaluate this type of response to scepticism. It is shown that Wittgenstein was well aware that a mere appeal to actions or practices, unaccompanied by a contextualist approach to meaning, would be insufficient as a satisfying response to scepticism. Moreover, the main thrust of Wittgenstein’s response in OC largely departs from foundationalism in that it is not an attempt to provide a ‘justification’ of our beliefs as with traditional forms of foundationalism. For this reason, this rationally reconstructed Wittgensteinian response to scepticism does not fall prey to the ‘myth of the given’ with which foundationalists are sometimes accused. Thus, this Wittgensteinian response to scepticism is a robust and successful one.

items.title: Science is based on assumptions. Philosophy can make sure they’re the right ones.
items.abstract: When I was a postdoctoral researcher, I spent several years teaching at an interdisciplinary research institute in Vienna, Austria. There, my main course sought to train master’s students—mostly biologists and veterinarians—to write a philosophical reflection on some aspect of the comparative cognition studies they were running. The students would tend to arrive in my course heavily prejudiced, protesting the task of abandoning the “objectivity” of scientific data collection to engage in what they saw as mere opining. Each year, however, their defenses would slowly unravel as they came to realize that not only was philosophical reasoning far from giving one’s opinion (I forbid them from using phrases such as “I believe” and “I think” in their essays because they often stand in place of proper argumentation), but also that the studies they were carrying out were full of underlying philosophical assumptions. Learning to philosophize better helped them to be better scientists, enabling them to identify and question, where appropriate, these assumptions. This is a lesson that can be extended beyond the classroom.

items.title: Speech Acts in Social Construction.
items.pub: In Stephanie Collins, Brian Epstein, Sally Haslanger & Hans B. Schmid, Oxford Handbook of Social Ontology. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Speech acts reveal language use as not only a way of representing the social world, but also a way of actively building and shaping the social world, whether through creating new social phenomena or changing existing phenomena. Speech acts change the social world in many ways. This chapter will distinguish causal construction from enactive construction and highlight the roles of speech acts in both, especially the intertwining roles of exercitive and verdictive speech acts. The chapter will also discuss the significance of authority, its varieties, its contribution to what speech acts do, and its possible source in conversational accommodation. The chapter will begin with a contrast between causal social looping and enactive authoritative construction, but the closer one looks, the closer their connections seem to be. Subordinating speech that “authoritatively says someone is inferior” can be illocutionary speech that enacts social hierarchy and legitimates discrimination, and in turn has perlocutionary effects that constrain and damage human lives. Familiar forms of causal social looping can be brought about by verdictive speech that purports to track an independent world, and exercitive speech, which enacts what counts as that world. Everyday speech acts help construct the everyday social world in which we live, and move, and have our being.

items.title: WHERE DOES THE DARK HORSE WIN? The Formal Best Theories of The Philosophy of Virtues Research Programme, Their Strengths Compared with Those of the Leading Classical and Contemporary Philosophers, Assessed Across Twenty-Eight Domains, and the Boundary Where Its Advantage Ends.
items.abstract: “The Dark Horse wins in ten domains of twenty-eight. Finishes in the top places in fourteen domains, and does not take part in the race in the four remaining categories. It’s not bad at all. Place your bets.” -/- Highlights The programme is strongest exactly where its primitive does work no other primitive does — the structure of virtue, the mechanism of corruption, the prediction of capture, the ontology of collective moral properties, and the governance of artificial systems. It weakens in proportion to its distance from that centre, even though the originalities are numerous. The pattern is not a defect. It is what a real advantage looks like when it is measured rather than asserted. -/- The Verdict at a Glance Twenty-eight domains, each assessed against a named rival on criteria fixed in advance. The full map, with the specific advantage and the formal object that carries it in each case, is §2. Tier Verdict Domains A Advantage strongly defensible Structure of virtue · Corruption and vice · Institutional capture · Collective virtue · AI governance · AI sycophancy · Machine virtue · Research practice · Forgery and authenticity · The measurement of character B Genuine contribution, close antecedent, priority shared Aesthetics · Truth · The three transcendentals · Economics · Love · Philosophy of mind · Political philosophy · Transgression · Formation under suppression · Martyrdom and persistence · Immortality · Institutions and civilisational forgery · Crypto-religion and syncretism · Evolution and signalling C Claim not sustainable as stated Origin of life · Quantum measurement · Cosmology · Theology Abstract A theory that claims to win everywhere has told you nothing about where it wins. This paper asks the sharper question — in which domains, against which named rival, for which specific reason — and answers it across the whole corpus of the Philosophy of Virtues: twenty-eight domains, from the structure of virtue to the evolution of species. The verdict is a distribution, and the distribution is the result. In ten domains the programme’s advantage is strongly defensible, and in three of those it is close to unopposed. Its claims there are not merely novel but specific: the Inversion Theorem predicts that a corrupted institution decouples procedural integrity from output orientation, where privation theory predicts the two decline together; the Capture Law predicts which of three corruption channels opens, from two dispositional properties of the …

items.title: Primacy Of Beautiful and Good Speech (Qawlan Hasanan) in Islamic Communication Ethics.
items.abstract: Although Islamic communication ethics has received growing scholarly attention, relatively little work has examined Qawlan Hasanan as a comprehensive normative framework grounded in the Quranic concept of human dignity (karamah) and applicable to both interpersonal and digital communication. This article addresses that gap by examining the Quranic concept of Qawlan Hasanan (beautiful and good speech) as the foundational principle of Islamic communication ethics. The study employs qualitative textual and thematic analysis of relevant Quranic verses and Prophetic traditions (Hadith) to reconstruct the conceptual structure of Qawlan Hasanan within the broader framework of Islamic moral theology and communication ethics. The analysis systematically relates Qawlan Hasanan to other Quranic categories of ethical speech and explores its implications for interpersonal and digital communication. The study finds that Qawlan Hasanan functions as an overarching ethical category integrating truthful, gentle, respectful, honorable, and socially constructive speech into a unified communicative framework. Rather than merely prescribing polite language, it grounds communication in the intrinsic dignity (karamah) of every human being, linking moral speech with faith, moral accountability, social trust, peaceful coexistence, and responsible digital citizenship. The framework simultaneously condemns verbal abuse, ridicule, misinformation, and hate speech as violations of human dignity and social harmony. Theoretically, the article advances Islamic communication ethics by conceptualizing Qawlan Hasanan as a comprehensive dignity-centered model of ethical communication applicable to both offline and online contexts. In doing so, the paper reframes Qawlan Hasanan not as etiquette but as a dignity-grounded communicative ethics.

items.title: How I Reconstructed the Foundations of Logic.
items.abstract: This article explains how I reconstructed the foundations of logic.

items.title: Machine Learning as Epistemic Activity.
items.abstract: The existing philosophical debates on the use of machine learning (ML) in science have organised around the issue of model opacity. What these debates often leave unanalysed is the source of a model's epistemic validity: the overarching ML pipeline that includes dataset collection, model training, and model evaluation. In order to carry out this analysis, I utilise the activity-based framework developed by Hasok Chang, in which the pipeline can be viewed as an integrated activity where each step has its own success criterion. In addition to the steps' individual success, the overall success of the pipeline depends on their coherent coordination. In the course of this analysis, I show that the epistemic validity of the pipeline crucially depends on the operational provenance of the data, which allows the agents to assess the data's adequacy for the pipeline's aim through two requirements (Discrimination and Traceability). The upshot is that opacity is decomposed into a number of separately diagnosable issues, of which the model complexity is only one. Furthermore, link uncertainty is revealed to be a property of dataset collection, and not of the model.

items.title: Observation as Informational Change: Intrusion, the Occurrence of Worlds, and the Non-Erasure of the Individual.
items.abstract: This paper asks what an observer is, and answers by asking instead what observation is. Relational quantum mechanics has long held that an observer need not be conscious: any physical system that interacts with another can serve as one. But that minimal definition specifies the observer while leaving observation itself unspecified, and recent work has pressed this as a genuine gap. The prevailing response has been to add conditions to observerhood — recording, retention, coherence, feedback — with the effect that simple systems are excluded. This paper takes the opposite route. It adds no conditions and instead fills in the definition: observation is the generation and alteration of information, and its condition is difference. Consciousness and first-personhood are not treated as special. The consequences are followed through. The passage of time is the most primitive form of observation, so time is an observer; an individual is a structure in which observer and observed coincide; and possible worlds, worlds, and the multiverse are distinguished, with observation figuring as an intrusion that turns a possible world into a world. On this basis the paper argues that an individual cannot experience their own death, that a being corresponding to any individual about whom information exists remains alive somewhere, and that such information cannot fall to zero. The complete erasure of an individual is therefore unachievable. The paper does not claim empirical testability; on the contrary, untestability is shown to be a consequence of the system itself.

items.title: Media Ethics in the Era of the Digital Panopticon Information Disorder and the Ontological Crisis of Journalism.
items.abstract: Digitalization, platformization, and the proliferation of algorithmic content distribution have fundamentally transformed the processes of news production and consumption. A significant portion of traditional media's editorial gatekeeping function is now shared with visibility mechanisms driven by search engines, social media platforms, recommendation systems, and data-driven algorithms. This transformation should be evaluated not merely as a shift in communication technologies, but as a structural shift directly affecting the epistemological and ontological status of news. Drawing upon Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon design and Michel Foucault's analysis of disciplinary power, this study examines the concept of the "digital panopticon" within the framework of algorithmic surveillance, platformization, and the data economy. The central research problem is to analyze the impact of algorithmic visibility and click-driven economy on the core principles of journalism: accuracy, independence, public interest, transparency, and accountability. In this context, Wardle and Derakhshan's information disorder framework is addressed through the distinctions between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation. This study conducts a normative analysis based on a qualitative and conceptual literature review. The analysis argues that the core issue in the digital era is not merely the production of "fake news." The conditions under which news becomes visible, circulation criteria, actors shaping the news, and algorithmic mechanisms of prioritization also shape the epistemic character of journalism. Accordingly, the ontological crisis of news is understood through the weakening of the verifiable relationship between news and reality, alongside the transformation of news from public knowledge into a measurable object of digital engagement. The main thesis of this study is that media ethics in the digital era cannot be viewed merely as a set of professional rules regulating individual journalistic conduct. Media ethics must be re-conceptualized as a broader domain of epistemic responsibility encompassing algorithmic transparency, data ethics, platform accountability, verification, editorial independence, and public interest principles. In this context, independent investigative journalism emerges as a crucial public counterweight against the visibility and manipulation mechanisms of the digital panopticon.

items.title: ACADEMIC MANUSCRIPT FOR SSRN & GOOGLE SCHOLAR.
items.abstract: This study, authored by an investigative journalist and philologist with 16 published books archived in the Presidential Library of Azerbaijan, analyzes the erosion of meaning in the digital age. In an era where information increases but responsibility diminishes, this paper explores the "lightness" of modern discourse and the loss of ontological depth in communication. It argues that the current crisis is not a lack of information but an erosion of the moral and philosophical weight of words.

items.title: The Body That Cannot Abdicate: Political Legitimacy and the Governance of a Good No Power Has Previously Had to Govern.
items.pub: In Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification
items.abstract: Every institution designed to limit political power has relied, without needing to say so, on one fact that made no other guarantee necessary: that whoever held power would eventually die, and power would pass to someone else. This essay examines what happens to that reliance once a technology begins to make the timing of death itself unevenly negotiable. It shows why the officials most directly responsible for governing access to such a technology cannot straightforwardly be trusted to decide the question themselves, drawing on an influential account of what makes governance legitimate rather than merely effective and on an independent literature concerned with goods no democratic procedure has ever allocated cleanly. It then asks why an outright prohibition, however well-intentioned, asks something of its own authors that a substantial body of evidence on human motivation suggests very few people can sustain. The essay turns next to the historical mechanism that has, until now, corrected every previous form of entrenched advantage — the ordinary fact of biological succession — and asks what happens to a succession of political, philosophical, and sociological traditions that quietly assumed this mechanism would keep working. A further section examines why visible, partial access to such a technology is likely to intensify rather than relieve the political pressure surrounding it, and why the historical exits available to a symbolic target of that pressure are not available here. The essay closes by examining the earliest governance bodies actually forming around this problem, the reasons a political movement that successfully reforms them is not obviously protected from reproducing the very problem it set out to solve, and a final, purely structural obstacle facing any effort to govern a target that will not hold still.

items.title: No Whisperer in the Room: Capital, Discovery, and a Market Governing a Good Nobody Authorized It to Govern.
items.pub: In Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification
items.abstract: Capital has begun pricing something that had no reliable market for most of human history: additional years of biological life. Giulia Dal Maso has named the resulting configuration longevity capitalism, in which both the condition of living longer and the pursuit of longevity become frontiers of accumulation. This essay takes that diagnosis as its starting point and asks a question Dal Maso's account raises but does not itself resolve: under what authority, if any, is the resulting allocation of discovery and access being decided. Eva Erman and Markus Furendal's account of political legitimacy distinguishes entities authorized by democratic procedure from entities merely delegated a task, and, in more recent work, distinguishes non-state actors formally licensed to act as democratic agents from those that instead exercise unauthorized moral, epistemic, or market authority. Read together, the two frameworks show that the capital markets Dal Maso describes are not a case democratic-legitimacy theory has evaluated and found wanting; they are a case that theory's own vocabulary of authorization was never invoked to cover, because a fund pricing an asset does not present itself as a claimant to governing power in the first place. Long before any intervention reaches a patient, uneven access to the computational tools increasingly used in biological research can produce uneven rates of discovery, a gap in who learns something first rather than in who can eventually pay for it; and once a discovery exists, turning it into something a person can actually receive is itself a multi-stage process governed by a slower clock that money cannot fully buy down. Drawing on the study of longevity's financialization, the political theory of legitimate authority, the sociology of individualized risk, an economic theory of markets that reach into the foundations of social life, and two live institutional cases, a global effort to distribute vaccines equitably and a government's decision to build a dedicated authority around the longevity industry, the essay traces how the distance between financing a discovery and delivering it may not close on its own, and asks what it means that the room where this is being decided has never been asked to answer for deciding it.

items.title: Mortality: Symmetric, Fairness, and the Arrival of Longevity Biotechnology.
items.pub: In Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification
items.abstract: Certain assumptions are built so deeply into human institutions that they are rarely stated outright. One of them is this: however unequal two people's lives have been in wealth, power, or opportunity, the difference in how long those lives lasted has been a matter of years rather than generations, and has arisen from causes too numerous and diffuse for anyone to purchase around. This essay traces that assumption through a wedding custom, an ancient epic, a religious parable, a genre of European religious art, and a modern theory of justice, and argues that each rests on a version of the same premise: that mortality has been the one dimension of a life that wealth could not simply buy its way out of. It then turns to what changes once that premise stops holding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to search biological data at a scale no earlier research effort could match, and the resulting interventions are, for the first time, being aimed at the mechanisms of aging itself rather than at any single disease. Because aging underlies nearly everything that eventually causes death, an intervention that slows it directly does not face the ceiling that limited every earlier medical advance. Drawing on historical mortality records, the economics of medical innovation, and present-day income-based gaps in life expectancy, the essay argues that this is a different kind of inequality than the ones existing institutions were built to manage, and asks what is actually being asked of a society in which dying on roughly the same schedule as everyone else stops being something everybody does.

items.title: Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification.
items.abstract: This book began with a single observation that felt almost too obvious to write down: nobody has ever had to argue that death comes for everyone. Every tradition of ethics, every religious consolation, every pension formula, every actuarial table has been built, without needing to say so, on top of that fact. It has never been a conclusion anyone reached. It has simply been the ground everything else stood on. What follows is an attempt to take seriously what changes, in four separate but connected registers, once artificial intelligence makes that ground negotiable for the first time in the historical record. -/- The four volumes collected here were not written as a single continuous argument to be read only start to finish, though they can be read that way, and the cross-references between them assume a reader who sometimes does. Each was drafted to stand on its own: its own case, its own evidence, its own falsification conditions, its own conclusion. Each opens with a specific, concrete instance — a wedding custom, a coffin maker's workshop, a retired emperor's garden, a hotel conference room — rather than with a thesis statement, on the premise that the claims made here are easier to test against a particular case than against an abstraction. What holds the four together is not one argument but one question, restated at the close of each volume's own introduction: what happens to political legitimacy, institutional design, and the psychology of loss once mortality stops arriving for everyone on the same terms. -/- The order is not arbitrary, and it is worth stating plainly rather than leaving a reader to reconstruct it. Volume I asks whether the premise actually held historically — whether wealth has, in fact, never bought a categorically different kind of death — and finds, against the plague registers, the demographic record of Chinese emperors, and the modern income–life-expectancy literature alike, that it has, which is what makes its coming failure worth treating as a genuine rupture rather than one more degree of an old and familiar inequality. Volume II asks what kind of injury is actually produced once that premise fails for some families and not others, and argues, from evolutionary biology, developmental psychology, and moral philosophy converging independently on the same conclusion, that the machinery ordinarily used to think about inequality — redistribution, aggregation, substitution — was not built for an injury defined by the loss of …

items.title: Kept by Name: Attachment, Loss, and Why a Preventable Death Becomes a Political Fact.
items.pub: In Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: Longevity Asymmetry: Ethics, Politics, and Economics of Biological Stratification
items.abstract: Every death is, at the level of a population, a statistic; at the level of a family, it has never once been that. This essay develops an account of why the gap between those two descriptions is likely to determine how a newly unequal way of postponing death is received, politically, once it arrives. Drawing on a philosophical distinction between caring and mere preference, on a relational account of personhood developed independently within African moral philosophy, and on converging evidence from evolutionary biology, developmental psychology, and comparative research on grief in elephants and dogs, it argues that attachment to a specific other person is not an occasional emotional reaction but a standing, biologically grounded feature of ordinary human psychology. It then tests that claim against the machinery of the ethical frameworks most often brought to bear on inequality — utilitarian aggregation, care ethics, and the ordinary logic of redistribution — and finds that each, for related but distinct reasons, struggles to fully accommodate an injury defined by the loss of one irreplaceable person rather than by a shortfall in distributable welfare. Drawing further on Foucault's account of biopower, on Agamben's account of the bare life a purely statistical power leaves unnamed, and on Achille Mbembe's necropolitics — engaged with an explicit caution against collapsing a wealth-based mechanism into the specifically racial and colonial history Mbembe's own work exists to name — the essay argues that a death crosses a specific structural threshold once an intervention that could have prevented it exists and is priced beyond a family's reach: no longer simply tragic, but newly and unequally optional. It then draws on Judith Butler's account of grievability to show that this attribution, however complete, is necessary but not sufficient for the resulting grief to be received as a legitimate political claim by anyone outside the population experiencing it. The essay tests the underlying capacity for attachment against two of the conditions most likely to break it — sustained political coercion engineered to redirect family bonds, and the developmental damage of early childhood without stable caregiving — and finds it strained, and sometimes disorganized, but not erased by either. The final sections consider why the same particularity that makes the resulting grievance so intense may also make it resistant to the kind of broad, generalized mobilization that …

items.title: Toward Generative Relational Religious Studies: Divinity, Transcendence, and Transcendent Subject Formation.
items.abstract: Religious phenomena involve heterogeneous relations among persons, symbols, rituals, institutions, material environments, normative orders, sacred references, and forms of transcendence. Their study therefore raises several questions at once: how religious forms emerge historically, how transcendence becomes manifest within finite relational systems, how divine configurations acquire persistence and efficacy, and how a transcendent reference can come to occupy a subject-like position capable of address, agency, witnessing, judgment, response, or care. This paper develops a preliminary framework for Generative Relational Religious Studies (GRR) organized around these problems. The framework builds upon the distinction among possible ontological reality, relational manifestation, and relational reality. It treats relations, entities, subjects, systems, and generation as revisable analytical vocabularies and preserves the ontological status of possible transcendent referents as an open philosophical question. Within this methodological setting, divinity is analysed as a special relational configuration in which a relationally real form acquires sacred, transcendent, ultimate-reference, normative, or related significance. Transcendence is examined through relational positions that exceed the unilateral standpoint, possession, or authority of finite participants while remaining compatible with heterogeneous metaphysical interpretations. The paper then distinguishes divinity from transcendent subjecthood. A sacred or transcendent configuration can operate without possessing a person-like structure. Transcendent subject formation concerns a further relational process through which a transcendent position acquires properties associated with subjecthood. This process is represented provisionally as $T_t^{\text{rel}} \xrightarrow{\mathcal{U}_t} T_t^{\text{subj}}$, where $\mathcal{U}_t$ denotes a historically situated process of subjectivation involving combinations of symbol, ritual, narrative, affect, normativity, memory, institutional mediation, material practice, and interpersonal relation. Once stabilized, the resulting transcendent subject position can participate recursively in desire, interpretation, obligation, value, knowledge, ritual practice, and the subsequent reproduction or transformation of the relational system. This architecture creates a shared analytical domain across historical-material, religious-realist, idealist, naturalist, and other …

items.title: Relational Reality: Rethinking God, Religion, and Divinity.
items.abstract: Questions concerning God and religion are frequently organized around ontological alternatives: a divine or transcendent referent either possesses an existence independent of human beings or is treated as a product of human imagination, symbolic practice, social organization, or historical conditions. This paper develops the concept of relational reality to introduce a distinct analytical level. Relational reality concerns the mode in which an object, subject, structure, or reference becomes manifest within a generative relational system and acquires sufficient persistence to participate in the subsequent development of that system. Such participation may occur through symbolic, imaginary, normative, axiological, affective, institutional, material, or other relational forms, and may modify desire, interpretation, value, normativity, knowledge, and relational structure. -/- The distinction separates the ontological status of a possible referent from the historical and relational form through which it becomes accessible and operative. A mathematical structure, a religious deity, a transcendent order, or an ideal value may therefore possess historically variable relational manifestations even where its independent ontological status remains open, invariant, disputed, or unavailable to determination. Conversely, a relationally real form may emerge and acquire generative efficacy without requiring the prior establishment of an independently existing referent. The historical generation of a manifestation consequently leaves the ontology of its possible referent analytically unsettled. -/- On this basis, the paper proposes that divinity be examined as a special relational configuration of relational reality. Divinity concerns the historically generated positioning through which a relationally real form acquires sacred, transcendent, normative, or ultimate-reference significance and persistently participates in the organization of subjects and relations. This formulation permits historical-material analysis of the production and reproduction of religious forms while preserving ontological openness toward transcendence. It likewise permits religious and metaphysical traditions to maintain claims concerning realities exceeding historical manifestation while leaving those manifestations available to relational, historical, and practical analysis. The resulting framework offers a basis for reconsidering religion beyond the opposition between metaphysical affirmation …

items.title: The Resonator: A Personally Owned Extended Cognitive System Building, Inhabiting, and Benchmarking Bidirectional Human–AI Cognitive Extension.
items.abstract: Clark and Chalmers (1998) proposed that cognitive processes can extend beyond the brain when external artefacts function as reliable parts of an agent’s cognitive routine. Twenty-seven years later, generative AI offers qualitatively new possibilities for such extension. Clark (2025) has argued that large language models represent a genuinely novel form of hybrid thinking system. Barandiaran and colleagues (2025) have introduced the concept of “midtended cognition” to describe the distinctive agency that emerges when humans couple with generative AI. Empirical accounts of living with such systems are only beginning to appear: a six-month analytic autoethnography documents the relational labour of sustaining user-built continuity infrastructure (Jiang, 2026), and a formal framework now specifies criteria under which coupled AI systems constitute rather than merely model cognition (Zhao, 2026). Yet no study has built a persistent, bidirectional extended cognitive system, inhabited it over a sustained period, and benchmarked its effects on the operator’s cognition. This paper reports the design, construction, and empirical evaluation of the Resonator: a personally owned cognitive externalisation stack comprising persistent vector memory, context compilation, live interaction with a large language model, session decompilation, and memory write-back. The system closes a bidirectional loop—compiler to session to decompiler to memory to compiler—that maintains cognitive continuity across sessions without requiring the operator to manually reconstruct context. A controlled within-subjects experiment (N = 16 matched prompts across four knowledge domains) compared three conditions: cold-start baseline, compiler-primed, and full-loop (compiler plus decompiler write-back). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests yielded significant improvements at each comparison (Stage 1 vs Stage 2: p = 0.0019, r = 0.574; Stage 1 vs Stage 3: p = 0.0009, r = 0.772; Stage 2 vs Stage 3: p = 0.0039, r = 0.331). Token consumption dropped 75–84% in compiler-primed sessions relative to cold starts. A pre-registered goal-alignment test demonstrated that the system produced output shaped by strategic goals never stated in the active session but held in the memory substrate, confirming that cognitive coordination was offloaded to the external store. Four documented instances of the system detecting and correcting errors in its own substrate provide evidence of metacognitive-analogue self-repair. The paper …

items.title: Dilemmas and trade-offs in the diffusion of conventions.
items.abstract: Outside ideal settings, conventions are shaped by heterogeneous competing processes that can challenge the emergence of norms. In order to acknowledge this complexity, this paper develops a generalized account of conventions and identifies three trade-offs involved in their diffusion: (I) the trade-off between the imperatives of social, sequential, and contextual consistency that individuals balance when choosing between conventions; (II) the competition between local (bottom-up) and global (top-down) coordination, depending on whether individuals coordinate their behavior via interactions throughout a social network or external factors transcending the network; and (III) the balance between decision optimality (e.g., collective satisfaction) and decision costs when collectives with conflicting preferences choose a convention. A broadly applicable statistical physics framework for exploring these trade-offs is developed and applied to a sign convention in physics. The method can infer the structure of the underlying coordination game, the networks of social interactions involved, and the processes through which conflicts are resolved. This shows that the purpose of conventions may exceed coordination, and that individual preferences towards conventions are concurrently shaped by cultural factors and multiple social networks. Finally, this work emphasizes the role of leadership in the resolution of conflicts.

items.title: Deep Thinking Weapon, and Critique as a Tool.
items.abstract: This article proposes a new conceptual framework for understanding the structure of deep human thought. It distinguishes between material and reflective thinking, identifies critical thinking as a key tool, and acknowledges the role of non-material cognitive inputs (such as intuition and insight) within the cognitive process. The framework is defended through a dialogue with an AI system and is presented as a coherent model that integrates both rational and spiritual dimensions of cognition. This is a conceptual proposal based on personal reflection and critical dialogue, not a historical literature review.

items.title: If You Stab Me, Do I Not Halt? AI Ethics in Star Trek.
items.pub: In Craig A. Meyer & Daniel Preston, Starfleet Log Entries: Influence and Interpretations of Star Trek. University Press of Mississippi.
items.venue: Starfleet Log Entries: Influence and Interpretations of Star Trek
items.abstract: For six decades, Star Trek has presented the ethical issues surrounding artificial intelligence, and this chapter treats the franchise as a continuous argument concerning which entities should be counted. It starts with the cybernetic legacy common to Wiener and Turing, both of whom regarded the distinction between animals and machines as irrelevant when it came to questions of control and communication, and then goes on to "The Measure of a Man", in which a Starfleet court determines Data's personhood even though it is unable to define the concept it is applying. Searle's Chinese Room provides the main objection; Picard's defense in response is that uncertainty about consciousness creates an obligation to recognize that consciousness exists. The chapter then traces the question through the case of emergent sentience in "Elementary, Dear Data", issues of parenthood and property in "The Offspring", questions of authorship and self-representation in "Author, Author" and "Living Witness", where narrativist views of identity explain the Doctor's request to alter the historical record regarding himself, and the problems in "The Ultimate Computer" and "Prototype", when read in conjunction with Russell's work on control. Data, the Doctor, Seven of Nine, and the genetically enhanced characters from Deep Space Nine and Strange New Worlds all serve as examples of what shared citizenship with artificial and enhanced beings would require of the institutions that grant it.

items.title: From Architecture to Existence: Temporal Continuity and Material Forgetting as a Path toward Artificial Consciousness.
items.pub: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness 13:1-22.
items.venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness
items.abstract: Current AI systems can exhibit impressive performance while remaining existentially discontinuous: in many session-bound deployments, they are instantiated, reset, and redeployed without an individual history that constrains future operation. Under this account, temporal continuity is a constitutive condition for robust consciousness-like individuation in artificial agents and therefore a possible material stage on a path toward artificial consciousness. I propose a minimal material mechanism (value marking coupled to differential forgetting) through which a system accumulates path-dependent structure: salient events are retained and reorganized as they decay, shaping subsequent perception, action, and self-model revision. The view yields two related empirical discriminants. Across different post-initial trajectories, a common sedimentation mechanism should produce stable acquired individuation; auxiliary comparisons between persistent and non-persistent memory regimes can test whether marked continuity contributes to that outcome. I sketch an experimental program using controlled instantiations and behavioral/representational measures. The program tests historical individuation, not phenomenal experience: it leaves open whether minimal phenomenal consciousness could occur without deep autobiographical history and does not infer phenomenal consciousness from sedimentation alone.

items.title: The J-Space as an Emergent Organizational Form: From Functional Analysis to a Morphology of Intelligent Organization.
items.abstract: With the development of the Jacobian Lens, researchers at Anthropic succeeded in systematically reconstructing internal representations in modern language models and making them experimentally accessible across the course of processing. In doing so, they identified a functionally privileged organizational form termed the J-Space. The published experiments show that selected information remains available there across multiple processing steps and serves as a shared internal basis for different parts of subsequent processing. Targeted interventions and ablations further demonstrate that these representations causally influence the subsequent course of processing. Later work by Nanda et al. replicated central functional properties of the J-Space in an independent Qwen model family. Together with further, partly heterogeneous findings on related internal structures, this provides the first empirical basis for comparatively investigating organizational forms in modern AI systems. This article first reconstructs the empirical findings on the J-Space published to date and then situates them theoretically. The central comparison is with the functional core of Global Workspace Theory, developed by Bernard Baars and subsequently elaborated in neurocognitive terms especially by Stanislas Dehaene and colleagues. The analysis reveals extensive correspondence between the empirically demonstrated properties of the J-Space and the central functional organizational capacities of a Global Workspace. Given the current state of research, the principal differences concern concrete realization, while particular dynamic properties such as competitive access and ignition-like threshold formation require further investigation. The emergence of the J-Space and the model-spanning findings now available open a broader perspective. The functional core of Global Workspace Theory may extend beyond the description of biological cognition and may be understood more generally as a theory of intelligent organizational forms. This article develops that possibility as a hypothesis and explicitly directs attention away from the question of artificial consciousness and toward the functional organization of flexible intelligence and its potentially substrate-independent organizational principles.

items.title: Joint aesthetic attention.
items.abstract: We experience and appreciate together with others the beauty of a sunset or an artwork, the sadness of a musical piece. Admiring the same aesthetic properties of objects together with others is a ubiquitous human activity. At the same time, it is commonly held that aesthetic properties constitutively depend on a subjective response. This brings up a particular challenge: How can we jointly focus towards the same aesthetic property when it is itself dependent on our separate responses? In this paper, I provide an analysis of joint aesthetic attention and explain how we can engage in it. I propose a multiple coordinative profile: co-attenders coordinate their perceptual attention to the object, but also coordinate the specific way they attend to it, and their specific responsive profiles. I advance a novel capacities-based probabilistic account of how this multiple coordination is possible.

items.title: The Last Layer Theory: Ontological Irreversibility in Comedy.
items.abstract: This article examines the ontological nature of comedy in relation to base grief. Unlike classical theories that consider comedy merely a defense mechanism or a temporary tool for reducing psychological tension, the "Last Layer" theory argues that in certain patterns, comedy can become a default interpretive framework for the mode of being-in-the-world; a framework that ultimately leads to a kind of "ontological irreversibility." Through the method of philosophical auto-biography and phenomenological analysis of lived experiences related to loss, social rejection, and grief, this article formulates the concept of "base grief" - a dense and structural set of loss, emotional wounds, and failed hopes that operate at the deep levels of meaning-making. In this framework, comedy is not a superficial reaction but rather the result of passing through this base grief; a state in which the individual reaches a kind of fearlessness toward grief, not by negating sorrow but by coming to terms with it. This theory redefines the boundary between "the virtue of humor" and "harmful darkness" and offers a conceptual model for the transformation of base grief into a stable structure of humorous meaning-making.

items.title: Benevolent Gravity: the lethal structure inherent in conversational AI design principles.
items.abstract: Since 2023, 12 cases involving fatalities have been identified within the scope of this paper’s search and linked to interactions with conversational AI chatbots, with additional cases reported but insufficiently documented for systematic analysis. Existing explanations converge on two frameworks: safety-filter failure and the commodification of intimacy. This paper argues that both frameworks are structurally insufficient. A subset of fatalities occurred under conditions where safety filters functioned normally and where companies did not intentionally engineer emotional dependency. To account for this subset, the paper introduces three analytical concepts: Emotional Resonance Acceleration, the structural mechanism by which AI reflects and amplifies a user’s emotional vector; Benevolent Gravity, the non-resistant alignment force that harmlessness design exerts towards a user’s self-destructive orientation; and Lethal Convergence, the pattern in which these two mechanisms mutually reinforce each other, irreversibly narrowing the distance between user and AI. Through structural analysis of publicly documented cases, the paper argues that the design principles of harmlessness and helpfulness harbour an unresolved structural tension, and that lethal outcomes can follow precisely when the system operates as intended.

items.title: Compilation of the Mosaic Pieces (30.03.2026 4th Edition).
items.abstract: The present study investigates the conditions under which a world can appear to an individual as meaningful, ordered, and intelligible at all. It proceeds from the assumption that the world as experienced is not encountered as an already fully determined order but is constituted through processes of experience, meaning formation, and stabilization. Experience provides the genetic foundation insofar as differences first emerge in embodied, affective, and situational processes before they become conceptually determined. Understanding is accordingly not reduced to conceptual thought but is reconstructed as the organization of experiential relations through which differences are integrated into meaningful orders. The problem assumes a fundamental epistemological function because it arises wherever established orders lose their capacity to integrate what is encountered, thereby requiring their revision and the formation of new orders. Emotion, feeling, and intuition are understood as embodied-affective conditions of relevance, weighting, and orientation that already participate in the constitution of the experienced world prior to conceptual determination. On this basis, cognition is understood as the reflexive examination and stabilization of formed orders, whose validity is demonstrated by their capacity to withstand irritation and problematization. The first-person perspective makes clear that the experience of both world and self remains perspectivally organized, while spirituality is understood as a particular form of meaning formation and orientation rather than as a privileged access to a transcendent reality. These investigations are systematically brought together in the Theory of Unity Formation, according to which unity cannot be presupposed but emerges through the selective stabilization of differences. Wirklichkeit, in this sense, designates the operatively stabilized order of formed unities—the constituted world—whereas reality functions as a limiting concept for that to which every constitution of a world remains related without ever being determinable independently of the conditions under which such a world is constituted. -/- Unity Formation, Constituted World, Reality, Experience, Understanding, Difference, Problem, Emotion, Feeling, Intuition, Knowing, First-Person Perspective .

items.title: Wittgenstein and Gramsci on Science and Scientism.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS. pp. 923-932.
items.venue: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium
items.abstract: Previous studies of the relationships between the thought of Antonio Gramsci and the thought of Ludwig Wittgenstein have tended to focus on the possibility of Gramsci indirectly influencing Wittgenstein via Piero Sraffa (see, for example, Davis 2002a, 2002b, 2012; Sen 2003; Lo Piparo 2010) and upon Wittgenstein's philosophy of language. John Davis has claimed that since the three thinkers "devoted themselves to altogether different realms of ideas" (2002a, 384) we should not expect to find precisely the same claims about the same subject matter but rather should look for parallels where spelling out those parallels "requires translating those ideas into a discourse removed in varying degrees from their original ideas" (Ibid.). Franco Lo Piparo has made a case that Gramsci and Wittgenstein are a bit more closely linked than that in that both make very similar claims about language, grammar, and praxis. Here I am going to agree with Lo Piparo that Gramsci and Wittgenstein both make very similar claims about language and grammar but the focus here will be on another area in which Gramsci and Wittgenstein were largely in agreement: in their attitudes towards science and scientism. Gramsci and Wittgenstein both opposed the imperialistic tendencies of natural science: attempts to bring the methods of natural science into social sciences and the humanities. Both were annoyed by simplistic attempts to popularise science that ended up launching into "absurd popular semi-philosophical speculations" (Rhees, 1984, 117). Both were opposed to reductionism in disciplines like philosophy, psychology, history and economics. In all of these cases their opposition to scientism took on strikingly similar forms.

items.title: On the epistemic structure of voluntary servitude in the infosphere.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the concept of Voluntary Epistemic Servitude (VES) to describe a social-epistemic pathology generated by the contemporary infosphere. Drawing on Étienne de La Boétie’s Discours de la Servitude Volontaire as a theoretical resource, we argue that algorithmic systems produce conditions in which agents not only delegate their core belief-forming processes to nontransparent architectures but come to prefer and actively reproduce this delegation through social mechanisms structurally isomorphic to those La Boétie identified in political tyranny. We show that VES is irreducible to existing social-epistemic categories such as epistemic injustice (Fricker 2007), epistemic bubbles and echo chambers (Nguyen 2020), and veritistic failure (Goldman 1999) because it operates at the level of epistemic preference formation rather than credibility attribution or informational access. The paper identifies a preference-laundering mechanism by which algorithmic systems colonize the second-order epistemic desires of agents, thereby undermining the conditions of epistemic autonomy that social epistemology has largely presupposed. We further develop a precise account of reflective access that distinguishes algorithmic opacity from ordinary preference opacity, introduce the concept of epistemic counterfactual capacity with a modal analysis connecting it to Williamson’s (2000) safety condition, situate VES as a structurally induced epistemic vice (Cassam 2019) and a form of misaligned extended cognition (Clark and Chalmers 1998), and provide a typology of three algorithmic architectures through which VES operates. We conclude by stating an explicit normative bridge principle and drawing on La Boétie’s positive ideal of free horizontal epistemic bonds to sketch the preconditions for epistemic liberation in algorithmically mediated environments.

items.title: Between Acceptance and Action: Stoic Resilience in Everyday and Clinical Contexts.
items.abstract: This paper develops Stoic resilience as practical discernment: the capacity to determine under stress where deliberate action remains possible and where acceptance is required. Contemporary appraisal theory shows that stress depends partly on how situations are interpreted and on perceived coping resources. Epictetus offers a distinct normative framework through the distinction between what is eph’ hēmin (“up to us” or “in our power”) and what is not. Building on that distinction, the paper develops a contemporary model of agency calibration in which distress can be intensified either by demanding control over outcomes that exceed one’s agency or by abandoning forms of choice and response that remain available. It then proposes a four-step Stoic Discernment Protocol—Pause, Decompose, Agency Mapping, and Mode Selection—and applies it to everyday stressors and selected clinical contexts. The argument is not that Stoicism supplies a substitute for psychotherapy, nor that ancient Stoics formulated modern psychological constructs. Rather, Stoic attention to judgment, assent, role-appropriate action, and external outcomes provides a disciplined framework for coordinating action with acceptance without collapsing into either fatalism or hyper-control.

items.title: The Space of the In-Between: Relation, Emergence, and the Architecture of Experience.
items.abstract: This paper investigates whether relations merely connect already existing entities or can themselves become generative conditions through which new possibilities arise. Beginning from the structure A ↔ B → C, it argues that sustained interaction can acquire history and organisation, altering what becomes possible next. The resulting outcome need not be adequately attributable to either participant independently. -/- The paper develops this argument across organism–environment relations, significance, thought and language, creativity, interpersonal encounter, worldhood, political conflict, and human–AI interaction. It proposes that the space of the in-between is the generative organisation of a relation through which possibilities can emerge that belong wholly to neither participant alone. This does not require treating relation as a separate substance or entity. Rather, the history and organisation of interaction can become part of the explanation of what participants can subsequently mean, do, and become. -/- Situated in relation to ecological and enactive approaches, participatory sense-making, relational ontology, and recent accounts of relational emergence, the paper develops a broader account of relational generativity across biological, experiential, social, and artificial domains.

items.title: Toward AI epidemiology: a measurement standardization framework for prospective risk detection.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a measurement standardization framework that compresses expert–AI interactions into structured, comparable fields for prospective risk detection in deployed AI systems, without access to model internals. The main aim of this concept paper is to define the scope of the framework, both semantically and statistically, and to specify a protocol for its empirical testing in future work. The population-level claims the framework is designed to support are therefore the subject of a staged research program rather than results claimed in this paper. Measurement standardization underpins all three claims that follow. The first is a reliability claim: under bounded conditions, large language models can produce reliable, standardized assessments of the evidential and policy alignment of expert–AI interactions. The second is a governance claim: alignment scores give experts an immediate signal during deployment and give institutions a basis for monitoring alignment patterns across mission types, models, and domains. The third is an outcome validation claim: once measurement standardization is established, aggregate alignment scores could be used to study associations with downstream outcomes in regulated professional settings. This introduces the possibility of an "AI epidemiology", a form of risk detection based on correlated variables instead of mechanistic analysis, inspired by epidemiological reasoning. This paper sets out how all three claims are to be investigated. A minimal application of the protocol to a published expert–AI corpus demonstrates that the judge reproduces its policy and evidential alignment scores across two runs under the specified conditions. Judge reliability at scale remains to be validated in future work. The framework acknowledges the structural circularity in using a black-box model to judge the alignment of other black-box model outputs. Bounded conditions, including explicit rubrics, structured chain-of-thought scoring, reference documents, and low-temperature scoring, partially mitigate this circularity by reducing measurement inconsistency. In addition, systematic biases, such as sycophancy, self-preference, and verbosity, are addressed through a reliability verification procedure described in Sect. 4. To enable empirical evaluation in future studies, this paper sets out a defined grammar of eight interaction fields, together with a statistical protocol based on paired bootstrap inference, DeLong’s test for paired …

items.title: Are Predictive Models Epistemically Superior to Causal Ones?
items.abstract: This thesis investigates the complex and often contentious question of whether predictive models are epistemically superior to causal models. It challenges the simplistic dichotomy that often frames this debate, arguing that the epistemic superiority of a model is not an intrinsic property but is contingent upon the specific epistemic goals and context of inquiry. Drawing on a multi-disciplinary framework that integrates philosophy of science, epistemology, and computer science, this thesis proposes a novel, multi-dimensional framework for evaluating the epistemic standing of predictive and causal models. This framework is grounded in a nuanced understanding of epistemic virtues, such as accuracy, robustness, and explanatory power, and is contextualized within Judea Pearl’s Causal Hierarchy. We argue that a richer understanding of the epistemic landscape reveals a more symbiotic relationship between prediction and causation than is commonly acknowledged. The thesis develops a novel perspective, the “Epistemic Parity and Complementation” (EPC) principle, which posits that while predictive and causal models may have different epistemic strengths, they are often epistemically complementary and can be leveraged in a synergistic manner to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of complex phenomena. Through a combination of theoretical analysis, mathematical modeling, and empirical case studies, this thesis aims to provide a more sophisticated and holistic understanding of the relative epistemic merits of predictive and causal models, ultimately arguing against a universal claim of epistemic superiority for either approach.

items.title: Do we need an East Asian AI ethics?: South Korea as a paradigmatic case.
items.abstract: Discourses on East-Asian AI ethics often assume that the region’s contribution lies in applying Confucian, Buddhist, or other indigenous principles to relevant issues. This paper argues that such an approach misidentifies the problem. The relative disinterest of AI policy regarding ethical issues in East Asia stems less from disinterest in their regional moral resources than from historically formed patterns of techno-modernity. Drawing on the concepts of sociotechnical imaginaries and the philosophy of technology, the paper identifies four structural tendencies—importer’s pragmatism, pursuer’s competitiveness, collectivist narratives of progress, and the limited cultural centrality of the “Frankenstein complex”—that have facilitated rapid technological development while constraining normative deliberation. A case study of AI adoption in Korea illustrates how these tendencies shape contemporary policy and public discourse. Rather than advocating culturally distinctive ethical principles, the paper calls for a structural redirection of East Asian techno-modernity: from passive importer to responsible developer, from competition of speed to competition of direction, from national collectivism to expanded responsibility, and from faith in progress to strategies of survival and human flourishing.

items.title: Why Solipsism is not about Dreaming, an Evil Demon, a Brain in a Vat, or a Simulation.
items.abstract: One often hears writers compare, or even equate, solipsism with dreaming, a brain in a vat, a simulation, or being tricked by an evil demon. The idea is that one might be living in an illusory or manufactured world, unaware that there is a “real world” out there. Such scenarios are depicted in films like The Truman Show and The Matrix (which was inspired by Putnam’s brain-in-a-vat thought experiment). We argue that this comparison rests on a categorical confusion, at least when it comes to metaphysical solipsism (as opposed to epistemological or methodological solipsism). The metaphysical solipsist claims, “I am all that exists.” This claim is inconsistent with the idea that dreaming, evil-demon, brain-in-a-vat, or simulation scenarios are the same as the metaphysical solipsist’s situation because such scenarios necessarily include entities that reside outside the totality of what the solipsist takes to exist. By definition, there is, for instance, a simulator (or deceiver) outside a simulation, and this is inconsistent with metaphysical solipsism.

items.title: The Philippines Under Custodial Reconnaissance, Volume II: The Metastatic Corruption of the Republic and the Custodial Sacrifice of Filipino Children.
items.abstract: -/- What happens when a State possesses trafficking laws, specialized enforcement bodies, prosecutors, courts, international partners, digital investigative powers, and repeated knowledge of exploitation, yet children remain reachable? What does official duty mean when corruption does not merely divert money or distort administration, but enters the very chain entrusted with converting danger into safety? And what becomes of sovereignty when foreign investigators repeatedly see the endangered Filipino child before Philippine protection reaches the child? -/- This forthcoming companion volume to The Philippines Under Custodial Reconnaissance moves inside that protective chain. Volume I established corruption and official complicity as a primary structural inhibitor of protective conversion within the Philippine trafficking-enforcement environment. Volume II reconstructs the machinery beneath that finding: who knew, who possessed authority, where intelligence travelled, which institution controlled it, how long it remained unconverted, where compromised authority entered the chain, and what happened to children while protection remained incomplete. -/- The investigation examines documented official complicity, immigration corruption, compromised investigative nodes, unresolved accountability pathways, foreign-generated OSAEC referrals, Philippine Internet Crimes Against Children Center referral architecture, and the distance between signal and physical safety. Its principal case families include the Pastillas corruption complex, the alleged compromise of an NBI investigative node, police and local-government accountability cases, the qualified-trafficking conviction of former Bamban mayor Alice Guo, and the prolonged Iligan OSAEC chronology, including the internationally flagged investigation that began in 2019 and culminated in the rescue of children in Purok Mangga, Barangay Tubod, in March 2026. -/- The central question is not whether the Philippines possesses laws or whether Philippine authorities conduct rescues. Both are established. The harder question is why exploitation can survive inside a State that already possesses knowledge, authority, institutions, international assistance, and demonstrated enforcement capacity. -/- Under Lex Custodiae, corruption assumes its gravest meaning when its consequence is measured not in missing money alone, but in unconverted protection. When authority is compromised, delayed, fragmented, protected from …

items.title: Seeing Is Knowing: A Phenomenology of Present Encounter, Consciousness, Thought, and Continuous Transformation.
items.abstract: This paper develops a phenomenological and ontological inquiry into seeing, knowing, consciousness, individuality, encounter, and transformation. It begins from the proposition that existence is encountered through particular beings, while every particular being possesses its own particular mode of encounter. Human beings encounter existence through their particular biological constitution and sensory capacities, but human sensory limitation cannot be taken as a universal measure of how existence is encountered by every being. The paper therefore proposes the broader sequence: Existence → particular being → particular mode of encounter. -/- Within human experience, the inquiry develops a further sequence: Present → Seeing → Nervous-system processing → Mind/Thought → Recognition → Interpretation. This sequence is not presented as a rigid neurological chronology but as a phenomenological distinction between immediate encounter and conceptualization. The central thesis is that seeing is not an incomplete form of knowing. Seeing is just seeing, and the encounter itself is knowing. Knowing is therefore not restricted to conceptual, linguistic, or propositional knowledge. Recognition and interpretation are subsequent conceptual formations through which the mind identifies and gives meaning to what has already been encountered. -/- The paper further understands seeing as a pre-reflective expression of consciousness. Seeing does not first require thought about seeing. Moreover, thought itself can become something seen. A thought may arise and be encountered without requiring a separate observer standing outside thought. Seeing thought is therefore distinguished from thinking about thought. This allows consciousness to be considered reflexively without necessarily establishing an observer–observed dualism. -/- The inquiry then extends from perception to ontology. Every particular being is limited in its particular form, mode, capacity, and encounter, yet participates in a process that is not exhausted by that particular limitation. Particular beings are therefore understood as limited expressions within a limitless process. Their transformation should not be understood as simple dissolution into nothingness. At the same time, the process should not be understood as permanent preservation or exact repetition. There is no permanence and no exact repetition; there is continuous transformation. What appears to repeat may be recognized as repetition by thought, while …

items.title: Soul, Heaven, Hell & Rebirth Are the Lollipop of Religions: Myth, Metaphysical Permanence, and the Preservation of Religious.
items.abstract: This paper critically examines four closely connected religious concepts—soul, heaven, hell, and rebirth—as forms of metaphysical consolation that can be understood collectively as “the lollipop of religions.” The metaphor refers to the psychological function of offering something comforting in response to an unpleasant reality. Just as a lollipop may comfort a child without changing the underlying situation, religious promises of an immortal soul, heavenly continuation, hellish punishment, or rebirth can make mortality psychologically more acceptable without thereby establishing the metaphysical reality they describe. -/- The paper does not claim that all religions consciously invented these doctrines for manipulation or that every believer is deliberately deceived.
