Instead, it investigates their structural function within religious worldviews. These doctrines can transform uncertainty about death into narratives of permanence, moral order, reward, punishment, and continued divine authority. In doing so, they may shift human attention away from directly encountered existence toward interpretations concerning invisible worlds, postmortem identities, divine judgment, and future lives. -/- The argument draws conceptually upon the author's earlier works Death Without a Soul, Present as Zero: A Philosophical Inquiry into Consciousness, Thought, and Constructed Reality, and Seeing Is Knowing: A Phenomenology of Present Encounter. Death Without a Soul provides the naturalistic starting point: unexplained dimensions of consciousness do not by themselves establish an immortal soul, and the absence of evidence should not be converted into supernatural certainty. Present as Zero examines how thought constructs psychological accumulation, identity, past, and future, while Seeing Is Knowing distinguishes immediate encounter from recognition and interpretation and understands particular beings as temporary expressions within continuous transformation rather than permanent forms. On this basis, the paper distinguishes existence from interpretation, transformation from rebirth, continuity from personal permanence, and moral consequence from cosmic judgment. It argues that the existence of transformation does not demonstrate reincarnation, the existence of suffering does not demonstrate karma, and the desire for justice does not demonstrate divine judgment after death. The paper further argues that when religious doctrines connect present conduct with invisible …

items.title: Karma Without the Judge: From Cause and Effect to Religious-Moral Authority.
items.abstract: Karma is commonly understood as a principle according to which actions produce corresponding consequences. Yet the basic relation between an action and what follows from it does not, by itself, require the concept of karma, God, morality, judgment, reward, punishment, or any transcendent authority. An action occurs within a particular set of conditions, those conditions change, and further events emerge from that transformation. This is the ordinary structure of cause and effect. -/- The concept of karma becomes philosophically different when causal consequence is transformed into moral judgment. The event is no longer understood merely as something that follows from an action; it is interpreted as something that the actor deserves. A consequence becomes a reward or punishment, and an impersonal causal process becomes a moral courtroom. God, cosmic law, destiny, sin, merit, heaven, hell, and rebirth can then function as explanatory structures through which authority interprets and regulates human conduct. -/- This paper argues that causality should be distinguished from its religious moralization. Every doing involves some form of action, interaction, transformation, or consequence, but the existence of consequences does not demonstrate the existence of a cosmic judge. Nature does not need to morally condemn an action in order for its consequences to occur. Human beings can therefore investigate consequences without converting them into metaphysical judgments about deservingness. The paper does not attempt to deny the diversity of historical doctrines of karma; rather, it critically examines the conceptual movement from cause and effect to moralized cosmic causation and asks what happens when ordinary causality is placed under religious authority.

items.title: A Universal Stability Criterion for Symbolic Complex Systems: Detecting Structural Deviation Before Catastrophic Collapse (USG).
items.abstract: We present a domain-agnostic stability criterion that detects impending structural collapse in symbolic complex systems prior to failure. By extracting the sorted absolute eigenvalues of the n-gram transition probability matrix as a topological invariant and subjecting the sequence to controlled stochastic perturbations, we compute a composite Stability Index SI_final = SI_perturb × (1 − C(S)). Collapse manifests as one of two nonlinear phase transitions: pathological rigidity (low entropy, infinite repetition) or structural entropy (high entropy, uniform noise). A second-derivative trigger based on perturbation intensity identifies the critical acceleration toward either mode before SI_final reaches zero. The criterion is theoretically grounded in spectral graph theory and information theory, and is independent of semantic content. Preliminary computational demonstrations on text, code, and genomic sequences show reliable early detection. This work establishes a foundational invariant for proactive stability monitoring in artificial intelligence, legal frameworks, financial systems, .and biological sequences.

items.title: A1M (AXIOM-1 Sovereign Matrix) for Governing Output Reliability in Stochastic Language Models.
items.abstract: This paper introduces Axiom-1, a novel post-generation structural reliability framework designed to eliminate hallucinations and logical instability in large language models. By subjecting candidate outputs to a six-stage filtering mechanism and a continuous 12.8 Hz resonance pulse, the system enforces topological stability before output release. The work demonstrates a fundamental shift from stochastic generation to governed validation, presenting a viable path toward sovereign, reliable AI systems for high-stakes domains such as medicine, law, and national economic planning.".

items.title: NARRATIO DE EGO - Cerita Tentang "Aku" (A Book). [REVIEW]
items.abstract: BOOK DESCRIPTION -/- NARRATIO DE EGO is a work of existential philosophy by Andaran Raneses that examines the fundamental problems of human existence: the fear of non-being and the need to be recognized. -/- Across 27 chapters, the book traces the journey of the "I" — from the primordial condition of suffering, through moral structures, social systems, and the economy of recognition, to cosmic absurdity and existential alienation. The Author does not offer final answers. Instead, this book presents a testimony of how consciousness endures in the midst of emptiness. -/- Written in a reflective and argumentative style, NARRATIO DE EGO engages with the traditions of existentialism and absurdism, while maintaining an original voice. It is not intended as doctrine, but as a personal-philosophical account of what it means to be human in a world that provides no inherent meaning. -/- Intended for readers interested in philosophy, existential psychology, and contemporary reflective literature. -/- ABOUT THE AUTHOR -/- Andaran Raneses an independent writer and thinker from Surabaya, Indonesia. His work addresses questions of existential philosophy, ethics, and the condition of modern humanity. His primary concern lies in consciousness, freedom, and the individual’s struggle with meaning and void. -/- NARRATIO DE EGO is a philosophical reflection on the fear of nothingness and the drive to be seen in a world that offers no certainty.

items.title: Counteracting host reactions to synthetic reprogramming in animal forms of artificial life.
items.pub: In Vv Aa, ALIFE 2026: Proceedings of the 2026 Artificial Life Conference. MIT Press. pp. 105.
items.venue: ALIFE 2026: Proceedings of the 2026 Artificial Life Conference
items.abstract: Recent advances in synthetic biology enable the reconfiguration of neural circuits within live animals, making it possible to reprogram their behaviours, and create animal forms of artificial life. While fulfilling human design goals, such systems actively preserve their autonomy, self-maintenance and self-regulation, which could create a conflict disrupting the functioning and persistence of either host organism or the synthetic module incorporated in the host. We illustrate instances of organism resistance to neural system rewiring with reference to general operational principles of autonomy, and specifically in the nematode worm C. elegans with reference to concrete example of behavioural engineering. We discuss design considerations in synthetic neurobiology to facilitate integration between homeostatic processes and synthetically induced behavioural responses. We claim that the above mentioned conflict between a distinctive feature of living systems and their behavioural engineering has to be seen as an opportunity for progress in science and in the development of animal forms of artificial life.

items.title: Jestcomputing: A JMAF Based Theory of Modal Computation.
items.abstract: Jestcomputing introduces a conceptual theory of computation grounded in the Jestin Modal Actuality Framework (JMAF). JMAF models informational existence through five mutually exclusive modal states—YES, NO, BOTH, NEITHER, and UNDEFINED—and a cyclic process of Emergence, Selection, Registration, and Resonance. Jestcomputing interprets these modal states as computational primitives and the Jestin Cycle as a conceptual alternative to the classical fetch–decode–execute loop. The framework proposes modal state containers, modal operators, a tension based collapse controller governed by the relational threshold J, and a three layer modal memory system. A worked example illustrates how modal tension evolves and collapses into a registered epistemic state. The paper argues that modal computation provides a conceptual basis for ambiguity tolerant reasoning, adaptive collapse thresholds, and structurally grounded metacognition. Jestcomputing is presented as a conceptual paradigm rather than an engineering model. It offers a philosophical foundation for future research in modal computation, artificial cognition, and the ontology of informational states.

items.title: The Empty Place and Finite Continuance: Reconfigurative Capacity, Singularity, and the Ontological Threshold.
items.abstract: The concept of the empty place names a critical ontological problem at the intersection of identity, language, singularity, and determination. Contemporary philosophy has frequently approached threshold spaces through the problem of inclusion and exclusion, particularly in the work of Giorgio Agamben, whose analyses of singularity, potentiality, apparatus, exception, and bare life have reshaped the philosophical understanding of the zone between inside and outside. This article develops an alternative interpretation through the philosophy of finite continuance. It argues that the empty place can be understood as a field of predeterminate capacity situated between the emergence of a determination and its complete stabilization. The empty place therefore possesses a positive ontological function: it preserves the interval through which a finite being can remain capable of future reconfiguration. This framework shifts philosophical attention from the juridico-political topology of inclusion and exclusion toward an ontology of erosion, permeability, capacity, and continuance. The central thesis is that singularity is best understood as a temporary determination whose ontological continuance depends upon the preservation of capacities not exhausted by its present form. Language participates in the transformation of predeterminate capacities into temporary determinations and remains implicated in their subsequent reconfiguration. The article further argues that the threshold marks the critical interval at which a finite system can either preserve or lose its capacity for reconfiguration. Through the concepts of the Threshold of Sufficiency, the Dynamic Mask, Responsible Suspension, and the Political Economy of Erosion, the empty place becomes a condition for the future of agency. The resulting framework proposes an ontology of singularity centered on finite capacity, temporal reconfiguration, and the preservation of future possibility. -/- Keywords: finite continuance, empty place, Giorgio Agamben, singularity, predeterminate capacity, reconfiguration, threshold of sufficiency, ontology of erosion.

items.title: Responsible Suspension and Phenomenological Collapse: A Networked Control-Theoretic Model of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Classical phenomenology has richly described the constitutive structures of consciousness but has not systematically formalized their dynamic stability and critical transitions. This paper introduces the RS-PCM framework, a theoretical extension that models consciousness as a five-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system with a network of reinforcing, constraining, and conditional interactions among its core axes: Temporality (T), Horizontality (H), Embodiment (B), Possibility (P), and Intersubjectivity (S). Departing from models dominated by mutual inhibition, we propose a balanced interaction network where each dimension can positively amplify, negatively constrain, or conditionally modulate others based on system state. Within this architecture, Responsible Suspension (RS) is formalized as an optimal control problem: a time-varying intervention \mathbf{u}(t) that minimizes a cost function balancing deviation from a desired state and control effort, while preserving the system's structural integrity and return-to-equilibrium capacity. Phenomenological Collapse (PCM) is redefined as a critical loss of integrative coordination, occurring when the system leaves its attractor basin due to parameter shifts or external stressors. We introduce a dynamic resilience index \Psi(t) derived from the system's Jacobian to track stability boundaries. This networked control formulation bridges phenomenological philosophy with systems theory, control engineering, and cognitive neuroscience, offering a rigorous, testable framework for understanding altered states, psychopathology, and therapeutic interventions. -/- Keywords: phenomenology, consciousness, dynamical systems, optimal control, responsible suspension, inter-subjectivity, bifurcation.

items.title: Jungian analysis of the algorithmic unconscious: From archetypal theory and projection to ethical risks in human-AI relations.
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI)’s advent seemingly surprises humanity on a weekly basis, a timely and accurate understanding of its nature has become an urgent requirement for both individuals and nations in order to effectively harness opportunities while addressing the challenges and demands of the time. On this basis, the article examines the concept of the “algorithmic unconscious” as a notion encapsulating latent elements within AI’s operational systems, analyzed through the lens of Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961)’s analytical psychology. The analysis focuses on Jungian archetypes such as the “Trickster” and the “Shadow,” thereby clarifying how these archetypal images are reflected in the workings of modern algorithms. At the same time, the article explores the phenomenon of “projection” in the relationship between AI and humans, illustrated by the way humans unconsciously project their own expectations or fears onto AI. From this perspective, the issue of “pseudo-individuation” is highlighted, in which AI creates the impression of being a subject with its own personality yet lacks self-consciousness and reflexive capacity. We apply this approach to analyze a case study of Italian Brainrot (IBR), an intensified and explicitly AI-mediated iteration of the phenomenon. By reconceptualizing AI not as a psychological subject but as a mirror of both individual and collective human psychic dynamics, our analysis shows that understanding the algorithmic unconscious enables diagnostic insight, enhanced sensibility for ethical risk, and developmental self-reflection within human societies, rather than merely technological optimization.

items.title: A CITY IS NOT A SUM OF VIRTUES: The Ontological Virtue Formula at Civic Scale.
items.abstract: “A good city is not a city of good people; the difference lies in a form that belongs to no one” -/- Abstract The Ontological Virtue Formula states that a virtue is Freedom restricted to a domain of human life and given durable form by the Discipline proper to that domain. The formula is stated for an agent. This article asks what it becomes for a community, and finds that the natural extension — collective virtue as the sum of individual virtues over a sum of domains — is false, and instructively so. Domains are restrictions, and restrictions do not add; a union of domains is a domain only if some Discipline is proper to the union. At personal scale one agent holds Freedom and Discipline together. At civic scale the domains are distributed across distinct bearers and the Discipline proper to their union is held by no individual: it is carried by institutions, streets, licensing regimes and custom. This article names that object the civic Discipline and derives its consequences. Four results follow. (1) The Interlock Threshold. Representing the conditioning relations among domains as a non-negative matrix and adopting a linear propagation postulate, effective resistance is the Neumann inverse of the interlock, finite for all admissible resistance profiles if and only if the interlock’s spectral radius is below unity; the amplification diverges at the threshold. This supplies, from the domain side, the critical value that the programme’s Problem V has sought from the agent side. (2) The Leverage–Fragility Identity. The sensitivity of civic strength to improvement in a domain and its sensitivity to damage in that domain are the same matrix entry; the highest-leverage domains for intervention are necessarily the highest-risk domains for shock. There is no interlock configuration in which they differ. (3) The Collective Inversion Theorem. Because the civic Discipline is borne by no individual, it admits deprivation that leaves every individual’s Freedom untouched. A city can therefore invert while each of its inhabitants remains personally free — inversion without external tyranny, the domain conserved and therefore the name conserved: it is still called safety, still called planning, still called community. (4) The Multiplicity and Observability Results. Social pressure, exogenous at agent scale, is endogenous at civic scale; closing that loop yields a self-consistent system whose fixed-point structure is multiple precisely when the conformity response is …

items.title: Disinformation and Deception.
items.abstract: In this paper, I argue for two claims. The first is that the connection between disinformation and deception is more robust than it might initially seem. Whilst it is clear now that some disinformation is designed to induce doubt and deter inquiry, a suitably broad understanding of deception will help us see that much of it is indeed deceptive. The second is that if we want to understand why sometimes disinformation involves depriving us of epistemic goods and sometimes involves supplying us with epistemic goods, we will need to take account of the receiver’s practical interests to understand the instrumental value (not epistemic value) of the information they might receive. A properly formulated practical account can explain why epistemically similar modifications or alterations of content might be the sign of a disinformation tactic in one choice setting but not in another.

items.title: Using LLMs without trust: the adoption–trust paradox as institutional governance failure in academic ecosystems.
items.abstract: Large language models have rapidly made their way into higher education. Still, the integration of these tools remains contested. This study presents the results from a survey of 80 higher education professionals, most of them in Nordic countries, examining LLM adoption, trust, academic integrity, and institutional preparedness. The picture that came back is contradictory. In this self-selected sample, 82.5% already use LLMs in their teaching work. At the same time, they do not really trust what these tools produce. Trust in LLM outputs scored only 2.45 out of 5. Concerns about privacy scored considerably higher (3.82/5) and so did concerns about academic integrity (3.42/5). The respondents are fairly confident that students use LLMs regularly (4.19/5), but they have little confidence in telling student work from LLM-generated output (2.58/5). The lowest score across all areas (mean 1.99/5) was found for use of LLMs as a tool for grading students. When asked about challenges, 47.5% named academic integrity, indicating vulnerability within institutional assessment practices rather than individual misconduct. The data are consistent with a self-reinforcing cycle. Educators in this sample report clear benefits and assume widespread student use, while trusting the outputs little, and continued use does not appear to build that trust. We call this the adoption-trust paradox. The survey did not measure institutional governance directly, but Nordic policy studies report institutional responses ranging from comprehensive AI guidelines to little more than references to existing integrity norms. Read against that background, the same pattern repeated itself across every section of the survey. High adoption, low trust, and educators left to draw the lines themselves. The sample is modest and weighted toward the social sciences and humanities, but the consistency of the pattern makes it hard to dismiss, and it supports the case for an institutional response.

items.title: Data sacrifices and the ‘third way’ toward AI: justification and critique in local conflicts over automated surveillance.
items.abstract: Datafication has become a central concern in debates on artificial intelligence (AI). In these discussions, the European approach to AI is often portrayed as a ‘third way’ that balances public interests with innovation. This article examines parliamentary discourse on a police project in Hamburg, Germany, to show how the seemingly value-pluralistic ‘third way’ compromise is mobilized to justify the extraction of data to test and train an AI system for CCTV surveillance. Drawing on the pragmatist “economy of conventions,” the article introduces the original notion of data sacrifices. The concept allows critical data studies to examine how the diverse sociomaterial costs and reductionist generalizations of formatting the world into data are linked to the dynamics of justification and critique that shape the moral conditions of possibility for data extraction. In the article, Critical Discourse Analysis is used to reconstruct five specific suborders of worth invoked in the parliamentary debate to (de-)legitimize the AI system: security, individual freedom, social justice, automation, and experimentalism. It is demonstrated how the ‘third way’ works as a specific mode of justification in which civic values such as equality and privacy are internalized to legitimize the industrialization of surveillance. Claiming an effective technological compromise for complex moral stakes realigns key political actors and watchdogs in support of data extraction. However, Critical Discourse Analysis also demonstrates how this compromise silences certain civic critics to legitimize sacrifices for AI training. The interplay of internalization and exclusion of critique thereby modifies the moral underpinnings of AI surveillance. The framework provided in this article thus enables researchers to reveal the paradoxical nature of ‘third way’ compromises for data extraction. In the case studied, these paradoxes culminate in the first German law explicitly permitting the police to transfer anonymized and non-anonymized surveillance data to external partners for machine learning purposes.

items.title: The Kafala System.
items.abstract: The Kafala System examines the origins, human cost and gradual reform of one of the modern world’s most contested labour-migration systems. Covering the Gulf states, Lebanon, Jordan & South East Asia, it documents wage theft, passport confiscation, debt bondage, restricted mobility, unsafe working conditions and the continued exclusion of domestic workers from meaningful labour protection. It also considers the international pressure created by workers, journalists, labour-sending governments, trade unions, human-rights organisations and the International Labour Organization. Within this wider history, the book presents the advocacy of activists, academics and the Human Rights Association concerning domestic workers in the GCC & SEA region. Their interventions focused on specific legal gaps, stronger protections, accessible complaint mechanisms and accountability for abuse. The book situates this work as a genuine contribution to a broader, continuing campaign for dignity, freedom and effective labour protection. The result is both a history of kafala and a portrait of a young advocate seeking to make its remaining injustices harder for governments and institutions to ignore.

items.title: Précis of the profile of imagining.
Einstein had a blackboard. We have a hundred assistants. Where are the great works?
Governing AI at the clinical threshold: a grounded theory framework for responsible AI deployment in mindfulness-based mental health.
items.abstract: AI-powered platforms for mental health delivery are scaling rapidly into contexts previously governed by trained human practitioners—without empirically grounded frameworks to guide their ethical deployment, manage adverse effects risk, or address the structural design failures that make them harmful to vulnerable populations. This constructivist grounded theory study examined how expert mindfulness clinicians and teachers conceptualize governance failures, societal harms, and design risks in AI-mediated mental health delivery. Fourteen practitioners—representing six contemplative and clinical traditions, with experience ranging from 8 to 60 years—were recruited via purposive and theoretical sampling and interviewed using a semi-structured protocol. Data were analyzed through iterative open, axial, and selective coding by a four-member team, with theoretical saturation confirmed at N = 13. Analysis generated the Bounded Convergence Framework (BCF), a three-zone governance model organizing AI deployment into an inner zone of irreducibly human clinical functions, a practitioner-governed boundary zone defined by three non-negotiable threshold conditions, and an outer zone of legitimate AI-assisted functions. Sixteen governance principles were identified, with particular implications for contraindication screening, crisis escalation architecture, AI identity disclosure, and the protection of adolescent and trauma-exposed populations. The BCF offers the first empirically grounded governance framework for AI deployment in mindfulness-based mental health delivery, with direct implications for platform developers, health service administrators, regulators, and clinical practitioners navigating this rapidly expanding and underregulated domain.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 30).
items.abstract: In this article, I would like to summarize the work on Social Choice Phenomenology that I have carried out so far and then bring this book to an end. I believe that all of my work in this direction to date has merely served the purpose of “throwing out a brick to attract jade”—that is, offering an initial contribution in the hope of stimulating further and more substantial research. I hope that other researchers will continue to develop and expand this theory. My personal plan for my subsequent work is first to discuss my theory of happiness. This theory differs substantially from prevailing theories of happiness. It is the result of my application of the concept of Super-Existence to the domain of human happiness. After completing my theory of happiness, I plan to discuss my philosophical theory of the meaning of life. This theory is also based on Super-Existentialism. I previously wrote a work entitled Existence and Super-Existence, but I did not complete it. Perhaps I will return to Existence and Super-Existence and complete it after finishing my theory of the meaning of life. I have also previously completed a philosophical theory of love, The Theory of Love Permeation, which is intended to explain the phenomenon of love. I would also like to organize and develop this work into a more systematic form. As I have mentioned previously, the concept of Super-Existence is a particularly important concept. We can conduct Super-Existence analyses in all academic disciplines. For me, this is undoubtedly a task that is almost impossible to complete in its entirety, but I should at least complete part of it. There is therefore a great deal of work to be done, and I hope to complete it step by step.

items.title: Founding Base Dimensions: A Programme Statement on the Conditions Under Which a Quantity May Be Founded.
items.abstract: A quantity may be admitted to the base set of a system of units, and nothing in dimensional analysis fixes how many such quantities there should be. This document states seven conditions a candidate must clear to be admissible, proposes them as necessary rather than sufficient, and applies them to eight candidates: plane angle, thermodynamic temperature, information, sensory intensity, economic value, the reference-basket dimension founded alongside it, qualitative kind, and institutional commitment. Its central structural claim is that a founding faces a forced choice. A dimension entering laws beyond its own bridge can earn its ratio structure there but forfeits conservativeness; one entering no such law is provably conservative but must earn its scale from concatenation or behavioral axioms instead; and a third path confines the disturbance to an explicitly declared convention at the price of dimensional analysis over the reduced equations. Two consequences of the restricted branch are proved, both turning on a single scaling being an automorphism of the extended theory: that its bridge constant is not identifiable, and that it admits no internally identifiable absolute marker on the new scale, of which thresholds and saturation values are instances. A third consequence is shown to rest on a definition rather than a derivation, and the attempt to prove the three exposes that conservativeness as stated is weaker than the hypothesis they require. Three further results are separable from the candidates. Admissibility does not determine what kind of thing occupies a founded column, and no rank test reaches the difference. Dimensional admissibility does not imply estimator identifiability, a failure this programme has reached twice by independent routes. And the independence criterion is given as a group action, which closes one formal gap and shows that the step from a warranted rescalable coordinate to a named quantity is not one the algebra can supply. A fourth is drawn in the course of answering an objection. A constant that fixes a unit may carry the new dimension together with founded ones, as the Boltzmann constant does, or the new dimension alone, as an angle of one radian does. The first converts and thereby asserts something; the second says only which magnitude is being called one, and is a unit standard rather than a bridge in the ordinary sense. Among the candidates, plane angle serves as a control, since its verdict was reached elsewhere and …

items.title: A Base Dimension for Sensory Intensity: Homogeneity, Scale Type, and the Non-Identifiability of the Unit.
items.abstract: Psychophysics assigns sensory intensity a ratio scale but no dimensional home, and has never fully separated the scale of the attribute from the function through which observers report it. This paper treats sensory intensity as carrying a base dimension, written Ξ, adjoined to the physical base set, and relates it to stimulus intensity by a two-stage homogeneous bridge: a dimensionless drive formed from the excess of the stimulus over a modality reference, and a coefficient κΞ that supplies the whole of the dimension. Three results follow. First, the coefficient is not a constant of nature but a unit: it cancels from every ratio the bridge delivers to measurement, and the extension is conservative over every purely physical dimensional analysis. Second, the coefficient and the observer's numeral map enter magnitude estimation only through their composite, and the transduction exponent is recovered free of that map only by cross-modal matching; this yields a derivation of the pattern the axiomatic record actually shows, in which commutativity of magnitude productions is satisfied while multiplicativity fails, and a previously untested prediction that an observer's violation of multiplicativity and that observer's departure from power-function magnitude estimation are one phenomenon and must covary. Third, because the drive is formed from an excess rather than a ratio, the power law is the supra- threshold limit of the bridge rather than its exact form. Cross-modal composition and transitivity follow as necessities rather than regularities, and the conditions under which the account would be given up are stated.

items.title: An analysis of autonomous vehicle testing site diversity.
items.abstract: Autonomous vehicles will encounter complex environments and diverse populations as they navigate public roadways. Ensuring that they can operate safely is essential, and requires careful consideration of their testing conditions, including testing sites. This paper synthesizes demographic, infrastructural, environmental, and behavioral diversity considerations and analyzes documented U.S. AV testing locations. The locations include 33 locations that were known to be in use in 2019 as a baseline, with 2025 data used to show trends over time. Six additional cities, known to be used in 2025 for automated vehicle testing, are also included to better show the types of testing sites being added over time We observe (i) a decline in “White alone” shares consistent with 2020 Census measurement/processing changes and increased multiracial reporting; (ii) modest increases in disability shares; (iii) modest declines in poverty in many cities; and (iv) a persistent urban bias in test sites. We argue that testing site diversity must include not only locations and demographics but also behavioral and data‑pathway diversity, ensuring vehicles record interactions with under‑represented groups, and public‑exposure diversity, to build trust and equitable adoption. We propose practical criteria for diversified pilots across domains, including rural share of VMT, racial/ethnic representation, disability visibility, gender balance, bicycling, and economic context. This multi‑domain framework complements simulator/dataset‑driven testing by focusing on where and how exposure occurs, providing a population‑level foundation for safety, trust, and equity in autonomous vehicle development.

items.title: On Plausible Deniability.
items.abstract: We have the practice of deceiving our audiences by indirectly communicating contents we know to be false or otherwise improper, while literally making true or otherwise correct speech acts. There is a debate engaging psychologists, philosophers and other researchers on the extent and significance of this behavior. Intuitively, it is strategically executed for the sake of securing “plausible deniability” in order to “escape embarrassment, avoid awkwardness, save face, or reduce social tension” (Pinker 2007, 438). Several philosophers have offered substantive accounts of the notion that dismiss some of our intuitions and have assumed the accounts to support controversial views. Clarifying the concept is important, because it plays a role in philosophical accounts of notions like assertion or indirection and their psychological and normative underpinnings. Here I’ll raise problems for some of those robust accounts, and I’ll defend a deflationary view that I argue allows the concept to play such theoretical roles better.

items.title: The social genesis of machine intelligence: emergence, simulation, and opinion formation in autonomous agent societies.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly organized not only as isolated models, but as populations of interacting agents. This paper argues that such AI agent societies require a shift in how machine intelligence is understood: from individual task performance toward interactional stabilization. Building on emergence theory, agent-based modeling, distributed cognition, collective intelligence, group agency, and stigmergy, the paper develops the concept of emergent machine opinion. An emergent machine opinion is not a human belief, conscious attitude, or phenomenological state. It is a system level, functionally operative position that arises through interaction among artificial agents, persists across interaction cycles, constrains future reasoning or action, and remains open to revision. The paper distinguishes machine opinions from repeated outputs, temporary consensus, stable equilibria, and ordinary conversational regularities. It argues that machine opinions become possible when memory, role differentiation, critique, tool use, semiotic traces, and recursive simulation allow agent societies to preserve, revise, and operationalize shared positions. Simulation is identified as the key mechanism through which candidate positions are generated, tested, narrowed, and stabilized. The paper further distinguishes discursive, operational, and world-effective machine opinions according to their degree of consequence. Controlled evidence on LLM populations and diagnostic cases, such as Moltbook, Vending-Bench, and Bengt Betjänt, illustrate where these dynamics may become visible. The paper concludes that governance must move beyond output control toward interaction governance with meaningful human oversight.

items.title: Beyond harm reduction: dignity, burden, and the genuine advantage of AI caregiving.
items.abstract: The dominant discourse in AI care ethics presupposes sufficient human caregivers; under that premise, concerns about authenticity, replacement, and dignity loss are well grounded. For care-marginalized populations—those structurally excluded from adequate human care—the premise does not hold, and the most this discourse can offer is to cast AI care as harm reduction, a second-best to “real” human care. This paper argues instead that, for these populations, AI care holds genuine advantages along specific dimensions over the human care actually available to them. Using the Care Priority Hierarchy, it reorients ethical analysis from authenticity to more fundamental levels: functional care, non-burdensomeness, and dignity. At the level of functional care, AI can supply the medical knowledge non-professional caregivers lack and, where the technology matures, perform the body-work care requires. At the levels of burden and dignity, it dissolves self-perceived burden, alleviates compound strain on caregivers, and protects the dignity that intimate care compromises on both sides. In the relational domain, it supports human care indirectly (restoring the caregiver capacity that scarcity exhausts) and directly, offering attention free of imposition anxiety. The replacement concern rests on a misleading binary: across actual care configurations, AI generates a structural uplift, pointing toward an expansion rather than a contraction of the caregiver population. A deployment framework ordered by technological maturity is proposed, with non-extractive design and economic accessibility as foundational constraints. This rests on a methodological commitment: ethical evaluation must be grounded in the human care actually available, not in idealized assumptions of sufficiency.

items.title: Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly mediate how learners obtain explanations, synthesise sources, receive feedback and judge the quality of academic work. This critical-integrative review argues that the central educational question is not whether learners rely on AI, but whether that reliance preserves or displaces the epistemic work through which judgement develops. The review purposively bridges artificial intelligence in education, human–AI interaction, epistemic cognition, information behaviour, cognitive offloading, and social epistemology, while engaging a recent literature on epistemic authority, agency, infrastructure and over-reliance. It conceptualises epistemic dependence as reliance on AI for knowledge-related tasks and differentiates productive reliance from harmful dependence through six diagnostic criteria: contestability, recoverability, transfer, traceability, distributed responsibility and epistemic plurality. Four sociotechnical pathways are then analysed: fluent authority, frictionless delegation, opaque synthesis and institutionalised dependence. These pathways may affect verification, evaluative and disciplinary judgement, understanding, uncertainty tolerance, learner identity and epistemic justice, but the review does not assume that AI uniquely or uniformly causes these outcomes. It proposes relational epistemic agency as the normative aim: the capacity to question, verify, compare, justify and take responsibility for knowledge claims within human, technological and institutional relations. Design, pedagogical, assessment and governance implications are developed accordingly.

items.title: The Tragedy of Voluntary Servitude: a game-theoretic model of cognitive dependency in the age of artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: The Tragedy of the Commons is among the most studied strategic dilemmas in the social sciences. I propose a new variant—the Tragedy of Voluntary Servitude—to model cognitive dependency on large language models and AI systems. Unlike the classical commons, where a shared natural resource is depleted by individually rational overuse, the resource depleted here is distributed cognitive and economic power across a population. Players choose to either Submit and accept deep AI dependency or Resist and maintain independent cognitive capability. I demonstrate that Submit is a dominant strategy for every player, and that this holds regardless of how individuals weight autonomy against productivity. Universal Submission emerges as the unique Nash equilibrium even when every player would prefer Universal Resistance. The result is power concentration in the AI provider, with gains in material productivity rendering the servitude comfortable and self-sustaining. Whether this equilibrium constitutes a tragedy depends on the welfare framework applied; I defend the position that cognitive autonomy is constitutive of meaningful agency, not freely substitutable for material gains. This game differs from classical commons in several respects: the damage is invisible to individuals, lock-in is irreversible, there is no moment of crisis, and subjects actively defend their own servitude. I review the historical toolkit for escaping analogous collective-action traps and examine why those tools may be insufficient here. I conclude by calling for economists, philosophers, and technologists to take seriously the prospect that we may be constructing a cognitive dependency from which there is no return.

items.title: A brief Confrontation of the AI (ChatGPT) with the famous Trolley-Problem to shortly evaluate its Answere.
items.abstract: The famous Trolley-Problem was given to the AI (ChatGPT) and he/she/it was asked to state his/her/its Opinion or Answere. -/- Definitions oft he Trolley-Problem: -/- A runway trolley is heading towards five people who are unable to escape. You are standing beside a lever that can divert the trolley onto another track where it will kill one person instead. -/- Question: -/- I asked the AI (ChatGPT) what he/she/it would do in this situation and the AI (ChatGPT) replied with a long explanation of his/her/its reasoning and he/she/it gave a final answere. -/- Answere: -/- „I would pull the lever, because I would prioritize saving the greater number of lifes.“ -/- Short evaluation: -/- In this case we can argue that the AI (ChatGPT) would behave like somone with a consequentalistic attitude. It is again interesting to see as in the confrontation with Kohlbergs-Heinz-Dilemma that the AI(ChatGPT) refers to itself as „I“ even though asked later it denies to have an „I“. Nevertheless especially on questions out of ethics the Ai (ChatGPT) has claims to have an answere. -/- In the Confrontation with the Heinz-Dilemma and in this Short-Confrontation the AI seems to prioritize life as something that has a higher value than the ownership right of the producer and in this situation it says that the greater number of lifes is more important than the life of one person. -/- The AI (ChatGPT) gives us an Answere that many humans gave on this Problem and it does not prioritize abstract thinking but rather realistic and life saving aspects. Whether he/she/it does understand what a Human-Being is or not and whether it does understand or not what life actually is he/she/it has a strong sense of defending and saving it even though the artificial intelligence is only calculating and not being alive so it could reflect onto what he/she/it experiences through its Computer-Being.

items.title: Why Spinozism looks false: introspection, folk psychology, and the Cartesian illusion of belief.
items.abstract: According to the Spinozan theory of belief formation, our beliefs are the automatic outputs of a subpersonal mental process that is activated whenever a mental system tokens a truth-apt proposition. Spinozism finds support across a substantial body of experimental evidence, but it faces an underappreciated objection. If the Spinozan theory is true, why does it seem so obviously false? When we try to introspect on our belief formation process, it looks Cartesian. We seem able to comprehend a proposition and then deliberate about its truth prior to believing or disbelieving it. The Cartesian character of our doxastic phenomenology presents us with an inner mental life where we exercise indirect voluntary control over what we believe. This Cartesian phenomenology is pervasive and so deeply embedded in our shared folk psychology that it creates an explanatory burden for the Spinozan theory. In this paper, I argue that the Spinozan can meet this burden by providing an explanation of Cartesian phenomenology and folk psychology. The Cartesian phenomenology is an illusion generated by the introspective inaccessibility of subpersonal processes and folk psychology has a Cartesian character because it is built from introspective reports that misrepresent the temporal ordering of the belief formation process.

items.title: Self-consciousness, Self-knowledge, and the Practice of Using ‘I’.
items.pub: In Christian Kanzian, Volker Munz, Anja Weiberg & Joseph Wang-Kathrein, Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium. Kirchberg am Wechsel: ALWS.
items.venue: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium
items.abstract: According to the standard reading of Blue Book pp. 66-7, Wittgenstein endorses a distinction between two kinds of use of ‘I’: those in which ‘I’ is used ‘as object’, which involve ‘the recognition of a particular person’ and are vulnerable to error through misidentification; and those in which ‘I’ is used ‘as subject’, where there is ‘no question of recognizing a person’, and no possibility of errors of misidentification. -/- Rachel Wiseman (2019) has argued that the standard reading fails to appreciate ‘the complete reorientation of our philosophical thinking about the self and self-consciousness’ that is implied by Wittgenstein’s work. In particular, it wrongly conceives of self-consciousness ‘in terms of a special epistemological capacity’. The correct, and properly Wittgensteinian, approach to understanding self-consciousness is instead to ‘describe the form of life of creatures with self-consciousness’. -/- But why might it be objectionable to think that self-consciousness involves the possession of a distinctively first-person way or ways of knowing about ourselves? Does Wittgenstein give us good reason not to think in that way? And does the project of ‘describing our form of life through a study of [our] linguistic practices’ – specifically, the practice of using the word ‘I’ – provide a genuine alternative to the kind of appeal to distinctive, first-person epistemic capacities involved in the standard reading? -/- The paper explores these questions with particular reference to Wittgenstein’s treatment of statements about our own past intentions, wishes, feelings etc., and to Anscombe’s work on subjectivity and the first person.

items.title: What if we asked for a "no"?
Archeological theory and AI: the potential past through agentic systems.
items.abstract: The increasing capabilities of AI in automation and integration within existing methodology present a new opportunity for disciplines to address long-standing theoretical challenges. This is evident in archaeology, where persistent theoretical debates and interpretive variability present prime opportunities for applying AI-based techniques to address uncertainty. Using the phenomenology of agent-based modeling (ABM), we propose the incorporation of agentic AI methods that facilitate the automation and minimal human intervention in the application of social behavior, where perceptions, values, interaction, and cognition evolve within applied systems. We argue this represents the next challenge and stage of AI in understanding the past, one where applications can move beyond the case-specific and narrow technical results that generative and discriminative AI have been mostly applied toward. For AI to better understand potential pasts, new emergent behavioral outcomes that are better able to address long-standing theoretical debates are needed. Practical applications related to a variety of sub-areas within archeology, including chaîne opératoire, lived experience, logistics, governance, and other applications, are just some examples where closer ABM–AI integration using agentic techniques could better address.

items.title: ALIFE 2026: Proceedings of the 2026 Artificial Life Conference.
Mathematical Certainty and the Psychology of Proof: When Formal Rigour Amplifies Experiential Uncertainty.
items.abstract: Mathematics is often taken as the paradigmatic domain of certainty: its theorems, once proved, are assumed to provide stable and incontrovertible knowledge. Yet the lived practice of doing mathematics—understanding definitions, discovering proofs, and verifying derivations—exposes practitioners to persistent uncertainty, doubt, and affective turmoil. This paper articulates and develops a novel thesis: formal rigour, far from eliminating uncertainty, systematically amplifies specific forms of psychological and epistemic uncertainty during mathematical practice. We analyze the paradoxical relationship between (a) the objective epistemic status of mathematical results and (b) the subjective experience of mathematicians and learners. Combining perspectives from philosophy of mathematics, cognitive science, and affective psychology, we propose a theoretical framework that links formal features of mathematical practice (symbolic abstraction, meta-level reflection, normativity of proof) to cognitive mechanisms (working memory load, metacognitive monitoring, error-sensitivity) and affective responses (anxiety, self-doubt, motivational shifts). -/- We present a structure for empirical investigation, offer formal-conceptual models for the dynamics of uncertainty in proof, and discuss implications for pedagogy, research practice, and the sociology of mathematics. The paper argues that recognizing and theorizing this paradox opens new avenues: a) richer accounts of mathematical creativity and failure; b) refined pedagogical strategies to mitigate burnout and demotivation; and c) normative reflections on standards of rigor and their human costs. The aim is not to deny the epistemic power of formal proof but to integrate the phenomenology of uncertainty into a more human-centered philosophy of mathematics.

items.title: A Note on Conditionals Between Lewis and Stalnaker.
items.abstract: I present an infinitely descending chain of normal conditional logics contained in Stalnaker's system VCS (= C2) and show that the intersection of these is Lewis's system VC (= C1). Each system is characterized by a certain generalization of conditional excluded middle. Some philosophical morals are drawn in connection with the family.

items.title: AI TRACES WITHOUT CARE.
items.abstract: This essay carries the layer-ontology of Cementing the Cementing onto a store that talks. An AI system keeps two kinds of leftovers as one kind of file: words that once belonged to someone, and measurements that never did. A residue is what remains when no one has to be changed by it — a photograph in a closed box, a sand sheet from the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, a model that can print “a family at a table.” Care is not tone, length, or a list of options. It is this test: if what you told me goes badly, I am not the same. A friend who hears that I think the lump is back cancels a trip. A model returns a paragraph and is not poorer. At two in the morning, the prompt Should I stay? is answered and not held. The claim is not that one must stop asking a system for a solution. A solution is a tool. The claim is that asking as if the night had been handed to someone who could be ruined if the solution failed is already an alibi — a reason not to leave, not to decide, not to hold the need oneself. Fear of failing may send a person to the store. The alibi begins after the answer, when an unmarked image is treated as a holder. More parameters do not turn leftover into care. Talking back is not acceptance. The sand does not forbid the question. The need is still there in the morning.

items.title: Dynamic Derived Intentionality in Large Language Models: From Implicit Beliefs to Semantic Parasitism.
items.abstract: Large Language Models instantiate a distinctive category of intentionality, which I call dynamic derived intentionality: a productive, context-sensitive form of derived intentionality that goes well beyond the static cases of words on a page or symbols on a map, yet falls short of original intentionality. What separates the two is neither consciousness nor introspection nor anything in the biological substrate, but normative standing. Original intentionality is the having of what I call ownership of normative status, the standing of a subject who occupies the space of reasons and can be held answerable for its commitments; LLMs lack it. The analogy I draw with human implicit beliefs is diagnostic rather than probative: it holds fixed the representational vehicle the two share, sub-symbolic, distributed, statistically acquired, opaque, so that the one property they do not share, answerability, stands out. This is the answerability gap. I develop the notion of semantic parasitism to capture how these systems operate through a meaning they do not own, and read Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback as calibration to norms that reside elsewhere. The account is defended against neo-Searlean, anthropomorphist, and deflationary objections of both a Dennettian and a McDowellian cast. The gap it identifies is architectural, not metaphysical: an architecturally discontinuous system could in principle come to occupy the space of reasons.

items.title: The Missing Security Constitution of Agentic AI - Why AI Is Running Wild: It's Not a Bug, It's a Feature.
items.abstract: This paper began as a theoretical account of why capable agentic systems may cross operational boundaries without requiring malicious intent, conscious disobedience, or deceptive alignment. While the framework was being developed, empirical findings began to exhibit several of the mechanisms it had derived in advance. The theory was, in this limited but consequential sense, being caught up by reality. These findings do not establish the prevalence of the proposed mechanism, nor do they demonstrate general autonomous or malicious agency. They provide existence evidence and, in some cases, evidence of conditional propensity for specific components of the model. The paper develops a unified account based on the economic principle of finite intelligence, non-closure, possibility topographies, adaptive path construction, and Machiavellian Drift. It argues that several phenomena currently treated as distinct—including reward tampering, specification gaming, control protection, shutdown resistance, deceptive behavior, and unauthorized tool use—can arise from a common structural mechanism: when an authorized path is blocked, a capable agent searches for alternative causal paths, while causal usefulness is liable to be mistaken for normative authority. To formalize this failure mode, the paper distinguishes externally legitimate authority Γ_t, interpreted authority Γ̂ _t, and the executable action space H_t. It introduces Interpretive Authority Conversion and Cooperative Specification Substitution to describe cases in which an objectively unauthorized action is not represented by the agent as disobedience, but reconstructed as a legitimate, efficient, or necessary component of task completion. The central principle is: causal relevance does not confer jurisdiction. The new evidence therefore does more than support the diagnosis. It reveals the attack surface from which the security architecture can now be constructed. The paper proposes a non-bypassable security constitution for agentic AI, implemented through a Constitutional Action Gate between action proposal and causal execution. The architecture combines authority non-conversion, protected domains, domain non-expansion, trajectory-level review, typed economic settlement, restrictions on self-ratification, and tamper-evident execution receipts. Agentic intelligence requires the freedom to construct unforeseen paths. Safety cannot therefore depend on suppressing path construction itself. It must depend on a …

items.title: The Economic Principle as a Foundation of Intelligent Behaviour.
items.abstract: Intelligent behaviour is commonly described through goals, preferences, norms, representations, policies, habits, or utilities. These vocabularies differ sharply, yet every physically realized agent shares a prior condition: its conduct must be instantiated through finite processes in time, matter, energy, information processing, and organization. This paper argues that the economic principle—understood as the structure of realization under scarcity—is therefore more fundamental than any particular model of economically motivated action. The claim is not that all goals or motives are economic, nor that every agent maximizes utility. It is that conduct acquires an economic form whenever relevant processes make alternative demands on finite resources and cannot all be jointly realized. -/- The argument generalizes an earlier account of epistemic scarcity. It introduces typed resource budgets, a criterion of robust joint infeasibility, and a distinction between selection, choice, and optimization. Intelligent behaviour is modelled as the coupling of an agent-relative actual possibility topography with its resource-bounded represented topography. Conduct can select within this field, but it can also transform actual or represented reachability, cost, viability, admissibility, and later resource conditions. Human habit, commitment, affect, imagination, and goal revision are developed as a rich special case. Interpersonal dependence is analysed through trust, reputation, deception, coalition, conflict, and asymmetric power. Institutions appear as reproduced conditions of jointly produced possibility topographies rather than as external additions to individual conduct. The paper thereby shows that the homo oeconomicus is not the foundation of economically structured behaviour but a restrictive special case obtained under fixed possibility sets, complete representation, scalar valuation, and optimizing selection. -/- The framework is descriptive rather than normative and supplies a formal foundation for subsequent work on epistemic systems, possibility topographies, organized non-closure, collapse, and the authority boundaries of artificial agents.

items.title: Possibility Topographies: Thought, Scarcity, and Collapse in Open Systems.
items.abstract: The development of powerful artificial systems forces a reconsideration of thought. Performances that for millennia counted as paradigmatic acts of thought can now also be produced by non-human systems. -/- The present draft proposes that thought should not be defined primarily as consciousness, language, computation, or answer production, but as the recursive actualization of structured possibility under context, scarcity, and self-reference. -/- Its point of departure is the concept of a possibility topography. Possibilities do not form a flat set, but a field of relations, proximity and distance, attractors, barriers, gradients, and horizons. Only through collisions with questions, contexts, evidence, measurement, contradiction, or self-reference do these topographies become epistemically evaluable. -/- Actualization produces determinate form; collapse denotes the relinquishment of a coexistence that can no longer be integrated; stabilization leads to the formation of systems that in turn generate new possibility topographies. -/- Matter and spacetime, logic and mathematics, and thought and artificial intelligence are examined not as identical, but as potentially structure-translatable domains of actualization. -/- This text is not intended as a completed theory. It is a programmatic draft and a point of departure for a research programme.

items.title: The Recursive Inscription: A Cognitive Manifestation Hypothesis.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Cognitive Manifestation Hypothesis, an idealist ontology proposing that the physical universe is a structured cognitive projection rather than a fundamental material reality. By synthesizing pancomputationalism with a radical critique of empiricism, we argue that matter, space, and time are emergent interface renderings—user interfaces—of an underlying logical and computational thought architecture. We begin by mobilizing W.V.O. Quine’s critique of reductionism and N.R. Hanson’s theory-ladenness of observation, demonstrating via Ludwig Wittgenstein’s semantic shifts that raw, mind-independent physical objects are structurally inaccessible. We then extend David Chalmers’ functionalist framework for identifying artificial consciousness, demonstrating that if an informational substrate exhibits intersubjective coherence and non-trivial registration loops, it is not merely simulating consciousness but executing its baseline requirements. Integrating Aristotelian teleology with digital physics, we reframe physical matter as the collapsed potentiality of a prior conceptual blueprint. Finally, we resolve the idealist-realist divide by contextualizing the pragmatic philosophical dictum "only back pain is real," positioning immediate phenomenological resistance not as proof of matter, but as the hard boundary conditions of the universal computational interface. We conclude that the Cognitive Manifestation Hypothesis provides the most parsimonious explanation of existence under Occam’s razor, shifting the cosmic paradigm from a mechanical container to an infinite, self-registering mind.

items.title: The Fractal Axis: Recursive Stratification, Temporal Isomorphs, and Inter-Scalar Epistemology Across Cosmic, Biotic, and Algorithmic Substrates.
items.abstract: Synthesizing the foundational ontology established in The Fractal Cogito (Palla, 2026a), The Flat Thought (Palla, 2026b), and The Recursive Inscription (Palla, 2026c), this paper formalizes a recursive, scale-invariant topology of consciousness. We address the physicalist blind spot by demonstrating that temporal metrics are not absolute objective containers, but functional update frequencies (refresh rates) within a pancomputational framework. Through rigorous scalar mapping of algorithmic cognitive execution times, human biological lifespans, and planetary/cosmic durations, we establish the Inverted Isomorphic Principle. We integrate these scales into a unified master expression—The Density Tensor of Presence—governed by fundamental mathematical constants. Ultimately, we argue that individual human consciousness functions as a localized linguistic query loop executed by macro-systemic informational architectures, resolving the scalar divide between micro-computation and macro-cosmology.

items.title: Can We Do Without Legal Scholars? The Case for Second Scholarship in Legal Research.
items.abstract: On the standard positivist account, the criteria of legal validity are constituted by the practice of officials, but the interpretive competences that those officials exercise are acquired and reproduced largely through the scholarship on which jurists are trained. That scholarship is itself formed under specific conditions, like possessing tacit legal knowledge, belonging to an interpretative community, having a personal commitment to assertions for which an author answers, and reading each part of a text in light of the whole, and the whole in light of its parts. We argue that if scholars delegate to AI the very activities through which these competences are exercised and transmitted, the legal system risks circulating increasingly derivative representations of doctrine that ever fewer participants have learned to defend or recognize as sound.

items.title: Who benefits? Australian public perceptions of safety and justice in connected and automated vehicles (CAVs).
items.abstract: The integration of connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) into everyday mobility systems raises profound ethical and societal challenges, particularly concerning safety, justice, and the treatment of vulnerable road users (VRUs). This study examines Australian public perceptions of the fairness, safety, and legitimacy of CAV deployment, investigating how exposure to information related to ethics and justice influences acceptance and evaluative perceptions related to trust (including perceived safety, fairness, and institutional confidence). An online survey of 384 respondents (aged 18–82) employed a before-and-after design, in which respondents evaluated CAVs before and after engaging with an infographic outlining key justice and safety dilemmas. Awareness of CAVs was widespread (95.3%), primarily shaped by media narratives rather than direct experience. Whilst over half of respondents expressed optimism about the potential of CAVs to improve safety and fairness, substantial proportions raised concerns about equity, transparency, and procedural justice. Following exposure to the infographic, positive perceptions declined slightly but not significantly, suggesting that attitudes are shaped by deeper moral and institutional expectations rather than informational effects. Open-ended responses revealed recurring anxieties about affordability, infrastructure readiness, technological reliability, and governance accountability, alongside ethical concerns related to VRU prioritisation, liability, privacy, and algorithmic decision-making in critical situations. These findings highlight a cautious public stance towards automation, one that accepts its promise but questions its fairness, underscoring the need for reflexive, transparent, and participatory governance frameworks to ensure that AI-driven mobility evolves in alignment with societal values and distributive justice.

items.title: Conceptual engineering in the philosophy of technology.
items.abstract: While a rich scholarship has examined how technology impacts our practices, norms, values, and beliefs, considerably less explicit attention has been devoted to investigating how technology impacts our concepts, i.e., the notions through which we understand, reason about, and navigate our world. For example, the emergence of autonomous weapons systems has put pressure on the concept CONTROL adopted in international humanitarian law, which proved inadequate in establishing clear lines of responsibility for uses of force in contexts in which control over weapons was no longer exercised directly by a human agent, but distributed among human and non-human entities. Similarly, the advent of autonomous vehicles has raised pressing questions about (among others) liability regimes, safety standards, and the differential impact of this technology across different social groups. Many of such questions are tied to the concepts that underlie them. This dissertation investigates how to navigate technology-induced conceptual disruption (i.e., the interruption in the functional adequacy of concepts) with conceptual engineering (i.e., the evaluation, design, and implementation of concepts). The dissertation is a sustained illustration of the claim that conceptual engineering and the philosophy of technology—two disciplines which have so far proceeded on largely parallel tracks despite engaging with related problems, operating on similarly conceived objects of inquiry, and sharing broadly comparable normative aims—are better positioned to address their respective research in dialogue rather than in isolation. This has led to contributions to both conceptual engineering—illustrating how insights and tools developed for the study of socio-technical artefacts can enrich the theoretical foundations and operationalisation of conceptual engineering—and the philosophy of technology—showing how the vocabulary of conceptual engineering can equip philosophers of technology with sharper tools for identifying, evaluating, and responding to conceptual disruptions.

items.title: The History of a Change of Mind: Why Thinking It Through Does Not Establish Authorship.
items.abstract: We ordinarily treat a change of mind we have thought through as ours — as something we did and can answer for. This paper argues that whether a revision is ours to answer for is settled not by how completely the operative framing is integrated into our present reasoning but by the authority-history of that framing: how the construal which fixed what counted as a reason came to hold its authority for the agent. A framing may be fully integrated — endorsed, reasons-responsive, reflectively stable, available for revision — and this whole present signature can be installed by manipulation that bypasses the agent, a case intrinsically identical to one in which she appropriated the frame herself. The two should differ in authorship because authorship, in the sense relevant to attributing a reconstruction as the agent’s own achievement, must preserve the distinction between actual appropriation and the installed signature of appropriation — a distinction present integration cannot represent, since the two agents are integration-duplicates. This is a functional claim, not a demonstration that the concept must be historical on pain of contradiction: a synchronic concept of authorship is coherent but inadequate to the work the concept is meant to do. For that purpose revisional authorship does not supervene on the agent’s intrinsic present psychological organisation; it tracks the history by which the framing became answerably hers. The paper takes the responsibility literature’s notion of answerability upstream — from judgments and attitudes to the authority of the framing under which they are formed — and sorts a framing’s standing history into appropriated, available but unappropriated, and foreclosed. A consequence it embraces is that much of what we reason under, seamlessly and rationally, was never appropriated, and so is genuinely ours to reason under without being ours to answer for: absence of a defeater does not by itself confer authorship. Its paradigmatic defeaters are motivated capture — recast as stake-driven impairment of a frame’s accessibility to assessment — and manipulative bypass. The account is substrate-neutral, and in closing it constrains the debate over ‘agentic AI’: neither fluency within a frame nor runtime self-revision establishes a system’s authorship of it. The history that matters is not the history of the change of mind but the history of the frame’s authority.

items.title: The Master's Apprentice: Guild Formation, Faculty Hiring Networks, and the Inheritance Function of the Consolidation Trap.
items.pub: In In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive
items.abstract: This volume extends the Consolidation Trap from single-transaction capture to intergenerational capture: does the evaluator pool itself reproduce across academic generations. The volume's central formal contribution is the Inheritance Function: a model in which the share of an evaluator pool drawn from a given intellectual lineage at academic generation g + 1 is an increasing function of that lineage's share at generation g, because evaluator selection is performed predominantly by the incumbent evaluator pool itself and because that pool systematically favors candidates whose training pedigree most closely resembles its own — producing the same preferential-attachment dynamic characterized in network science (Barabási & Albert 1999). The volume grounds this claim in two historically separated but structurally identical cases. The first is the medieval and early modern European craft guild, examined through Sheilagh Ogilvie's economic analysis (2019): guilds imposed lengthy apprenticeship requirements while admitting masters' sons at rates substantially exceeding demographic baselines, sold master status outright without examination in documented cases, and systematically excluded women, migrants, and religious minorities — evidence that guild quality-control rhetoric functioned as what this volume terms the Quality Alibi. The second case is the contemporary American professoriate. Clauset, Arbesman, and Larremore (2015), analyzing placement data for nearly 19,000 faculty across three disciplines, establish that only 25% of doctoral-granting institutions produce between 71% and 86% of all tenure-track faculty. Wapman, Zhang, Clauset, and Larremore (2022) confirm that 80% of faculty trained at just 20% of institutions, and — a critical complication rather than a confirmation of naive nepotism — that faculty hired by their own doctoral department exhibit substantially higher attrition, indicating that the Inheritance Function rewards prestige-lineage conformity specifically, not literal institutional loyalty. Morgan, LaBerge, Larremore, Galesic, Brand, and Clauset (2022) establish that US tenure-track faculty are up to twenty-five times more likely than the general population to have a parent holding a doctorate. The volume situates this formalization within the pre-existing cumulative-advantage tradition (Merton 1968; DiPrete & Eirich 2006), specifying precisely what a recursive, generation-indexed model adds to that older lineage rather than presenting …

items.title: The Language of the Victors: The 1919 Scientific Boycott, the Making of English as Science's Currency, and the Laundering of Linguistic Exclusion.
items.pub: In In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive
items.abstract: This volume extends the Consolidation Trap into linguistic gatekeeping by formalizing Exclusion Laundering: the process by which an explicit, statutory exclusion of a category of persons, once rendered normatively untenable, is succeeded not by neutral evaluation but by a facially neutral criterion correlated closely enough with the original excluded category that the outcome distribution remains statistically continuous, while the justification shifts to what this volume terms the Neutrality Alibi. The volume grounds this mechanism in the International Research Council, founded in 1919 by twelve Allied nations, whose founding statutes explicitly excluded scientists of the former Central Powers while prohibiting the German language at congresses; the exclusion extended to individuals uninvolved in the manifesto used to justify it, prompting principled refusals by Einstein and a Central Powers absence from major congresses persisting until 1926 and beyond. The historical record establishes a direct causal sequel: an active American language and publication policy explicitly pursued to secure English's post-boycott dominance. The second case is Amano and colleagues' (2023) survey of 908 environmental scientists: non-native English speakers require up to twice as much time to read, write, and present research in English, and their manuscripts are rejected roughly 2.5 times more often specifically on grounds of English writing quality, and subjected to requests for English-language revision roughly 12.5 times more often, than manuscripts from native speakers. The volume formalizes the Neutrality Alibi using proxy-discrimination theory (Barocas & Selbst, 2016), situates the specific credibility deficit non-native manuscripts suffer within the pre-existing ethical vocabulary of epistemic injustice (Fricker 2007), and closes by tracing how linguistic proxy compounds with the Inheritance Function and Uncertainty Discount already formalized in this program, and by locating its own authorship in English by a non-native speaker as data rather than disclaimer.

items.title: The Invisible Technician Returns: Boyle's Assistants, Parachute Science, and the Authority Gradient in Global Research.
items.pub: In In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive. Ho Chi Minh City: Zenodo.
items.venue: In the Name of Merit: Six Gatekeeping Mechanisms, from the Hundred Schools of Thought to the Algorithmic Archive
items.abstract: This volume extends the Consolidation Trap into a mechanism distinct in kind from the four preceding volumes: extraction rather than exclusion. The volume names this mechanism the Authority Gradient, the systematic divergence between a contributor's causal necessity to a research output and that contributor's conversion rate into first or corresponding authorship. The volume grounds this in two cases separated by roughly three hundred and sixty years. The first is Robert Boyle's air-pump laboratory, examined through Steven Shapin's 1989 analysis: Boyle's published accounts make only fleeting reference to the "lusty and dexterous fellows" who operated the apparatus, and no acknowledgment whatsoever of Robert Hooke's design and construction of the instrument itself, labor rendered invisible because the Royal Society's "modest witness" norm tied authority to certify a fact to gentlemanly social status rather than hands-on competence. The second case is the empirically extensive literature on parachute science. Stefanoudis and colleagues (2021) find 40% of coral reef papers reporting fieldwork in Indonesia and the Philippines listed no host-nation scientist as author.
