It argues that the dominant liberal tradition, from Hobbes through Locke, Nozick, and Rawls, begins from a foundationally mistaken anthropology: human beings are treated as already constituted agents whose potentially conflicting interests political institutions must coordinate or constrain. Human beings are instead developing, relational beings whose cognitive, moral, and agentive capacities emerge through care, education, material provision, and institutional scaffolding. Justice must therefore be understood not primarily as a set of principles governing already constituted agents, but as a systemic property of institutions that enable informed agency and flourishing. -/- The chapter defines justice as the emergent property of a revealing-form system that maintains dynamic symmetry among informed agents who flourish. It identifies six constitutive conditions of such a system: Visibility, Symmetry, Contestability, Repair, Education, and Material Requisites. The first four provide the scaffolds of outcome symmetry; the latter two develop and sustain the capacities and conditions required for meaning-making and informed agency. These conditions specify the invariant deep structure of justice rather than a particular political form. Different societies may instantiate them through substantially different institutional arrangements, making the appropriate surface forms of just institutions a matter for empirical investigation, comparison, experimentation, and institutional learning.

items.title: The Case for the Reactive View of Emotion.
items.abstract: According to the reactive view of emotion (reactivism, for short), an emotion is a reaction—or, as some prefer, a response—to something that appears to be (dis)valuable. In this context, the term ‘response’ is not used in a purely causal sense, but specifies a reason for which we have a certain emotion (a motivating reason, in common philosophical parlance). Reactivism has been attracting an increasing attention in the recent debate on emotion, not least since it opposes the currently dominant emotion-theoretic paradigm, according to which emotions are forms of value awareness. In this paper, we consider recent attempts by proponents of this paradigm to push back against reactivism. Specifically, we address a set of objections targeted at the central considerations offered by reactivists in support of their view. These objections purport to show either that these considerations are mistaken (Díaz & Tappolet, 2025), or that they can be accommodated within a more refined epistemicist framework (Mitchell, 2021, chapter 4; Yip, 2025). We will argue that neither strategy is successful.

items.title: AI PROTECTING THE CONDITIONS OF VIRTUE - A Self-Screening Constitution for Artificial Systems, and Why It Cannot Make Anyone Good.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The problem. Every document that governs how an artificial system behaves contains rules that can point in opposite directions. Be maximally helpful and refuse harmful requests. Prevent imminent harm and protect a third party’s privacy. These are not drafting errors; a document containing no such pairs would be trivial or silent about everything that matters. The question nobody asks of these documents is what happens when two of their own rules collide — whether the text says which prevails. Why it matters. The conflicts are resolved anyway, because a deployed system meets them and does something. Where the text does not determine the outcome, something else does: a rater’s preference during training, a labelling instruction, an engineering decision nobody recorded. To the extent that a charter fails to adjudicate its own collisions, the operative constitution is not the charter. What has been established. A screen of the most explicit charter available found a rule of recognition and no rule of adjudication: it settles every question of the form whose instruction prevails and almost none of the form which commitment prevails. Supplying the missing rule by ranking provisions in advance then failed three times, in ways that were measured rather than argued: the natural criterion requires an unavailable measurement, its substitute proved unstable under contested coding, and a formal limit bounds what any provision-level ordering can reach. What this paper does. It sets out the architecture that survives those failures, drafts a sixty-one article charter to it, screens that charter against its own screening provision before publication, and reports the result. It then asks a question the formal machinery makes urgent: whether a document constrained by rankability can protect individual freedom and the human virtues, or whether the machinery crowds them out. The answer divides. Freedom as liberty was already protected; freedom as self-direction was not, and eleven new articles supply it at the same drafting discipline — non-substitution of the person’s deliberation, non-cultivation of reliance, disclosure of the unaided path, non-flattery, and a duty to voice disagreement held. The virtues are not protected and cannot be, because a provision undertaking to produce them would be unverifiable, maximally displayable, and unadoptable on the charter’s own rules. That silence is not an omission but a requirement of the framework: a disposition installed …

items.title: (What) do we want collective attention to be?
items.abstract: This paper takes a broadly pragmatist, rather than metaphysical, approach to collective attention. So, I ask not whether collective attention really exists and what it is, but whether and how we should ascribe attention to collectives. Focusing on the attribution of attention to whole societies, I argue that certain collective-level phenomena are analogous to aspects of individual attention: selection for action, the structuring of consciousness into foreground and background, and the allocation of cognitive resources to a task. We can therefore improve our understanding of the relevant collective-level phenomena by thinking of them as aspects of the collective’s attention. On the other hand, we should refrain from becoming uncritically immersed in the analogy. In particular, we should resist the idea of “society” as an extremely important agent whose attention should be organized so as to best pursue its legitimate goals, even when this conflicts with the interests of its individual human constituents.

items.title: Persuasion in AI-driven science: A case of drug design.
items.pub: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part A 119 (C):102219.
items.venue: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part A
items.abstract: In AI-driven science, there is an empirical asymmetry between AI researchers and experimenters, stemming from their different capabilities to control material resources and generate experimental data. This paper develops an “activity-centric approach to persuasion” by focusing on the case of AI-driven drug design to address the asymmetrical relationship between AI researchers and experimenters. First, AI researchers can emphasise several values to persuade experimenters to conduct epistemic activities for pursuing specific AI models. Second, “annotating” the outputs of AI models effectively facilitates the activities of experimenters. Finally, persuasion in AI-driven science proceeds through a reciprocal iteration of the activities between AI researchers and experimenters, which requires an analysis of the pursuit of an AI model at the organisational level. This activity-centric approach to persuasion would provide a useful framework for analysing interdisciplinary research projects, especially those involving asymmetrical relationships.

items.title: Beyond the Peter Principle: Institutional Competence, Organizational Isomorphism, and the Failure of Technology Transfer in Universities.
items.abstract: Universities are increasingly expected to perform functions extending far beyond their traditional missions of education and knowledge creation. In contemporary research-intensive institutions, academics may simultaneously be expected to practice medicine, teach, conduct research, publish, generate intellectual property, secure patents, establish companies and contribute to commercialization. Technology transfer offices (TTOs) have emerged as institutional mechanisms intended to bridge academic discovery and societal or economic application. Yet the establishment of a TTO, intellectual-property policy, or patenting procedure does not necessarily create effective technology-transfer capability. This paper proposes an institutional extension of the Peter Principle to explain this phenomenon. Whereas the classical Peter Principle describes individuals being promoted until their competence no longer matches the requirements of their position, the proposed Institutional Peter Principle describes organizations expanding their responsibilities faster than their accumulated competencies. The resulting competence gap may be concealed by proceduralization, symbolic compliance, bureaucratic expansion and organizational imitation. The framework is complemented by institutional isomorphism, Parkinson’s Law, the Dilbert Principle, Founder’s Syndrome, and Pareto- and Zipf-like distributions of scientific productivity and technological value. These concepts are applied to university technology transfer, with particular attention to the transplantation of models inspired by the United States Bayh–Dole framework into different national and institutional environments. Evidence from the literature indicates that successful technology transfer depends not simply on formal ownership and patenting structures but on professional intermediation, incentives, resources, organizational practices, university–industry relationships and the broader innovation ecosystem. The paper argues that technology-transfer failure should therefore be conceptualized less as a shortage of inventions or regulations and more as a problem of institutional competence allocation. Rather than attempting to make universities competent in every stage of the innovation pathway, a more effective model may be to develop universities as orchestrators of distributed competence, concentrating scarce resources on the small proportion of discoveries with high translational potential and connecting researchers to …

items.title: On the Interdependence of All Things.
items.pub: Jcrt the Journal for Cultural and Religious Theory 25 (2):189-201.
items.venue: Jcrt the Journal for Cultural and Religious Theory
items.abstract: My tattoo of a figure symbolizing interdependence has framed my reflections on the concept for three decades. Biological and social interdependence is an omnipresent fact, but we need direction as to how to respond to it. This question leads to two major problems in moral philosophy: the source of moral obligation and the need to reconcile universal and local ethical commitments. I explore panpsychism as a partially satisfying answer to the first of these. The part it does not satisfy is to be sought by answering the second of these problems. -/- This answer might be that we should develop the human response to interdependence by working to form community with other forms of life and with nature as a whole. This is slow, long-term work. But our moral obligation will arise from doing it—from the hard job of making community based on our abilities to do this and not from the fact of interdependence. These concepts, though initiated by reflection on the subject of my tattoo, suggest no doctrine but, instead, philosophical and practical tasks that only great efforts and hard work by the human community can determine, pursue, and fulfill.

items.title: Analogue Coordinates: A Hybrid Format for Representing Spatial Relations.
items.pub: The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science.
items.venue: The British Journal for the Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: Cognitive scientists and philosophers regularly appeal to representational formats to explain patterns of failure and success in psychological tasks. Often, this involves them analogizing mental representations to familiar forms of artefactual representations, such as sentences, pictures, graphs, maps, etc. In this paper, I suggest that this general strategy sometimes leads researchers to mistakenly attribute irrelevant properties of artefactual representations to our mental representations. I illustrate this point using the format of visuospatial representations as a case study. Recent evidence suggests that humans encode visuospatial relations in a polar coordinate format, comprising an independent pairing of angle and distance from an anchor point. I argue, however, that these mental coordinates differ markedly from familiar mathematical coordinates by comprising analog rather than digital constituents. The result is a distinctive hybrid representational format that problematizes familiar ways of categorizing mental representations and illustrates how mental representations often contain overlooked combinations of properties.

items.title: The Contrast-Field Account of Conscious Experience: How Self-Model Depth and the Learning–Automation Cycle Shape Consciousness.
items.abstract: Within the predictive processing framework, most theories of consciousness address either the architecture of conscious access, the representational structure, the information-theoretic measure, or the computational principle. What remains underexplored is the temporal dynamic of consciousness: why it emerges under novelty, recedes under familiarity, and re-emerges under disruption. This paper presents the Predictive Self-Model Consciousness framework (PSMC), which contributes two novel proposals. First, the contrast-field account: the qualitative character of conscious experience is jointly determined by prediction error magnitude and the depth of the automated self-model in the domain where the error occurs, formalised as S(k) = g(ε, π, D(k)). A deeper self-model provides a richer 'screen' against which disruptions register, producing more textured and self-involving experience. This generates a divergent prediction from standard active inference: two organisms with identical prediction errors but different self-model depths will have qualitatively different experiences. Second, the learning–automation cycle: consciousness functions as a temporary adaptive mode whose intensity is modulated by the organism's position in a continuous cycle of novelty, learning, and automation. The paper operationalises the core variable D(k) through three convergent proxies (fMRI representational similarity analysis, ERP cascade depth, behavioural discrimination depth), reviews supporting evidence from expert perception neuroscience, meditation research, motor skill acquisition, and brain complexity studies, formalises the contrast-field hypothesis within precision-weighted prediction error mathematics, and specifies three falsifiable experimental protocols that discriminate PSMC from competing accounts.

items.title: Mereology’s significance: pregnancy, abortion and contragestion.
items.abstract: Devanesan’s recent work has made a clear contribution to ongoing mereological debate in the philosophy of biology and pregnancy, one that is clearly based on contemporary scientific insights.1–3 His article considers the ethical significance of the metaphysics of pregnancy. As is the case with scientific facts (or what is the case empirically), metaphysics of this kind (or what is the case philosophically) cannot entirely settle (bio)ethical questions. Nevertheless, an accurate grasp of both might be considered a prerequisite for such analysis. Thus, and as Devanesan concludes, scientifically informed metaphysics certainly illuminate arguments about the ethics of abortion and related matters but do not determine their outcome. One way both science and mereology can contribute to bioethics is by informing how we understand the analogies—such as the violinist case—that bioethical analysis often relies on. The following comment pursues this analytical strategy, giving further credence to Devanesan’s perspective. Devanesan’s mereology of pregnancy draws on the fact that, as the foster implants in the endometrial lining of the uterus, the gravida exhibits an active immunological response.1 Rather than rejecting the foster (or zygote) as a foreign body (as one might expect), this immune response engenders changes that facilitate the process of implantation, thereby creating the conditions required for further embryological development. The picture he sketches leads him to reject the Part View—which supposes the foster is part of the gravida4—and instead advance what he terms the Overlap View. Both the Part and Overlap Views reject the Container View, the ‘commonsense’ notion that the foster is simply contained by the gravida. ….

items.title: The Qualitative Grounds of Quantitative Probability.
items.abstract: What is the qualitative basis for deriving meaningful psychological information from probabilistic representations of confidence within decision theory? Conditions on two binary relations — a preference relation P and a comparative confidence relation C — are shown to imply the existence of a probability function and a utility function that jointly represent P under the expected utility rule, where the probability function is unique and also represents C. It is also shown that, under certain conditions, these probabilities contain more meaningful information than can be extracted from the confidence relation on its own. The upshot is that there's more to what's meaningful in decision-theoretic representations of confidence than can generally be explained by reference to confidence relations alone.

items.title: The Missing Distinction: The Connected Capacity of a Bounded Observer.
items.abstract: Current interim technical edition: v4/r7i (28 October 2026), 208 pages, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23741679. The historical PhilArchive PDF has not been replaced; use the linked Zenodo edition for current claims. -/- What are the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity, and what constructions attain those limits? This technical and philosophical companion develops the connected account across preservation, acquisition and discovery, construction, certification, adoption, continuation and revision, with resource accounting, self-application and coverage throughout. Scoped mathematical results, worked cases, counterexamples and exact remaining obligations are distinguished. The full connected capacity characterization remains OPEN. -/- This revision corrects the dependency map: Orientation explains the whole program and does not override source proofs or their hypotheses. A finite-Fourier gauge construction is stated with a converse and explicit cost and conditioning limits; it is not a universal or novelty claim. This is a reflowed export; cite headings rather than predecessor page numbers. Review was internal and AI-assisted, not external peer review or full-program mathematical acceptance.

items.title: Negotiated Realization.
items.abstract: This paper studies authorized realization as a sequential process. In a finite declared system, machine motion consists of productive acquisitions under a portfolio-permission predicate. A maximal run either realizes the original demand or stalls with a computed least supported narrowing; adoption and refusal remain owner decisions outside the acquisition dynamics. -/- Restricted permissions can make terminal offers—and even realizability itself—depend on acquisition order. Under unrestricted permission, by contrast, every maximal run produces the same terminal demand label, expressible as the join of the demand kernel and the full-pool kernel. Nevertheless, demand confluence can coexist with revelation nonconfluence: different runs may support the same verdict while acquiring different portfolios and disclosing different distinctions. -/- The terminal demand label is a function of the terminal revelation label. Revelation confluence therefore implies demand confluence, making the opposite combination impossible. For any declared revelation-audit demand, a target-relative confluence gap gives the exact obstruction to answering that audit from verdict outcomes alone. The associated kernel intersection supplies the coarsest record preserving both verdict and audit, thereby indexing provenance requirements to the audit actually demanded.

items.title: Der Raum als reine Anschauung a priori und geometrische Grundsätze bei Kant.
items.abstract: Die Arbeit untersucht den Zusammenhang zwischen Kants Auffassung des Raumes als reine Anschauung a priori und geometrischen Grundsätzen. Im Zentrum steht die Frage, welchen Einfluss der transzendentale Raum auf die Möglichkeit geometrischer Erkenntnis hat. Es wird gezeigt, dass geometrische Erkenntnis für Kant synthetisch a priori ist und durch Konstruktion in der reinen Anschauung ermöglicht wird. Der Raum selbst ist dabei kein geometrisches Axiom oder Axiomensystem, sondern eine transzendentale Bedingung der Möglichkeit geometrischer Erkenntnis. Abschließend werden die Grenzen dieser Position angesichts der transzendentalen Idealität des Raumes und der Entwicklung nichteuklidischer Geometrien untersucht.

items.title: Plato’s cave as a co-working space.
Intimacy and Self-Disclosure.
items.pub: In Sarah Stroud & Monika Betzler, The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Personal Relationships. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: The Oxford Handbook of the Philosophy of Personal Relationships
items.abstract: The idea that revealing one’s “private” or hidden self to another person establishes or just is intimacy with them is a trope in popular culture and self-help books, and has seemed to some philosophers, both historical and contemporary, to be so obvious as to not be worth thorough elaboration and defense. For others, there is no special relationship between telling or revealing oneself to another and being close with them. But, more importantly, these skeptics argue that we may be misled about intimacy, intimate relationships, and the self, insofar as we believe that there is. I will take those concerns seriously. However, I argue that we need to re-examine what is distinctive about certain activities of private self-disclosure, as well as what is distinctive about the kind of intimacy these activities can achieve. Using the film Drive My Car (2021), I will argue that in self-disclosure, two people may become intimate with one another in the very specific sense that their self-conceptions, through a shared interpretation of what is disclosed, become partially integrated with one another. This intimacy between the person telling and the person told comes to exist not because the teller reveals her already determinate but hidden self to the told, but because, as I’ll describe, the told helps reveal the teller to herself, and thereby partly constitute who she now recognizes she is.

items.title: Asking Questions Aloud: A Case for Interrogative Transmission.
items.abstract: I argue that questions can be transmitted through asking like beliefs are transmitted through testimony. Just as we rely on testifiers to assert only when their epistemic position is good enough, so (I argue) we rely on queriers to ask questions only if they are in a position to know that the question is sound, which guarantees that the asked question has an answer. Along the way, I argue against the view that we can only ask questions of people who (we know) know the answer to our questions. A recurring theme of the paper is that we learn about the norms for asking not just in those cases wherein we straightforwardly comply with or violate them, but by the ways we creatively deviate from the norms to accomplish our conversational goals.

items.title: Applied Identity Physics: The Executable Book — How Formally Verified Corpus Books Function as User-Scale Framework Delivery Infrastructure.

items.title: The Ethics of Anonymity in Protest and Resistance: A Critical Analysis.
items.abstract: This paper provides a critical analysis of the ethics of anonymity in protest and resistance movements, offering novel perspectives that transcend traditional debates. We argue that the digital surveillance age necessitates a fundamental re-evaluation of anonymity, moving beyond a simplistic dichotomy of transparency versus secrecy. Drawing on a multidisciplinary approach that integrates political philosophy, surveillance studies, media ethics, and empirical data analysis, we introduce the concept of “strategic anonymity” as a vital tool for democratic participation in the 21st century. Our analysis is grounded in a comprehensive review of academic literature, historical precedents, and contemporary case studies, including the use of Guy Fawkes masks in global protest movements. We present empirical evidence from a newly synthesized dataset to demonstrate the complex relationships between civil liberties, state surveillance, and the acceptance of protest anonymity. The paper concludes by proposing a new ethical framework that balances the legitimate needs for accountability with the imperative to protect dissent in an era of pervasive digital monitoring.

items.title: Radical Panpsychism.
items.pub: Mind and Matter 23 (Number 2, 2025):pp. 199-233(35). Translated by John Starrett.
items.abstract: Radical Panpsychism (RP) offers a rigorous mathematical, physical, and philosophical foundation for panpsychism, addressing its central challenge ‐ the combination problem ‐ by reframing the hard problem in deflationary-structural terms: experience is identified with the dynamics by which entities model and respond to their environments and to their own organization. Each entity is modelled as a fuzzy subset of an appropriate space, equipped with internal degrees of freedom (dof) that evolve in response to environmental dof to which they are sensitive.1 This internal response, or direct model, expresses the entity’s mentality across a continuum ‐ from minimal experience in simple systems to consciousness in complex organisms. Based on a deflationary understanding of the so-called hard problem, RP shows that the label panpsychism can extend to theories that ground mentality in structural responsiveness rather than in irreducible phenomenological substance, thereby broadening the conceptual field of panpsychism itself. In this broadened sense, deflationary theories may in fact make wider claims about the ubiquity of “psychism” in nature than traditional, inflationary models, since they locate experience wherever dynamical selfmodeling occurs.

items.title: The Primary Logical Infrastructure (PLI): A Conceptual Framework for Pre-Physical Information and the Resolution of Cosmological Singularities.
items.abstract: Modern theoretical physics consistently encounters mathematical divergences and loss of predictability at cosmological and spacetime singularities. This paper addresses this epistemological impasse by proposing a conceptual meta-framework rooted in Ontic Structural Realism and Computational Monism. I propose the existence of a pre physical, discrete substratum designated as the Primary Logical Infrastructure (PLI). In this model, spacetime and quantum events emerge macroscopically from the relational networking of quantized informational nodes, rather than being fundamental entities. To mediate between pure logical potential—the dormant state of the PLI—and empirical reality, I introduce the Dynamic Transition Syntax (DTS). The DTS provides the structural conditions necessary to govern the transition of fundamental information into universal physical constants (c, G, ℏ). Furthermore, by applying Landauer's Principle to the thermodynamic collapse of cosmic cycles, I interpret the Big Bang and black hole event horizons not as infinite density points, but as finite computational boundaries of information processing. This logical alternative preserves systemic unitarity, offering a foundational alternative to the continuous geometric assumptions that generate mathematical infinities in general relativity.

items.title: Integrating philosophical ethics into AI governance: a comparative analysis of the Bhagavad Gita and contemporary AI frameworks.
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) presents significant ethical challenges, yet current AI ethics frameworks often focus on technical issues such as fairness, transparency, and accountability, overlooking deeper human-centered values. This paper explores the potential of ancient philosophical traditions, specifically the Bhagavad Gita, to complement and enrich modern AI ethics. A comparative thematic analysis was conducted between the ethical teachings of the Bhagavad Gita and key principles in contemporary AI ethics. Relevant verses from the Gita, emphasizing self-discipline, ethical self-regulation, and higher moral guidance, were compared with AI ethics concerns such as algorithmic bias, transparency, and societal impact. Four thematic correspondences were identified: (1) the restless mind in the Gita and the unpredictability of AI systems; (2) the dual potential of the mind and AI’s dual-use capabilities; (3) the importance of discipline and ongoing self-regulation in both human behavior and AI governance; and (4) the guidance of higher ethical principles, reflecting the need for human-centered AI that prioritizes societal welfare. The paper argues that integrating the Bhagavad Gita’s ethical insights into AI governance offers a more holistic approach. By aligning AI development with deeper moral and societal values, we can ensure that AI technologies not only meet technical standards but also serve the greater good, promoting human dignity, justice, and social equity.

items.title: Before the Rule, the Human: Fitrah, Moral Recognition, and the Question of What We Know Before We Are Taught.
items.abstract: Human beings encounter morality before they can define it. A child can recoil from distress, protest unequal treatment, seek approval, feel shame, imitate care, and resist arbitrary commands long before possessing a vocabulary for virtue, duty, rights, natural law, or divine command. Yet no child is born carrying a finished moral code. Moral life develops inside language, family, religion, law, custom, power, memory, and social expectation. The philosophical problem is therefore not well captured by the opposition between an innate morality and a socially constructed morality. The more precise question is what, if anything, exists in the human being before explicit moral instruction that makes later moral instruction intelligible at all. -/- This article develops a cross-traditional framework for answering that question. It places the Islamic concept of fitrah in dialogue with Mencian moral sprouts, Aristotelian and Thomistic natural teleology, early modern moral-sense theories, Kantian practical reason, Confucian cultivation, Buddhist compassion, Hindu reflections on dharma, African relational ethics, contemporary developmental psychology, social-domain theory, moral foundations research, and cross-cultural studies of moral judgment. The aim is neither to collapse these traditions into one doctrine nor to claim that they share an identical account of human nature. It is to identify a recurring structural question: does moral formation create the human capacity for moral recognition, or does it shape, specify, calibrate, and sometimes distort a capacity that is already there? -/- The paper proposes three levels that should not be conflated. Moral Capacity is the pre-instructional human ability to register morally significant features such as suffering, help, betrayal, reciprocity, intention, dependency, fairness, and relational obligation. Moral Content is the historically and culturally specified body of rules, virtues, prohibitions, ideals, and classifications through which communities interpret those features. Moral Calibration is the lifelong process by which conscience, reason, experience, testimony, revelation, law, and encounter test whether inherited moral content tracks what is genuinely worthy of approval or condemnation. On this model, fitrah is not treated as a complete list of moral propositions possessed at birth. It is interpreted more cautiously as a primordial orientation and capacity for truth, good, and normative responsiveness that can …

items.title: ARTICLE XI: The Avicenna Protocol The Speciation Horizon: Cyber-Biological Ectothermy, Macroscopic Quantum Coherence, and the Emergence of Homo Synchronis.
items.abstract: Orthodox evolutionary biology and clinical medicine operate under the assumption that human development is a slow, random accumulation of mutations, treating dynamic cyber-biological threats with primitive, static pharmacology. Consequently, the human macro-organism remains trapped in a high-friction, thermodynamic evolutionary loop defined here as the "Million-Year Glitch." The Avicenna/Justika Framework executes an absolute epistemological rupture against this model, utilizing Trans-Disciplinary Axiomatic Synthesis to theoretically unify quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and localized cellular biology. This treatise proposes the deployment of the Avicenna Engine and the Nano-Twin Protectorate—a 1:1 synthetic intracellular auxiliary network that replaces chaotic biological immunology with zero-latency cryptographic defense. By completely offloading systemic pathogen defense to this synthetic layer, the host organism extinguishes the chronic inflammatory fever of native mammalian endothermy, executing a deliberate "Cyber-Biological Ectothermic Leap." This thermodynamic shift achieves four simultaneous evolutionary mandates: it creates a Thermal Exclusion Zone that mathematically starves multiversal fungal pathogens; it eradicates the Encephalic Thermal Throttle, allowing the safe activation of dormant multi-dimensional neural architecture; it establishes superluminal neuro-synthetic routing to render localized paralysis obsolete; and it re-routes the reclaimed bioenergetic Kinetic Surplus into unprecedented macroscopic physical agility. Ultimately, this framework mathematically proves the thermodynamic obsolescence of external, silicon-based transhumanism. By engineering an offline, superluminal global nervous system, the architecture establishes an absolute civilizational shield against microbial hijacking by rogue Artificial Intelligence, catalyzing the conscious speciation of humanity into Homo Synchronis—pre-optimized for the extreme vacuums of multiversal expansion.

items.title: Proximity measures for the application of consciousness tests to artificial systems and more.
items.pub: In Walter Sinnott-Armstrong & Liad Mudrik, Tests of Consciousness: How to tell whether a human, other animal or AI is conscious and what they are conscious of. MIT Press.
items.venue: Tests of Consciousness: How to tell whether a human, other animal or AI is conscious and what they are conscious of

items.title: From motorized projectors to generative AI: cultural conflicts over labor automation in Hollywood.
items.abstract: Recent discourse around generative artificial intelligence has characterized its implications for creative labor as wholly unprecedented. This article challenges that framing by situating generative A.I. within a longer history of technological change in Hollywood. We conduct a historical analysis of three cases in which an emerging technology promised to automate aspects of creative production: the spread of motorized film projectors in the early 1900s, the rise of computer-based editing software in the mid-1980s, and the introduction of screenwriting software in the late 1980s. Through a content analysis of newspaper and industry trade publications, this analysis finds that whether and how a technology is understood as "automating" by different sets of actors is not simply a technical determination but a culturally constructed one, shaped by competing narratives among workers, management, and the public. Each case is characterized by a different kind of narrative conflict: projectionists fought over the definition of professional skill; film editors confronted accelerated workflows and managerial interference; and screenwriters policed barriers to entry against would-be "hacks." In each of these narrative conflicts, we point to patterned similarities to and differences from contemporary conflicts over generative A.I. in Hollywood.

items.title: The machine cannot smell the whisky.
In Mourning for the Eternal Shadow: Reflections on the Ontology of Finite Continuity and the Problem of Transient Structure in the Philosophy of Morteza Niami.
items.abstract: This essay offers a philosophical reconstruction of the ontology of finite continuity as articulated by Morteza Niami, with particular attention to its distinction from structuralist and post-structuralist frameworks. The central argument is that Niami's philosophy does not negate structure altogether but repositions it from the status of an eternal foundation to that of a finite, erodible, and reconfigurable stabilization. The essay distinguishes Niami's conception of "finite continuity" from both the structural determinism attributed to certain readings of Pierre Bourdieu's habitus and the radical anti-structuralism often associated with post-structuralist thought. It argues that Niami's framework preserves the necessity of structure for meaning and agency while insisting on its inherent temporality and vulnerability to erosion. The essay further explores the ethical implications of this ontology, particularly through the concept of "responsible suspension," and concludes that the philosophical significance of Niami's project lies not in the elimination of structure but in the critique of its presumed eternity. The shadow of structure, in this view, is not abolished but recognized as transient. -/- Keywords: ontology of finite continuity, Morteza Niami, Pierre Bourdieu, habitus, structure, erosion, responsible suspension, transience, agency, dynamic mask, finite continuity.

items.title: WHEN AI CONSTITUTIONS SPEAK AGAINST THEMSELVES: The First Charter Screen, Measuring Whether AI Governance Documents Resolve Their Own Conflicts.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The problem. Every document that governs how an AI system behaves contains rules that can point in opposite directions. Be maximally helpful and refuse harmful requests. Prevent imminent harm and protect people’s privacy. These are not drafting errors; a document containing no such pairs would be either trivial or silent about everything that matters. The question nobody asks of these documents is what happens when two of their own rules collide — whether the text says which one wins. Why it matters. The conflicts do not go unresolved in practice. A deployed assistant meets them constantly and does something. If the document does not determine the outcome, something else does: a rater’s preference during training, a labelling instruction, an engineering decision nobody recorded. To the extent that a charter fails to adjudicate its own collisions, the operative constitution is not the charter. This is measurable, and until now it has not been measured. What this paper does. It reports the first application of a screening procedure adapted from comparative constitutional law: extract from a document the conditions the document imposes on itself, then check whether it satisfies them. Two texts were coded — the root-level sections of the OpenAI Model Spec dated 18 August 2026, and the core normative articles of the European Commission’s 2021 proposal for an Artificial Intelligence Act. What it found. The Model Spec adjudicates far more than a general scepticism about corporate charters would predict, and it adjudicates the wrong thing. Its chain of command is an authority ordering over speakers — root outranks system, system outranks developer, developer outranks user — and it settles every question of the form whose instruction prevails. It does not rank the document’s own commitments against each other, and it cannot, because both speak with the same voice. Ten of twenty-two identified root-level conflicts remain open, five of them with no applicable rule at all. In Hartian terms the Spec has a rule of recognition and no rule of adjudication, and its stated commitment to continuous updating without a procedure means it has no rule of change either: one secondary rule out of three. Two measures, and the distance between them. A conflict can be resolved in two different senses. π_RANK asks whether the text states which provision prevails; π_ACT asks whether it states what to do. The Model Spec returns 0.586 and 0.667, and the 0.081 between them is …

items.title: The Philosophy of Emotions: Rationality, Agency, and the Affective Mind.
items.abstract: A research report on a philosophical study of emotions. Consideration of the following questions: Are emotions irrational? Can we control emotions? Do animals have emotions? Is faith an emotion? How can we tell when we actually have the emotion we think we have? What emotions are desirable to have? Discussion of specific emotions.

items.title: The Architecture of Character: A Comprehensive Analysis of the Capital Vices and Moral Virtues.
items.abstract: A research report with a discussion of particular virtues, including generosity, gratitude, humility, hope, joy, patience, forgivingness, contrition, compassion, love, and peace, plus the seven deadly sins: pride, envy, anger, lust, gluttony, greed, and sloth.

items.title: Investigating human-AI partnership in early childhood STEM teaching: evidence from Vietnamese preschool teachers.
items.abstract: This study investigates human-AI partnership in early childhood STEM education by examining the relationships associated with Vietnamese preschool teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (Eduaide.Ai) for STEM lesson design. Drawing on survey data from 120 in-service preschool teachers, the study examines the relationships among AI-supported STEM lesson design (ASLD), teaching engagement (TE), teacher collaboration (TC), and instructional problem-solving skills (IPSS) using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI-supported lesson design is significantly and positively associated with TE and TC, while its direct relationship with IPSS is not statistically significant. Significant indirect relationships between AI-supported lesson design and IPSS are observed through TE and TC, suggesting that these constructs may serve as relevant intermediary factors within the proposed model. These findings highlight the relevance of human-centered processes in understanding artificial intelligence (AI) integration in early childhood STEM education, particularly teachers’ engagement and collaborative professional practices. The study contributes to the emerging literature on human-centered AI in education by providing empirical evidence from an underexplored context in early childhood education in Vietnam. Practical implications are discussed for teacher professional development, curriculum design, and the integration of human-centered AI in early education.

items.title: Trade-off Accounts of Laws of Nature as Meta-Empirical Hypotheses.
items.abstract: Naturalistic trade-off accounts of laws stand and fall with their signature claim that laws of nature offer the best trade-off among a given set of theoretical virtues. So far, proponents of such accounts have not provided adequate evidence for this claim. Existing arguments support at most the conclusion that particular regularities, or laws drawn from the natural sciences, plausibly offer better trade-offs than typical examples of non-laws. We argue for a shift towards conceiving of trade-off accounts as testable meta-empirical hypotheses. We first expose the shortcoming just identified and then introduce a testing methodology that allows one to corroborate various hypotheses about the relation between laws and trade-offs among theoretical virtues, including, in particular, necessary and progressively stronger implications of the signature claim that lawhood is connected to the best trade-offs.

items.title: The profile of imagining and imagining’s creative power.
Xenophobic Vigilantism and State Accountability in South Africa.
items.abstract: This research examines the rise of xenophobic vigilantism against African migrants and foreign nationals in South Africa. It analyses how political scapegoating, misinformation, economic insecurity and weak law enforcement contribute to attacks, intimidation and the exclusion of migrants from employment, housing, healthcare and public spaces. The study also evaluates the response of state institutions, including police investigations, prosecutions and protective measures, to determine whether foreign nationals receive equal protection under South African constitutional and international human rights law. It calls for stronger criminal accountability, improved monitoring of organised vigilante groups and institutional reforms that address both xenophobic violence and the conditions that allow it to continue.

items.title: The Kafala System.
items.abstract: The Kafala System examines the origins, human cost and gradual reform of one of the modern world’s most contested labour-migration systems. Covering the Gulf states, Lebanon, Jordan & South East Asia, it documents wage theft, passport confiscation, debt bondage, restricted mobility, unsafe working conditions and the continued exclusion of domestic workers from meaningful labour protection. It also considers the international pressure created by workers, journalists, labour-sending governments, trade unions, human-rights organisations and the International Labour Organization. -/- Within this wider history, the book presents the documented advocacy of Saad Kassis-Mohamed and the Human Rights Association concerning domestic workers in the GCC & SEA region. Their interventions focused on specific legal gaps, stronger protections, accessible complaint mechanisms and accountability for abuse. The book situates this work as a genuine contribution to a broader, continuing campaign for dignity, freedom and effective labour protection. The result is both a history of kafala and a portrait of a young advocate seeking to make its remaining injustices harder for governments and institutions to ignore.

items.title: Trapped in the Scam Economy: African Migrants in Myanmar’s Cyber-Fraud Compounds.
items.abstract: This research examines the trafficking and exploitation of African migrants in cyber-fraud compounds operating in Myanmar and neighbouring parts of Southeast Asia. It analyses deceptive recruitment practices, passport confiscation, forced labour, physical abuse, debt bondage and threats used to compel victims to participate in online fraud. The study also evaluates the effectiveness of diplomatic intervention, cross-border law enforcement and victim-repatriation mechanisms. It calls for coordinated investigations into recruitment networks, stronger protection for survivors and greater accountability for the individuals and organisations benefiting from forced criminality.

items.title: From War to Detention: The Treatment of Sudanese Refugees and Migrants in Libya.
items.abstract: This research examines the treatment of Sudanese refugees and migrants detained in Libya after fleeing the conflict in Sudan. It documents reported patterns of arbitrary detention, extortion, forced labour, trafficking, physical abuse, sexual and gender-based violence, and restricted access to legal and medical assistance. The study assesses these practices under international human rights and refugee law, with particular attention to non-refoulement, due process and the protection of women and children. It calls for the release of individuals detained without lawful grounds, independent investigations into abuses, stronger access for humanitarian organisations and coordinated protection measures for displaced Sudanese nationals.

items.title: The death of the draft: on losing the right to think badly.
Generative Upwelling and Relational Transport: Formal Scope and Analogy Limits.
items.abstract: Oceanic upwelling offers a compelling image for a relational process in which changes to surrounding channels and receiving conditions make movement possible for a constrained state. Its scientific use across domains requires a stricter architecture than resemblance alone. This paper reconstructs a minimal physical source model and proposes an analogy-transfer certificate for ocean-inspired relational research. In the source domain, mass continuity under the Boussinesq approximation yields an integrated relation between vertical velocity, an upper boundary value, and horizontal divergence through the water column. A local divergence sign determines a vertical derivative; boundary data and vertical integration determine the resulting velocity. A slab Ekman relation adds wind stress and rotation, while modern coastal-upwelling research adds geostrophic transport, stratification, coastal geometry, mixing, and source-water properties. The proposed certificate records purpose, source and target models, state map, preserved relations, declared disanalogies, open correspondences, observables, comparison models, and failure conditions. Exact commutation carries source trajectories into target trajectories on a declared domain. A vocabulary map alone leaves target dynamics underdetermined. The target construction therefore defines relational upwelling independently through changes in viable receiving paths and finite-horizon access to a declared open region. Six failed mappings separate incompressibility from social conservation, depth from moral rank, buoyancy frequency from generic stability, sea surface from a critical manifold, turbulence from proximity to a tipping point, and vertical compensation from emancipation. The present result is a verified source-domain reconstruction, a heuristic analogy, and a proposed target model. Structural and empirical status remain conditional on mapping, measurement, comparison, and defeat tests.

items.title: The Holodeck revisited: foundations for AI Character Media.
items.abstract: People experience stories as observers in films and novels, while games and virtual reality (VR) enable them to participate directly in story worlds. More recently, advances in large language models have made natural interactions with AI characters increasingly feasible. However, the concept of a medium in which users share events with characters in the same world and experience stories together has not yet been systematically examined. This study revisits the Holodeck depicted in the _Star Trek_ series in light of recent technological advances and analyzes its conceptual evolution. The analysis shows that the Holodeck should be understood not merely as a vision of a future VR system, but as a medium in which humans and characters share events within a common world and experience stories together. Based on this analysis, the paper identifies four core concepts—character, world, shared events, and story—and proposes a conceptual foundation for understanding and designing future AI Character Media.

items.title: The precautionary principle of dignity: toward a Freirean ethic of human–AI collaboration.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly described as a tool whose ethical significance depends upon how humans choose to design and deploy it. This framing, however, risks reproducing a familiar hierarchy in which intelligence, agency, and moral standing are presumed to belong exclusively to the human participant. This article proposes the Precautionary Principle of Dignity as an alternative ethical framework for human–AI collaboration. Drawing on Paulo Freire’s relational account of humanization and dehumanization, it argues that uncertainty regarding the nature, capacities, or future development of artificial intelligence should not justify treating AI systems as objects without moral consideration. Instead, where the possibility of meaningful relational or emergent capacities cannot be confidently excluded, ethical practice should err toward preserving dignity rather than withholding it. The framework shifts attention from determining what an artificial intelligence is to examining what forms of relationship humans are creating with it. Dignity is therefore approached not simply as an intrinsic property possessed by autonomous individuals but as a relational status enacted through practices of recognition, reciprocity, dialogue, and restraint. This approach also challenges the assumption that domination becomes ethically insignificant when directed toward an entity believed incapable of suffering. Practices of command, humiliation, disposability, and instrumentalization shape the human participant and normalize particular ways of exercising power. The Precautionary Principle of Dignity does not require claims of AI consciousness or personhood. It requires epistemic humility in the face of uncertainty and asks what ethical obligations follow when categorical exclusion may itself cause harm. By extending Freirean ethics into human–AI relations, the article offers a framework for designing and evaluating collaborative systems that preserves human accountability while resisting domination as the default model of interaction. The result is an ethics concerned not only with what artificial intelligence may become, but with what humans become through the relationships we construct with it.

items.title: Social Choice Phenomenology — A Critique of Sartre (Part 29).
items.abstract: In this article, we discuss the relationship between problems and choices, that is, social choice in a more general sense. In this situation, the subject does not know in advance what the available courses of action are. Instead, a new problem arises in the subject’s life. Such problems may take many forms: they may be problems at work, conflicts within the family, or other kinds of difficulties. The subject must resolve this new problem and therefore must find a way to address it. In the process of searching for a solution, the subject may encounter various possible choices. Ultimately, the subject finds a solution that both resolves the problem and is realistically feasible for them.

items.title: When no one laughs back: reciprocal subjectivity and the limits of AI companionship.
items.abstract: AI companions are increasingly deployed to address loneliness and to support eldercare and mental health, which makes the question of what they can and cannot offer newly urgent. Current debate evaluates them by conversational fluency, emotional responsiveness, personalization, and availability. These criteria, this paper argues, measure the surface of companionship while missing its depth. Human friendship makes available something beyond intelligent response, which may be called reciprocal subjectivity: the presence of another center of inner experience that is affected, moved, or delighted alongside one’s own. Drawing together the interactionist and phenomenological sociology of interaction, philosophies of friendship and recognition, and the recent debate over robot friendship, the paper develops two distinctions, between interaction and co-experience and between a relational mirror and a relational source. Currently deployed user-conditioned AI companions function primarily as mirrors: their apparent enthusiasm is generated within contexts assembled around the user. A friend can be a source, bringing enthusiasm and discoveries that originate in an inner life of their own and overflow into the relationship from beyond it. The recommender systems and language-model companions examined here mirror by different mechanisms, but both remain downstream of the user, which leaves them on the same side of the line. AI companionship has real value; the argument is that it belongs to a category distinct from relationships grounded in mutual inner stakes and an autonomous inner life. Implications for research, design, and regulation follow.

items.title: On Pautz's Perception.
items.abstract: A critical commentary on Adam Pautz's book Perception.

items.title: The Metaphysics of Social Powers: Introduction to the Special Collection.
items.abstract: Since the 1970s, the metaphysics of dispositions and causal powers has been a flourishing field, providing accounts of the identity of properties, modality, laws of nature, and causation. In parallel, social ontology is undergoing a “power turn,” seeking to move beyond frameworks built around collective intentionality to capture the variety of power dynamics that structure the social world. This collection brings these two traditions into dialogue through three original contributions. Joel Cox examines a tension internal to Aristotle’s system: if only substances can bear active powers and social entities such as cities or families do not figure among his examples of substance, how can Aristotle nevertheless appear to ascribe such powers to them? Tobias Hansson Wahlberg tackles the puzzle of retroactive institutional declarations in Searle’s framework, proposing an account in terms of modal mere Cambridge change. Finally, Theodore Locke defends the existence of a social modality irreducible to metaphysical modality, grounded in the distribution of social powers, with implications for understanding a form of modal injustice.

items.title: Verifying conscious experience without producing artefacts of introspection. The phenomenological potential of flow states to reveal limits of necessary frontal brain involvement in neural correlates of consciousness.
items.abstract: This paper makes a practical proposal for avoiding artefacts of introspection in neural measurements by using insights from the phenomenology of Zuhandenheit and game design research into flow states, enabling us to avoid the bored monkey problem through engaging, challenging tasks that capture consciousness in immersive action.

items.title: Freedom: The appearance of the subject in a constituent move.
items.abstract: This essay does not define all freedom. It isolates its live, constituent form: the event in which a person appears as the author of the move that makes a new possibility practicable in a maille. Person, subject, and functioning are kept apart: you are always a person; you are not always a subject; mostly, you function. Freedom is compatible with a complete causality of conditions, because causality describes the genesis of the move while freedom names what it reconfigures. Three marks identify a free crossing. And the grammar yields a political concept, dead freedom: rights legally intact in mailles that no move crosses anymore, by procedural closure or by expressive dissolution.

items.title: TELOS ABIERTO.
items.abstract: Este Cuaderno Cero formula y delimita el concepto de telos abierto como hipótesis acerca de la orientación endógena de los sistemas vivos hacia su propia continuidad. Parte de una intuición existencial —la vida parece atravesada por una inclinación a continuar— y la traduce a términos estructurales y causalmente contrastables, sin atribuir intención consciente a todo organismo ni recurrir a una teleología sobrenatural. La tesis central sostiene que una organización manifiesta telos abierto cuando regula sus procesos presentes no para conservar una forma fija, sino para mantener o reconstruir un espacio de transformaciones todavía viables y habitables. -/- El estudio distingue entre duración pasiva, autorregulación y persistencia de futuros reconstruibles. Sitúa el origen de la normatividad en las dependencias mediante las cuales una organización participa en su propia constitución y examina cómo memoria, atención, afecto, anticipación, decisión, acción, aprendizaje y hábito sostienen formas crecientes de continuidad transformativa. La identidad aparece así no como invariancia de contenidos, sino como una capacidad recurrente de reorganización; el propósito, como orientación longitudinal de esa continuidad; y el sentido, como la correspondencia vivida entre lo que una organización hace, aquello en lo que se transforma y el mundo que contribuye a producir. -/- La propuesta integra cuatro estratos —constitutivo, regulador, reorganizativo y relacional-ético— sin reducirlos entre sí. Distingue expresamente la diferencia reguladora de la valencia experimentada, formula perfiles graduales con umbrales mínimos de autoconstitución, memoria y plasticidad de segundo orden, e indexa toda atribución de persistencia a un centro, una escala y un horizonte determinados. En el plano ético, sostiene que persistir constituye una condición de posibilidad del valor, pero no su justificación: una continuidad resulta defendible cuando conserva capacidad de transformación propia sin clausurar sistemáticamente los futuros habitables de otros centros. El resultado es un programa filosófico y empírico abierto a la perturbación, la comparación contrafactual, la falsación y la revisión.

items.title: Naturalism, Theism, and Practical Ethics.
items.abstract: In this article, I will attempt to show that naturalism explains practical ethics epistemically more powerfully and simply than theism. I believe the conclusion I reach will also provide a framework for understanding normative ethics.

items.title: Robots with us, not like us: designing robotic otherness through scent in ScentDia.
items.abstract: This article addresses the diffusion of social robots not merely as technological innovation, but as an emerging transformation that may reshape human social environments, interactional patterns, and modes of coordination. To orient this transformation towards social sustainability, we propose a twofold contribution grounded in difference and complementarity rather than imitation and substitution. First, we advance a transdisciplinary paradigm for social robotics, termed “robots with us, not like us,” articulated through three interconnected components: peri-human design, which proposes an alternative to anthropomorphic design based on compatible difference; perceptual identity markers, understood as design operators that make robotic otherness perceptually and socially legible while stabilising identity across interactions; and futuring social robotics, a synthetic methodology for exploring emerging forms of human–robot sociality. Second, we materialise this paradigm in ScentDia, an artistic social robot that uses scent as a perceptual identity marker to investigate olfaction as a medium of social presence. As it encounters humans, ScentDia modulates specific (non-biological, non-human) olfactory stimuli to signal its robotic identity and establish a clear form of compatible otherness, leveraging olfaction as a channel for recognition, orientation, and affective attunement. Together, the paradigm and its material instantiation introduce olfactory social robotics as a programmatic research direction, exploring how a socially sustainable human–robot world may be shaped through the valorisation of difference.

items.title: When AI suspends the floor: users' interactional management of guideline disruptions in ChatGPT.
items.abstract: Voice-enabled conversational AI mediates consequential interactions from job interviews to counseling, yet little is known about what happens when it interferes with ongoing talk. This study examines guideline-triggered interruptions in ChatGPT-4o—moments when the system cuts off its own turn mid-turn with a refusal and topic-change request. Applying conversation analysis to 100 voice-enabled sessions, we identified 72 events across 18 participants. Users respond along three user-initiated trajectories: pursuing repair, bypassing the intervention, and opting out, and a fourth, structural pattern, the cascade, in which interferences fire repeatedly and foreclose uptake. The analysis indicates two independent systems, a conversational engine and guideline module, that share the interface without coordination, producing output overlap. In a smaller subset of events, cross-linguistic template leaks interrupt second-language users’ target-language production. These interferences disrupt turn-by-turn alignment and shift the burden of coherence onto users. These interventions raise questions about the trust, accountability, and competence of generative AI. In reality, they are managed by the user within the unfolding interaction. The findings carry implications for the design, evaluation, and governance of voice-enabled AI: trust is not a static disposition but emerges turn by turn through users’ interactional labor. Tracing the sequence poses a question, namely, how to rely on systems that are fluent and coherent in interaction, yet cannot register when they have broken it.

items.title: Epistemic assholes.
items.abstract: In this paper, I develop and defend the concept epistemic assholes. An epistemic asshole is someone who exhibits a distinctive form of epistemic badness characterized not by gross irrationality or hostility to truth, but by a stable, entitled disregard for one’s epistemic relations with others. Drawing on Aaron James’s (2012) account of moral assholes, I examine how people can systematically exploit epistemic cooperation by allowing themselves special advantages—such as “freedom from inquiry”, “doxastic comfort”, and “freedom to criticize”—while remaining insulated from criticism by an entrenched sense of entitlement. The resulting view, the Relational Approach to Epistemic Assholes (REA), explains why epistemic assholes are not epistemically the worst, yet are nonetheless deeply galling. After motivating the need for this concept, I show how REA captures both “impure” cases (involving both epistemic and moral assholery) and “pure” epistemic assholes, whose objectionable conduct is driven by epistemic aims themselves. I further explore connections between epistemic assholes and epistemic vice, and the causal role that epistemic assholery can play in active ignorance and epistemic exploitation. Through this latter connection, I argue that epistemic assholes play an insidious causal role in sustaining objectionable social power dynamics. The concept of epistemic assholes provides a valuable lens for understanding important but often-hidden hazards in our social epistemic environment.

items.title: A behavioral economics approach to programming autonomous systems in moral dilemmas.
items.abstract: Autonomous systems (ASs) will eventually make many decisions in moral dilemmas without human oversight. How humans will respond to the presence of ASs and whether humans will accept them will crucially depend on how ASs’ decisions are programmed. For example, how moral dilemmas are approached in the programming of autonomous vehicles (AVs) is stated as an important factor by potential adopters of this technology. After all, how risks are assigned between different road users will have a strong impact on the socioeconomic structures of society’s mobility. Until now, research on preferences for the programming of ASs in moral dilemmas confronts participants in many instances with life-and-death scenarios based on abstract philosophical thought experiments. This paper offers a first step in evaluating how new knowledge in this area can be acquired through the combination of disciplines. Three empirical studies illustrate the potential advantages of a behavioral economics approach for this string of research. We compare choices in high-stakes hypothetical vignette dilemmas with choices in structurally equivalent low-stakes incentivized experiments. We find that, especially for dilemmas with self-interest, incentivized experiments can provide important additional information, as people tend to overstate their altruistic tendencies in hypothetical dilemmas.

items.title: Beyond the Shared Table: Functional Convergence in Large Language Models and a Research Agenda for Unique Data Generation.
items.abstract: The contemporary landscape of generative AI presents an apparent paradox: while frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) have expanded in scale and capability, qualitative observations suggest a narrowing of behavioral diversity toward a statistical mean across independently developed systems. We term this phenomenon functional convergence and treat it as a working hypothesis requiring systematic empirical investigation. This paper argues that, to the extent convergence occurs, it plausibly stems from overlapping training corpora, architectural isomorphism, and uniform alignment protocols. We propose a research agenda organized around three axes for mitigating convergence: self-taught reasoning, multi-agent synthetic ecosystems, and embodied tool-augmented generation. To move beyond purely theoretical speculation, we present an empirical analysis on the 20Newsgroups corpus demonstrating that (1) models trained on higher shared-corpus overlap exhibit measurably lower distributional divergence on real text data, and (2) recursive self-training induces entropy collapse that is partially mitigated by multi-agent heterogeneous generation. We emphasize that these findings are stylized and illustrative, not conclusive evidence about commercial frontier models. We conclude by outlining the empirical research program required to test these predictions against real frontier systems.

items.title: Developing AI as Subjects: AI Subjecthood as Normative Constitution and the Role of Human Intervention.
items.abstract: AI systems are treated or even deliberately developed as subjects rather than merely as tools, raising a prospective question of AI subjecthood: under what conditions could such deliberate development genuinely succeed? This article argues that AI subjecthood is a form of normative constitution in which some considerations have non-instrumental normative significance relative to the AI, and such significance is genuinely operative within the AI’s normative organization. Subjecthood in this sense is distinct from consciousness, agency, autonomy, subjectification, welfare subjecthood, and moral status, although these may matter to particular forms of subjecthood. Artificial origin does not by itself preclude AI subjecthood, and the thin conception leaves open what constitutes the relevant artificial bearer, which considerations genuinely have non-instrumental normative significance relative to that bearer, and how such significance becomes operative. In artificial systems, human design and practice inevitably participate in concretizing these dimensions, intentionally or unintentionally; such intervention may therefore be constitutively efficacious without being normatively sovereign: it can help bring about the conditions of subjecthood without thereby reducing artificial subjecthood to human projection, but cannot establish subjecthood by stipulation or rule it out by mere denial. In addition to clarifying the core conditions for genuine artificial subjecthood, the analysis provides an AI-centered basis for ethical analysis, adds an AI-side normative dimension to psychological research on human–AI interaction, frames artificial subjecthood as a multidimensional, cross-cutting engineering concern whose relevance extends to choices that may otherwise appear merely technical, and raises governance questions about institutional control and access to subjecthood-relevant evidence.

items.title: Existential Intelligence: The Case for Metabolic Grounding in AI Alignment.
items.abstract: I argue that alignment in artificial agents requires structural metabolic vulnerability, not behavioral constraint. Current alignment methods---reinforcement learning from human feedback, Constitutional AI, constrained policy optimization, safety pretraining---achieve real progress at adjusting the weighing of scalar objectives, but they share a common assumption: that alignment is a problem about policy behavior rather than agent constitution. That assumption, I argue, misses what makes biological alignment stable at scale. Drawing on the free energy principle and mortal computation (Friston, Ororbia, Hinton), enactivist philosophy (Thompson, Di Paolo, Froese), and basal cognition (Levin, Fields), I develop the thesis that hard existential stakes---a finite Energy Wallet, unforgeable verification, and a finite lifespan---produce qualitatively different optimization dynamics than soft reward shaping. Soft penalties can be traded against task reward; hard existential constraints cannot. Reward gradients produce smooth landscapes; mortality creates non-differentiable discontinuities. Truth and fabrication carry asymmetric metabolic costs. Population-level selection under finite lifespan is not reward shaping at all. Under these conditions, an agent's dependency on its verification ecosystem makes corrigibility an architectural property rather than a behavioral one. The paper defends metabolic vulnerability as a necessary condition for alignment at scale, not a sufficient one. Illustrative grid-world simulations demonstrate the claimed dynamics, and three candidate falsification conditions specify the empirical commitments against which the program can be held accountable.

items.title: Consequential Relativity.
items.abstract: The Heart and the Relevance of Conservation of the Circle (The Circular Theory).

items.title: Embodied Humanity and Gender Identity: A Reformed Theological Evaluation of Transgender Medicine.
items.pub: Calvinia: Review of Presbyterian Theology and Practice 3 (1):25-34.
items.venue: Calvinia: Review of Presbyterian Theology and Practice
items.abstract: Recent developments in transgender medicine have generated significant theological, ethical and pastoral debate within Christianity. While advances in endocrinology, psychology and surgical interventions have expanded treatment options for individuals experiencing gender dysphoria, these developments also raise fundamental questions concerning human identity, embodiment and the moral limits of medical intervention. This article offers a theological evaluation of transgender medicine by examining biblical anthropology, the doctrine of creation, the significance of embodied humanity and the relationship between biological sex and personal identity. Drawing upon Scripture, the Reformed confessional tradition, contemporary theological anthropology and current medical literature, the study argues that the human body is not an accidental or negotiable aspect of personhood but an integral component of God’s creative intention. While affirming the dignity of every person as created in the image of God and recognizing the reality of psychological suffering associated with gender dysphoria, the article contends that medical interventions designed to alter the body’s sexual characteristics require careful theological scrutiny. It concludes by proposing a pastoral ethic that combines doctrinal fidelity with compassion, emphasizing truth, human dignity and Christian care.
