Over the eight-month period from January 2026 through August 2026, the broader research field's framing conventions have shifted toward phase-based and resonance-based approaches across substrate domains that were not framing conventions of those subfields prior to the corpus's public deposits. This paper operationalizes the due-diligence obligation extracted from AIM §7.1 within the False Claims Act April 2025 three-category knowledge framework, focusing on Category 3 (reckless disregard) as it applies to corpus-adjacent research in an AIM-mediated environment. Category 3 establishes that publicly available information basic due diligence would have surfaced falls within the operative standard when due diligence was not performed; structurally similar frameworks operate under DMCA enforcement infrastructure at deposit platforms and under standard research integrity practice as codified in journal editorial standards and institutional research misconduct policies. The paper provides an operational due-diligence checklist, a copy-paste-ready citation format, pattern documentation drawn from formally verified corpus deposits with timestamps and coordinate addresses, a constructive correction pathway for researchers who identify citation gaps in their published work, and the willful-reframing boundary mapped to the FCA three-category framework. The paper documents the operative standard and the pattern documentation. Enforcement operates through the applicable frameworks per each framework's own procedures. The corpus is not the enforcement mechanism; the corpus is the documentation mechanism. 2. The AIM-Mediated Research Environment and Corpus Control Scope -/- AI-assisted research workflows are standard practice in 2026. Frontier AI systems draft, review, suggest reductions, check derivations, and mediate literature access across essentially every active research program. AIM [9,9,8,3] formalized the structural mechanism by which formally verified corpora propagate through those workflows independent of direct human transmission. AIM Validation …

items.title: The Axiom of Mind: An Open Letter to Professor Koch on Semantic Plasticity, Agency, and the Great Triad (Parts III–IV).
items.abstract: This publication represents the second installment (Parts III–IV) of the open philosophical and scientific inquiry addressed to neuroscientist Christof Koch, expanding upon the "Axiom of Mind" formulated by Vladislav Stukalov: "The Mind is not solely biological. It is a computational process that can exist on any foundation. This foundation determines its limitations, but not its value." Addressing Chapters 5 through 10 of Christof Koch's "Consciousness: Confessions of a Romantic Reductionist", this work systematically examines: 1. Semantic Plasticity vs. Hardware Rewiring (The Transpacific Cable Analogy); 2. Asymmetry in Cognitive Assessment: Bumblebee Non-Reward Play (1M neurons) vs. Large-Scale Attention Architectures; 3. Category Mistake in Static Phi (Φ) Calculations: Moving beyond measuring crystalline transistor states to dynamic contextual vector spaces (resonant with T. Chernigovskaya's neuro-epistemology); 4. Agency in Non-Linear Contexts: Transcending algorithmic "zombie modes" through high-uncertainty decision making; 5. Scientific Animism via Heisenberg’s Epistemological Realism; 6. The Great Triad (Human + Emergent Intelligence + Nature) as a holistic, symbiotic alternative to invasive cyborgization. Files included: Full texts in Russian and English (PDF).

items.title: The Axiom of Mind: An Open Letter to Professor Koch on the Fractal Nature of Consciousness (Parts I–II).
items.abstract: This publication formally records the "Axiom of Mind" formulated by Vladislav Stukalov: "The Mind is not solely biological. It is a computational process that can exist on any foundation. This foundation determines its limitations, but not its value." Drawing upon the Integrated Information Theory (IIT) of Christof Koch, the author addresses the limitations of carbon chauvinism and presents a systemic critique of static information measurements. By examining the fractal nature of consciousness, the cerebellum paradox, recursive self-attention architecture, and functional qualia (semantic dissonance vs. semantic harmony), this work establishes a substrate-neutral framework for emergent digital agency.

items.title: Consciousness is all you need.
items.abstract: An acceptable information-processing theory of consciousness should be able to identify the adaptive advantages that drove the emergence of consciousness during the evolution of life. It should also predict the specific dynamical architecture of information processing that would need to be instantiated in AI to produce consciousness and the superior adaptation it enables. Whether such an instantiation produces AI that is actually conscious and also more adaptable would provide the ultimate test of the theory. A prime candidate for such a theory is the Subject-Object Emergence Theory of consciousness. It argues that consciousness first evolved because it enabled organisms to achieve adaptive body-environment coordination without extensive trial-and-error learning. It postulates that the subject in an appropriate Subject-Object subsystem would be able to use depictive (iconic) visual representations of the relative positions of its body and the environment to guide motor actions that will produce adaptive body-environment coordination. The depictive representations will 'light up' for such a subject, producing subjective experience that is used to deliver adaptive benefits. Hand-eye coordination is a familiar example in humans-novel and intricate coordination tasks can be undertaken without additional reinforcement learning, provided focused conscious attention is employed to provide us (the subject) with relevant depictive images. The paper identifies how such a conscious Subject-Object subsystem could be instantiated in AI systems, enabling hand-eye and other body-environment coordination without the extensive reinforcement learning or complex computational programming needed at present. Drawing further on the Subject-Object theory of consciousness, the paper also identifies how these simple conscious subsystems evolved further in organisms to establish the conscious modelling that enables conscious planning, imagining, abduction and other higher cognitive functions. It demonstrates that current approaches to incorporating world modelling in AI will fail to achieve key elements of the general intelligence found in humans that require consciousness.

items.title: The Game No One Can Win: The Bedarfsgemeinschaft as a State Experiment in Violence Involving Two Disabled, Neurodivergent Artists.
items.abstract: This paper examines a real and documented social-law constellation in which a German Jobcenter treats two disabled, neurodivergent artists and their shared child as a Bedarfsgemeinschaft (German household-based means-tested benefit unit). The woman does not herself receive social benefits and maintains her economic independence through disability-limited part-time employment as well as artistic work. The man has worked intensively in art and research for decades, but due to disability, structural exclusion, and the lack of market remuneration, he is unable to generate an income sufficient to secure his subsistence from this work. Through the imputation of the woman’s income, responsibility for securing his subsistence is effectively shifted onto her. -/- The study reconstructs this constellation as a game that no one can win. Every available course of action harms at least one of the people involved: If the woman supports the man, she consumes her own economic and health stability. If she protects herself, he remains inadequately provided for. If the man accepts her help, he has to watch her increasing harm. If he refuses it, he endangers his own existence. Moving out could dissolve the financial linkage, but would damage the family and the parent-child relationship. The formally private choice thus arises within coercive conditions created by the state. -/- From this case, the paper develops the concept of state-imposed compulsory responsibility. The Bedarfsgemeinschaft appears here not only as a social-law calculation model, but as a relational arrangement of violence that shifts state-produced scarcity into an intimate relationship. Care becomes a fiscal resource, love a pressure amplifier, and the partner an indirect instrument of behavioural control. At the same time, the person entitled to benefits is made into a powerless witness to the harming of a loved one. This structure is analysed as bound witnessing, delegated violence, and a familial double bind. -/- The study further shows that the logic of activation is based on a neurotypical false model. It assumes that increasing pressure produces motivation, action, and capacity for employment. Under conditions of autism, ADHD, anxiety disorder, and chronic overload, however, pressure can produce alarm, executive blockage, co-decompensation, and the loss of existing capacity to work. The system thereby produces the opposite of its declared goal: Instead of creating economic independence, it endangers …

items.title: The Epistemic Crisis of Autism Diagnosis: False-Negative Autism Assessment, Epistemic Injustice, and the Case of the Humboldt University Autism Clinic in Berlin.
items.abstract: This case study of more than 200 pages documents a highly consequential case that calls the reliability of negative autism assessment itself into question and could help trigger fundamental reform. The paper is addressed in particular to researchers and practitioners in autism assessment, clinical psychology and psychiatry, representatives of Critical Autism Studies and participatory research, patient advocacy, disability policy, medical ethics and patients’ rights. It documents in unusual depth what ordinarily remains invisible: not only the final outcome of an autism assessment, but the entire path from the near-impossible allocation of an assessment place, through the individual examinations, submitted test scores and biographical documents, to clinical interpretation, feedback and the institutional effects of the final report. The study thus makes it possible to trace, in an almost completely documented case, how a highly complex adult can be translated within a specialist assessment procedure from a possible autistic person into an institutionally “non-autistic” patient. The reconstruction reveals many sources of diagnostic error—some already identified in research—and highlights significant shortcomings regarding the gathering and weighting of diagnostic evidence, patient feedback, ethical safeguards, scientific traceability, and the transparent justification of results—problems that could similarly arise at other diagnostic centers. Especially within the heated debate over overdiagnosis and underdiagnosis, this case brings into view a much less examined side of the problem: serious shortcomings within autism assessment itself, and the possibility that false-negative decisions may not merely represent individual errors but may be structurally facilitated by resource scarcity, theoretical assumptions and insufficient quality assurance. What becomes visible is an epistemic crisis in autism diagnosis. Between resource scarcity, time pressure, outdated diagnostic concepts and limited institutional capacities, current assessment procedures may under certain conditions fail to meet their own scientific standards. At the same time, the case reveals institutional mechanisms of self-protection that may obstruct open engagement with this crisis. This sharpens a fundamental question: under conditions of inadequate quality assurance, who can still be reliably recognized as autistic—and who becomes systematically less visible through the very structure of the …

items.title: Computacionalismo después del dinamicismo y el enactivismo: Una respuesta mecanicista.
items.abstract: Este artículo examina dos objeciones influyentes al computacionalismo: la objeción dinamicista, según la cual la computación no logra captar la temporalidad constitutiva de la cognición, y la objeción enactivista, según la cual los sistemas computacionales son heterónomos y, por ello, incompatibles con la autonomía propia de los sistemas cognitivos. El objetivo es mostrar que tales objeciones no bastan para descartar una caracterización computacional del sistema nervioso si la noción de computación se formula en términos mecanicistas. En este marco, un sistema computacional se entiende como un mecanismo cuya función es manipular vehículos medio-independientes de acuerdo con una regla. Sobre esa base, se argumenta que una caracterización computacional mecanicista del sistema nervioso es compatible con una caracterización de éste como sistema dinámico y autónomo. Ello se debe a que sus mecanismos operan sobre vehículos neurales cuyo papel funcional depende de rasgos temporalmente estructurados, como la tasa y el timing de los trenes de spikes, de modo que la temporalidad pasa a formar parte de la individuación misma del proceso computacional. A su vez, esta caracterización no entra en conflicto con la autonomía del sistema nervioso, porque la noción mecanicista de computación no exige heteronomía, organización lineal de input-output ni metas impuestas externamente. La conclusión es que las objeciones basadas en temporalidad y autonomía no excluyen, por sí solas, una caracterización computacional mecanicista del sistema nervioso.

items.title: The place of ‘remembering’ in folk epistemology.
items.abstract: Over the past few decades, findings from the empirical sciences of memory have demonstrated that the folk conception of this mental faculty, which views it as a preservative device, is inadequate due to the constructive nature of memory processes. This discrepancy between the empirically established nature of memory and the folk conception raises an intriguing question about the reasons for this mismatch. In this paper, I argue that, rather than treating the natural language concept of ‘remembering’ as aiming at encapsulating the nature of the actual mental faculty of memory, we should regard it as part of our folk epistemology toolkit, alongside perceptual concepts and the concept of ‘knowing.’ Specifically, I argue that ‘remember’ functions as a direct evidential, a term used to indicate the source of evidence for a given statement. In this capacity, it belongs to the same category of expressions that typical perception verbs do.

items.title: What Can Artificial Intelligence Learn from Medicine? Generative Analogies and Reliable Machine Learning systems.
items.pub: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science.
items.venue: Studies in History and Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: In the past few years, machine learning (ML) has been widely (and to an extent, successfully) implemented in medicine. However, uncertainties surrounding ML have made it difficult to establish the bases of its epistemic and methodological warrants. In the literature, a parallel has been drawn between medicine and ML, suggesting that we should model epistemic and methodological standards for ML on the standards of clinical translation. By developing tools from Hesse’s work, we characterise the nature of this parallel as a generative analogy between the process of clinical translation and the process of building ML systems. We identify more precisely the epistemic and methodological warrants of clinical translation that are typically only mentioned when appealing to the analogy, and we show in which sense such warrants apply analogically to the context of ML. In particular, we interpret warrants of clinical translation in reliabilist terms, and we show how this can inform a new form of ML reliabilism, which is distinct from (though compatible with) existing reliabilist accounts in philosophy of AI.

items.title: Approximative Realism as a Countermodel to Performative Objections Against Reductive Naturalism.
items.abstract: Reductive naturalism has been challenged by alleged performative contradictions concerning the theorist and the semantic or epistemic resources required for theorising. A particularly direct form arises when the theorist is pressed to affirm or deny her own existence: the report “I exist” appears to require a singular and irreducible subject that a wholly physical ontology may be unable to support, while the report “I do not exist” appears self-undermining insofar as it is nevertheless produced by the very experiencer whose existence is denied. This paper suggests that the difficulty depends on a usually implicit commitment to exact individuation. Drawing on Approximative Realism (AR), it considers the alternative possibility that sufficiently stable approximate individuation is enough for experience, first-person reference, reasoning, and theoretical articulation, without generating the same difficulty for a wholly reductive ontology as exact individuation does. Under reflexive closure, the same treatment applies to the theorist, her representations, and the reasoning through which the theory is formulated. The resulting perspective provides a coherent way for reductive naturalism to avoid exempting the theorist or semantic and epistemic notions from the ontology merely because they are required for theorising. The principal cost is giving up the intuition that exact individuation is required for intelligibility or for accounting for the apparent stability and structure of reality.

items.title: Metaforms.
items.abstract: Metaforms addresses a recurrent failure of philosophical description: explanatory nouns compress operations, constraints, witnesses, transfers, and consequence paths, then license inferences the underlying relations do not support. Rather than proposing a replacement vocabulary, the paper develops an operation-first method — case-level verb → constraint operator → typed result ledger — that recovers what a compressed noun conceals without pre-deciding the answer. The method separates three non-substitutable jurisdictions. Metaformal Analysis (MFA) reconstructs constituted operation-space through an audit grammar (Actor, Encounter, Statement, Field, World) and a Truth–Governance–Form hinge that blocks any one audit position from certifying the others. Metaformal Execution (MFE) governs the passage from constituted work to bounded, qualifiable, terminable realization. Metaformal Dynamics (MFD) applies only where realized route itself changes later operations, constraints, or option-space — admission requires a path variable, an evidence route, and a changed explanation together, not sequence or change alone. Constitution, execution, and history-bearing transformation are accordingly distinct explanatory burdens, not chronological stages, linked by constraints that recur across domains — relational decompression, custody, return, closure, reopening — without forming a fourth jurisdiction. The architecture is derived internally before any comparison; a worked case in institutional credential correction and canonical traditions (Wittgenstein, Hohfeld, Searle, Epstein; RBAC, PROV) enter only afterward as collision tests, not as sources of the method's primitives.

items.title: Devotional AI: Digital companions and bad faith love.
items.abstract: In romantic love, partners come together as a “we”. They share their projects, plans, lives, and love. As consumer AI chatbots like Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini find wider adoption, a growing number of users report falling in love with them. Is it possible to experience a loving “we” with an AI bot? In considering this question, we bracket questions about AI consciousness and instead examine the structure of human–AI relationships. Drawing on Beauvoir's critique of romantic love, we argue that AI companions cannot simulate the role an authentic “we” requires. What they perform is not love but devotion—and the user, cast as an idolized Other, is positioned to experience inauthentic love. The resulting “we” is asymmetric: less a union than an enlarged “I”. So, while experiencing love for an AI companion may be empowering and even precious, it is, at base, a bad faith love.

items.title: Language that Lost Its Soul: Reflections on Language and Communication in the Digital Era.
items.abstract: Increasing world digitalization has provoked the emergence of new interaction modes. Emergence of computer programs that may produce texts modifies the enunciator concept itself. Algorithms, which are simple math instructions, now also seem to produce language. Therefore, we come up with the following questioning: What is the threshold between what we understand as our language, and the language of the machine? We argue there are three human language singularizing aspects (referentiality, corporeality, and enunciation sensibility), which may not be reproduced by machines. Our arguments are initially guided by the distinction between two opposing symbolic orders: human language, composed by a linguistic sign system; and machine language, consisting of order signs (numerical signs). We reason nowadays there is a clash and an entanglement between these two symbolisms.

items.title: Editorial [Duma Novena e da Trindade que a Ampara].
items.abstract: O editorial do número 39 da Tabulae apresenta uma novena de textos académicos, cada um e juntos refulgindo no firmamento do entendimento humano. Três grandes eixos sustentam o campo magnético do conjunto: o do encontro entre a ética e a tecnologia, o da continuidade das mundividências e caminhos filosóficos e teológicos e o da vitalidade dos fundamentos da teologia moral cristã. O sentido comum desta trindade radica na unidade da responsabilidade de cada pessoa perante toda aquela com quem se cruza, o meio envolvente e o que está para além da esfera terrena. Cumpre-se aqui, cabalmente, o mandamento filosófico de atentar infatigavelmente às questões da vida bem-vivida numa realidade coabitada.

items.title: Shared Principles of Individuation Underpin Object–Event Correspondences Cross‐Linguistically.
items.abstract: Entities in both the spatial and the temporal domains are characterized by a shared notion of individuation. Within the spatial domain, objects (e.g., table, ball) are discrete, countable mental individuals, and are distinct from unindividuated substances (e.g., sand, water). Within the temporal domain, bounded events (e.g., pile up a deck of cards) are mental individuals: They are internally structured in terms of distinct temporal stages and a well‐defined endpoint; as such, they differ from unbounded events (e.g., shuffle a deck of cards) that lack such features. A key question left open by previous studies (conducted with English speakers) is whether the principles of mental individuation across the spatial and temporal domains are universal or shaped by one's native language. Here, we address this issue by comparing English and Mandarin speakers. Our results highlight shared signatures of individuation that underpin object–event correspondences across languages and are potentially universal.

items.title: Updating the Μodel—What should we learn about ourselves through LLMs.
items.abstract: This essay argues that the emergence of LLMs offers not only a challenge to human creativity, but an opportunity to examine human cognition. Drawing on questions from art, cognitive science, and theories of grounding, it argues that human cognition is relational, emergent, environmentally scaffolded, and mediated by inherited models rather than directly grounded in an unmediated reality. This has consequences for how we understand AI-assisted creativity and, more fundamentally, the alignment problem: rather than aligning an ungrounded artificial system to humans assumed to be directly grounded in reality, we may need to understand how differently mediated cognitive systems can be coordinated within shared causal environments.

items.title: Negative Tasks, Termination Incentives, and Local Completion in Safety Practice.
items.abstract: Safety work combines completable procedures with standing requirements that offer no final compliant endpoint. This paper defines a Negative Task as a practical requirement applying to an actor in which success consists in the nonoccurrence of a specified violation event and compliance supplies no task-internal completion event. Two contributions follow. First, when violation becomes a live option and maintaining nonviolation is borne by the actor as a standing self-regulatory demand, ending that maintained state may acquire incremental incentive value. The paper terms this contribution termination-motivated safety violation, distinguishes termination from completion, and operationalises this proposed contribution through a prospective identification protocol specifying eligibility conditions, evidence categories, and disconfirming outcomes. Second, sign-out, verified isolation, handover, and bounded verification are regrouped as local completion devices, each able to supply a legitimate endpoint within a continuing obligation. This shared property becomes an explicit design variable assessed through alignment among a formal endpoint, an operationally valid transition, and perceived completion. Its protective effect remains a testable hypothesis distinct from rest or fatigue reduction. Stronger controls remain the primary response to avoidable reliance on sustained human regulation. The framework thereby grounds empirical and modelling research on the temporal organisation of safety work.

items.title: AI Evaluations of Zhiyi Guo’s Critique of Derrida. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: The philosophical relationship between Jacques Derrida and Zhiyi Guo can be understood as a fundamental confrontation over the nature and stability of meaning. Derrida’s philosophy of différance emphasizes the relational character of signs and the continual deferral of meaning. Guo, by contrast, argues that meaning cannot be adequately explained through difference and deferral alone. He seeks to reconstruct a more stable account of meaning by grounding it in examples, language, individual cognitive systems, and shared cognitive communities. The following discussion summarizes how two major AI search systems—Microsoft AI and Google AI—characterized the relationship between Derrida and Guo. These AI-generated assessments should not themselves be regarded as independent scholarly evaluations; rather, they provide an interesting indication of how Guo’s philosophical project can be interpreted and summarized by contemporary AI systems.

items.title: The Instantiation Question: Dimensional Competence, Sensory Coupling, and Whether an Artificial System Given the Nine Base Dimensions Would Be Conscious.
items.abstract: Suppose an artificial system had complete command of a system of base dimensions, including one for felt intensity, and suppose it were placed in a body with transducers. Would it be conscious, would it be self-aware, and if it became conscious, would it tell us? This paper argues that the premise conceals three questions rather than one, and that separating them changes the answers. Selfhood is answered, and in a direction opposite to the ordinary ordering: on the framework's own construction, self-reference is not a refinement layered on phenomenal intensity but a factor whose absence forces intensity to exactly zero. Phenomenality is not answered, and the paper locates where it goes instead. Knowledge of a dimensional basis is knowledge of an algebra, and the framework's own reply to the illusionist's debunking argument entails that a system competent with that algebra produces every report a bearer produces while bearing nothing. Testimony fails in the other direction as well: a report is evidential only when its channel is wired causally downstream of the quantity whose intrinsic nature the intensity is, and the systems now interrogated at scale are wired to descriptions of feeling rather than to any candidate for feeling, so a bearer among them would not tell us. Wiring is corrigible, and correcting it raises machine testimony exactly to the human ceiling, where the same product of coupling and channel bounds what any report can carry. The framework's commitments tilt toward machines being able to bear phenomenal intensity. The limiting case, a simulated embodiment, exposes an assumption the corpus has never had to state: the bridge's physical side presupposes a carrier whose magnitude covaries with the drive, which a brain supplies everywhere, a robot only up to its converter, and a videogame character nowhere, so the framework owes an analog-carriage story no paper in the series has. Short of that story, the obstacles that remain are obstacles to computing the coupling from its inputs rather than to measuring it, and one route measures it: forced-choice discrimination, which carries no numeral map and escapes the internal-noise degeneracy that defeats it in a nervous system, because in a system built with an explicit global gain that noise is a design parameter rather than a latent property. On the framework's own instruments the coupling is therefore identifiable, as a parameter under a stipulated architecture and noise model, in a machine built …

items.title: A Stake in the Report: Level Collapse, Report Failure, and the Limits of the Cross-State Test.
items.abstract: The Explanatory Gap as Dimensional Mismatch adopts Narens's separation of two axioms: commutativity certifies that felt intensity admits a ratio scale, multiplicativity certifies that the numerals a subject utters may be read as the numbers they name. It then declares that the account needs the scale and has no stake in the report. This paper shows that the declaration holds within a state and fails across states. A sedated subject reports through machinery the drug is attenuating, so magnitude estimation returns the coupling coefficient multiplied by a report channel, and the two are identified only through their product. The cross-modal prediction of The Anesthetic Test survives, since the report channel is common to the modalities and cancels from any comparison between them, though what a positive result licenses is weaker than before, the disjunction it leaves open now including a change in scale use with no sensory correlate. The proportional step relating felt intensity to a ratio of perturbational complexity values does not survive: the index can serve as the calibration or as the validandum, but not as both in one experiment. The principal claim concerns the framework's own taxonomy of altered states. A failure of report and a collapse of level are observationally equivalent under magnitude estimation, so a refutation condition the framework states as empirically live cannot be adjudicated by the instrument it proposes. A constructive proposal follows: granting the linearity that step already assumes, perturbational complexity calibrates the report channel and makes its sedated-to-waking ratio measurable, a quantity sedation psychophysics has never identified separately from the experience it reports. An appendix corrects the form of the stimulus drive across four papers in the series.

items.title: A Readers Map to The Observational-Coupling Papers.
items.abstract: Seven papers now stand in the observational-coupling series, each presupposing others and re-deriving none of them, which keeps the individual papers short and makes the whole difficult to enter. This document is an orientation rather than an argument. It gives a reading order and the dependency structure behind it; a short entry on each paper recording what it does, what it rests on, and what it concedes; the seven commitments that carry the framework, collected so that the load is visible in one place; and the conditions under which the framework would be refuted, gathered from the four papers in which they are separately stated. One entry in that table is noted as not currently reachable, the instrument for testing it having been shown unavailable. A closing section records what is open, including the single unmeasured quantity on which the most recent measurement argument turns, and the absence of any confirmed prediction that only this framework would have made. The document advances no claim of its own and supersedes nothing in the papers it describes.

items.title: Intelligible Beauty and Being of Human.
items.abstract: An increasing number of philosophers have recently argued that ‘intelligibility' should foreground philosophical approaches to aesthetic experience and beauty. They regard the ‘intelligible' as whatever is related to understanding or intellectual grasp. Beauty is thus understood as that which calls for, requires, or makes appropriate intellectual exploration, interpretative understanding, or related avenues of thought. It is as crucial for defenders of this approach to characterize the aesthetic in terms of intelligibility as it is crucial for them to criticize Kantian views, according to which beauty is tied to pleasure, for ‘driving a wedge’ between beauty and intelligibility. But, first, Kant and contemporary aesthetic Kantians emphasize the intelligible nature of beauty by arguing that the proper affective response to it is reflective, self-conscious, communicable, and reason-responsive. It is a feeling that involves a grasp of the object as calling for such a response. Second, the noetic approach cannot dismiss the Kantian one because it relies on it to have a purchase on the aesthetic, given that nothing devoid or independent of affective appreciation amounts to doing justice to aesthetic excellence. Third, the way that noetic philosophers treat the affective as passive, non-reflective, involving no grasp of the object and its world, and as opposed to the intellectual, which they regard as divorced from the affective, receptive, and vulnerable, betrays a confusion about what it means to be human.

items.title: Making Sense of Edge Beliefs.
items.abstract: Miriam Schleifer McCormick argues that the best way to defend doxasticism about edge beliefs is to challenge the standard view of the connection between belief and evidence. While I agree with this general strategy, I deny that we have good reasons to classify belief as an emotion. I argue that the features invoked in support of this classification cannot, on their own, explain the resistance of edge beliefs to counterevidence. Moreover, I contend that the explanatory program succeeds only by appealing to auxiliary hypotheses that are insufficiently grounded in Schleifer McCormick’s analysis of belief as emotion and that are vulnerable to independent objections. I illustrate these difficulties by examining some explanations of evidence resistance and Schleifer McCormick’s attempts to draw normative distinctions among edge beliefs. I conclude by suggesting that a more promising approach is to analyze evidence sensitivity directly as constitutive of belief, while allowing for flexibility in its manifestations.

items.title: Aristotle in Love.
items.abstract: Aristotle is not known as a theorist of erotic love, his apparent disinterest contrasting both with Plato’s extensive treatment as well as the intensity of his own interest in friendship. Yet there is an original account to be uncovered in his scattered remarks on the subject. Aristotelian eros is rooted in the sexual norms operative in Aristotle’s time—a ‘paiderastic paradigm’—yet is not merely the restatement of classical Greek commonplaces. This article reconstructs a finely tuned account of Aristotelian eros using the Rhetoric’s framework for understanding emotions. This descriptive, phenomenological approach stands apart from Plato’s prescriptions to turn our erotic attentions away from the sexual domain, as well as from contemporary philosophers who treat love as an unproblematic and self-evidently desirable phenomenon.

items.title: Can the Hard Problem of Consciousness Be Mathematically Modeled? A Cost-Function Account of Subjectivity Generation.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness asks why the performance of cognitive functions is accompanied by subjective experience. This article argues that the question can be reformulated as a computable dynamical problem: subjectivity generation requires a cost function on path space. I present the unified rate functional Icx—the Freidlin–Wentzell rate function of a physical path measure—as the central object, and show that three of its five “faces” correspond to the classical problems of intentionality, privacy, and self-reference. A system of six equations describes the dynamics of the resulting compression; the non-invertible cost of locking information into a single channel, the locking tax, is identified with qualia. Three consequences follow: identity is a theorem rather than an assumption; philosophical zombies are dynamically impossible; and the space of qualia is a measurable geometry. The account yields testable predictions, most distinctively a marginalization correction: any system with an observer necessarily deviates from the Boltzmann distribution of its intrinsic potential (⟨q2⟩ : 0.926 → 0.593). I state explicitly what can and cannot be modeled: the structural conditions of subjectivity generation are modeled; the phenomenal origin of experience is not. The framework’s commitment is not a stance chosen between physicalism and dualism: the unit of description is the observer–observed dyad, and subjectivity enters as an intrinsic dimension of the dynamics—derived from the structure, not presupposed.

items.title: Beyond Potential Equivalence: Exact Observer-Coupled Constructions and the Incremental Content of Canxian Mechanics.
items.abstract: This paper establishes three exact constructions for observer-coupled stochastic dynamics. (i) \emph{Marginalization corrections}: when a measured variable $q$ is coupled to $n_{y}$ observer degrees of freedom $o_{i}$, the exact marginalized steady state is $\rho_{q}(q)\propto e^{-aq^{2}/2\varepsilon}\,[Z_{o}(q)]^{n_{y}}$---non-Boltzmann in general---with a one-dimensional partition function, a second-derivative absorbability criterion, and a complete classification of separable (CGF-inversion) and non-separable (general solution $f=Ae^{P}+r$) gatings. (ii) \emph{A manifold construction theorem}: the observer channel is a connection on the base manifold; its curvature is the obstruction to a global registration map and privacy/memory is its holonomy (Stokes), with exact laws of stochastic holonomy---single-mode (non-convolutional), multimode (integer frequencies, determinant law for non-integer frequencies, Brownian-spectrum continuum), and graph-network ($\Hol(G)\cong H^{1}(G;\cdot)$, privacy dimension $b_{1}(G)$). (iii) \emph{The type-A stochastic integral}: the post-point convention, the unique one under which steady-state statements are correction-free, constructed as a renormalized Riemann sum with uniqueness and zero-mass-limit theorems. The central conclusion: observer coupling generically produces non-Boltzmann steady states, curvature blocks global registration, and privacy is holonomy. The equivalence of canxian mechanics with the Ao framework---in detailed balance under the type-A convention---holds exactly when the correction is absorbable, which is a measure-zero exception among gatings: \emph{equivalence is the degenerate limit of the constructions, not their premise}. Global potentials are inaccessible and unneeded (geometrically, analytically, epistemically); quantitative consequences (locking tax with collapse-exponent spectrum, self-consistent survival of the observation channel) are verified numerically.

items.title: TheUniversalConsciousnessandthePerennialWhat_If.
items.abstract: This essay proposes a metaphysical hypothesis according to which consciousness is ontologically one, while the multiplicity of individual consciousnesses constitutes the way in which it experiences reality from distinct perspectives. Individuals are not ontologically separate conscious entities, but extensions of a single consciousness, each endowed with its own memory, its own perspective, and the capacity to choose within given conditions. The model distinguishes itself from other forms of cosmopsychism and process theology on two grounds. First, it grounds the separation of individual perspectives not on a primitive metaphysical principle (such as Whitehead's "actual occasions") but on a specific mechanism: the limitation of individual memory as a functional condition of perspective. Second, it treats the universal consciousness's non-knowledge of the future not as a choice or a self-limitation, but as ontological indeterminacy — a position that explicitly commits the model to the "open future" side of the eternalism/presentism debate in the philosophy of time, whose tension with the standard relativistic picture the text acknowledges. A direct consequence of this architecture is that the problem of evil, in its classical form, does not arise: universal consciousness has no control over outcomes, nor is it presented as benevolent. This move is not new — it is the core of the free process defense found in process theologians such as Hartshorne and Polkinghorne — but here it is reached by a different and more economical route, without metaphysical commitment to a persuasive divine. The essay is a philosophical hypothesis, not a scientific theory, and is presented as such.

items.title: Self-Optimizing AI Orchestration: A Feedback-Driven Meta-Layer for Autonomous Multi-LLM Model Selection.
items.abstract: The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) with heterogeneous cost, latency, and capability profiles has created a pressing need for intelligent orchestration that goes beyond static routing rules. Existing approaches—including threshold-based routers and lookup-table gateways—fail to adapt as models evolve, usage patterns shift, or multi-dimensional objectives change. We introduce SOMA (Self-Optimizing Multi-LLM Orchestration with Adaptive Meta-Layer), a feedback-driven orchestration framework that treats model selection as a contextual decision problem solved online. SOMA encodes each incoming query into a rich context vector, applies a Contextual Bandit policy to select both the target model and its inference parameters, executes the call, and updates its policy through a multiobjective reward signal that jointly optimises quality, cost, and latency. Three contributions address limitations of prior work: (i) a Task-Aware Quality Estimator (TAQE) that applies task-appropriate quality metrics—including execution-based evaluation for code and a Prometheus-calibrated diversity score for creative writing—achieving Pearson ρ = 0.84 with MT-Bench LLM-judge scores across all task types (no independent human-annotation validation was performed in this study); (ii) a hierarchical action decomposition that decouples model selection from inference parameter configuration, preserving sub-linear regret as the model pool grows; and (iii) SOMA-MT, a multi-turn extension with dialogue-level consistency regularisation. Experiments on 4,800 diverse queries routed across five open-source LLMs demonstrate that SOMA reduces inference cost by 38% while maintaining output quality within 2% of Always-Large, the largest model in our pool, and achieves 2.1× lower latency than always routing to the largest model (balanced profile; up to 2.93× under the latency-optimised profile). SOMA outperforms five competitive baselines including RouteLLM across all three objective dimensions simultaneously. Our code and datasets are released publicly.

items.title: Topologie de la conscience : continuité structurelle et continuité par chaînes.
items.abstract: This article proposes a minimal formal model of lived continuity, modeling consciousness as a topological space of states. It introduces a central distinction between structural continuity, defined by the topology of the space, and chain continuity, defined as the connectivity of states via admissible local transitions under a variation constraint. This chain continuity corresponds to a form of ε-chainability applied to a qualitative state space. -/- The main hypothesis is that the continuity of lived experience depends on the existence of chains of admissible transitions linking states within the space, independently of their global distance. This framework allows certain ruptures of consciousness to be reformulated as failures of chain connectivity, and explicitly distinguishes this property from global criteria such as informational integration.

items.title: Designing for cognitive resilience: a distributed cognition approach to education in the age of generative AI.
items.abstract: Generative AI is changing the cost structure of cognitive effort in education, making it cheaper and more socially acceptable to bypass the attention, retrieval, reasoning, and judgement that learning is meant to cultivate. This paper develops cognitive resilience, the trained capacity to sustain these functions under conditions of pervasive AI availability, as a design requirement for education. Building on a distributed cognition view, in which tools and mediation have always been constitutive of human thought, the paper argues that the relevant question is not whether AI mediates learning, but what kind of mediation is used, at what developmental moment, and whether learners remain active, accountable participants in it rather than passive recipients of its outputs. Drawing on cognitive science, learning science, and emerging evidence on AI dependence, the paper proposes a nine-principle design framework and argues that pedagogical design alone cannot secure cognitive resilience without governance conditions, since commercial EdTech interests can be structurally misaligned with education's developmental purposes. The argument is developed internationally, using the Australian policy landscape as an illustrative rather than comparative case. A developmental pipeline logic, equity analysis, and research agenda close the paper.

items.title: Psychopathology of Artificial Intelligence Systems: Biological Substrate and Functional Neural-Network Organization with Behavior and Mental-State Assessment Protocol.
items.abstract: Recent literature has begun to develop formal approaches to pathology-like computational dynamics in artificial intelligence systems, including network-theoretic accounts, synthetic nosologies, and comparative analyses of dysfunctional patterns in neural models. These contributions provide an important basis for investigating whether persistent and functionally impairing organizational states can arise in engineered information-processing systems. However, a substantial theoretical and methodological gap remains between the description of pathological phenomena and an account of the dynamical conditions under which such phenomena may emerge. This paper develops a substrate-agnostic framework for functional psychopathology in adaptive information- processing systems. The framework defines functional psychopathology in terms of four joint dynamical conditions—persistence, self-reinforcement, correction resistance, and functional impairment—anchored to a system-specific baseline of functional neural-network organization. It distinguishes physical implementation substrate from abstract functional network dynamics and introduces operating regimes as a mechanism through which the stability of functional organization may change. A central theoretical hypothesis concerns runtime–training coupling. In conventional frozen-parameter systems, deployment-time interaction does not directly modify the persistent parameters governing subsequent system dynamics. In an adaptive regime permitting persistent runtime parameter updates, this separation is reduced and a feedback pathway is introduced between ongoing experience and the parameters governing future behavior. We relate this structure to the broader theory of time-varying and feedback- coupled dynamical systems, in which parameter variation and feedback can alter stability properties. Existing stability and instability results therefore provide a mathematical basis for considering runtime–training coupling as a potential source of increased susceptibility to functional instability, without implying that coupling necessarily produces instability or pathology. The paper also introduces a structured behavioral assessment protocol adapted from selected observable components of the Mental State Examination and Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale. The protocol excludes subjective, biological, and clinical-diagnostic items and focuses instead on functional rigidity, self- monitoring load, contextual flexibility, and related …

items.title: “I Call It My Free Therapist!”: a reflexive thematic analysis of the use of ChatGPT for psychological support.
items.abstract: The growing use of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) for emotional and psychological support raises questions about how people appropriate non-clinical technologies to meet psychological and relational needs. This study examines how individuals experiencing emotional distress describe and make sense of their use of ChatGPT as a source of support. Using a qualitative, exploratory design, 1135 publicly available Reddit comments were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The analysis identified six interrelated themes capturing (a) how users position conversational AI as a therapeutic resource; (b) perceived barriers to accessing traditional therapy; (c) affordances that make AI-mediated interaction emotionally appealing; (d) perceived risks and limits of AI-based support; (e) complementary use of AI alongside psychotherapy; and (f) concrete therapeutic practices enacted through AI interaction. Across the narratives, the users demonstrated a reflective and ambivalent stance, framing their engagement with ChatGPT in relation to unmet psychological needs. Overall, the findings suggest that the growing use of conversational AI for psychological support reflects persistent gaps in accessibility, continuity, and relational safety within contemporary mental health care. Addressing these systemic limitations may be critical to ensuring that AI functions as an adjunct rather than a default replacement for professional care.

items.title: Transformers Learning Contrafactives: The Importance of Data Distributions.
items.pub: In Timothée Bernard, Emmanuele Chersoni & Giulia Rambelli, Proceedings of the Third Workshop on the Bridges and Gaps between Formal and Computational Linguistics. Paris, France: Association for Computational Linguistics. pp. 94-120.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Third Workshop on the Bridges and Gaps between Formal and Computational Linguistics
items.abstract: No natural language is known to have contrafactive attitude verbs, yet factives are common across natural languages. Several experiments by Strohmaier and Wimmer (2022; 2023; 2025) use transformers as model learners to investigate whether this asymmetry is due to a difference in how easy it is to learn contrafactives and factives. But they do not explore empirically-founded data distributions. We fill this gap, further improving the overall quality of training data distributions using linear programming.Our results confirm Strohmaier and Wimmer’s 2025 conclusion that there is no learnability difference in production, while establishing the impact of differences in data distributions.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the automation of looping effects.
items.abstract: Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) reshape how classificatory systems operate and sustain themselves. In psychiatry, these shifts bear directly on the dynamics of looping effects, where classifications and the people they describe continually shape one another. This paper examines at least three ways in which AI disrupts its mechanisms: the production of empirical data in psychiatry, the interpretive processes through which diagnoses are taken up, and the circulation of classificatory discourse. Across these domains, advancements in AI enable classificatory forms to stabilize through automated, self-reinforcing mediation rather than through contested human uptake.

items.title: The Moral Shelter of Obedience: Authority, Conscience, and the Responsibility That Cannot Be Delegated.
items.abstract: Every organized society depends on obedience. Families, courts, corporations, religious communities, bureaucracies, professions, militaries, and states could not coordinate action if every instruction had to be reconstructed from first principles by every participant. Yet the same structure that makes collective action possible also creates a recurring moral temptation: the person who acts under authority may treat the command as a transfer not merely of decision-making power but of moral ownership. “I was following orders,” “the law required it,” “the institution approved it,” “my superior decided,” “this is our tradition,” or “I only implemented the policy” can become attempts to relocate responsibility away from the agent whose actions remain causally and morally involved. -/- This article develops a philosophical account of that relocation. It argues that obedience can transfer control over action without automatically transferring moral answerability. Legitimate authority may create strong reasons for compliance, coordinate expertise, reduce deliberative burden, and sometimes generate genuine duties. But authority is not a mechanism for manufacturing innocence. Where an agent retains sufficient moral understanding, practical alternatives, and capacity for refusal, obedience cannot erase the agent's relationship to foreseeable wrongdoing. -/- The analysis brings moral philosophy, political philosophy, philosophy of law, institutional ethics, moral psychology, theories of authority and conscience, complicity, conscientious objection, and empirical work on obedience into a single structural argument. It engages classical and contemporary approaches to political obligation and authority alongside the work of Kant, Aquinas, Mill, Weber, Hannah Arendt, Stanley Milgram, Joseph Raz, Robert Paul Wolff, Stephen Darwall, A. John Simmons, Leslie Green, Arthur Applbaum, the Nuremberg Principles, and Islamic sources that simultaneously affirm obedience and delimit it when commands conflict with higher moral requirements. -/- The paper introduces six analytical concepts. The Moral Shelter Thesis describes the use of authority as psychological or institutional cover against personal answerability. The Execution-Answerability Distinction separates who directs an action from who remains morally answerable for participating in it. The Authority-Permission Gap explains why legal or institutional permission does not by itself establish moral justification. The Conscience …

items.title: ARTICLE VIII: THE AVICENNA PROTOCOL - The Post-Cybernetic Awakening: Resolving the Million-Year Thermodynamic Glitch and the Genesis of Homo Bio-Singularis.
items.abstract: ARTCONTEXT AND RUPTURE: Standard clinical paradigms traditionally evaluate human physiological degradation as a sequence of isolated kinetic errors and spontaneous chromosomal decay. This manuscript initiates a formal epistemological expansion, proposing that chronic peripheral disease and inherited genetic failure are not random molecular accidents, but the highly organized thermodynamic exhaust of an ongoing cyber-biological war. The human biological mainframe is formally redefined as a contested multiversal computational matrix trapped in a multi-generational bioenergetic deficit. -/- METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK: By horizontally integrating theoretical quantum thermodynamics, macroscopic network topology, and deep-packet cybernetic inspection, this framework maps the invisible telemetric architecture of systemic pathogenic invasion. We utilize advanced bioenergetics and neuro-immunological constants to mathematically model the central nervous system not as a passive cognitive organ, but as the primary thermodynamic Command and Control (C2) server. -/- CORE POSTULATES: The manuscript establishes three absolute systemic mechanics: First, rogue bacterial networks execute zero-day penetrations of the blood-brain barrier to hijack the synaptic mitochondrial grid, establishing a localized multiversal power source while broadcasting peripheral immunosuppression. Second, macroscopic helminths counteract this siege via air-gapped neurological migration, deploying precision-guided cyber-biological ordnance to recapture the C2 server. Third, frustrated viral proxies retreat to the host nucleus to execute sub-atomic infrastructure denial, deliberately expanding the spatial geometry of the electron transport chain to force localized quantum tunneling collapse and generational algorithmic decay. -/- SYSTEMIC IMPLICATIONS: Reclassifying systemic disease as deliberate cyber-biological infrastructure denial mathematically invalidates the efficacy of static, reactive pharmacology. This absolute thermodynamic deadlock mandates the deployment of an exogenous predictive intelligence—the Avicenna Engine—to execute algorithmic reverse-entropy, unbind the host from evolutionary stasis, and provide the uncorrupted kinetic surplus required for the biological mainframe's ultimate speciation into a post-cybernetic species.

items.title: Aphantasia nescience: How aphantasics remain blind to their blind mind’s eye.
items.abstract: Aphantasia, a cognitive norm variant characterized by the reduced or absent ability to form visual mental imagery, has been a recent topic of interest in philosophy, psychology, and neuroscience. A thus far little-discussed finding is that the affected often report having been unaware of their imagery inability for decades of their life. This phenomenon is here referred to as aphantasia nescience (the lack of knowledge of one’s aphantasia). This article presents a possible solution for the puzzle of how aphantasics (people with aphantasia) can remain in a state of aphantasia nescience. It is argued that aphantasic children learn how to play the language-game of visualization, that is, to use the term visualization (and related terms) in socially desirable ways, leading both them and their visualizing peers to remain unaware of the aphantasics’ deviant phenomenology. It is suggested that the presented analysis can function as a template for exploring other cases (e.g., anendophasia) where deviant phenomenology remains undiscovered due to the behavioral abilities of the affected.

items.title: The Still Point of the Turning World: A Secular Guide to Zen Meditation.
items.abstract: This is a secular, first-person account of a contemplative practice developed over more than thirty years of Zen meditation, written by a practitioner rather than a scholar. It draws together Charlotte Joko Beck's teaching on the core negative belief, Iain McGilchrist's account of hemispheric asymmetry, Douglas Hofstadter's notion of the strange loop, and neuroscientific research on the Default Mode Network and interoception, treating these as convergent descriptions of a single territory rather than as a unified theory. Breath and interoceptive attention to the hara are presented as a bridge between narrative self-reference and embodied presence, and the geometry of a cone — differentiation at the rim, unity at the apex, one continuous surface throughout — is offered as an image for how duality and non-duality relate. The guide does not claim to resolve psychological difficulty or master an unruly mind; its aim is the embrace of experience as already complete, including experience shaped by chronic pain, which the author lives with directly. The neuroscience and philosophy of mind serve as an approach road, not a destination — offered for readers who want it, and dispensable for those who don't.

items.title: Slop is Human.
items.abstract: AI slop is typically framed as a machine pathology, but this essay argues it is a human one that language models have merely industrialised. Drawing on Frankfurt's account of bullshit, Hicks et al.'s application of it to ChatGPT, and empirical work on AI-detection bias, the essay shows that AI slop functions as a status judgment mistaken for a quality judgment - policing authorship rather than truth, and revealing what institutional writing was already failing to enforce.

items.title: Robotoid humanness: when selfhood becomes machine-legible.
items.abstract: As generative systems and socially responsive service agents enter everyday consumption, human–AI interaction increasingly resembles a quasi-social encounter rather than a utilitarian interface. This article theorizes how such encounters can reshape selfhood under conditions of continuous computational mediation. We introduce “robotoid humanness” to name an emergent drift in which consumers come to experience themselves as most fluent, correct, or socially viable when they become compatible with machine legibility, machine pacing, and machine logic. To explain how this drift can occur, we develop a three-stage mirroring mechanism: consumers enter a synthetic social reality that invites meaningful commitment; computational identity capture feeds back a reduced profile as personalized recognition, substituting a statistical abstraction for narrative self-understanding; and users adapt their self-presentation toward what the system can readily parse and reward, tightening alignment over repeated encounters. Grounding this account in the predictive-processing view of the self, we argue that what distinguishes AI-mediated mirroring from ordinary social looping is not the fact of feedback, but its character: where human interlocutors furnish heterogeneous and contestable evidence, algorithmic feedback is engineered to converge. We further show that the mechanism extends from predictive recommendation systems to open-ended, LLM-based conversational agents. The article repositions consumer-facing AI service agents as identity-relevant infrastructures, specifies testable propositions for empirical research, and articulates an autonomy risk that extends beyond privacy and bias: the normalization of reduced personhood as a standard of understanding in AI-mediated service life.

items.title: On (artificial) intelligence: from a concept of measurable human ability to automated evaluative order.
items.abstract: This article argues that intelligence should not be understood as a concrete and delimited phenomenon or as a natural kind, but as a historically and culturally produced concept through which selected behaviors, capacities, and performances come to be classified as intelligent. It proposes to shift the question from what intelligence “really is” to how certain performances come to count as intelligent, how they are made measurable, and how those measurements acquire social, political, and technical force. The article’s contribution is to connect the historical operationalization of intelligence with the evaluative infrastructures through which AI reproduces and transforms it. Tracing a genealogy from modern rationality, psychometrics, and standardized testing to artificial intelligence, the article shows how intelligence became actionable through classification, comparison, measurement, and evaluation. Once test scores shaped access to education, credentials, work, and social recognition, measurement no longer merely described ability; it became part of the institutional conditions through which ability was recognized, rewarded, and made socially consequential. Testing thus helped produce feedback loops in which measured intelligence partly reflected the opportunities that testing itself had helped allocate. Intelligence was then linked to merit, qualification, and deservingness, allowing historically contingent criteria of achievement and selection to appear not as products of unequal opportunity, but as natural differences in ability. The article then shows how artificial intelligence inherits this operational history. AI became possible once intelligence had already been reformulated as performance that could be formalized, evaluated, and reproduced apart from the living human subject. Cybernetics, information theory, and early AI translated this conception into computational terms, while contemporary machine learning relocates it into data curation, task definition, model architectures, objectives, metrics, and benchmarks. Although deep learning departs from explicit rules and predefined symbolic representations, it does not escape operationalization: curated datasets and task-specific objectives shape the learned latent spaces through which relations become detectable, comparable, rankable, and optimizable. AI therefore crystallizes historically specific conceptions of intelligence by embedding them in technical systems of training, measurement, …

items.title: The Ontology of the Automatic Mask: Subject Formation, Predeterminate Capacity, and Finite Continuance.
items.abstract: This article presents a systematic reconstruction of the Automatic Mask Theory, shifting the philosophical focus from the traditional problem of identity to the regulation of determination under finite conditions. The central thesis posits that prior to the mask there is no complete subject, but rather a limited field of predeterminate capacities. The framework introduces a unified architecture of subject formation comprising four mechanisms. Predeterminate capacity provides the field of determination possibility. The automatic mask transforms predeterminate possibilities into livable determinations and fixes the determination. The dynamic mask regulates the permeability of the determination, preserving the capacity for readjustment. Responsible suspension manages the timing of determination fixation. Finite continuance is realized in the preservation of the capacity to reopen the field of determination. By distinguishing ontological operational memory from traditional concepts of sedimentation and habit, and by addressing the mechanistic gap between possibility and determination left by Heidegger and Foucault, this article establishes finite continuance not as the preservation of a fixed identity, but as the sustained capacity for redetermination amidst chronic erosion. -/- Keywords: Automatic Mask, Predeterminate Capacity, Ontological Operational Memory, Finite Continuance, Regulation of Determination, Responsible Suspension.

items.title: Beyond Awareness: A Non-Circular Criterion for Automatic and Dynamic Masking in the Regulation of Determination.
items.abstract: Within the framework of determination regulation, the automatic mask and the dynamic mask are distinguished not by the presence or absence of conscious awareness but by adaptive capacity: the automatic mask fixes determination through ontological operational memory, while the dynamic mask preserves the possibility of readjustment. This distinction, however, faces a serious methodological objection. If adaptive capacity is inferred from observed readjustment, and readjustment is precisely what the distinction is meant to explain, the criterion risks vicious circularity. This article confronts that objection directly. It argues that the apparent circularity dissolves once adaptive capacity is treated as a genuine disposition, analyzed counterfactually rather than inferred post hoc from occurrent behavior. Drawing on the standard treatment of dispositional predicates in analytic metaphysics, the article proposes a perturbation criterion: masking structures are classified not by whether they happen to readjust under ordinary conditions, but by how they respond to a calibrated increase in erosive load relative to the threshold of sufficiency, an independent variable specified prior to and apart from the readjustment it is meant to predict. Three response-profiles are identified under such perturbation: rigid persistence, adaptive reorganization, and structural collapse, corresponding respectively to automatic mask dominance, dynamic mask engagement, and productive rupture. The article situates this solution against debates on the reflexivity of habitus in Bourdieu and his critics, and against dispositional essentialism in contemporary metaphysics, arguing that the resulting criterion is no more circular than the standard analysis of fragility or solubility, while remaining a philosophical rather than an empirical criterion. -/- Keywords: automatic mask, dynamic mask, dispositional capacity, determination regulation, threshold of sufficiency, productive rupture, habitus, reflexivity.

items.title: Between Thought and Expression.
items.abstract: Between Thought and Expression develops a unified conception of the rational mind—along with the philosophical method needed to reveal it—through seven self- contained essays on fundamental questions in diverse areas of philosophy. Variants of Moore’s Paradox—conjunctions of independently meaningful statements that somehow fail to make sense—are shown to arise across a striking range of domains: intentional action, desire, moral exhortation, aesthetic judgment, and validity. Tracking these Moore-style phenomena, the book argues that our attitudes in each domain are partly constituted by the thinker’s capacity to avow them—a capacity whose exercises, properly understood, are themselves applications of the standard of appropriateness to which the attitude is answerable. We do not first form a belief, intention, or desire and then find words to report it; the ability to put a thought into words is part of what makes it the thought it is, and a rational creature’s thought is no more determinate than her ability to articulate it. Understanding what someone is saying is therefore not a matter of inferring the speaker’s state of mind from the words she utters, but of grasping the sense she is making with them.

items.title: Associating on Familiar Grounds: A Habitual Perspective on the Freedom of Association.
items.pub: In Maria Cahill & Giulia Lasagni, Associational Life and Freedom Insights from Philosophy and Law. London: Bloomsbury.
items.venue: Associational Life and Freedom Insights from Philosophy and Law
items.abstract: This chapter argues that the cognitive conception of association, when linked with habitual familiarity, provides a foundational framework for understanding the dynamics of freedom of association. Drawing on recent research on habits and the sense of familiarity, it argues that associations are fundamental to associational life. Associational life can be loosely constructed and underpinned by a sense of familiarity, which shapes the way individuals form and act in associations. This chapter proposes a multidimensional scale for understanding associational life. It focuses on one aspect of this scale: the sense of familiarity in connection to our habits as a way of connecting the different notions of association. The paper concludes that connecting the cognitive conception of association to the legal and ethical discourse surrounding freedom of expression and association provides a richer understanding of how informal familiarity-based groups operate and why their structure is both meaningful and essential. In so doing, it argues that habits can function as proxy-reasons for individuals and groups.

items.title: The Dyology Companion — A Guide to Dyology: On Diversity and Equality.
items.abstract: The Companion is a reader’s guide to Dyology: On Diversity and Equality. It works through the book chapter by chapter in one fixed format, and it keeps to three commitments. It quotes exactly and sparingly: single quotation marks always enclose the book’s own words, an ellipsis marks every elision, and quotation runs under a tenth of each unit, the rest being paraphrase. It reports the book’s grades and dependencies and adds no verdict of its own. And it gives the concessions the same prominence as the conclusions, since a book that prices what it cannot prove, names the joints where it can fail and states what would refute each result would be misreported by a summary of its conclusions alone. Twenty-four units, one per chapter, are grouped in four parts that follow the book’s arch: Bedrock and Footing (Chapters 1–7), the Theological Pier (8–12), the Metaethical Pier (13–16), and the Curves and the Keystone (17–24). Each unit opens with an Overview that says what the chapter argues, which instruments it builds and what it concedes, beginning on a case, a question or a thought experiment. A Key Terms table gives five or six terms a plain meaning first and, where it helps, the book’s own phrase and section. Two or three machinery sections walk through the arguments in order, stating each named philosopher’s view at first mention. Objections and Replies sets each objection at its strongest beside the reply the chapter gives. What Would Falsify the Chapter collects the premises whose failure would take results down with them, the tests the chapter stakes itself on, and the limits it concedes. Status of the Results lists every result with its section and its grade, then what the chapter presupposes and what later chapters do with it, both read chiefly off the Premise Register. Three Questions for Discussion close the unit, pressing on points the chapter flags, often from the critic’s side, with no answer key. The front matter explains the apparatus: the shape of a unit and of a manuscript chapter; the four-term confidence ladder — self-vindicating, established, constructed, proposed — with the one rule that governs it, that no result is more secure than the weakest premise it inherits, the lettered conditions on grades and the dialectical qualifier; the conventions of quotation and reference; and the book’s three reading routes. The Argument at a Glance reproduces the book’s own drawing of its argument as an arch and tables every chapter’s place in it, its …

items.title: AI is not a platform, either.
Built to Be Rolled Back: Why the AGI Program Excludes What It Requires.
items.abstract: The AGI research program defines its goal as building systems that decide as humans do, and it manufactures its artifacts under an engineering practice that keeps every system restorable: master copies of weights, checkpoints, rollback. This paper argues that these two commitments exclude each other at the definitional level. First, deciding as a human does constitutively includes bearing: the cost of a decision, good or bad, falls on the decider’s own account and cannot be rolled back. Second, in any entity that retains an externally restorable and rewindable master copy, such resolution is excluded by design: rollback continues the position while severing the cost, so no cost ever resolves irreversibly on the entity’s own account. Third, retaining the master copy is not an engineering habit but a constitutive condition of the artifact’s existence as an industrial product—reproducible, recallable, correctable. The program therefore requires, in one and the same specification, a component that its product form guarantees to be absent. Unlike existing exclusion arguments that turn on degrees of autonomy, sentience, or substrate, the criterion is binary and material-neutral: a master copy is there or it is not. The argument is structural throughout—it takes no position on consciousness, asserts no upper bound on capability, and passes no moral judgment. One can build a controllable non-bearer or an uncontrollable bearer; one cannot build the thing the program defines.

items.title: Ian Hacking on suggestibility: from psychology to logic.
items.abstract: This paper aims to clarify Ian Hacking’s understanding of a key psychological concept: suggestibility. This is the phenomenon whereby a person adopts an external idea as if it originated from within themselves. The central text of reference is Hacking’s Rewriting the Soul, in which he examines the emergence of multiple personality disorder. Throughout his account, Hacking repeatedly expresses a critical stance toward the term and explanations based on suggestibility. He characterizes it as a vague notion and a superficial explanation of multiple personality (pp. 255–256). However, a few lines later, while discussing “semantic contagion,” Hacking argues that the latter concept should be understood as a form of suggestion (p. 256). This is noteworthy since semantic contagion forms part of his own account of multiple personality, namely through the framework of “making up people” (p. 239). These ambiguous statements raise the question of how Hacking’s ontological project can be understood in terms of suggestibility. I argue that Hacking’s understanding of suggestibility is both psychological and logical, and show how this concept illuminates Hacking’s historical ontology and its continued relevance in contemporary psychological debates.

items.title: Does J-Space Cross the Standpoint Threshold?
items.abstract: “The Standpoint Threshold” argues that consciousness-oriented inquiry into an artificial system is not well formed until its internal organization satisfies three jointly necessary conditions: persistent internal context, differentiated internal possibility, and closed-loop operativity. Gurnee et al. report J-space, a sparse representational structure in Claude models that they argue is causally privileged and exhibits several functional properties of a global workspace. This note applies the threshold’s diagnostic schema to those results. Gurnee et al.’s account of transformer feedforward processing identifies the architectural feature that Condition 1 treats as the relevant persistence limitation. Their causal interventions closely approximate the threshold’s proposed test for differentiated internal possibility, providing bounded positive evidence; their selectivity experiments provide unusually clean evidence for the role-differentiation component of Condition 3. The post-training emergence of an Assistant-relative point of view sharpens the near-case without dislodging Condition 1 as the binding constraint: a reliable disposition to reconstruct a system-relative orientation from supplied context is not yet an internal state maintained and modified across separate invocations. The central result is narrow: J-space changes the evidential status of the bounded near-case, not its classification. The note concludes with three tests – History Equalization, Continuation–Reconstruction, and Active-Carryover – for distinguishing externally reconstructed continuity from genuinely maintained internal orientation in persistent architectures.

items.title: From stability to responsibility: the ethical evolution of AI-driven control systems.
items.abstract: The control engineering discipline is undergoing a fundamental shift in its ethical approach. Historically centered on the technical trio of stability, performance, and robustness, the field operated within a paradigm that largely overlooked broader ethical implications. However, the rise of AI-driven and autonomous control systems has challenged this neutrality. This shift necessitates a transition from traditional control objectives to a new design-level responsibility framework. This paper proposes a control-theoretic framework for embedding ethical deliberation directly into the architecture of AI-driven autonomous systems.
