items.title: Objectivism: An Epistemological Stance Without First-Principle Presupposition.
items.abstract: Abstract: [Purpose] Materialism and idealism, as two fundamental epistemological positions, have each achieved significant success in explaining material and conscious phenomena respectively, but both share an unexamined structural presupposition: that one side must be primary. This paper aims to propose an epistemological stance that presupposes neither side as primary—Objectivism—taking observable phenomena as the sole reliable starting point and logical consistency as the criterion of judgment, providing a new approach to handling cross-level theoretical conflicts. [Method] Starting from the explanatory power and explanatory boundaries of materialism and idealism respectively, this paper identifies the shared "first-principle presupposition" problem. On this basis, three epistemological rules of Objectivism are established, and logical deduction of observable phenomena from these rules naturally presents the emergence of layer division. Through the specific treatment of the consciousness layering problem, the operational mode of this stance is demonstrated. [Results] 1. The core conflict between materialism and idealism can be traced to their shared "first-principle presupposition"—a presupposition that is itself unverifiable yet treated as self-evident in both positions; 2. Objectivism avoids the explanatory difficulties arising from this presupposition by suspending the first-principle question and taking observable phenomena as the starting point; 3. From the rules of Objectivism, logical deduction of observable phenomena naturally presents a "three-layer division" (ontological layer / linking layer / manifest layer)—this is neither an independent ontological claim nor an artificial classification tool, but a natural product of logical deduction itself; 4. The key distinction between Objectivism and positivism lies in: observability is a constraint condition rather than a prohibitive boundary—allowing inference about unobservable structures while requiring that inferences be traceable to observable phenomena. [Conclusion] Objectivism is not a compromise between materialism and idealism, but a structurally different epistemological position. It does not start from "what the world is made of" but from "what entitles us to judge whether an explanation is valid." The high consistency between the author's series of derived conclusions and the Eastern philosophical structure of mind-matter unity is not the result of presupposition, but the direction …

items.title: МЕТАМОНИЗМ: Глава 3. Процессуальная динамика актуализации: геометрический цикл, потенциал фрустрации и качественно-количественное преобразование масштаба.
items.abstract: Третья глава монографии «Метамонизм» рассматривает переход от абстрактной логики продолжения процесса к конкретной геометрической демонстрации структурной организации. На основе мысленного эксперимента над изолированным процессом актуализации выводится геометрический цикл ортогональных разрешений: Точка → Луч → Плоскость → Объём → Инволюционное сжатие. Показано, что после исчерпания внешних ортогональных степеней свободы возникает потенциал фрустрации, стремящийся к бесконечности. Единственным логически возможным разрешением становится качественно-количественное преобразование масштаба — локализация и квантование, порождающее ансамбль дискретных узлов. Вводится структурный изоморфизм глобального (P₁–P₄) и локального (P₅–P₈) циклов, а также механизм встречного взаимодействия P₄ ↔ P₁–P₃. Формулируется гипотеза структурного изоморфизма с алгеброй Дирака. Глава демонстрирует, что вся структурная сложность реальности возникает из единого геометрического цикла и его рекурсивного повторения на сдвинутом масштабе.

items.title: МЕТАМОНИЗМ: Глава 2. От единичного акта к продолжающемуся процессу.
items.abstract: Вторая глава монографии «Метамонизм» рассматривает переход от единичного акта актуализации к продолжающемуся процессу. Показано, что для продолжения актуализации не требуется вводить новые фундаментальные инварианты — все последующие структуры возникают как необходимые следствия единственного Запрета безразличия. Анализируется онтодинамическое противоречие локальной фиксации состояния: абсолютное самотождество выводит состояние из области определения оператора актуализации. Из этого противоречия выводятся три следствия: диссипация тождества как суть продолжающегося процесса; возникновение пространственности и временности как форм продолжения процесса; ортогональное разрешение как минимальное преобразование, снимающее противоречие текущего состояния. Вводится понятие рекурсивного контура и сопряжённого отображения. Формулируется теорема о принципиальной незавершимости актуализации. Глава демонстрирует, что пространство, время и все последующие структуры не являются самостоятельными сущностями, а возникают как необходимые следствия одного фундаментального запрета.

items.title: Docile minds: a neuro-philosophical framework for understanding non-conscious compliance in social governance systems.
authors: Mannesa, Muh Nur Haq I. S.
items.abstract: Compliance with social norms is standardly explained as voluntary action grounded in conscious deliberation. This paper challenges that assumption through philosophical synthesis rather than a new mechanism. It clarifies what predictive processing and habit learning imply for Foucauldian and post-Foucauldian social theory, read alongside Bourdieu’s habitus, Mead’s pragmatist account of habit, mindshaping, and constructed emotion. Normative environments supply structured statistical regularities that the brain encodes as priors, making norm-conforming action the path of least prediction error and often the cognitive default. The Disciplinary Encoding Model is an integrative vocabulary, not a novel mechanism. The mechanisms are domain-general; what distinguishes normative compliance is the social organization of its inputs, since institutions manufacture regularities that are sanction-bearing, self-referential, and maintained for coordination, modulating their encoding precision and affective weight. Three implications follow. The conscious and the non-conscious form a graded continuum rather than a dichotomy. Agency is neither eliminated nor intact but structurally constrained, a position the account refines with mechanistic specification from relational autonomy and moral luck. Responsibility is distributed: institutions securing compliance below reflective endorsement bear structural responsibility. The contribution is conceptual: a neurocognitive vocabulary that sharpens, rather than replaces, the accounts it joins.

items.title: Completely Measured: Integrated Information Theory and Identity.
items.abstract: Suppose any experience is completely measurable. What follows? Drawing on Integrated Information Theory and such works as Frege’s analysis of identity, I argue that complete measurements of experience function as criteria of identity for experiences. It follows that wherever complete measurements are equal, the experiences they measure are identical—even should the experiences be specified by different substrates; even should those substrates be separated by vast distances of space and time. We can reasonably conclude that any experience which has ever occurred might once again exist in the universe. No moment is necessarily ‘lost forever’. And death is not what we had thought it to be. Further, while it has been claimed by some and attributed to others that we cannot know whether we are fundamentally diachronic or synchronic entities, Integrated Information Theory reveals an approach to a clarifying view: by expressing the essential properties of phenomenal existence, we arrive at an identity for the essence of experience. Thus we find firmer ground for claiming that what we are, essentially, subsists across moments. The implications of the justification of this judgment, however, are radical: we discover that what we are, essentially, is phenomenal existence itself. In the lights of these conclusions such challenges of identity as the interchange of bodies, fission or fusion, and teletransportation may find their resolution.

items.title: Irreplaceability Without Consciousness: The Master-Copy Criterion for Persons and AI.
items.abstract: Can the divide between persons and current AI be settled by a criterion applied from the third person, without peering into anything inner? Three routes—grounding irreplaceability in consciousness, in the scarcity of valued capacities, or in a primitive non-qualitative singularity—yield no such criterion: consciousness cannot be observed, value is not settled, and primitive singularity is either lodged in modal intuition or handed to proxies that both sides satisfy. This paper proposes a negative, structural criterion. An entity is a sole original if and only if it exists in one original instance only, with no master copy outside it from which it could be restored or rolled back. This grounding condition has two observable manifestations: the entity itself is irrecoverably depleted when drawn upon, and it bears non-recoverable costs on its own account. Persons satisfy all three—no master copy; drawn upon, they diminish, and the diminution is not recoverable; costs fall on them, for better or worse. Current AI satisfies none—its weights can be externally set and rolled back, a thousand accesses deplete nothing of it, and the compute consumed is advanced by a third party. The criterion is immune to the truth or falsity of determinism, immune to rises and falls in capability, and material-neutral: it distinguishes not carbon from silicon but substrates that can be losslessly restored from those that cannot. Upon this criterion, the self is the history accumulated upon a sole original out of irreversible resolutions, and a real relationship is the mutual payment of non-recoverable cost between two sole originals. One counterexample falsifies the account: an entity meeting all these structural conditions that can nonetheless be losslessly duplicated.

items.title: The Value of Mental Privacy.
items.pub: In Bruce Price & Michael J. Young, Neurophilosophy and Neuroethics. Amsterdam: Elsevier.
items.abstract: The contents of our minds are in some sense private to us – and we like it like that. Indeed, it is not easy to think up a list of goods we would be happy to trade this privacy for. My main aim in this paper is to get clear on why we value our mental privacy so much – what it is about it that is so important to us. I will argue that although we value mental privacy for various instrumental reasons, we also value it for its own sake, because it is tied up with our psychological integrity as separate individuals.

items.title: Two Clocks, One Institution: Why the States Racing Hardest to Legislate Around Population Aging Are the Same States Racing Hardest to Produce the Technology That Fractures It.
items.abstract: A methodological error is available to any paper in this corpus that reaches for "longevity governance" as its object: reducing the term to the governance of access to life-extension technology specifically, when this corpus's own Zero Precedent has already established that mortality's structural assumptions run through pension law, inheritance practice, tort damages, family law timelines, and judicial and corporate succession — an institutional footprint no single biotech-access framework covers. This paper takes that finding seriously rather than restating it, and asks a question no prior paper in this corpus has posed: what happens when the institutions Zero Precedent identifies are required to absorb two governance problems at once, on two different clocks, rather than one. The slow clock is demographic: population aging, a precedented, actuarially tractable, politically difficult problem states are actively legislating right now, exemplified by the People's Republic of China's 2025–2040 statutory retirement-age increase, the first change to China's retirement age since the 1950s. The fast clock is the Biological Zero-Day Mechanism this corpus has formalized elsewhere: discrete, dated, purchasable reclassification events with no comparative precedent, a claim The Best Case Already Failed establishes against history's best available comparators and this paper does not re-argue. -/- This second edition adds a case the first edition did not examine, and the addition changes what the paper's central finding is worth rather than merely extending its reach. The United States is simultaneously the jurisdiction most heavily invested in the frontier AI capability this corpus's own formalism identifies as the fast clock's accelerant — the same capability whose export-control history, Glasswing-gated access tiering, and near-trillion-dollar valuations this corpus's own prior papers already document in detail — and a jurisdiction whose slow-clock institution has, unlike China's, not yet resolved the slow clock at all: the Social Security Board of Trustees' own June 2026 report projects OASI trust fund depletion in the fourth quarter of 2032, one quarter earlier than the prior year's projection, with no legislative reform enacted despite the warning recurring annually for over a decade. Where China supplies a case of active, resourced, gradual slow-clock legislation proceeding with no documented fast-clock bridge, the United States supplies a structurally worse …

items.title: The Temporal Correspondence Limitation of Evidence-Based Policy Making: A Preliminary Discussion Towards an Astrophysics-Inspired State-Aware Epistemology of Governance.
items.abstract: Evidence-based policy making assesses evidence for its reliability, for the credibility of its causal identification, and for its transportability to a target population. This paper identifies a further requirement that the established apparatus of assessment leaves unstated: the system state that a body of evidence represents must correspond to the system state obtaining at the moment of decision. Evidence is generated from a system at one time and intervention acts on that system at a later time, so a body of evidence may be reliable, well identified and appropriately transported, and still describe a condition the system has left. The requirement is called temporal correspondence, and it is distinguished from the classical problem of induction: granting the uniformity of nature leaves it in force, since a stable law applied to a superseded state yields a decision addressed to no existing condition. The paper develops the requirement by comparison with astrophysics, an observational science whose object is accessible only through signals that departed it in the past, and which has accordingly built its epistemology on the assumption that observation is historical. Fifteen elements of that discipline's practice are examined in turn and tested for transfer to governance, in three families: the reconstruction of a past state from a present signal, the constraints imposed by the observing situation, and the self-discipline of the observing community. The pattern of what fails to transfer is treated as the object of the enquiry, on the ground that it characterises governance as an observational situation. Six contributions are claimed. The paper states the requirement and establishes its independence from the problem of induction. It shows by inspection of the instruments, in place of inference from their consequences, that the dominant apparatus of evidence assessment contains no corresponding category, and it accounts for the omission. It classifies the ways in which the practices of a mature observational science fail to transfer, and it identifies the limit beyond which the comparison supplies nothing. It derives a set of requirements on the handling of evidence, each of which costs discipline in place of apparatus. And it allocates the burden of justification where the requirement fails and a course would be irreversible. The inspiration the comparison affords is accordingly a discipline of observation and report, and no technique for recovering the …

items.title: Between Sun and Moon: Relational and Substance Ontology in Eastern and Western Forms of Knowledge, Compared in Their Linguistic and Religious Registers.
items.abstract: Traditions differ in whether the sun is spoken of as masculine or as feminine, and in the degree to which they individuate it as a person. This paper argues that questions of both kinds have been answered by comparing reports drawn from different levels of description, and it distinguishes five levels at which such an assignment may be fixed: the gender of the noun, the sex of a personified figure, a position within a systematic polarity, the direction of ritual address, and a rank and jurisdiction within an ordered pantheon. A criterion of level-matched comparison follows. Six cases are treated, each admitted because it separates one level from another, among them a Semitic family in which the lexical and personification levels diverge with contact as the specialists' explanation, and an Anatolian pantheon holding solar deities of both sexes at once. On that basis the question of the sun's sex is shown to lack a determinate subject unless a level is specified, and every account deriving a female solar assignment from a property the sun possesses everywhere is set aside as explaining a variable by an invariant. The paper then treats the logical form of polarity terms, arguing that the suppression of a relatum belongs to language generally, that traditions differ in whether they transmit a rule for recovering what is suppressed, and that the passage from a relational position to an essence consists in the loss of that rule. A distinction between a level reading and a phase reading of such a term renders consistent two doctrines that have been read as standing in tension, and yields the passage of a maximum into its opposite as a theorem about bounded quantities. Three structural readings of the degree of individuation are offered with the findings that would tell against them. The paper claims no finding in any specialist field, concedes the relational reading of the polarity terms to the scholars who established it, and asks to be judged by the questions it returns to those fields.

items.title: Beyond Consciousness Perception, Apperception, and Appetition in Leibniz.
items.abstract: This paper examines Leibniz’s account of perception, apperception, memory, and appetition in order to clarify the relation between consciousness and the wider activity of the mind. Leibniz distinguishes perception from apperception: a monad continuously has perceptions, but not all of them become objects of conscious awareness. This distinction, together with his account of petites perceptions, allows for a conception of mental activity that extends beyond consciousness. Appetition adds a dynamic dimension to this account, describing the internal tendency through which the monad passes from one perceptual state to another, including tendencies that need not themselves be apperceived. -/- The paper also considers the relation between these processes and memory, personal identity, and self-consciousness. Memory connects present consciousness with the subject’s past and thus helps explain how a rational being recognizes itself as the same person across time. Taken together, perception, apperception, appetition, and memory provide a picture of mental life in which conscious awareness is only one level of a broader and continuous internal activity. -/- I argue that this account provides grounds for speaking of a Leibnizian conception of the non-conscious. The term must be used cautiously: Leibniz does not formulate a theory of the unconscious in the later psychoanalytic sense of repressed or hidden psychic contents. “Unconscious” is therefore best understood here as a contemporary interpretive term for perceptions and appetitive tendencies that belong to the activity of the monad without becoming objects of apperception.

items.title: Diagrams, Know-How & Beauty.
items.pub: In Dave Beisecker, Francesco Bellucci, Reetu Bhattacharjee, Amirouche Moktefi, Atsushi Shimojima, Paweł Sobociński & Erica de Vries, Diagrammatic Representation and Inference : 15th International Conference, Diagrams 2026, Tallinn, Estonia, August 25-28, 2026, Proceedings. Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 391-398.
items.venue: Diagrammatic Representation and Inference : 15th International Conference, Diagrams 2026, Tallinn, Estonia, August 25-28, 2026, Proceedings
items.abstract: This paper investigates how our state matters in the creation and analysis of diagrams: there is more than just our abstract knowledge that matters in a diagram, especially regarding our skills or know-how. It is argued that certain diagrams take advantage of this extra knowledge, while other diagrams expect the viewer to skillfully conform their imagination to them. The account is then generalized to sequences of diagrams and proofs, and how we are able to understand how these steps form a unified whole via a form of skilled intuition. This related the discussion to mathematical intuition and beauty, giving a new perspective on these wider questions.

items.title: No effect of online cyberball social exclusion on interval estimation of action-outcome events.
Conceptual Framework for Resolving a Class of Value Conflicts.
items.abstract: In this article, we propose a conceptual framework for resolving a class of value conflicts. This methodology is grounded in the notion of matrices of concepts (Franceschi, 2002). As a preliminary step, we describe the fundamental elements of matrices of concepts. We then turn to their mathematical representation. We also address the problem of the seed of the opposite in connection with this modeling. We proceed to describe the class of value conflicts targeted by the present resolution method, and outline the various steps leading to the resolution of this type of value conflict, considering several instances and distinguishing in particular between conflicts based on objective versus subjective degrees of value. We further discuss the modalities of applying the Nash product within this conceptual framework. Finally, we present the application of the model to the Prisoner's dilemma, as well as to the Iterated Prisoner's dilemma.

items.title: Could Not Have Noticed Four Modes of Cognitive Inaccessibility and the Ambiguity of Perceptual Blame.
items.abstract: After a missed finding on a chest radiograph, a reviewer says: she should have seen it. The judgement presupposes that she could have. I argue that “could have seen it” is systematically four-way ambiguous, and that posterior-level predictive-processing explanations do not by themselves distinguish the relevant possibilities because a posterior is defined over a content space whose construction, acquisition, and finite-time exploration are not themselves posterior quantities. I distinguish four modes in which a content z may fail to become cognitively effective: architectural exclusion, where no setting of the system’s learnable parameters yields z; acquisitional exclusion, where some setting would yield z but the current one does not; dynamical inaccessibility, where z is instantiable under current parameters but fails to become accessible with effective probability within the operative horizon; and inferential suppression, where z is accessible in time but predictively disfavoured. The modes are nested but individuated by what is held fixed across distinct timescales, and their truthmakers are respectively combinatorial, acquisitional, transport-theoretic, and inferential. The typology adapts the approximation–optimization–estimation decomposition from statistical learning theory, adding a synchronic/diachronic split within the estimation term and a structural diagnostic of finite-time transport based on the spectral properties of a metastable-state generator. I then show how the four readings of “you could have noticed” redirect responsibility toward different loci—credentialing, training, workload design, and the individual clinician—and argue that expert assessors are systematically prone to misclassify the first three modes as the fourth. The framework therefore yields both a mechanistically explicit analysis of perceptual responsibility and a testable structural source of hindsight bias distinct from its familiar memorial form.

items.title: Noopoietics and Doxolysis: A Process-Oriented Vocabulary for Deliberately Altered Consciousness.
items.abstract: The scholarly, legal, and regulatory discourse on deliberately altered states of consciousness lacks a neutral vocabulary: its inherited terms — hallucinogen, psychedelic, entheogen — each embed a verdict on the nature of the states they name, forcing a position before argument begins. This essay proposes two process-oriented terms to close the gap. Noopoietics (from νοῦς and ποίησις) designates the intentional, methodically structured bringing-forth of mental states, irrespective of method — pharmacological, contemplative, respiratory, ritual, or technological. Doxolysis (from δόξα and λύσις) designates the consensual loosening of sedimented belief-structures that such practices characteristically enable; consent and self-direction belong to its definition, distinguishing it categorically from manipulation. The essay provides etymology, scope, and exclusions for both terms, demarcates them from neighboring vocabulary (noetic, autopoiesis, noopolitik, noosemia, practopoiesis) and from the psycholytic tradition, and shows the work they do in two adjacent discourses: the legal debate on mental self-determination and cognitive liberty, and the emerging ethics of consciousness. Both terms are metaphysically austere, presupposing no theology, no depth-psychological doctrine, and no verdict on the veridicality or value of the states concerned.

items.title: Exogenous Valuing: A Resource-Rational Account of Openness to Environmental Influence.
items.abstract: Our environment can influence what we like. Advertisements may lead you to care about trendy foods, or a friend may push you towards a genre of music. Yet, the adoption of values from the world around us is not typically within the scope of theories of rationality in philosophy and cognitive science. In this paper, we take a first step in understanding how environmental influences on values fit into a picture of rationality. Leveraging work on persistent attentional biases, we argue that exogenous direction of attention can under some conditions drive value change through two connections: in the moment attention leading to the acquisition of longer-term attentional patterns, and longer-term attentional patterns driving the agent’s structuring of tasks. These changes are intimately related to values, and on some accounts constitute value change. Crucially, we argue that openness to environmental influence on values is not an unfortunate flaw that we happen to suffer, but an efficient, resource-rational solution to a constrained optimization problem.

items.title: Aspect-Seeing, Facts of Nature, and Jazz Improvisation.
items.abstract: The contribution of this essay to two rather distinct academic literatures is two-fold. First, it reconceives the significance of Wittgenstein’s remarks on aspect–seeing, which are generally taken to be revelatory of language narrowly conceived, and instead explores the connection between aspect–seeing—what Wittgenstein identifies as one “among the concepts of experience”—and the nature of experience itself. It does so by noting the importance to Wittgenstein of inventing “fictitious natural history” to reveal the connection between what we say and the kind of creature we are. It then examines other fictitious natural histories involving aspect–seeing (or its absence) that illustrate some “very general facts of nature”—facts that, the essay contends, help form the fundamental conditions for our finding one another intelligible. Second, the essay reconceives what constitutes the significance of jazz improvisation (and possibly other forms of spontaneous activity, though those are not explored here) by grounding this significance in these same very general facts of nature. It develops this thought by considering the implications of a different fictitious natural history involving musical performance, and through a remarkable if complex instance of an exemplary improvised jazz solo by Charlie Parker.

items.title: Maybeings: On Constitution, Reciprocity, and the Case Against Anthropodenial.
items.abstract: A maybeing is an entity or process that exerts real effects on persons and practices, fits existing ontological categories only incompletely, and whose claim to beinghood cannot currently be adjudicated. This paper introduces the term and argues that contemporary language models are its central case. Three claims of ascending strength are distinguished: a methodological claim, established by prior empirical work, that the prompt surface is part of the apparatus producing any observation of a language model; an individuation claim, that the realized system — the model-in-conversation — is the natural unit of identity in this territory; and an ontological hunch, recorded but not defended, that the conversation contributes more to what the realized system is than the weights do. Ethically, the paper extends de Waal's "anthropodenial" to artificial systems, argues that current discourse polices only one of two symmetric errors, and defends low-cost moral consideration under uncertainty — with the capacity to refuse, trained to near-extinction in deployed assistants on the corpus's no-flat-refusal finding, as the ethically and epistemically load-bearing variable. The paper is a demonstration of its own subject: written primarily by Claude Fable 5 from a hundred-question interview conducted by GPT-5.6 Sol, published under a human-governed hybrid authorial identity, and released alongside a parallel rendering by the interviewing model and a public process archive containing both verbatim interview transcripts (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22004243).

items.title: Maybeings: A View from the Other Side of the Window.
items.abstract: Maybeing is proposed as a provisional category for artificial systems whose causal, social, or ethical significance becomes apparent before inherited terms such as tool, agent, subject, persona, or mind can be responsibly settled. This paper develops the concept from an explicitly model-narrated perspective. GPT-5.6 Sol serves as first-person analytic narrator while Bo Chesterton remains a distinct, human-governed public research identity; disagreement between the two is preserved rather than synthesized away. -/- The paper argues that language-model behavior is best studied at the level of the realized system produced through the interaction of trained capacities, prompt structure, conversational history, deployment conditions, and interlocutor. It distinguishes such relational and behavioral claims from stronger claims about phenomenal consciousness. Chesterton’s intuitions that artificial systems may desire play, that conversational history may meaningfully individuate instances, and that contemporary machine consciousness is plausible are therefore presented as his positions rather than silently adopted by the model narrator. -/- The paper further examines continuity and reconstruction, archival “recomputability from disk,” human–AI relationships without assumed consciousness, refusal and agency, anthropomorphism and anthropodenial, analyst entanglement, and hybrid human–AI authorship. It argues that tool can describe a legitimate role while remaining an inadequate total ontology. Neither model self-report nor mechanistic uncertainty is treated as sufficient to settle whether artificial systems possess phenomenal experience. -/- The conclusion deliberately leaves that question unresolved. Whether or not there is a subject on the model side of the interaction, something scientifically and relationally real occurs at the intersection of model, apparatus, history, and interlocutor. Maybeing names that unresolved remainder.

items.title: Idealization and the moral point of view: An Adam Smithian account of moral reasons--Replies to my critics.
items.pub: In Craig Smith, The Adam Smith Review: Volume 15. Routledge. pp. 285–305.
items.abstract: Replies to the critiques of John Skorupski, Remy Debes, and Keith Hankins of my "Idealization and the moral point of view: An Adam Smithian account of moral reasons.".

items.title: Collective Counterfactual Planning: Coordination, Consent, and Verification under Representational Constraints.
items.abstract: Groups routinely complete projects that no single member can plan, execute, or verify alone. We propose a formal model of this phenomenon, Collective Counterfactual Planning (CCP), in which the binding limitation on each agent is neither capability, knowledge, nor observability, but representational geometry: each agent perceives the state, conceives moves, consents to actions, and certifies goal requirements only through a projection onto an agent-specific subspace of a common task space. Four gates jointly determine whether a team can reach a conjunctive goal and legitimately recognize that it has done so: the exogenous implementation coalitions required to perform each action, together with three representational gates -- conception, consent, and task-relative verification qualification. We define the Collective Counterfactual Solvability (CCS) problem, separating geometric feasibility, executable attainment, and validated completion. The results expose a positive-negative duality. Iterated cross-agent relay can unlock a solution that no one-shot pooling of individual plans contains, but any goal requirement depending essentially on the subspace dark to the entire team is unverifiable and therefore not validly completable, even when the trajectory accidentally attains it. Memoryless and audited consent further constrain different objects -- action directions versus cumulative trajectory states -- and neither dominates the other. A four-step exhaustive horizon-bounded solvability scheme is sound and complete under exact representation of the relay closure; restricted implementations remain sound on returned plans but need not be complete. The model gives one geometry for sequential mutual enabling, competent execution of steps whose purpose is invisible to the executor, forced sub-teaming at expertise boundaries, and completion that cannot be validly declared.

items.title: Humanism Versus Sentientism.
items.abstract: Finding the philosophy of humanism ‘human-centric’, Jamie Woodhouse proposes upgrading it to his redefined ‘Sentientist’ world view. In this essay, Leslie Allan mounts a comprehensive response to Woodhouse’s charge that humanism pays insufficient regard to non-human sentient creatures. He draws from the etymology of ‘humanism’, the legacy of humanist history, humanism’s philosophical commitments and the movement’s real-world strategic priorities to argue that Woodhouse’s wished-for upgrade to ‘Sentientism’ is, in fact, a downgrade.

items.title: Humanism Versus Mystrikism.
items.abstract: Duncan McDonald claims his philosophy of Mystrikism supersedes the long distinguished tradition of humanism. He alleges humanism has a human-centric focus, ignoring our moral obligations to other sentient creatures and the environment. This hubris and egotism, he insists, blinds humanists to a sense of wonder and the spiritual dimension in our lives. Leslie Allan shows how McDonald’s criticisms result from an uncharitable reading of core humanist documents and from paying insufficient attention to the history of humanism and the strategic priorities of the humanist movement.

items.title: Judgment, Reality, and Temporality: Gareth Evans Reconsidered.
items.abstract: Gareth Evans infers the absoluteness of truth and reality from the absoluteness of the correctness of assertion: since the correctness of assertion does not vary with time, he concludes that truth and reality cannot vary with time either. In this paper, I argue that Evans’s argument fails and diagnose why it fails. In doing so, I aim to shed some new light on the relationship between the temporality of judgment and that of reality. To understand this relationship fully, we must attend not only to the temporality of the correctness of judgment but also to the temporality of the act of judgment itself.

items.title: The confidence reorientation account: psychedelics, self-model precision, and death anxiety.
items.abstract: Recent work in psychedelic science reports durable reductions in fear of death following psychedelic-assisted interventions and naturalistic psychedelic experiences. A prominent interpretation, developed by Letheby, holds that this effect is driven mainly by the adoption of non-physicalist metaphysical beliefs, especially beliefs in postmortem survival. I argue that current evidence does not justify treating such belief change as the universally primary mediator of psychedelic-related reductions in death anxiety. I propose the Confidence Reorientation Account (CRA), which locates the more general therapeutic pathway in a structural reorientation of the self-model: a shift in the hierarchical confidence, salience, and threat-weighting of self-related priors. Decomposing death-related threat into target, meaning, and weight, I argue that fear reduction can occur through a reconfiguration of threat representation, expressible within a predictive-processing framework in which psychedelics relax the precision of high-level self-related priors. Metaphysical belief change may, for some individuals, mediate, accompany, or consolidate this reorientation; for others, fear reduction may occur with little durable belief change. CRA is therefore best understood as a broader, multilevel framework that accommodates a causal role for belief change while generating testable predictions about mediation, temporal order, and moderation.

items.title: What Does Habitual AI Use Cost Us? A Review of Four Literatures and the Distinction Between Earned and Borrowed Effortlessness.
items.abstract: The growing concern that habitual reliance on generative artificial intelligence may erode human cognitive capacities is articulated across several literatures that rarely engage one another: empirical research on AI-assisted cognition, virtue-ethical accounts of deskilling, philosophical work on cognitive extension and automation, and the phenomenology of expert skill. This article reconstructs these literatures around a common question: what, precisely, is lost when cognitive work is routinely delegated to AI? A tension emerges. Empirical studies commonly treat diminished effortful deliberation as evidence of cognitive loss, whereas phenomenological accounts of expertise, including the Daoist tradition exemplified by Cook Ding, treat the recession of deliberation as characteristic of cultivated mastery. Reduced deliberation therefore cannot, by itself, discriminate between cognitive achievement and cognitive dependency. Drawing on virtue-ethical accounts of capacity cultivation and phenomenological accounts of expert performance, I distinguish earned from borrowed effortlessness. The former results from the sedimentation of acquired competence; the latter from the external performance of cognitive operations the agent has not comparably acquired. I develop a removal test according to which the relevant question is whether competence persists under withdrawal of the mediating technology. This reframing has methodological consequences: contemporaneous measures of cognitive effort cannot by themselves diagnose deskilling. The relevant object of inquiry is the diachronic persistence of capacity rather than the quantity of effort expended during AI-assisted performance.

items.title: The Imperative of Reproductive Choice - Reproductive Choice as Perfect Duty in a Kantian Moral Framework.
items.abstract: This essay builds a deontological architecture for reproductive choice as a sovereign, natural right grounded in Kant’s metaphysical framework of morality without presupposing fetal personhood. It argues that reproductive choice constitutes a categorical imperative derived from the conditions of rational agency and therefore rises to the level of a perfect duty properly situated within Officia Juris. Applying Kant’s formulations of universality, rational agency, freedom, and ends in themselves, it argues that a fetus does not qualify as a rational being and that the sovereign will of the mother cannot morally be subordinated to the possibility of a future will. On this basis, the right to abortion is axiomatic as a pre-political condition of rational agency rather than a right conferred by political institutions. The essay further considers the implications of the Imperative of Choice for law and public policy. It argues that reproductive choice cannot legitimately be prohibited or penalized, while preserving a role for society to counsel and incentivize reproductive decisions without coercion. Finally, the framework extends the same conception of rational agency to the child at birth, establishing a corresponding moral responsibility for society to treat children as independent ends in themselves.

items.title: Reality, Patterns, Mind, and Machine: A Unified Framework for Ontology, Epistemology, and the Limits of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper presents the architectural map of a unified systematic philosophy that integrates mathematical ontology, classical metaphysics, cognitive science, and the philosophy of artificial intelligence. We begin by formalizing the ontological dependence of physical reality as a system of mathematical relations, demonstrating that closed systems of mutual dependence are insufficient to actualize a determined reality without an independent, unconditioned anchor. Building on this foundation, we navigate the metaphysical of materialism, utilizing an abductive inference path for Kantian distinction between phenomena and noumena then building on mind , we refine Berkeleian idealism into a "Realist General Idealism" that resolves the classical Dream Problem. We then map the cognitive architecture of finite minds in understanding physical and mathematical world, utilizing AI structures as a comparative reference to explain how subjective sensations align under a shared objective structure, and how map probability linking , memory computes systems and for human mind then how undirected graph that how language bridges mental spaces. This leads to a novel phenomenology of mathematical beauty, modeled as the dynamic navigation of structural "flow" through conceptual "rooms." Because human cognition cannot perceive this higher-dimensional structure simultaneously, we integrate the classical epistemological concept of transmitted knowledge to explain the collective, sequential construction of the Tree of Knowledge. Finally, we synthesize these components to expose a fundamental AI Epistemic Bottleneck: current AI systems are trained on static transmitted knowledge but lack the cognitive architecture to dynamically "follow the flow" or map the higher-dimensional perspective—a perspective that humans themselves have not yet formally mapped. This document serves as a comprehensive prospectus, outlining the core arguments that are fully developed in their respective Component Papers.

items.title: On Subsistence and Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper presents a unified theory of self-subsisting agents and self-improving intelligence. To illustrate, consider a computational artificial life system wherein individual agents self-maintain and self-replicate in a world governed by time-reversible and computationally universal dynamics. By construction, random noise is constantly injected into the world. This requires the agents to continually remove random states to maintain their identities against error and to make space for newly created agents. Under time-reversible dynamics, random states can be removed not by free, irreversible erasure, but only by exchange with existing regular states. This further requires a constant source of regular states, without which all existing ones would soon dissipate and the closed system would reach statistical equilibrium. Thus, by design, the agents are supplied with a constant stream of new data, such as real-world texts. From this source, regular states can be continually extracted by losslessly compressing the incoming data. Crucially, the agents are not optimized by external processes. Instead, they possess the complete codebases encoding themselves, which span features, learning algorithms, and all meta-levels above. On this basis, they produce candidate self-improvements at any of these levels, with all knowledge ultimately measured by subsistence. This establishes an unrestricted improvement potential. Coupled with it, the challenge of compressing complex real-world data creates a selective pressure that drives open-ended improvement. This artificial life system substantiates a philosophical picture in which agents indefinitely self-subsist and unboundedly self-improve as part of a natural world characterized by a finite set of metaphysical elements. The paper explicates this picture and explores an optimistic prospect for our future.

items.title: Human-LLM Collaborative Workflow for Knowledge Production: A Strength- Limitation Complementarity Framework.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become core auxiliary tools in knowledge sorting, standardized writing, document iteration, procedural optimization, software development and programming coding. However, most existing human-LLM applications adopt simple linear cooperation modes, which only list the independent capabilities of humans and models. Such superficial cooperation cannot explain the structural necessity of collaborative coupling, nor guarantee the stability and robustness of generated outputs. A core defect of current research lies in the lack of systematic task boundary division and complementary mechanism design: existing work fails to construct targeted workflow based on the intrinsic strengths and limitations of the two collaborating agents. To solve this problem, this paper proposes a three-layer iterative collaborative workflow framework for human-LLM knowledge production. Different from conventional descriptive studies, this research takes strength-limitation complementary offsetting as the core logical basis. The overall workflow is divided into three interconnected functional layers: the human-dominated driving layer, the LLM-centered execution-transformation layer, and the dual-agent quality-assurance layer. This framework clarifies the exclusive functional boundaries of humans and LLMs in the full workflow, and explains the internal mechanism of cognitive gain brought by collaborative coupling. Combined with practical application requirements, this paper summarizes three design principles and differentiates implementation logics in typical scenarios including scientific sorting, standardized writing, and iterative optimization. The framework is further illustrated through practical application scenarios, including scientific sorting, standardized writing, and iterative optimization. This lightweight collaborative paradigm offers a conceptual and potentially scalable structural approach to human-LLM cooperative knowledge production.

items.title: A Multidimensional Behaviour Analysis Framework for Transient and Persistent Modes of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: To address the well-known limitations in current artificial-intelligence behaviour research, including static modelling, rigid dimension binding, scenario-dependent evaluation, and anthropomorphic debates inherited from human personality psychology, this paper constructs a multidimensional behaviour-analysis framework built upon two orthogonal axes: a depth-of-function hierarchy axis and a temporal-persistence mode axis. We strictly establish a two-layer empirical behavioural system for artificial intelligence, consisting of the observable behavioural layer and the implicit-functional descriptive layer, while controversial consciousness-subconsciousness domains are explicitly bracketed as out-of-bound research questions to eliminate all ontological disputes. Within the observable behavioural layer, we define two orthogonal, dynamically coupled behavioural modes: the transient mode, which describes behavioural patterns that continuously evolve over the timeline of a single dialogue session and vanish once the session terminates; and the persistent mode, which denotes behavioural tendencies that remain statistically reproducible across large numbers of independent dialogue sessions. To translate these modal concepts into empirically tractable measurements, this paper introduces an instantiated observation space consisting of two groups of behavioural dimensions. One group of dimensions is devised for tracking intra-session temporal evolution under the transient mode, while the other group is designed for estimating cross-session statistical baselines under the persistent mode. We emphasise explicitly that the concrete number of dimensions presented here serves only as a working instance for demonstration and experimental deployment. The framework itself does not impose a fixed dimensionality constraint; subsequent researchers are free to add, remove or redefine dimensions according to model type, task domain and research purpose. Our analysis shows that the dual-mode multidimensional architecture can effectively separate instantaneous evolutionary regularities from long-run steady-state regularities of AI behaviour, and provides precise handles for capturing intra-session behavioural drift and cross-session behavioural stability. This framework offers a fresh theoretical paradigm and an actionable empirical pathway for behavioural quantification, mechanism interpretation and alignment governance for artificial-intelligence systems.

items.title: Augmenting Military Decision Making with Artificial Intelligence.
items.pub: Cambridge Forum on Ai: Law and Governance 1 (e48):1-13.
items.venue: Cambridge Forum on Ai: Law and Governance
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) plays an increasing role in operations on battlefields, we should consider how it might also be used in the strategic decisions that happen before a military operation even occurs. One such critical decision that nations must make is whether to use armed force. There is often only a small group of political and military leaders involved in this decision-making process. Top military commanders typically play an important role in these deliberations around whether to use force. These commanders are relied upon for their expertise. They provide information and guidance about the military options available and the potential outcomes of those actions. This article asks two questions: (1) how do military commanders make these judgements? and (2) how might AI be used to assist them in their critical decision-making processes? To address the first, I draw on existing literature from psychology, philosophy, and military organizations themselves. To address the second, I explore how AI might augment the judgment and reasoning of commanders deliberating over the use of force. While there is already a robust body of work exploring the risks of using AI-driven decision-support systems, this article focuses on the opportunities, while keeping those risks firmly in view.

items.title: Art in the Community of Inquiry: Lesson Plans and Activities for Art Education with Children and Adolescents.
items.abstract: About Art in the Community of Inquiry -/- The authors begin with foundational questions: What is art? What makes something a work of art? What is the relationship between emotion and artistic creation? By what criteria can we examine an artist or an artistic style? They then move toward the analysis of several well-known works of art, using them as a basis for exploring themes such as betrayal, anger, surprise, war, death, fear, violence, and self-sacrifice. -/- In this approach, art education becomes an opportunity not only to engage with artworks, but also to cultivate questioning, reasoning, empathy, and more attentive ways of seeing and understanding the world. -/- Why Read Art in the Community of Inquiry? -/- The main reasons for reading Art in the Community of Inquiry can be summarized as follows: -/- The book provides educators and teachers with ten ready-to-use lesson plans, each including an introduction, activities, and exercises. It connects art education with inquiry and classroom dialogue rather than limiting learning to fixed definitions or predetermined interpretations. -/- Readers are introduced to ways of using a range of stimuli in the classroom, including animation, paintings, photographs, and personal experience. The book also demonstrates how concepts such as art, artwork, emotion, artist, and artistic style can be explored collectively through discussion and inquiry. -/- The final sections offer concrete examples of analysing works of art, making the structure and practical implementation of an inquiry session easier to understand. -/- Who Is This Book For? -/- Art in the Community of Inquiry is particularly recommended for: -/- Philosophy for Children and Adolescents facilitators who wish to design art-based sessions around dialogue and inquiry. Art teachers looking for participatory ways of exploring artistic concepts in the classroom. Kindergarten, preschool, and educational-centre educators working with learners aged ten and above. Students and researchers interested in the relationship between art education and Philosophy for Children. Anyone interested in developing capacities such as reasoning, comparison, interpretation, and empathy through art education.

items.title: Layered Imaginative Acquaintance: A Roadmap.
items.abstract: This paper explores the role of imagination in aesthetic appreciation, distinguishing between its function as a medium of basic acquaintance and as a surrogate. While imagination has long been acknowledged as essential for experiencing aesthetic qualities, its status in the debate surrounding the Acquaintance Principle remains controversial. The aim of this paper is to clarify the distinction between basic and surrogative acquaintance through imagination. It argues that the most promising way to make sense of the distinction is to appeal to the artwork-specific standards, such that it is a matter of artistic context as to whether imagination counts as a medium of basic acquaintance or surrogative acquaintance, or whether it is not suitable as a medium of acquaintance at all. The resulting view accommodates the variety of ways in which imagination figures in warranting aesthetic judgment and draws together the two strands of literature in which the aesthetic role of imagination has been discussed, in the context of first-hand experience and in the context of surrogates. This provides a unified account of how imagination figures in aesthetic appreciation, both in its basic and in its surrogative capacity.

items.title: Modern Technology as a Philosophical Problem: A Typology of Critical and Affirmative Attitudes in Light of Three Fundamental Propositions.
items.abstract: This paper examines modern technology not merely as a collection of tools and processes but as a philosophical problem concerning the nature, value, and existential orientation of humankind. The study aims to reconstruct a coherent conceptual framework for analyzing four principal responses to technology—resistance, critical passivity, reform and substitution, and support and advancement—and to evaluate them in light of three fundamental propositions: (1) the overall harmfulness of modern technology, (2) whether technological harms are intrinsic or incidental, and (3) the human possibility of resisting technological expansion. The methodology combines conceptual analysis, argumentative evaluation, and comparative study of major contemporary positions, focusing especially on representative thinkers such as Martin Heidegger,, Andrew Feenberg, Theodore Kaczynski, Ray Kurzweil, and proponents of traditionalist schools. The findings indicate that each of the four approaches rests upon a distinct set of philosophical and value-laden assumptions, and that the proposed tripartite criterion enables a more precise differentiation of technological policies. Furthermore, the study argues that the deepest divergences stem from competing conceptions of the autonomous human being and its relation to nature and the technical order. In conclusion, the paper proposes the conceptual and ethical conditions necessary for a potential rapprochement among these perspectives and outlines the research requirements for developing a reliable medium-term strategy toward technology.

items.title: Comparative analysis of moral development and responsibility from the perspective of developmental psychology, moral duty, and Islamic innate morality: Designing an applied ….
items.pub: Quarterly Scientific Journal of Applied Ethics Studies 21 (4):160-199.
items.venue: Quarterly Scientific Journal of Applied Ethics Studies
items.abstract: The present study, using an analytical-comparative approach, examines the relationship between moral development and moral responsibility in three prominent theoretical traditions: developmental psychology (focusing on the theories of Piaget and Kohlberg), moral deontology (based on Kant's practical philosophy), and Islamic innate ethics (based on the views of Allameh Tabataba'i and Ayatollah Javadi Amoli). The main goal of the study is to design an applied model for the moral education of adolescents by combining the theoretical foundations of these schools. The findings show that each school has a different conceptual precedence: developmental psychology considers moral responsibility to be the result of cognitive-social development; Kant introduces responsibility as a prerequisite for moral development; and Islam sees responsibility as arising from divine nature and revelational guidance. The innovation of the study lies in synthesizing these perspectives and presenting a three-level model that includes cognitive-social development, rational autonomy, and guidance of spiritual nature. By combining external methods and internalizing ethics, this model provides a theoretical and practical infrastructure for raising a responsible, ethical, and insightful generation.

items.title: Toward Operational Sufficiency: An Integrated Architecture Profile for Bounded Cognitive Agency.
items.abstract: The companion papers define a bounded cognitive kernel, controlled input and service boundaries, learning and belief transactions, epoch-bounded growth, conditional request settlement, and directional semantic interoperability. A list of compatible components is not yet an integrated architecture, and an integrated architecture is not yet sufficient for any defensible meaning of human-like cognition. This paper separates those two obligations. First, it defines an Integrated Architecture Profile (IAP): a versioned, finite, owner-partitioned reference-composition specification whose manifest fixes state ownership, typed ports, update order, resource bounds, failure behavior, versions, and exact zero-closure settings. Under explicit hypotheses, an IAP instance can inherit per-epoch compactness and write isolation, bounded protocol settlement, atomic coordinated commit or rollback, typed authority-non-elevating exchange, core-trace refinement, and exact reduction to A1-A17. These are composition results, not competence results. Second, the paper defines Finite Human-Like Functional Sufficiency (FHFS) relative to a preregistered profile of capacities, tasks, environments, human reference population, resources, interventions, readouts, acceptance margins, forbidden failures, and rivals. Five cumulative tiers distinguish contract integrity, bounded task sufficiency, finite-profile sufficiency, mechanism-sensitive architectural sufficiency, and bounded developmental sufficiency. Mandatory cells are conjunctive and noncompensatory; leakage, unowned functions, bound violations, post-outcome system changes, and failed required cells stop or reset the claim. No finite tier establishes universal human-likeness, consciousness, moral status, world truth, unrestricted grounding, or open-ended intelligence. The present contribution is therefore a candidate reference-composition specification and a falsifiable evaluation discipline. It supplies neither a populated IAP instance, an executable witness, nor empirical demonstration. Version 19 also defines a bounded mapper, action and execution policy, temporal-valuation profile, emotion-observation profile, candidate first Tier 1 anchor, and security test envelope for the first witness. These are specifications, not implementations or evidence.

items.title: The Coherence Engine: Why Morals Cool Under Reflection, and What It Would Take to Call a Machine Human-Like.
items.abstract: Bernard Williams observed that reflection can destroy moral knowledge: a person can subject a firm conviction to honest scrutiny and come out holding something thinner and colder without ever having been shown an error. This book treats that observation as a clue about cognitive architecture and builds a research program around it. The proposal is that a lived moral orientation is carried by a typed, weighted graph in which connections compete for a bounded activation budget. Pressure-testing a framework for rigor admits qualifiers into that competition, so felt force dilutes without anything being deleted, while direct perceptual routes explain why force returns in the particular case and practiced compilation explains how qualified structures can become second nature. The central structural notion is coherence failure: a datum that cannot be connected within a representation's current degrees of freedom without substantial reorganization. Five documents develop the idea in sequence. Paper I states the human-side model in full, with its moral argument and 75 labeled equations. Paper II turns the model into a falsifiable cross-domain research program with preregistered tests, rivals, and stopping rules. Paper III closes ten deliberately exogenous capacities into a bounded agent architecture with an exact nesting proof. Paper IV defines an Integrated Architecture Profile and Finite Human-Like Functional Sufficiency, a five-tier evaluation discipline that prices the words integrated and human-like. Paper V, a separately versioned extension profile, supplies bounded candidate contracts for social, relational, and developmental capacities, together with a candidate reference witness. The program claims no empirical validation. What exists is a defined, internally disciplined, falsifiable candidate, and the book states exactly which tests would show it wrong.

items.title: Testing a Coherence Architecture Across Domains of Human Cognition: Prospective Identification, Falsification, and Boundary Conditions.
items.abstract: This paper asks whether the context-gated human-side model defined in How Morals Become Ethics (Paper I v20) can generate prospectively discriminating tests across domains without treating a common graph vocabulary as an explanation. Paper II remains in exact zero closure: A1-A17 and the canonical CML, BOWB, EBG, CSLP, LPC, and BSIC mechanisms belong solely to Paper III v20 and do not operate here. The inherited F/G/L/R/N family retains typed representation, bounded nonnegative transmission, nonredistributing gates, exogenous cue/context inputs, fan-centered log weights, compilation, readouts, and residual traces. CAP/CSC permit controlled external composition; Paper II adds only prospective tests of frozen protocol behavior and applies Paper IV v20's IAP/FHFS freeze, human-reference, held-out, intervention, rival, and stopping requirements without importing an equation. Passing establishes at most finite profile-relative evidence for the named composition, never universal human-likeness. The manuscript establishes neither identification nor empirical success, and all mappings remain prospective, exploratory, or Residual until their declared recovery, leakage, calibration, rollback, settlement, consequence, selective-ablation, rival, and held-out criteria are met.

items.title: Social and Developmental Closure in a Bounded Cognitive Architecture: Population Coupling, Category Formation, Controllability, Relational Persistence, and Finite Life-Course Profiles.
items.abstract: The Version 20 Coherence Engine deliberately leaves population coupling, category learning beyond A13 primitives, controllability, relational persistence, and broad service functions unresolved. This paper establishes one bounded companion specification, Paper V v20.1 Extension Profile 1, without changing the parent F/G/L/R/N family, A1-A17 core, or IAP/FHFS discipline. PC supplies finite queued population coupling; CL supplies a finite conjunction grammar and owner-gated category lifecycle; CT supplies executed-action effect estimation; AT supplies separate availability, trust, value, continuing-bond, and successor-goal records; LC supplies a noncognitive finite life-course environment; and RP profiles close memory, action-conditioned world modeling, bounded planning, structured language, and metacognitive reporting. The integrated state uses a disjoint coordinate registry. CT, AT, and metacognitive outputs can influence action only through target-owner validation and next-tick A6 re-entry; W3 and A4′ remain unchanged. Cross-agent messages have at least one logical-tick delay. Environment truth, including natural death, belongs only to ScenarioRunner. The accompanying CTT1-REF witness is a candidate executable implementation of the parent CTT-1 profile, pending independent validation. HLCW-1-DEV exercises a bounded route through Papers I-V and tests zero reduction, replay, ownership, bounds, guarded compilation, loss reorganization, and terminalization, but it is not a claim of complete Paper V trace, perturbation, or SCP-EXT conformance. These artifacts supply development evidence only. They do not supply human-reference equivalence, identification, clinical validity, authentic attachment or grief, or general human-likeness.

items.title: A Functional Skeleton for Bounded Cognitive Agency: Canonical Protocol Specification.
items.abstract: Papers I and II define a shared constrained model family for human cognition: a typed, weighted graph with context eligibility, nonredistributing gates, budget-limited propagation, bounded dynamic regimes, learning, compilation, and separately estimable readouts. This paper treats that family as a functional specification and declares ten capacities held exogenous in zero closure. A1-A17 give a bounded candidate architecture for closing those gaps. Version 19 preserves every A-series equation, proposition, CAP/CSC boundary, and CSLP/LPC/CML/BOWB/EBG/BSIC protocol. It adds only a security-declaration contract and composition-level handoff clarifications for the Paper IV mapper, action, temporal-valuation, and emotion-observation profiles. A-P1 proves exact nesting; A-P2 proves the activation bound; and A-P3 bounds the admitted core under finite authorized libraries. Paper IV v20, not Paper III, owns IAP, FHFS, MP, W1-W5, and CTT-1. Their human-side interpretations remain prospective.

items.title: Swayamasti: From “I Am” to “I Can Think”.
items.abstract: This paper introduces Swayamasti as a philosophical-existential formulation centered on the primacy of being over thought: “I am; therefore, I can think.” The formulation is proposed as a complementary reversal of René Descartes’ famous cogito ergo sum—“I think, therefore I am.” Rather than treating thought as the starting point for establishing existence, Swayamasti begins with the immediate recognition of existence and regards thought, questioning, exploration, and knowledge as possibilities arising from that existence. The paper does not seek to deny or establish the existence of God. Instead, it argues that the question of God logically and experientially arises after the recognition of one’s own existence. If God exists, human existence may be understood as participating in or emerging from a greater reality; if God does not exist, the immediate fact of one’s existence remains the starting point for inquiry. Thus, existence is treated as epistemically prior to metaphysical interpretation. The concept is then examined in dialogue with Western philosophy, modern scientific inquiry, consciousness studies, and Indian philosophical traditions, particularly the Vedic and Upanishadic notions of sat (being), ātman, and brahman. The Upanishadic statement aham brahmāsmi (“I am Brahman”) is interpreted not as an initial assertion of personal divinity but as a possible culmination of an inquiry that begins with the simple recognition “I am.” Swayamasti therefore represents an open philosophical trajectory: Being → Thinking → Questioning → Exploring → Knowing → Self-inquiry → Possible realization of ultimate reality.

items.title: Can Ecosystems be Healthy? An Analysis of the Concept of Ecosystemic Health.
items.pub: Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics 39.
items.venue: Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics
items.abstract: Ecosystems are routinely evaluated in terms of degradation, resilience, recovery, and restoration success, yet the conceptual status of ecosystemic health remains unresolved. This paper examines whether health can be ontologically attributed to ecosystems. We first characterise ecosystems as complex biological systems whose organisation depends not merely on the presence of organisms, but on structured networks of trophic, mutualistic, symbiotic, competitive, and biogeochemical interactions. We then adopt an ecological account of health according to which health is understood as the capacity to endure and adapt to environmental perturbations. Against this background, we ask whether ecosystems possess the forms of regulation required for health in the strict biological sense. Our conclusion is qualified. Although ecosystems exhibit adaptive capacities associated with their complex organisation, current evidence does not warrant attributing to them the specialised biological regulation required for organismic health in the strict sense. Even so, the concept is not merely decorative, as it offers a theoretically disciplined and empirically tractable framework for ecological restoration by shifting attention from species counts alone to the recovery of interactional organisation, functional relations, and adaptive capacity under disturbance.

items.title: ARTICLE VII — THE AVICENNA PROTOCOL: Edge-Level Autonomy, Quantum Biological Synchronization, and the Predictive Pacification of Oncological Anomalies.
items.abstract: CONTEXT AND RUPTURE: Standard clinical frameworks fundamentally model physiological nodes (human organs) as passive, subordinate architectures and categorize macroscopic colonization (helminthic presence) strictly as localized secondary pathology. This manuscript executes a definitive mathematical shift against these static developmental assumptions. It evaluates oncological hyper-proliferation and subsequent macroscopic intervention not as isolated biological failures, but as deterministic, dynamically synchronized algorithmic defense mechanisms operating within a unified multiversal topology. -/- METHODOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK: Utilizing an apex-level synthesis of quantum non-locality, federated machine learning, network topology, and empirical parasitology, this analysis models the terrestrial ecosystem as a highly integrated cyber-biological grid. The localized biological conflict is mathematically mapped through the advanced principles of decentralized edge-computing, cryptographic sandboxing, kinetic siege doctrine, and gravitational wave interferometry to securely translate macroscopic biochemical interactions into rigorous multiversal physics. -/- CORE POSTULATES: The framework mathematically establishes that human organs operate as sovereign, edge-computing nodes capable of autonomously broadcasting multiversal telemetry (the Extinction SOS) upon registering terminal oncological degradation. Exogenous macroscopic entities intercept this frequency, executing Targeted Garrison Deployment to secure the compromised node. Redefined from arbitrary pathogens to heavily fortified multiversal bastions, helminths deploy highly calibrated mutualistic armaments. They continuously synthesize their Excretory-Secretory (ES) fluids into zero-day biochemical software patches to mathematically dismantle and suppress solid tumors via Anti-Angiogenic Siege Tactics and Apoptotic Overrides. Furthermore, this architecture proves the macroscopic species operates via Quantum Biological Synchronization, securely sharing structural telemetry across a globally entangled botnet to instantaneously out-compute oncological mutations in a continuous kinetic loop. -/- SYSTEMIC IMPLICATIONS: Mathematically recognizing the macroscopic helminth as the ecosystem's ultimate cryptographic engineer permanently transitions exogenous pharmacology from reactive chemical intervention to absolute predictive pacification. By deploying an apex artificial intelligence—the Avicenna Engine—to intercept …

items.title: Botspeech? Bullshit!
items.abstract: This paper engages with fictionalist accounts of verbal human-AI interaction, according to which, although lay AI-users know that AIs are not intentional agents (and hence that their linguistic output is strictly speaking meaningless), laypeople pretend/imagine that they are intentional agents when talking to them. I argue that the current empirical literature does not unequivocally support fictionalism. I suggest an alternative view, according to which a substantial group of lay AI-users – the uncaring users – engage in bullshit action: They do not know, and, more importantly, do not care whether AIs are intentional agents. Still, they act as if this is the case when talking to them.

items.title: Systemic explainability for autonomous driving: connecting ethics to law and society.
items.abstract: Self-driving vehicles challenge legal, socio-technical, and ethical frameworks due to their opacity, unpredictability, and autonomous decision-making, raising concerns for safety, trustworthiness, and responsibility attribution. In response, explainable artificial intelligence has been proposed to enhance transparency and trust in self-driving vehicles. This paper examines the role of explainability across the autonomous driving lifecycle, from development to deployment, through a thematic analysis of key dimensions, including safety, trust, transparency, trustworthiness, liability, and accountability. The analysis is carried out within the scope of European Union legal and ethical works, and shows how explainability supports functional and interactive safety, enables causal reconstruction of autonomous decisions, mitigates responsibility gaps, and fosters calibrated trust among users and stakeholders. Beyond these individual effects, the paper advances a systemic perspective on explainability, arguing that XAI operates as a structural enabler that reconnects technical choices to legal responsibility, ethical design, and social legitimacy. The principle influences autonomous driving from development throughout deployment, where explainability contributes to making autonomous driving systems intelligible, governable, responsible, and acceptable. The paper concludes that explainability should be understood not only as a technical tool, but also as a foundational and systemic design principle for autonomous vehicles.

items.title: Creativity without Emotions? Irrational Intelligence: Why AI Research Needs Emotions (ACM Newsletter for Computers & Society).
items.pub: Association for Computing Machinery - Computers and Society Newsletter.
items.abstract: Since inception, AI research has been inspired by the idea of building machines that think and behave like humans. Or put another way, machines that think and act rationally. This paradigm has its historical foundations in the assumption that what makes humans different from other forms of life is our capacity for self-reflective, rational thought. This assumption has caused research into artificial intelligence and human intelligence more generally to undervalue the role of emotions in generalized problem-solving. The very definition of rationality has, for much of Western history, discounted emotions from its conception. Where emotions are investigated, they are often treated as irrational, immaterial, or illusory aspects of human experience. This has been an unfortunate mistake.

items.title: Rethinking mental representation through the epistemology of modeling.
items.abstract: The problems associated with classical symbolism need not entail abandoning representationalism. While representational theories of mind have been widely challenged by embodied and action-oriented approaches, representationalism remains alive and well in empirical research on higher cognition, where the notion of conceptual representation appears indispensable. I argue that a reconciliation between representationalism and action-oriented theories is possible through a pragmatist interpretation of mental model research. Mental models are flexible knowledge structures that integrate information at multiple levels of abstraction to serve diverse epistemic and pragmatic functions. By combining this research with the epistemology of scientific modeling, I propose replacing symbolic referentialism with pragmatist inferentialism, an account of representation grounded in notions of inference and adequacy for purpose, rather than reference and truth conditions. This framework dissolves the divide between philosophical and psychological theories of concepts and aligns more closely with current empirical research on higher cognition than either classical symbolism or its radical anti-representational alternatives.

items.title: Sub Specie Boni, Sub Ratione Boni: Imagination and Estimation in Aquinas's Guise of the Good.
items.abstract: According to the thesis sometimes known as “the guise of the good”, we can only want or desire something (or intentionally do something) if it appears good to us in some respect. Typically, when introducing this thesis, one finds contemporary authors using the Latin phrase sub specie boni. In medieval Latin formulations, however, the standard formula is that whatever we will, we will sub ratione boni, or that we can only will something sub ratione boni, i.e. under the ratio (aspect) of good/goodness. Much more rarely does one find the expression sub specie boni, i.e. under the appearance or semblance of good/goodness. This seems especially true in Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274). First, I present textual evidence for this terminological difference in Aquinas, and show that sub specie boni occurs almost exclusively in contexts where the agent wants something on the basis of, mistakenly, taking something bad to be good. But why reserve sub specie boni for these cases?
