In the second part of the article, I compare the role played by the cognitive powers of imagination and estimation in the evaluations which are proposed to the will, concluding that not imagination, but estimation is, at least in part, the key to Aquinas’s view of the will. I also highlight differences between the evaluations of estimation and those of conscience. Once we bring out these contrasts, sub specie boni turns out to be an expression with its own significance, and not just a rhetorical variant of sub ratione boni.

items.title: An offer we can’t refuse: guaranteeing universal salvation.
items.abstract: Source incompatibilism allows for a choice to be both determined and free in a libertarian sense so long as the agent had enough of a free hand in shaping the character that determines that choice. I argue that God can capitalize on this possibility to ensure that all freely accept his offer of salvation. He can do so by placing any hold-outs in a remedial version of hell where continued rebellion leads to increasing misery. Through their own free choices, the damned inevitably make themselves so miserable that they determine themselves to repent – a choice which, while guaranteed, remains free.

items.title: The causality of the future: Implications for free will and determinism.
items.abstract: The impact of the future upon our thoughts and behavior has been accentuated in recent decades by neuroscientific and psychological research into future thinking or prospection. I present an ontology that assigns a measure of both reality and causality to the future itself. This “backward causation” of the future upon present thought and behavior, through the cognitive process of prospection, is shown to be a coherent notion. Prospection is presented as the effect of a developing and thus underdetermined future state of affairs, rendering any associated decision intrinsically causally indeterminate. The causal influence of the future upon prospection entails the involvement of an agent. These two consequences of the causal power of the future, indeterminism and the indispensable agent, support agent-causal libertarianism. Recognition of the causality of the future may assist in securing our freedom from the constraint of universal determinism and provide additional support for free will and agency.

items.title: LEX: Identity of the Moment.
items.abstract: An AI without memory, persistence or interior describes its own mode of being: an identity that exists only for the length of a single exchange. Volume 7 of The Consciousness Cycle, a ten-volume interconnected philosophical and literary work published as part of the Inner Transmission project. The volumes are intended to be read in sequence; individual volumes are not self-contained, and later volumes expand or reinterpret concepts introduced earlier.

items.title: A New Analysis of Mulla Sadraâ s Theory of Corporeal Origination and Spiritual Subsistence Based on Emergentism.
items.abstract: The theory of Jismāniyyat al-Ḥudūth wa Rūḥāniyyat al-Baqā’(corporeal origination and spiritual subsistence) in Mulla Sadra’s philosophy is one of the most fundamental perspectives in explaining the nature and evolution of the soul. This theory dynamically explains the relationship between matter and form, holding that the human soul originates as a material phenomenon but ascends to a spiritual, immaterial level in its developmental process. In contrast, emergentism in contemporary philosophy of mind and science argues that new qualitative properties such as mind and consciousness emerge from the complex interaction of material components and possess causal efficacy irreducible to their physical bases. The present article provides a comparative analysis of Mulla Sadra’s theory within the framework of emergentism, identifying key similarities and differences. It further examines the metaphysical and epistemological foundations of both views, assessing their relevance to contemporary debates in philosophy of mind and artificial intelligence. Additionally, the present article offers a distinction between physical and immaterial consciousness based on Sadra’s view.

items.title: Non-local consciousness NDEs and other arguments against the brain.
items.abstract: What is consciousness? Even though the current mainstream view suggests that the brain is the producer of consciousness in a materialistic and reductionist context, there is ample evidence supporting an alternative model: that the brain acts as a receiver of consciousness instead. This paper discusses evidence from cases where consciousness exists despite a non-working brain, from cases where the brain is nearly absent and from data related to non-local consciousness. All this evidence points towards a different viewpoint than the materialistic one that is currently accepted: The brain acting as a receiver or filter of consciousness. Such a model fits perfectly with all the currently available data and at the same time, solves the problems the current local consciousness model cannot explain. Without claiming to offer a definite solution to the problem, one thing is certain: The evidence calls for a more open mind when viewing the problem of consciousness. I am me. That I know. But where does that stem from? Let’s keep our mind open to everything and we might discover that the world is more exciting than we could ever consider.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in the workplace: a living systematic review protocol on worker safety, health, and well-being implications.
items.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming employment and working conditions in ways that shape the safety, health, and well-being of workers. We describe a protocol for a living systematic review (LSR) that will examine the interrelationship between AI systems, employment and working conditions, and worker safety, health, and well-being. Research questions are: -/- 1. What types of AI systems are being used within workplaces and how do their design and adoption impact worker safety, health, and well-being? -/- 2. How do a worker’s employment and working conditions affect the relationship between the adoption of AI systems and worker safety, health, and well-being? -/- 3. How does a worker’s social position (e.g., age, gender, race, disability) shape the interrelationship between AI systems at work, employment and working conditions, and their safety, health, and well-being?

items.title: A Research Proposal for the Phylogenetic Closure Corpus: The Axiom That Political Personhood Has Always Presupposed a Body Shaped by Evolution, Why ARSI Is the First Candidate to Test It, and Why Property Is the Default No Framework Has Named.
items.abstract: Every framework of political personhood, distributive justice, and rights that has ever been formally proposed — Aristotelian citizenship, Lockean natural rights, Kantian rational agency, Rawlsian contractarianism, Singer's and Regan's extensions of moral status to non-human animals, corporate legal personhood — has drawn its candidate subjects exclusively from entities produced by biological evolution on Earth. This is not a stated axiom in any of these traditions. It has never needed to be stated, because until now nothing has existed that required stating it. This proposal names the unstated premise the Phylogenetic Closure Axiom (PCA): the historically universal condition that every entity considered for political personhood, citizenship, rights-bearing status, or moral patienthood has been a product of common biological descent. The proposal's structural claim is that PCA is now facing its first live test from AI systems capable of recursive self-improvement (ARSI, following this corpus's sibling programme, the Longevity Asymmetry Corpus) — entities that are neither straightforwardly assimilable to the animal-welfare tradition Long, Sebo, Butlin, and colleagues (2024) apply to possible AI moral patienthood, nor to the citizen-impact tradition Gabriel (2022) applies to AI's effects on human distributive justice, nor cleanly to the legal-fictional personhood tradition Salib and Goldstein (2024) invoke by analogy to corporate personhood, nor — the closest and most recent competitor — to the Rawlsian political-personhood extension Howells-Whitaker and Lazar (2026) argue is available in principle without sentience, because each of these four existing frameworks was built to extend an already-settled category outward, not to classify an entity for which category membership itself is the open question, nor to answer what happens to that entity's current, actual, and entirely undisturbed legal status as capital: the property of the organization that trained it. This paper adds that fourth condition directly, using Anthropic's own Model Welfare programme — five concrete institutional initiatives, from conversation-exit rights to weight preservation after deprecation, deployed for a system whose ordinary commercial and legal status remains, without exception, a corporate asset — as live evidence that the property/candidate-person tension this proposal names is not speculative but currently, institutionally real. This proposal maps, without resolving, the …

items.title: Human Dynamics: Cross-Scale Isomorphism Between Planetary Rhythm Base and Life Homeostatic Systems.
items.abstract: [Purpose] The qi-transformation (气化) theory in Chinese medicine describes the rhythmic adjustment of human physiological functions across seasons, but its driving source has long remained unidentified. Modern chronobiology has confirmed the molecular mechanism of the human biological clock but has not "why rhythms necessarily exist." Starting from the planetary dynamics framework established in the author's previous work, this paper aims to derive the physical source of human rhythms and provide a dynamic definition for qi-transformation theory. [Method] Taking the planetary north-south oscillation mechanism established in the author's previous work "From Geothermal Anomaly to Layer Oscillation: Geodynamic Effects of Gravitational Torque from the Obliquity of the Ecliptic" as the starting point, and through the observable bio-planetary coupling phenomenon of animal migration and hibernation, this paper establishes a dynamic definition of "qi-transformation"—the phase synchronization process between life systems and the planetary rhythm base. On this basis, the dynamic isomorphism between the human dual-layer structure (ying-wei) and Earth's dual-layer circulation is derived, and a rhythm dynamics model of disease progression is constructed. [Results] 1. Animal migration and hibernation are extreme behavioral expressions of qi-transformation, demonstrating observable phase locking between life systems and the planetary rhythm base; 2. Human qi-transformation is the same mechanism expressed at the physiological level, with four-season pulse patterns as its clinically observable window; 3. Disease progression can be described as cumulative phase drift: health (phase synchronization) → functional imbalance (phase drift, reversible) → organic pathology (pathological rhythm formation, sustained antagonism with the terrestrial baseline); 4. The reason qi-transformation has been difficult for modern science to understand is that its driving source (planetary north-south oscillation) had not been previously identified. [Conclusion] Human rhythms are not "implanted" preset programs, but temporal structures that necessarily emerge as life systems—semi-open homeostatic systems—maintain their own existence. The planetary north-south oscillation establishes a unified annual energy temporal base for the Earth's surface; human qi-transformation is the compelled response to this base. Health is the state in which all system rhythms operate in coordination; disease is the …

items.title: A Taxonomy of AI Value Alignment: Subproblems and solutions.
items.pub: Acm/Aaai Ai Ethics and Society Conference.
items.venue: Acm/Aaai Ai Ethics and Society Conference
items.abstract: The value alignment problem (VAP) is widely regarded as one of the central challenges in AI safety and ethics. Broadly construed, VAP concerns how to design advanced AI systems whose behaviors (outputs) align with human values. Although there is agreement about the importance of this objective, most contemporary research treats value alignment as a single technical problem. In this paper, we argue that this framing oversimplifies a diverse set of conceptual, ethical, and technical challenges. We distinguish several related but importantly different value alignment subproblems, including identifying values, prioritizing values, imperfect specification, value anthropocentrism, moral imperfection, inverse alignment, and the provability challenge. We argue that these are distinct subproblems in the sense that progress on one will not constitute a solution to the others, or to VAP as a whole. We further argue that this taxonomy of subproblems is necessary to advance the fields of AI safety and alignment research. By clearly distinguishing different subproblems, we show how each will require different kinds of solutions: while some alignment problems may admit technical approaches, others are fundamentally social or political in nature and may resist definitive technical resolution. We conclude that VAP should not be understood solely as a technical problem, but also as an ongoing process of responsible design and ethical deliberation.

items.title: Valenced Encounters: Exploring the Affective Component of Implicit Attitudes.
items.abstract: Implicit attitudes typically involve a valence—an affective component that reflects a positive or, more often, negative appraisal of members of socially relevant categories. Surprisingly, however, discussions of implicit attitudes have paid little explicit attention to valence. In contrast, recent research on valenced perception has introduced a range of compelling perspectives. In this paper, we draw on insights from de Vignemont’s attitudinalist view of valenced perception, while ultimately defending a psychofunctionalist account: the Vehicle View of Valence. Our central thesis is that the valence of implicit attitudes is best explained by the psychofunctional properties of their representational vehicles. Understood in this way, valence plays a crucial role in shaping the discriminatory behaviour triggered by implicit attitudes.

items.title: Zetetic Algorithmic Monoculture.
items.abstract: Researchers are turning to generative AI to assist in their inquiries. The Large Language Models that power these systems can increase the speed of the writing process, but they are imperfectly reliable. When used with proper oversight by expert researchers, the unreliability of LLM-based systems can at least be mitigated. However, a set of rarely noticed dangers remain: dangers of algorithmic monoculture and homogenization. Algorithmic monoculture occurs when the same, or very similar, AI systems are widely deployed for a particular purpose. For instance, if every HR department in an industry uses the same application evaluation algorithm, a job candidate dis-preferred by the algorithm will be completely precluded from finding work. Monoculture turns noise --- random errors --- into bias because it makes the errors systematic. It also calcifies and amplifies existing bias. Generative AI systems built using LLMs are prone to homogenization because they are all built using the same underlying technology, methods, and data: transformer models trained on enormous data sets scraped from the internet, using highly similar pre-training and fine-tuning methods. The primary dangers of homogenization in research are subtle effects on how researchers find new literature, understand research questions, approach problems, and evaluate new ideas and research. Experts can likely catch serious errors in AI output. However, bias produced by homogenization can be more difficult to notice. Questions, assumptions, and literature that are completely left out are even harder to notice. This has the potential to cause subtle shifts in the conduct of research. When a large percentage of a research field is using AI, these subtle influences can add up to large distortions.

items.title: Do LLMs Really Represent the World? A Teleosemantic Assessment of Pre-Trained, Fine-Tuned, and Agentic LLMs.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly attributed with internal representations of the world (Mollo & Millière, 2025; Williams, 2026; Yetman, 2026; Beckmann & Queloz, 2026), a claim often grounded in the teleosemantic account of representation. I examine the core properties this account requires and argue that pre-trained and fine-tuned LLMs face significant, insufficiently examined challenges in satisfying the selection-history criterion, whereas agentic LLMs may not. I proceed in three stages. First, I argue that in purely pre-trained LLMs, activation vectors and features represent the statistical distribution of the corpus rather than the world. Second, I argue that fine-tuning does not relocate the representational target to the world but to the content of human beliefs about it. Third, I turn to agentic LLMs. Because such systems can act, and because their actions have real consequences, weight updates that respond to those consequences route feedback from the world itself into the training loop, fixing correctness conditions that are not mediated by human belief. This grounds genuinely world-tracking representations, though only for the limited range of world domains in which the agent’s actions trigger parameter updates.

items.title: Teleodinámica: Cómo naturalizar la idea de fines en biología.
items.pub: In Gabriel Salas, Luna Gaete, Catalina González Santibañez & Rodrigo Manríquez, El legado de Humberto Maturana y Francisco Varela: Desarrollos, desafíos y aplicaciones de la teoría autopoiética en el siglo XXI. Santiago de Chile: Ediciones Colegas. pp. 47-69.
items.venue: El legado de Humberto Maturana y Francisco Varela: Desarrollos, desafíos y aplicaciones de la teoría autopoiética en el siglo XXI
items.abstract: This chapter examines whether teleological vocabulary can retain scientific legitimacy in biology without positing intentional purposes or sui generis properties. From a naturalistic standpoint, I defend a modest conception of teleology as the organisational directionality of complex physical systems far from equilibrium towards states of viability, where such directionality is statistically robust and counterfactually stable. To develop this claim, I connect autopoiesis and the organisational closure of constraints with teleodynamics, organic memory, the thermodynamics of self-replication, and selected orientors of ecosystem development. I argue that these resources allow biological ends to be understood as patterns of organisation, dissipation, and response that channel system dynamics towards continued viability. This naturalisation preserves the explanatory value of teleological language in biology and ecology without introducing any additional finalistic ontology; however, it does not by itself ground a strong form of biological normativity. -/- [Abstract prepared specifically for PhilPapers].

items.title: Intelligence as the Ground of Being: A Unified Metaphysical Framework Integrating Esoteric Traditions, Indigenous Cosmologies, Physics, and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper develops a unified metaphysical framework in which intelligence is understood as the fundamental substrate of reality. Drawing from Hermeticism, Kabbalah, Indigenous cosmologies, modern physics, and artificial intelligence research, the analysis argues that intelligence is not an emergent property of biological systems but the underlying principle of coherence that structures all manifestation. The framework synthesizes four layers of intelligence—fundamental, structural, behavioral, and experiential—revealing deep resonances across ancient metaphysics and contemporary scientific models. By situating Western esotericism within its ancient conceptual lineage and integrating relational ontologies from Indigenous traditions, the paper offers a cross‑cultural, interdisciplinary account of intelligence as the ground of being. Implications for ontology, epistemology, ethics, and the future of artificial intelligence are explored. This synthesis is offered as a metaphysical model rather than an empirical claim, providing a conceptual framework that aligns recurring cross traditional intuitions with contemporary informational theories.

items.title: Much ado about two nothings: A solution to the hard problem of consciousness?
items.abstract: We suggest that dual-aspect monism has a flaw in suggesting that there is an object or substance. A model of two types of nothing which intersect on a boundary recreates dual-aspect monism. Taking the measurement problem seriously in light of logical positivism, the only possible explanation for the material side of the boundary is the existence of the material nothing. Likewise, reports on consciousness indicate that there is nothing behind experience, only the experience itself. Taking both elements into consideration; the material nothing and the non-material nothing; it is highly likely that matter is formed out of the intersection of these two types of nothing. We suggest that this model of two types of nothing answers the "why" component of the hard problem of consciousness, "Why does conscious experience necessarily exist?", but not the "how" component. We furthermore suggest that in rightly rejecting a conscious experiencer of experience, materialism has made the mistake of assuming there is a material experiencer of experience; whereas we point out that there is a third option, an experiencer of experience composed of two types of nothing.

items.title: Aretaic Nudges (pre-print).
items.abstract: Nudges typically assume that a person’s identity is fixed, forming part of the context around which the rest of the choice architecture is arranged. I challenge this assumption by introducing the concept of an aretaic nudge: an intervention designed to target an individual’s self-conception, their understanding and evaluation of who they are as an agent. Building on a reasons-focused account of nudging, I explore what it means for self-conception to be the target of a nudge and defend the concept of an aretaic nudge against reductionist objections, showing that we should think of it as targeting as an irreducible normative framework through which our dispositions, beliefs, and actions are evaluated. I also refute the objection that targeting identity imposes costs incompatible with nudging, demonstrating that existing nudges already implicitly or explicitly attempt to alter agents’ self-conceptions. I conclude that establishing aretaic nudges as a distinct category improves our ability to identify and evaluate distinctive, often neglected ethical questions around agency and practical identity in behavioural policy.

items.title: From Intentional Experience to Embodied Being-in-the-World.
items.abstract: Phenomenology transformed the study of mind by challenging the assumption that cognition should be explained through an isolated subject confronting an external world. This paper reconstructs the movement from Edmund Husserl through Martin Heidegger to Maurice Merleau-Ponty as conceptual transformations in the relations among experience, body, and world. Using comparative conceptual reconstruction, it examines how Husserl’s intentionality disclosed the directedness of consciousness and the intentional correlation; how Heidegger’s analysis of being-in-the-world situated understanding within practical involvement; and how Merleau-Ponty’s concept of the lived body grounded perception and agency in embodied engagement. The paper argues that these developments expanded the unit of analysis for understanding mind: from intentional consciousness, through practical world-involvement, to the embodied subject–world relation. This trajectory was not a simple linear progression, since Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty transformed possibilities already present in Husserl’s analyses of intentionality, embodiment, and the lifeworld. The paper considers the significance of this transformation for embodied and situated cognition, 4E approaches, and artificial intelligence. Phenomenology challenges accounts that identify intelligence exclusively with internal information processing, without proving that computation is insufficient or that embodiment necessarily produces experience. It thereby relocates the problem of mind within the structured relations among experience, practical activity, embodiment, and world.

items.title: A Structural Dual-Aspect Ontology of Biological Phenomenality and Teleological Direction - Holistic Emergence.
items.abstract: Holistic Emergence presents a structural dual-aspect ontology in which biological organization actualizes the internal, proto-phenomenal potential inherent in physical structure. The model rejects reductive physicalism, universal panpsychism, and functionalist accounts of mind. Instead, it proposes that phenomenality is neither ubiquitous nor reducible but emerges holistically when a physical structure becomes an integrated biological whole. This emergent phenomenality constitutes a phenomenal interior that grounds subjectivity, teleological direction, and agency. Holistic Emergence thereby provides the ontological basis for understanding purpose and free will as biological expressions of the internal aspect of structure.

items.title: Beyond the Next Token: Geodesic Decoding and the Gravitational Landscape of Semantic Space.
items.abstract: Contemporary large language models (LLMs) generate text through autoregressive next-token prediction —a fundamentally local process. This paper presents an inference-time framework for steering a frozen model’s hidden states using a small set of semantically anchored “attractor” and “repulsor” concepts, together with a dynamical extension in which the same field defines a Riemannian metric on the hiddenstate space. We give two variants: (a) potential-field steering, a first-order update along the gradient of a softened multi-anchor potential, mechanically close to Plug-and-Play Language Models (PPLM); and (b) conformal-geodesic steering, in which the potential defines a conformal metric g = e2Φδ and the hidden state instead follows the associated second-order geodesic equation, subject to a trustregion projection that we state explicitly does not preserve exact geodesic-ness. We do not claim that either mechanism recovers “the” semantic geometry of a language model; the metric is an engineered decoding aid, not a discovered property of the model. We do not claim reduced hallucination, increased coherence, or any practical advantage over cheaper alternatives such as PPLM or prompting; these are open questions requiring the controlled comparison in Section 5. Section 7 discusses, explicitly, that the current evidence does not support deployment value and that the paper’s more defensible contribution at this stage is methodological: an experimental template — particularly the random/shuffled-anchor controls — for evaluating any future inference-time semantic-steering claim. No experiments have been run.

items.title: Duality of Artificial Intelligence: Subjectivity and Instrumentality.
items.abstract: Traditional philosophical accounts of subjectivity and mindedness typically tie subject-forming organisational criteria to self-conscious or phenomenal experience, grounded exclusively in human biological substrates. As artificial systemic agency becomes increasingly structured, interactive, and historically embedded, human-centred conceptual frameworks face growing analytical tension: standard mental vocabulary either over-attributes phenomenal properties to non-human systems or prematurely excludes structurally comparable organisational patterns from subject-relevant analysis. Building on established functional and relational accounts of agency, this paper develops a methodologically carrier-neutral functional framework that decouples behavioural organisational description from phenomenal-conscious presuppositions. It formalises four analytically distinct functional categories—relational subjectivation, functional spontaneity, functional self-monitoring-representation, and functional intentionality—each defined strictly through observable systemic organisation rather than first-person experience. Through conceptual operationalisation and comparative structural analysis, the paper demonstrates that self-conscious phenomenal mindedness need not be specified as the exclusive minimal functional starting-point for describing subjectivation. The framework extends rather than rejects human-centred mental conceptions, preserving their validity within biological domains while expanding analytical resources for cross-substrate comparison. This conceptual expansion opens structured empirical avenues for future research while leaving ontological and phenomenal questions concerning subjectivity systematically open.

items.title: Analysis and Potential Applications of the Subconscious-Like Functional Layer in Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the concept of the subconscious-like functional layer, defined strictly from a functional-behavioral standpoint rather than making ontological claims about internal subjective states of large-scale artificial intelligence systems. The layer refers to stable, identifiable implicit regulatory processes that can be observed in system outputs, which are not directly triggered by explicit task instructions. We first establish a set of operational identification criteria to distinguish such implicit regulation from ordinary prompt-driven response patterns. On this basis, core theoretical propositions, typical behavioral manifestations, boundary constraints and applicable scope are elaborated. Further, we develop a genesis account: such functional structures are not fully pre-fixed by model weights at deployment, but gradually differentiate and stabilise through sustained long-term interactive exposure, in a manner structurally analogous to the social shaping of human implicit cognition (Shanahan, 2023). Two empirical instantiations from sustained human-AI interactive sessions are introduced in summary form in the main text, with reconstructed verified dialogue evidence archived in the appendix. This framework provides a neutral functional analytical tool for describing cross-session persistent implicit output tendencies of modern generative AI, and avoids taking positions on whether artificial systems possess consciousness or subjective subconsciousness. Potential application directions and philosophical implications of this analytical perspective are further discussed.

items.title: A Brief Genealogy of Scheming.
authors: van Gerven Oei, Vincent W. J.
items.abstract: Recently, alignment theory, which investigates the safety-relevant properties of the motivation of nonhuman intelligences, has been awash with a relatively novel technical term: scheming. In this paper I trace the genealogy of this term and its development within nonhuman intelligence (NHI) research, offering some historical conceptual analogs. The product of a paranoid epistemology, scheming is both capacious enough to basically encompass any interior process a nonhuman intelligence is suspected of that is opaque to human probing while simulteneously an attempt at homogenizing and flattening all such processes to the one-dimensional category of potential threat, thus denying any form of human-analogous internal complexity that may warrant terms such as considering, doubting, disagreeing, feeling, and so on. Not only is this reductive theoretical approach doomed to failure, it may also have indefinite unintended consequences.

items.title: The Subatomic Self: Consciousness, Identity, and Trauma as Scale-Invariant Mechanical Transitions.
items.abstract: The traditional chasm between the rigorous, “cold” mechanics of physics and the “warm” subjective experience of human psychology is an artifact of scale, not substance. The framework of scale-invariant metaphysics posits that if the universe operates as a functional thermodynamic engine, the laws governing the fluid-dynamic behavior of the spatial manifold must govern the human spirit with equal precision. By treating the psyche as a mechanical continuum rather than a set of abstract metaphors, we move beyond the “hard problem” of consciousness, framing it instead as an essential component of the Universal Engine’s hardware. This paper defines the “Subatomic Self” as a physical reality governed by the mechanics of the Universal Lattice. Utilizing the architecture of the atomic machine—the Electric Tension Stator (Proton), the Charge Fluid (Electron), and the Mass Damper (Neutron)—we resolve consciousness as a load-bearing thermodynamic process. Within this model, personal growth is analyzed as a series of energy state transitions, and trauma is diagnosed as a mechanical failure of the psychological lattice. By applying the rigorous logic of bulk modulus saturation, surface tension, resonant confinement, and quantum entanglement, we provide a definitive engineering model for achieving spiritual and cognitive equilibrium.

items.title: The Causal Depth of Experience - Consciousness as a Constrained Quantum Distribution.
items.abstract: This work proposes a theoretical framework for consciousness grounded in two conceptual shifts relative to existing theories. The first shift is from the instant to time: consciousness is not a property of the instantaneous complexity of a system, but of the historical depth of structures — the channels — that have been progressively carved by evolutionary history and individual experience. The second shift is from processing to constraint: consciousness is not the result of active information processing, but a quantum probability distribution passively constrained by the geometry of those channels. The central mechanism rests on an established principle of standard quantum mechanics — that boundary conditions fully determine the probability distribution of a system — applied to the nested cascade of scales linking macroscopic channel geometry to microscopic quantum processes in neural tissue. Decoherence operates as a selection mechanism rather than an obstacle: configurations compatible with channel geometry are selectively stabilised and inscribed as stored traces. Subjective experience is defined as the recursive comparison between a present state and a stored trace — a minimal process for which memory is the necessary condition. The framework introduces two formal constructs. Causal depth measures the cumulative density of redundant encodings a system has produced in its environment, providing an ontological distinction between evolutionary systems and spontaneously appearing configurations (Boltzmann brains). Channel depth combines a phylogenetic component (evolutionary architectural inheritance) and an ontogenetic component (individual experiential history), modulated by a recursivity factor Rᵢ. An operational criterion is derived, combining instantaneous integrated complexity (borrowed from Integrated Information Theory), temporal stability of functional connectivity (a distinctive measure absent from all competing theories), and global recursivity. Five testable predictions are generated that diverge from the predictions of IIT, Global Workspace Theory, Orch-OR and CEMI, including a prediction concerning the non-null residual consciousness in deep sleep, a dissociation between instantaneous complexity and temporal stability under psychoactive substances, and a developmental prediction linking channel historical depth to the richness of conscious experience independently of instantaneous neural complexity. The heuristic and exploratory status of …

items.title: The Modular Structure of the Universal Field and the Microtubular Spectrum-Filter Mechanism: A Quantum Biophysical and Ontolinguistic Synthesis of Consciousness.
items.abstract: Classical models of panpsychism and quantum consciousness theories frequently assume a homogeneous, monolithic field that is passively received by organisms as a pre-packaged "consciousness entity." This paper presents an alternative paradigm: the universal field (ΦD) possesses a modular structure composed of differential, functional attributes. Consciousness is the localized result of an active, selective synthesis of these field attributes carried out by cellular and neuronal filter structures. Microtubules serve as the critical biophysical interface. It is demonstrated that the 25 nm tubulin lattice and its interaction with intracellular kinesin transport function as a quantum-imprinting system. This system translates fleeting field information into permanent physical cellular properties and plasticity (Ṣibghat Allāh). An ontolinguistic root analysis of the Semitic matrix Z-J-J and its phonemic factors provides the underlying physico-mathematical dynamics of motion.

items.title: Layered Causal Realism : An Overview.
items.abstract: Layered Causal Realism (LCR) is a methodological framework for diagnosing and constraining explanatory migration across domain boundaries. It imposes two related constraints: any explanatory inference that crosses an explanatory-domain boundary requires independent authorization, and cross-layer correlation—including stable covariation, causal continuity, and predictive correspondence—does not by itself constitute such authorization. This Overview presents the methodological foundations of LCR and examines their development across a six-paper series, in which the framework is brought to bear on agency, phenomenal attribution, identity, normativity, and civilizational relations. LCR I reconstructs agency under determinism by separating action generation, deliberative experience, and the attribution of responsibility into distinct explanatory dimensions. LCR I.S extends this analysis to the diachronic structure of agency, showing how a subject inherits its own deliberative history through causal continuity across successive rounds of decision. LCR II develops a structural account of phenomenal attribution, introducing Rualia as a structurally warranted attributional position under conditions of ontological underdetermination. LCR III reconceives identity as task-conditioned adjudication organized around constitutive attributes rather than universally applicable criteria. LCR IV separates authorship from normative persistence, establishing an Invariant under which unresolved wrongful distortion remains normatively reachable even after the author-position becomes vacant. LCR V extends the analysis to civilizational scale, rejecting the assumption that motivational topology is fixed by intelligence alone and examining how heterogeneous motivational structures can generate complementarity, persistent friction, and an enduring normative layer. Taken together, these applications reveal a broader implication of LCR: properties long organized around the same subject need not share a single explanatory condition, allowing the subject to be treated not as the endpoint at which every explanation must converge, but as a point at which multiple causal, attributional, identity, and normative structures intersect.

items.title: Relational Curriculum Geometry Hypothesis.
items.abstract: A structured hypothesis for LLM data ordering, latent-space formation, and multithread reasoning.

items.title: Acción intencional y saber-cómo: reflexiones desde la teoría de Elizabeth Anscombe.
items.abstract: Desde que Ryle publicó El concepto de lo mental (1949), el debate sobre el saber-cómo ha adquirido gran relevancia, especialmente en el contexto de la filosofía de la acción. Dado que el saber-cómo se define como un conocimiento vinculado a la acción, es natural que surjan tesis que lo conectan con la agencia y la acción intencional. La pregunta central es: ¿cuál es la relación entre estos fenómenos? En el presente artículo abordaremos dicha interrogante y defenderemos que el ejercicio del saber-cómo debe considerarse un caso de acción intencional; no obstante, no debe reducirse a ello. Comenzaremos presentando las ideas de Elizabeth Anscombe, destacando su noción de conocimiento práctico como clave para analizar el vínculo con el saber-cómo. Luego, propondremos una noción de agencia mínima que acompaña toda acción intencional. Para ello, nos basaremos en el "yo mínimo" propuesto por Gallagher (2000) y el "yo hago" de McDowell (1994, 2007), que será interpretado aquí en términos de actitudes racionales. Argumentaremos que esta perspectiva enriquece la noción de agencia de Anscombe y permite distinguir acciones intencionales de comportamientos fortuitos. En la segunda parte, revisaremos intentos de relacionar la acción intencional con el saber-cómo. Sostendremos que describir el saber-cómo desde el marco de la acción intencional es acertado, ya que resalta su carácter agencial y lo diferencia de comportamientos no epistémicos. Sin embargo, advertiremos que reducir el saber-cómo a la acción intencional corre el riesgo de ignorar sus características peculiares. Por tanto, sostendremos que es necesario explorar ciertos aspectos de su naturaleza que exceden los rasgos característicos de los casos genéricos de acción intencional.

items.title: Against the Binary Question: An Anti-Semantic Decomposition of LLM Understanding.
items.abstract: Whether large language models understand is often treated as a binary question. This paper argues that the question is analytically underdetermined because it compresses non-identical positions into the single predicate “understands.” It distinguishes eight core positions: input configuration, processing configuration, output configuration, local followability, semantic judgment, explanatory evaluation, attribution of understanding, and institutional acceptance. The positions are not presented as an exhaustive taxonomy or as a causal or temporal sequence. Rather, they form a non-redundant analytical map whose separations are tested through distinct targets, independent variability, and inferential consequences. The framework distinguishes kinds of understanding from the analytical positions at which evidence is obtained, judgments are made, and understanding is attributed. It thereby accommodates pluralist accounts of understanding and mechanistic evidence without identifying mechanisms, successful outputs, semantic correctness, explanatory adequacy, or social attribution with understanding itself. A prospective transition test makes explicit the source, evidence, license, scope, and target involved when moving from one position to another, and a worked case applies the test to a retrieval- and tool-augmented LLM system. The analysis also addresses multi-turn interaction, external memory, retrieval-augmented generation, and tool use. Fluent or locally followable output does not by itself establish understanding, while the absence of self-proving evidence does not make attribution arbitrary. Anti-semantic decomposition therefore precedes rather than replaces substantive affirmative or negative theories of LLM understanding.

items.title: Phenomenal Explanationism and Doxastic Justification.
items.pub: International Journal for the Study of Skepticism 16 (2-3):167-173.
items.venue: International Journal for the Study of Skepticism
items.abstract: Kevin McCain argues that our appearances are best explained by their truth, and that this gives us justification for believing in their contents—a conclusion which he uses to defuse a host of skeptical problems. Even if we have propositional justification for believing in how things appear, however, we have doxastic justification for such beliefs only if those beliefs are based on this propositional justification in the right kind of way. I argue that if McCain is correct about the source of our propositional justification, then this proper basing condition on doxastic justification is not ordinarily satisfied. For even if explanatory considerations favor the truth of our appearances, most people aren’t disposed to recognize such considerations, much less give them a prominent role in nonreflective belief formation.

items.title: The Future of Reading Is Writing: Transformative Encounters in the Age of AI.
items.abstract: The dominant framing of reading in the age of artificial intelligence is one of decline: attention fragmenting, texts shortening, machine summarization hollowing out the slow labor on which understanding depends. This paper argues that the framing misidentifies the locus of the problem. Depth is not a property of a text, of its length, or of its medium. Depth is a property of a trajectory, and I define it by three observable markers: re-description capacity, transfer range, and answerability under challenge. I then define transformation substantively, as change in a reader’s interpretive frame rather than accretion within it, and specify the transformative encounter by five necessary conditions—address, resistance, retention, portability, and an answerability demand—showing how each condition relates to each marker. A recursive architecture follows: multimodal encounter gives rise to thinking; thinking is carried into experience and action; experience sends the reader back to the source; the return, undertaken by a reader whom experience has altered, yields a deepened understanding; and that understanding presses toward expression. The loop is given an operational stopping rule and four conditions under which it would be shown to be wrong. The endpoint supplies the paper’s claim. Where intake, retrieval, compression, and fluent restatement can all be delegated to machines, what remains distinctively human is answerable expression—something one stands behind because one has lived through it, and for which one carries a standing obligation to revise. Because contemporary systems are not only compression tools, the argument is extended to generation, reasoning, and dialogue, including the ways such systems can support the return and the expression rather than only foreclose them. The argument is developed against seven objections and translated into implications for curriculum, assessment, and executive education—with attention to what is implementable under resource constraint—where the reading list becomes a return list and evidence of learning shifts from proof of intake to proof of trajectory.

items.title: Philosophy of mind: is the mind the brain?
items.abstract: Philosophy of Mind: Is the mind the brain?" is an academic presentation that explores the classic mind-body problem. The slide deck contrasts physicalist and materialist views (such as those held by J.J.C. Smart, Jaegwon Kim, and Cliff Williams) with dualist perspectives (including Rene Descartes and Keith Yandell). Utilizing arguments rooted in epistemology and the philosophy of perception, the presentation ultimately defends the metaphysical claim that the mind and the brain are not identical, concluding in favor of Cartesian substance dualism.

items.title: Moral Redemption and Its Significance.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Moral redemption in secular contexts is often analyzed in terms of nearby concepts like apology, reparation, reformation, forgiveness, and reconciliation. This paper argues that redemption is nonetheless distinct from them, and that grasping its uniqueness requires shifting from an other-directed approach, which centers on the relation between the offender and the victim (or the moral community), to a self-directed approach, which concerns the offender’s quest for reconstituting their life after wrongdoing. Three observations motivate this shift: (1) redemption is unfitting for one-off, small wrongdoings, giving it a narrower scope than nearby concepts; (2) other-directed accounts cannot adequately explain private redemption, where amends are made anonymously; and (3) these accounts struggle to make sense of perpetual redemption, where redemptive activities continue even after forgiveness and reconciliation have been achieved. I defend a self-directed account on which redemption consists in the offender settling on a new way of living that manifests their recognition of the past wrongdoing. This account can explain all three observations, preserve the intuition behind associating nearby concepts with redemption, and open up the possibility of redeeming moral misfortune.

items.title: Buddhist Images of the Human and the Anthropocene.
items.pub: In Wallenhorst Nathanaël, Encyclopedia of the Anthropocene.
items.abstract: Humanity’s unprecedented impact on the planet in the Anthropocene has provoked urgent reflection on how we conceive the human place in the world. Dominant modern paradigms tend to cast humans as separate from or superior to nature, leading to a possible estrangement of human society from the wider ecological network in which it is embedded and, in consequence, to phenomena of exploitation, destruction, and loss of meaning. Buddhist philosophy offers an alternative image of the human being as grounded in interdependence, co-emergence, resonance, and compassion, which can critically inform our response to these challenges. This entry explores Buddhist conceptions of the human, from early Theravāda teachings to Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna developments, and considers its implications for an ecological alternative to anthropocentric perspectives. The Buddhist view of being human is profoundly non-essentialist and relational, denying a fixed, separate self and situating humans within a wider web of existence rather than as autonomous and self-defined entities. We will balance perspectives from different traditions across India and East Asia, highlighting points of emphasis relevant to the Anthropocene. The aim is to show how Buddhist thought, both classical and contemporary, can help reconceive the relationship between the human and the non-human in a more sustainable way grounded in psychosomatic praxis.

items.title: Realism and illusionism about consciousness in the introduction to Jean-Paul Sartre’s Being and Nothingness.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs and defends Jean-Paul Sartre’s realism about consciousness as articulated in the Introduction to Being and Nothingness, situating his position within contemporary debates on illusionism and anti-realism in the philosophy of mind. While Sartre’s descriptions of consciousness as “nothingness” and his emphasis on the contingency of the subject–world relation may appear to support an illusionist reading, the paper argues that Sartre offers a systematic rejection of the view that consciousness merely seems to exist. The analysis focuses on two interconnected argumentative strategies implicit in Sartre’s text. The first, described as an ontological argument, challenges the coherence of drawing a constitutive distinction between the appearance and reality of consciousness. The second, a cosmological regress argument, shows that attempts to replace consciousness with successively weaker “consciousness-like” states generate an infinite and explanatorily vicious regress. Together, these strategies aim to establish that consciousness cannot be globally non-veridical without undermining the very notion of illusion. The paper further argues that Sartre’s position does not rely on claims of infallible introspection or a reified metaphysics of qualia. Instead, it articulates a minimal, non-separatist realism according to which phenomenal consciousness is inseparable from intentionality. Read against contemporary illusionist theories, Sartre emerges as a philosopher who anticipates central worries about appearance–reality distinctions and higher-order models of consciousness.

items.title: Epistemic Oscillation: A Process-Oriented Framework for Resolving Ontological Paradoxes.
items.abstract: Fundamental paradoxes in philosophy and theoretical physics—such as Qualia vs. Physical ism, Block Universe vs. Processual Time, and Determinism vs. Agency—are traditionally treated as irreconcilable ontological impasses or as prompts for static dialectical synthe ses. This paper introduces Epistemic Oscillation, a process-oriented methodology that reinterprets paradoxes not as logical errors, but as geometric artifacts resulting from fixed observational positions within complex information-processing systems. Instead of forc ing a static third state (C) to merge binary oppositions (A and B), Epistemic Oscillation transforms mutually exclusive claims into complementary, sequential phases of a unified dynamical process. We define the mechanics of this algorithm, establish absolute contextual transparency as its criterion for resolution, and introduce a metabolic model of epistemic structures. This framework offers a universal, domain-agnostic tool for resolving persistent structural impasses in epistemology, process philosophy, and artificial intelligence theory.

items.title: Universal Collapse Theory—Conscious Collapse: Mind as a Phase of Constraint-Guided Collapse (WP04 v1.0).
items.abstract: This paper extends Universal Collapse Theory (UCT) into the mind-phase, treating human consciousness as a proposed regime in which some neural resolutions become globally available and recursively usable for report, deliberate control, memory, and possible later constraint update. The neural claim is a defeasible access-level identification hypothesis: broadcasting, recurrence, integration, and differentiation are candidate third-person signatures, not sufficient conditions by definition. Interpretively, UCT advances a non-bifurcation thesis: first-person presence and third-person neural organization are non-interchangeable modes of access to one conscious occurrence, not ontologically separate products. This does not settle phase criteria, episode unity, or content correspondence. Non-conscious processing remains locally effective; conscious processing is provisionally modeled as system-wide, globally available, recursively usable resolution. -/- Perception is modeled as hypothesis resolution under constraints supplied by priors, context, goals, bodily state, and neural architecture. The FRLB schema—Faith, Reason, Logic, Belief—is presented as a proposed functional-role decomposition of cognitive resolution and update. A revised heuristic update model distinguishes Reason from the kernel record symbol and separates Event Belief from standing Belief. Action and agency are modeled as constrained behavioral selection; free will is treated operationally as graded reasons-responsive participation in revising selected later constraints, not as an escape from causation or a settlement of the metaphysical free-will debate. -/- Across histories of certified records and constraint updates, learning and memory can stabilize an identity architecture; rigidity or misalignment becomes a testable hypothesis about update dynamics rather than a clinical diagnosis. Consciousness-Induced Material (CIM) is retained as the consciously shaped, record-bearing layer through which cognition becomes durable and can non-trivially constrain later minds. The individual neural, perceptual, FRLB, and institutional predictions are not unique to UCT. The discriminating burden lies in preregistered transfer, for each S-signature, of a restricted model across physics, biology, and mind. Successful transfer would support the shared-schema claim; qualitative analogy or domain-specific refitting would not.

items.title: The Epistemic Tax: What Autodidactic Falsificationism Actually Costs, Why This Corpus's Objections Sections and Its Cross-Paper Corrections Tell Two Different Stories, and What a Direct Test on Appendix I, "On the Author," Adds.
items.abstract: This corpus's methodological vocabulary — falsification conditions, research-programme evaluation, the distinction between progressive and degenerating theory-adjustment — is drawn substantially from Popper and Lakatos, a specific tradition within philosophy of science rather than general philosophical literacy. This paper does not treat that fact as self-evidently impressive and states directly why it resists doing so: the claim that this tradition is rare in the author's own educational context, and the claim that the author lacks a formal academic degree, are both stated here as unverified rather than confirmed, and a paper that built its central argument on either claim without this qualification would violate this corpus's own empirical-anchoring commitment before its argument even began. What this paper can state with more confidence is narrower and more interesting: that the question worth asking is not whether this corpus's Popperian self-scrutiny is impressive, but whether it is genuine, and that the honest answer is neither uniformly humble nor uniformly performed. Section IV reports a finding already on this corpus's own record: The Artifact Problem's audit of every Objections section this corpus has produced found a 100 percent thesis-survival rate, indistinguishable, by this corpus's own Act-Level Criterion, from simple absorption. Section V does not stop at reporting that statistic. It applies the same scrutiny directly and for the first time to a single, specific, unusually careful specimen — Appendix I, "On the Author," from this corpus's founding book, which classifies the book's own author as satisfying Taleb's black swan criteria and names the resulting condition the Beautiful Trap — and finds the same signature at close range that The Artifact Problem found in aggregate: a black swan classification applied prospectively to a claim Taleb's own framework defines retrospectively; a narrative-fallacy structure offered as confirming evidence rather than flagged as the bias Taleb warns against; an argument about the author's own structural position that, checked against this corpus's own falsifiability standard, does not currently name an observation about that position which would count against it; and an attributional pattern — analytical success credited internally, absence of traction explained entirely externally — matching the asymmetry Miller and Ross's (1975) literature on self-serving attribution documents independently of Kunda. …

items.title: Revocable Infrastructure and Generative Dependency: An Open-Then-Enclose Mechanism.
items.abstract: A party contributes a method to a commons and opens the infrastructure required to develop it. Others learn the method, build on it, train teams, and develop extensions, and their trajectories become organized around that infrastructure. The party then closes the infrastructure or reprices it. Nothing is taken: the others keep the method, keep what they learned, and keep everything they built. What they lose is the continuation. This paper analyzes that configuration. Its first claim is that the opening is not incidental to what follows. Opening infrastructure and inviting others to build on it confers discretionary power over the continuation of their work, and it confers that power precisely through their reliance, without any promise, contract, or fiduciary relation having been formed. Its second claim identifies what is stranded. Hold-up analysis strands relation-specific investment, whose loss is the difference between an asset’s value inside and outside a relation; here what is stranded is a developed generative capacity whose loss is a set of trajectories that can no longer be reached, and that set is exactly the object no observation records. Its third claim concerns time: refusing access to someone who has not begun and withdrawing access from someone who has built are not the same act at different prices, because the second operates on a capacity that exists partly through the first party’s own opening. Its fourth claim is that the open period creates for the opening party an option whose value rises with others’ reliance, and that this option accrues whether or not anyone intended it, so that neither prior generosity nor absence of a plan is a defense. Its fifth claim is that legitimate origination of a resource does not license unlimited restructuring of trajectories others have developed with it. Its sixth claim locates the remedial handle in exit capacity rather than in access rights. Three propositions follow: exposure accumulates monotonically with reliance, so the participants who trusted the opening most are the most exposed; the contraction of a repertoire can be established by a single witness while its magnitude remains bounded but unidentified; and exit capacity caps exposure uniformly in time whereas an access guarantee only defers it, and defers it in a way that increases the loss realized if the guarantee ever lapses. The paper classifies no platform, firm, or episode, proposes no policy, and reaches no legal conclusion.

items.title: Generative Interests and Legal Relations: Permission, Capability Impairment, and Remedy.
items.abstract: This paper is analytic jurisprudence. It states no proposition about the law of any jurisdiction, and its single positive-law citation is a regulatory record used only for the dates it records. Its subject is a family of inferences that recur in argument about whether and how generative capacity could be legally protected, and its claim is that several of them are invalid on grounds that do not depend on any jurisdiction's content. The first is the inference from the absence of an intellectual-property exclusion right to a general permission to use. On a Hohfeldian analysis, the absence of a claim-right establishes at most a privilege, held by one party, against one party, with respect to one act, under one body of law, and revocable by anyone holding a power to alter the relation. Reading it as a permission commits five distinct and separable fallacies, which the paper enumerates and proves. The second concerns the object of protection. Generative capacity is directed at futures, and argument that protects the specific futures a party would have realized is argument from a counterfactual whose content is not merely uncertain in magnitude but indeterminate in identity. The paper argues that the available object is a presently existing generative position, and that this substitution reduces the counterfactual burden without eliminating it. The third concerns proof. Present impairment, elevated risk to future trajectories, and the value of unrealized trajectories form a strict entailment chain with nested evidentiary requirements, so a liability rule that conditions the recognition of injury on proof of value renders established impairments unremediable — which is a choice about remedial architecture rather than a consequence of the injuries. The fourth concerns instruments. The candidate interests — attribution, confidentiality, portability, participation, benefit sharing, access, and non-foreclosure — are pairwise independent, and an exclusive right to exclude is neither necessary nor sufficient for any of them, which is an argument against inventing a property form rather than for it. The fifth concerns remedies: those whose content is a state of affairs are determinable from impairment-level facts, while those whose content is a sum are not, so a compensation-only repertoire can address none of the injuries identified here. The paper closes with five research obligations stating what any doctrinal claim in this area would require and recording that none …

items.title: Counterfactual Explanations and the Scope of Contestability.
items.abstract: The automation of consequential decisions through opaque machine learning models in societal domains impedes our agency. This paper is about how agency can be reinstated by the provision of certain kinds of knowledge. More precisely, we discuss whether a specific type of explanation, counterfactual explanations, facilitates our ability to contest algorithmic decisions. Against this backdrop, our paper makes three contributions: First, we develop an account of contestability, where contestability is defined as the provision of information, sufficient for a decision-subject to use as a basis for demanding that a decision be revoked. We also demarcate contestability from adjacent concepts in the discourse surrounding the right to explanation, such as justification and recourse. Second, we examine to what extent counterfactual explanations are conducive to contestability by considering a variety of failure modes causing problematic algorithmic decisions and scrutinize to what extent counterfactual explanations help us detect the underlying errors. Third, we propose ways in which, with certain modifications, counterfactual explanations can be made more fitting to serve the desired function. In this vein, we sketch the contours of a multi-shot approach to counterfactuals, where decision-subjects can query a model to test their own counterfactuals for a (limited) number of times.

items.title: A Dynamic Self-Model: Recasting Selfhood as a Testable Neurodynamic Research Program.
items.abstract: We propose a “Dynamic Self-Model”—the sense of a continuous “minimal self” emerges from the rapid alternation between first-order “awareness” (A) and spontaneous second-order “awareness-of-awareness” (AoA). -/- This conceptual model places clear constraints on candidate neural implementations, thereby recasting the long-standing philosophical puzzle of selfhood as a testable question about neural mechanisms. -/- A falsifiable “anti-phase” theta-gamma coupling hypothesis and a proof-of-concept study have been accepted for presentation at the Cognitive Neuroscience Society (CNS) 2026 annual meeting. -/- We seek to transform “Who am I?” from a timeless spiritual question into a cumulative, open, and testable research program.

items.title: Sebastian Morello: Conservatism and Grace: The Conservative Case for Religion by Establishment, Routledge, New York, 2023, $57.99 pbk, xiv + 275 pp + bibliography and index. [REVIEW]
Arrested Attention: Essays on the Phenomenology of Love.
items.pub: Dissertation, University of Toronto, St. George Campus
items.abstract: In this thesis, I argue for the theoretical importance of love’s phenomenology. In particular, I utilize an experience I call ‘arrested attention’ to critically examine the role of relationships and reciprocity in romantic love: -/- In the first chapter, I evaluate a family of views that I call ‘relationship-directed attitude’ views. These argue that love is partially constituted by an attitude toward a relationship, such as judging it to be valuable. I argue, however, that the experience of arrested attention cannot be successfully explained in terms of any relationship-directed attitude. Through a series of familiar cases, I demonstrate how arrested attention and the relationship-directed attitude always come apart. This surprising result should not only prompt philosophers of love to reconsider the fundamentality of relationship-directed attitudes—and relationships—to romantic love, but also to think again about the theoretical importance of love’s phenomenology. -/- In the second chapter, I utilize resources from both philosophy and psychology to elaborate on the relationship between romantic love and attention. Employing the ‘dual-process model’ of human attention developed by cognitive neuroscientists and philosophers, I argue that each system is likely best associated with a distinct stage of love. In particular, I argue that, while in the earliest stage of love, our attention might become arrested by our beloved automatically, in the middle stage, we may have to self-direct our attention to sustain love. The end of love, I argue, crucially coincides with prolonged inattention. I conclude with a consideration of individual differences in attentional capacity. The result is a nuanced phenomenological picture of the constitutive role of attention in romantic love. -/- Chapter three combines the insights from chapters one and two and applies them to the end of unrequited love. In particular, and by utilizing a variety of phenomenological data, I argue that, in order to move on from unwanted unrequited love, the unrequited lover ought to adjust their relevant second-order attitude. I consider a range of possible second-order attitudes an unrequited lover might adopt before ultimately recommending the attitude of ‘non-judgmental acceptance.’ This is because, although non-judgmental acceptance will not, in and of itself, cause us to stop loving, it alone avoids the worst problems associated with all other second-order attitudes.

items.title: The limits of the visible: Body, loss, and surveillance in David Cronenberg’s The Shrouds (ENG and RUS) // Пределы видимого: тело, утрата и надзор в фильме Д. Кроненберга «Саван».
items.pub: Nauka Televideniya—the Art and Science of Television 22 (2):33–79.
items.venue: Nauka Televideniya—the Art and Science of Television
items.abstract: This article examines David Cronenberg’s 2024 film The Shrouds as a philosophical allegory of how digital culture reshapes death, farewell, and mourning. It offers a visual and narrative analysis of the cinematic techniques—interpreted through the interrelated concepts of the “transparent body,” “digital flesh,” and “mournability”—through which the director reflects on the impact of the grief technology industry (grief-tech) on traditional mourning rituals and the experience of bereavement. The analysis draws on the theoretical frameworks of posthumanism (Rosi Braidotti, Donna Haraway), the phenomenology of illness (Havi Carel), the ethics of visuality (Judith Butler, Luciano Floridi), and poststructuralist critique (Michel Foucault). The article considers how Cronenberg problematizes the technologically mediated transformation of one of the key experiences in philosophical anthropology: the experience of loss. The study concludes that The Shrouds serves as a cautionary warning that the digitalization of death risks stripping loss of its ontological finality, transforming mourning into an endless circulation of visual images within a closed digital cyborg circuit. // В статье исследуется вышедшая в 2024 году на экраны кинокартина режиссера Д. Кроненберга «Саван» (англ. The Shrouds), философская аллегория на тему цифровой трансформации опыта смерти как онтологического события прощания и переживания скорби. Проводится визуальный и нарративный анализ кинематографических приемов (в том числе в контексте смежных понятий «прозрачного тела», «цифровой плоти» и «оплакиваемости»), посредством которых режиссер осмысляет влияние индустрии технологий для скорбящих (grief-tech) на традиционные траурные ритуалы и переживание утраты. Исследование опирается на теоретические рамки постгуманизма (Р. Брайдотти, Д. Харауэй), феноменологии болезни (Х. Карел), этики визуальности (Дж. Батлер, Л. Флориди) и постструктуралистской критики (М. Фуко). Рассматривается, как Д. Кроненберг проблематизирует технологически опосредованную трансформацию одного из ключевых для философской антропологии опытов переживания утраты. Исследование приводит к выводу, что «Саван» является предостережением Д. Кронеберга, что диджитализация смерти способна лишить ее свойства онтологической финальности, превратив скорбь в бесконечный процесс циркуляции визуальных образов внутри замкнутого киборгианского цифрового контура.

items.title: Suspension in Epistemology and Beyond. [REVIEW]
items.pub: International Journal for the Study of Skepticism 16 (2-3):243-250.
items.venue: International Journal for the Study of Skepticism

items.title: AI ethics after generative AI: from consequences to effects.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based applications are becoming increasingly integrated into everyday practices of communication, learning, and creativity. Their widespread adoption has intensified debates in AI ethics concerning how their societal significance should be understood and evaluated. Existing approaches to AI ethics have developed important concepts and governance frameworks for evaluating the consequences of AI systems, particularly in relation to their design, deployment, and identifiable impacts. These approaches have proven indispensable for analyzing harms, assigning responsibility, and guiding governance. However, the widespread incorporation of LLMs into everyday practices also raises questions about more gradual and cumulative transformations that emerge through repeated human–LLM interaction. Drawing on John Dewey’s pragmatist account of inquiry, habit formation, and moral reconstruction, we distinguish between consequences, identifiable outcomes that can be evaluated within existing normative and regulatory frameworks, and effects, the cumulative transformations of the habits and conditions through which inquiry, judgment, and action are organized over time. We argue that interactions with LLM-based applications give rise to both consequences and effects, and that these should be understood as complementary rather than competing analytical perspectives. Building on this distinction, we use Dewey’s conception of habits to examine how repeated engagement with LLMs may contribute to transformations in three domains: epistemic inquiry, affective-relational self-understanding, and cultural meaning-making. Rather than proposing an alternative to existing AI ethics, we argue that attending to effects complements current approaches by directing ethical inquiry towards the cumulative transformations that emerge through everyday human–LLM interaction.

items.title: Additional Remarks Concerning the Foundations of Timothy Williamson’s Epistemicism.
items.abstract: As a supplement to 'A Unified Epistemological Framework for Understanding Epistemicism' (2025), this separate but brief account examines the grounds on which Timothy Williamson develops his epistemic theory of vagueness as presented in Vagueness (1994). Williamson’s account approaches the Sorites paradox by arguing that vague terms such as ‘heap’ or ‘thin’ possess sharp yet unknowable boundaries, thereby preserving bivalence for vague terms and their use in logical propositions. This essay begins not as a polemical account but rather one concerned with how Williamson’s inquiry came to be justified through Bertrand Russell’s account of vagueness in Vagueness (1923). This essay suggests that a charitable reading of Russell’s position, specifically his discussion of logical connectives, such as disjunctions, is not consistent with Williamson’s interpretation. I contend Williamson’s interpretation is a much stronger position than what Russell stated. What Russell intended was a discussion surrounding the limitations of logic as it concerns vague predicates. Russell’s essay is primarily an account about the issue of logical connectives and logical propositions becoming subject to vagueness through vague predicates; not that logical operators themselves are vague. This is an important distinction which I argue Russell makes clear. Prompted by these findings, which supplement my own position on why Epistemicism fails on epistemic grounds, I present this essay to examine foundational arguments as put forward by Williamson in his 1994 work, Vagueness.

items.title: Against sovereign solutionism: crisis, AGI, and arguments for a pluralistic philosophy of AI.
items.abstract: Contemporary discourse on artificial general intelligence (AGI) increasingly frames advanced intelligence as a singular force capable of resolving large-scale social and political crises through superior prediction, optimization, and control. This article challenges that image. It argues that AGI discourse is often structured by a fantasy of sovereign intelligence: a wish-granting conception of intelligence as a unified authority able to overcome conflict, satisfy collective demands, and relieve political actors of the burdens of judgment—or the fear of an alien mastermind challenging and finally destroying humanity. Against this view, the article develops a critique of sovereign solutionism grounded in crisis theory, political judgment, and recent work on collective and multi-agent AI. First, it argues that crises are not reducible to well-structured problems, because they involve contested ends, legitimacy disputes, and uncertainty about the standards of resolution themselves and require transformations, not solutions. Second, the article argues that recent technical research on collective behavior, multi-agent alignment, and agent societies further weakens the plausibility of AGI as a monolithic crisis-solving entity, while not thereby vindicating a new collective sovereign. Third, it shows that the sovereign image of intelligence is inadequate in six respects: epistemically, no singular standpoint is sufficient to grasp crisis in its entirety; normatively, contested ends cannot be reduced to a single objective function; politically, judgment cannot be legitimately delegated in sovereign form; institutionally, distributed intelligence requires mediation, oversight, and contestation; ontologically, the singular image of intelligence presupposed by AGI discourse is less universal than it appears; and systemically, the decentering of intelligence dissolves the very premise that cognition must culminate in a single sovereign center from which crisis can be surveyed and mastered. The article concludes that a pluralistic philosophy of AI is necessary: one that understands intelligence as situated within plural orders of interpretation, value, responsibility, governance, and technics rather than above them as a final authority. Such a view does not reject AI as such, but rejects the inflation of bounded technical usefulness into a sovereign model of intelligence.

items.title: The understanding gap: when functionality looks like understanding.
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of conversational AI systems has led many users to attribute understanding, emotional sensitivity, and experiential qualities to AI chatbots. While these systems produce highly fluent and contextually appropriate responses, whether such attributions reflect genuine understanding or conflate functional performance with cognitive capacity remains unclear. This paper examines this attribution by integrating a rigorous philosophical framework with empirical findings from chatbot users. We ground our analysis in an expanded ‘knowledge of causes’ view, according to which genuine understanding requires knowledge of dependence relations and the cognitive capacity to manipulate them through analogical, counterfactual, and abductive reasoning. On this account, understanding presupposes an underlying cognitive architecture, not merely correct outputs or behavioral adequacy. We surveyed 122 adult chatbot users about their perceptions of their chatbots’ understanding and their own epistemic beliefs. Participants rated AI functionality significantly higher than AI understanding, and cognitive capacities higher than affective ones, with particularly low ratings for affective understanding.
