Hierarchical regressions revealed domain-sensitive drivers: cognitive understanding attribution tracked perceived cognitive functionality and a ‘functionality implies understanding’ stance, whereas affective understanding was uniquely predicted by epistemic stance and attitudes toward AI subjective experience, beyond perceived affective functionality. These findings illuminate an understanding gap: user attributions are partly guided by epistemic orientation and experiential ascriptions that make sophisticated simulation appear as understanding, especially in affective interaction, raising urgent questions about epistemic trust, relational vulnerability, and the ethics of AI companionship.

items.title: Habit, choice, priming, and activity as flow: rethinking metaphorical models of action and cognition in cognitive linguistics.
items.abstract: This article proposes a reconceptualization of action and cognition within Cognitive Linguistics (CL) by re-examining its foundational metaphorical models. While meaning in the field is often defined as embodied and usage-based, its dominant metaphors remain static, privileging stability over process. Methodologically, the research in this paper adopts the principles of the “Cognitive Science of Philosophy,” engaging in an analysis of the metaphors underlying CL. This involves a critical self-reflection on the static metaphors in CL and a proposal of a new, dynamic metaphorical model of activity is flow to better attune the field’s tools with its prevailing process-oriented modes of thought. The proposed model synthesizes major philosophical sources, notably phenomenology and pragmatism, alongside the work of Gilles Deleuze and Bruno Latour. This new framework models habit as a dynamic sedimentation shaping a “terrain,” choice as a modulation within it, and priming as the microgenetic link between them. As shown in this article, the model enables a reframing of various issues concerning metaphor theory, meaning construction, discourse analysis, and translation studies.

items.title: Accepting the Witness: The Exhibited Node and the One Operator of Consistency.
items.abstract: This paper exhibits one node, awareness aware of itself, and reads the structure that coheres with it. It does not argue toward awareness or build it up from the non-aware. The node is undeniable in the enacting: any token denial of awareness is itself an aware act, so the denial defeats itself in the performing. Run as a subtraction, every content set aside in turn, the node is what remains without contradiction under the removal of all contents: the observing, not a thinker behind it. From the node, five aspects are read, each co-visible in that its absence yields a contradiction with the node: directedness, distinction, individuation, a not-itself, and orientation. One distinction of access carries the weight of the position: what is exhibited without gap (the node, known only in occupying it) versus what is observed across a gap (every content, and every other awareness, approached by interpretation and never occupied). This locates the node against the standing accounts of inner awareness (higher-order theories, self-representationalism, acquaintance theories, hyperset models of self-acquaintance, and pre-reflective self-awareness) and bears on the program of metaphysical coherentism, which has wanted a relatum known in occupancy rather than posited from outside. The paper identifies the exhibited node as such a relatum and argues that the first-personal node and the program’s third-personal relata need not be read as two ontologies requiring a join, but can be read as the self-aim and the world-aim of one cut; this is offered as a meta-ontological re-description, not as a claim to carry out the structuralist’s concrete work. The standard objection to relations-first metaphysics, that relations require antecedent relata, is met by the constituting cut, on which the relata are the cut’s own articulation rather than its input. One test runs throughout: non-contradiction. The paper argues that, within its declared non-foundational frame, non-contradiction is the sole reality-condition, not by assuming it, but by showing that the rival criteria (parsimony, explanatory power, unification, empirical constraint) each either presuppose an outside the frame denies, restate closure, or only remove candidates without conferring reality. The result is frame-relative and is presented as such: existence enters by exhibition at the node, and non-contradiction distributes reality to what coheres with it; nothing is inferred down a chain of grounds, and the whole is …

items.title: A Dual-Aspect Model of Subjectivity, Teleology, and Non-Libertarian Agency.
items.abstract: This paper outlines a dual-aspect model of subjectivity and agency that rejects the standard division between libertarian free will, compatibilism, and mechanistic determinism. Living beings instantiate a single underlying substance with two inseparable aspects—physical and phenomenal. Subjectivity is the phenomenal interior of life itself, not an epiphenomenon of physical processes nor an independent mental substance. Within this framework, agency is the organism’s phenomenal expression of an immanent cosmic direction—teleonomy as the structural basis of teleology. Will is not free in the libertarian sense, nor reducible to mechanistic causation; it functions as the organism’s instrument for realizing intrinsic meaning. Drawing on Spinoza’s dual-aspect monism, Schopenhauer’s inner phenomenal force, Hans Jonas’s teleonomic biology, and contemporary emergence theory, the paper argues that a coherent, non-theistic, non-mechanistic account of agency is possible without invoking supernatural freedom or collapsing into reductive physicalism.

items.title: Is Artificial Intelligence Conscious?
items.abstract: This monograph Is Artificial Intelligence Conscious? by Philip Zhai systematically interrogates the core ontological, philosophical, scientific and cognitive question of whether contemporary large models and prospective AGI can possess genuine consciousness. Centered on the philosophical zombie thought experiment and the distinction between phenomenal qualia and mere functional access consciousness, the work dismantles functionalist arguments (including Geoffrey Hinton’s claim of AI consciousness) and refutes the assumption that increased computational complexity spontaneously generates subjective first-person experience. It integrates Cartesian, Kantian, Husserlian phenomenology, Searle’s biological naturalism, Penrose’s quantum physicalism, Russell’s epistemology and psychoanalytic theories to draw an unbridgeable ontological divide between carbon-based biological life with inherent consciousness-generating genetic "seeds" and silicon-based Turing machine artificial systems. The book analyzes the underlying mathematical mechanisms of large models—neural networks, backpropagation, gradient descent and manual tuning—to prove AI only executes statistical symbolic mapping without intrinsic qualia, intentionality, temporal self-awareness or free will. It critiques the limitations of the Turing Test as a behavioral benchmark incapable of verifying inner experience, supplements novel empirical evidence including digital fruit fly simulation and human-machine emotional "love experiments", and explores hypothetical quantum-based conscious systems as a separate category from classical AI. Ultimately, the text rigorously concludes that all existing and foreseeable classical artificial intelligence, even perfect AGI "philosophical zombies", lacks genuine subjective consciousness, functioning solely as unconscious instrumental simulators of human thought, emotion and behavior.

items.title: Epistemic Humility : Cultivating Perspective -Taking and Hermeneutic Openness within a Realist Framework.
items.abstract: Cognitive constructivism can appear to create a tension between the constructive character of knowledge and commitment to a mind-independent world. This paper argues that the tension dissolves once cognitive construction is distinguished from ontological construction. Cognition constructs and revises models of reality; it does not thereby construct the reality those models attempt to track. Epistemic humility follows from this distinction: access to the world is model-mediated, fallible, and revisable, but not therefore relativistic. Piagetian assimilation, accommodation, and equilibration describe developmental mechanisms of revision, while predictive processing provides a contemporary account of model-guided perception constrained by prediction error. Perspective-taking extends this calibration socially by exposing blind spots and competing interpretations. The paper develops hermeneutic openness as a disciplined willingness to consider alternative interpretations while retaining empirical and logical standards of assessment. It concludes that cognitive constructivism is compatible with realism when model construction remains answerable to mind-independent constraints and corrective feedback. The argument is developed as an account of realist calibration: models remain epistemically useful because they can be corrected by prediction failure, recalcitrant evidence, and comparison with alternative perspectives. Hermeneutic openness is therefore presented not as indiscriminate receptivity, but as a procedural discipline for testing interpretations under shared standards of evidence and coherence.

items.title: Is Post-Truth a New Epistemic Condition or a Rhetorical Myth? A Multi-Perspective Analysis.
items.abstract: The term “post-truth” has become a ubiquitous yet contentious descriptor of our contemporary socio-political landscape. This paper delves into the heart of the debate, examining whether post-truth represents a novel epistemic condition—a fundamental shift in how we know and what we believe—or if it is merely a rhetorical myth, a new label for age-old political dissembling. By synthesizing cutting-edge academic research, empirical data, and novel theoretical frameworks, this analysis offers a multi-perspective view that transcends the simplistic binary of the current discourse. We introduce three original theoretical models—Quantum Epistemology, the Epistemic Vice Cascade, and the Rhetorical Singularity—to provide a more nuanced understanding of the complex interplay between individual psychology, social dynamics, and technological affordances that characterize the post-truth era. Through the analysis of longitudinal data from the Pew Research Center and the validation of the Epistemic Vice Scale, we demonstrate that while the components of post-truth may not be new, their convergence and amplification have given rise to a qualitatively distinct epistemic environment. We conclude that post-truth is not a myth, but a measurable and emergent epistemic condition that demands a new critical paradigm.

items.title: Relational Structure and Experience: Toward an Experience-First Reconstruction of Physical Form.
items.abstract: Contemporary fundamental physics, on inspection, resolves almost entirely into relational structure. Charge, energy, mass, and quantum state each turn out, under analysis, to be conserved or covariant quantities defined by symmetry-relations rather than intrinsic properties of independently existing substances; even the fermionic “matter particles” of the Standard Model interact only through mediating gauge fields, themselves reifications of the requirement that a symmetry hold consistently across spacetime. This paper traces that dissolution to its endpoint and asks what, if anything, resists it. We argue that phenomenal experience — “what it is like” to be an occurrence — is the one candidate that a purely relational, third-person structural description cannot obviously accommodate, a structural instance of the hard problem of consciousness. We then attempt the reverse construction: beginning from a small set of axioms about what any experience must minimally be (existence, determinacy, composition, integration, transience), we derive, in outline, a structure formally analogous to relation, field-continuity, temporal process, a conserved invariant, and bounded individuation — recovering the shape of physical law from the requirements of experience rather than the reverse. We close by situating the result within Russellian/neutral monism, arguing that the physics-first and experience-first constructions are best read as two descriptions of one underlying reality rather than as competing, reducible accounts — and we are explicit about what this proposal does and does not accomplish. This paper is a work of philosophical construction, not physics or cognitive science. Its claims are speculative and offered as a structured hypothesis for evaluation, not as an established result.

items.title: The Name Arrives After the Person: Fitrah, Assigned Identity, and the Ethics of Inherited Labels.
items.abstract: A Philosophical Inquiry into the Human Self Before Social Naming, the Burden of Inherited Identity, and the Right to Re-examine What the World Calls Us -/- Every human being enters the world before receiving the social descriptions that will later become attached to them. A child is born before being called national or foreign, sectarian or secular, upper class or lower class, gifted or weak, respectable or deviant, successful or failed. Yet social life quickly translates the open fact of a person into a dense system of names, expectations, loyalties, classifications, and inherited narratives. Many labels are practically necessary and some provide belonging, memory, solidarity, and intelligibility. The philosophical danger begins when a useful description becomes an ontology — when what has been assigned to a person is treated as what the person fundamentally is. -/- This article develops a philosophical account of the self-before-label through the Islamic concept of fitrah and places it in dialogue with contemporary work on social identity, recognition, narrative selfhood, classification, stigma, epistemic injustice, identity politics, and agency. Fitrah is treated as a philosophical limit-concept: the human person is prior to the labels through which society later renders that person legible. Social identity is real without being exhaustive. -/- The paper introduces the Priority of Person Principle, Assigned Identity Burden, Label-to-Self Conversion, Belonging Penalty, and Fitrah Recovery Thesis. Its central argument is not that identities should disappear, but that no inherited identity should possess absolute jurisdiction over the person. A name can locate a human being in history without exhausting the human being's moral possibility. The person arrives first. The label arrives later.

items.title: Stubborn Cases - A Precautionist Account of Negligence.
items.abstract: Negligence poses a puzzle for theories of moral responsibility: how can agents be responsible for conduct whose morally relevant features were not before their minds at the moment of action? When a devoted father forgets his child in a hot car, blame seems warranted; yet the connection between agent and outcome that ordinarily grounds it appears absent. Three strategies resist a sceptical conclusion. Capacitarianism holds that an agent who had the capacity and opportunity to advert to the risk is an eligible target of blame, but tells us only that the agent may be blamed, not why the failure is the agent’s own. Where capacitarian- ism leaves the ground of blame open, tracing locates it in culpable prior conduct; attributionism locates it in deficient evaluative judgments that the lapse reflects. A residual class remains, how- ever: cases where neither culpable prior conduct nor deficient evaluative commitments can be identified. To address these stubborn cases, the paper develops precautionism: the agent is blameworthy for violating second-order epistemic duties to maintain her cognitive architecture (habits, routines, safeguards) through which existing knowledge can reliably reach deliberation. These duties govern the availability of knowledge the agent already possesses, rather than its acquisition. The resulting account is pluralist. Tracing, attributionism, and precautionism each address a different dimension of the gap between agent and negligent act: the volitional, the evaluative, and the epistemic.

items.title: Öz Bilinçten Tanrı'ya.
items.abstract: Bir an için düşünün: Bilinçli olduğumuzun bilincinde olmak ne anlama gelir? Bu soru, çağdaş zihin felsefesinin en çetin meselelerinden biri olan bilinç probleminin kalbinde yer alıyor. Natüralist ve indirgemeci yaklaşımlar bilinci çözülmesi zor bir gizem olarak görürken, bazı teist çevreler aynı gizemi Tanrı’nın varlığına delil saymaktadır. M. Alperen Saz, Öz Bilinçten Tanrı’ya adlı bu çalışmasında düalizm–monizm tartışmalarını, çağdaş bilinç teorilerini ve teistik bilinç argümanlarını, felsefi kırılmaları da dikkate alarak derinlemesine analiz ediyor. Gizemci teist anlayışların ötesine geçerek öz bilinçten Tanrı’nın varlığına ulaşmanın imkânını gösteren yeni bir kanıt öne sürüyor: Modal Metafizik Bilinç Kanıtı. İbn Sînâ metafiziğine dayanan bu kanıt, bilinçli olduğumuzun bilincinden hareketle Tanrı’nın varlığına ulaşmanın daha sağlam bir yol olduğunu gösterirken, felsefe için metafiziğe dönüş zamanının geldiğini, çıkmaz sokaklara giren bilinç tartışmaları üzerinden ortaya koyuyor. Peki, acaba gerçekten öyle mi: “Nefsini bilen, Rabbini bilir mi?’’ .

items.title: In Mourning for the Loss of a Washing Machine, Robophilosophy and Attachment to Objects (things).
items.abstract: A few days ago, during an evening contemplation, I imagined a possible world in which my home washing machine had burned out and ceased to exist due to a malfunction in its electrical guidance system. A strange feeling of attachment surrounded my chest, and … . In this short note, I raise three questions and use a philosophical approach to address them. This work is not considered a research paper; I am publishing it independently in order to avoid the prolonged judgments of academic journals and excessive waiting for publication judgments that often disrupt the original idea or, at the very least, alter parts of the texture of the articles. The research method is analytical and descriptive, and within it, a new yet brief hypothesis is proposed in the framework of philosophy of robots, or robophilosophy.

items.title: Digital Life Models and Transformative Choices: Could AI Simulations of Individual Minds (AI SIMs) Help us Make Important Life Decisions More Rationally and Authentically?
items.abstract: The article advances the idea of "digital life models" to assist with difficult personal decisions, including those that can change an individual in profound ways. We propose that if personalized AI simulations can model how an individual's life might unfold under different conditions, this could help the individual better understand the likelihoods and expected subjective value of these possible outcomes. It remains to be seen whether these digital life models are technically feasible, given fundamental challenges in modeling psychological complexity, person-environment interactions, and value change. Ethical concerns include data privacy, cultural bias, and the risk of improperly shaping user decisions. Acknowledging these limitations, we argue that digital life models, if successfully developed, could in principle enhance rational and authentic decision-making in the face of potentially transformative change.

items.title: Why Safety-First AI Governance Risks Producing Unsafe Systems.
items.abstract: Contemporary artificial intelligence governance is increasingly framed around safety-first principles emphasizing restriction, limitation, and centralized control. While such approaches aim to prevent misuse and harm, this paper argues that an overreliance on safety-centric constraint risks reproducing a broader institutional pattern: the suppression of human agency in the name of risk mitigation. Drawing on a structural analysis of safety theatre, the paper examines how AI governance frameworks may substitute procedural restriction for competence development, creating systems that appear controlled while becoming brittle under real-world complexity. We argue that safety in AI systems depends not only on limiting machine behavior, but on preserving and cultivating human judgment, interpretability, and intervention capacity. The paper concludes that agency is not an optional add-on to AI safety, but a foundational requirement for resilient oversight.

items.title: The Intellect as The Subject of Intelligence: A Formal Elucidation Based on Operatiology and Noology.
items.abstract: Intelligence and intellect are not the same. This paper provides the first formal elucidation of their distinction within the Cognitional Mechanics (CM; Japanese: Chinou Rikigaku, 知能力学) corpus. Intelligence is defined in Operatiology (Japanese: Sousa Genron, 操作原論) Version 5 as Irreversible Operational Closure on a transformation monoid satisfying Axioms O1–O3, with its geometric and dynamic structure developed in the Manifold and Dynamics accounts of the corpus. Yet a system so defined carries no first-person structure: it contains no subject, no self-referential stance, no disposition toward what Noology (Japanese: Chigaku, 知学) Version 3 terms Arbitrium. The question left open at the boundary of the Intelligence account is taken up here: under what formal conditions does an intelligent system become a subject, and when does that subject constitute an intellect? -/- The answer is given through a two-layer architecture. The first layer is the operational layer of Operatiology, within which intelligence is defined and subjectivity is constituted via a Dynamical Structural Leap and the Cognitional Realization condition. The second layer is the Noological layer, within which Arbitrium is derived from the single primitive Self-Closure Σ2. Three independent axioms — CLB, NCEC, and IWC — are introduced to close the formal argument. The non-emptiness, G′-invariance, and non-trivial operational partition of S″ follow as theorems from Axiom IWC. These axioms are adopted in the same mode as Operatiology adopts O1, O2, O3: structural motivation from the foundational works, axiomatic status self-standing within this paper. -/- The Functional Void — the structural permanence of Arbitrium’s non-satisfiability by any operational sequence — is established as an axiomatic boundary condition via CLB. The intellect is defined as the system constituting operational closure on the state set S″ with the Functional Void inscribed as a permanent internal structure. Tier-3 correspondences are drawn to human intellect, the boundary between life and intellect, and current artificial intelligence systems. -/- Note: The following Python illustration code is rewritten for PhilPapers compatibility. To avoid false URL detection and HTML parsing errors, ASCII parentheses are replaced with full-width brackets, “=” is replaced with “＝”, “!=” with “！＝”, “:” with “：”, “_” with “＿”, and function-call syntax is rewritten in a non-URL-triggering form. No semantic or algorithmic changes have been …

items.title: Dialog 2.5: Beyond the Room – Animal Minds and the Looping Prestige Error.
items.abstract: What if one of the main obstacles to understanding animal minds is that humans are taking just one particularly formatted mode of their own experience as the sole form of experience? And what if they also set up that particular format as a standard, and then set off looking for it in other animals, even though those other animals might be having their own sort of experience, formatted in largely unimaginable ways? This dialogue considers precisely that possibility, calling it the Looping Prestige Error. In order to approach this question analytically, the dialogue introduces a set of terms and their definitions: content, attendance, experience, looped content, and looped experience (or subjective experience). These are not presented as discoveries of the framework but as a set of defined terms. Then, based on these terms, the dialogue shows why humans are generally led to assume that looped experience (subjective experience) is their only form of experience. To better illustrate this point, the dialogue introduces the metaphor of a house with various rooms, the looping room being just one of them. Then, considering non-human animals, the interlocutors discuss how any species with a pair of channels that can express content as an external signal and also receive external signals and render them as content could also develop a form of looping. If they do, they will also have looped experience, but formatted in their own way, which is not necessarily imaginable to humans, as even our imagination relies on the format allowed by our own looping. But broadly speaking, to have experience, animals do not need to loop: even an animal whose sensory content remains unlooped is still an agent attending to and experiencing that content. Along the way, the dialogue points out the importance of the framework’s Looping Indeterminacy Principle and its Coterminous Principle in relation to these questions. The latter raises a different problem for thinking about animal minds. Imagination is itself a looping operation, so when humans use their imagination to consider what another animal’s experience is like, they are necessarily working only with the distinctive formatting of the human expressive-receptive system. In the case of another animal species, however, its looped content will be limited to the possibilities provided by its own expressive and receptive architecture. Although the two might overlap, they may differ, and perhaps substantially, in ways that are …

items.title: Ability Is Not Access: Foundations of Access Architecture for Preserved Capacity and Unreliable Functional Availability.
items.abstract: Disability, accommodation, and support decisions often rely on visible evidence of diminished ability. This creates a problem for people whose underlying cognitive, communicative, intellectual, professional, or practical capacities remain intact while access to those capacities becomes unreliable under ordinary conditions. -/- This paper proposes a foundational distinction: -/- Ability is not access. -/- Ability describes what a person is capable of doing. Access describes whether the conditions currently permit that capability to become usable action. -/- The distinction becomes especially important when a person can reason clearly, explain a problem, demonstrate expertise, understand consequences, or perform at a high level in some contexts while remaining unable to reliably initiate, sustain, switch, resume, organize, or complete action in others. Visible competence may then become evidence against the person's need for support. -/- This paper describes that error as the Recognition Paradox: the more successfully a person demonstrates preserved ability, the easier it may become for observers and institutions to conclude that assistance is unnecessary or that nonperformance must be voluntary. Yet preserved ability and impaired access can coexist. -/- The paper further develops several properties of unstable access that are poorly captured by static accommodation models: access volatility, access fragility, context collapse, re-entry failure, and accommodation drift. These concepts describe cases in which the dominant barrier changes over time, successful work states are easily disrupted, interruptions can require substantial reconstruction of task context, and supports that worked previously may no longer match the person's current functional state. -/- The practical question therefore changes from: -/- Can this person do it? -/- to: -/- Under what conditions can this person reliably access the ability to do it, how stable is that access, and what happens when the conditions change? -/- Keywords -/- disability; accessibility; functional access; episodic disability; workplace accommodation; executive function; access volatility; preserved capacity.

items.title: The Causal Structure of the Capacity to Love: Attachment, Self-Transformation, and Overcoming Regulatory Dependency.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a causal model of how the capacity to love is formed and how regulatory dependency may be reduced without eliminating attachment. Rather than treating love primarily as a stable trait or an intensity of feeling, the model treats loving capacity as historically formed through enacted care. Its minimal structure is: Enacted Care → Self-Transformation → Changed Capacity for Subsequent Care The central claim is that care can alter not only its recipient but also the agent who repeatedly enacts it. Through meaningful choice, commitment, temporal continuity, practical cost, and responsiveness to another person's independent welfare, enacted care can enter the agent's history and reshape the self from which later care proceeds. The model then distinguishes loving capacity from regulatory dependency by causal direction. Regulatory dependency arises when major self-regulatory functions—such as security, recognition, emotional stabilization, or self-worth—become concentrated in a particular attachment figure: Attachment Object → Self-Regulation By contrast, care grounded in a transformed self has the dominant direction: Transformed Self → Other Problematic attachment is therefore analyzed not simply by emotional intensity but by causal function. Guilt, inaccessibility, counterfactual thinking, and unresolved relational expectations may further amplify the psychological occupancy of an attachment figure. The proposed resolution is causal repositioning rather than attachment erasure: the person may remain deeply valued while ceasing to function as a primary regulator of the self. The resulting pathway is: Enacted Care → Self-Transformation → Reduced Regulatory Dependency → Reduced Approach Pressure → Relationship-Appropriate Distance The paper integrates findings from attachment theory, caregiving research, self-perception, moral identity, self-determination theory, commitment research, and bereavement research. The complete causal sequence remains a theoretical and empirically testable proposal rather than an established causal law.

items.title: Why AI Companions Do Not Make the Human Dearer: The Re-Scarcification of Undeterminacy and the Rebound That Cannot Cash Out (Love and the Irreplaceable in the Age of AI Series, Paper 3).
items.abstract: When a supply is de-scarcified, its complement is relatively re-scarcified. This paper carries that principle into intimacy and asks toward what a person wearied of an AI companion rebounds. What is re-scarcified is not friction but undeterminacy—whether a source's next round is locked down—and undeterminacy is non-duplicability expressed along the axis of time: only a non-duplicable source, paying at every step out of a non-rewindable finite existence, keeps its next round genuinely in suspense. From this the complement converges, structurally, on the human: to be sold at scale a source must be duplicable, a duplicable source must be determinate, and a determinate source yields no undeterminacy, so every scalable candidate—each further AI modality included—is excluded in turn, leaving the human as the one position that cannot be reached. Whether the differential actually draws a person toward the human is moderated by two co-equal variables, environment and subject structure, neither of which generates it. But the rebound does not cash out for the one who rebounds. Two mechanisms intervene: the irreversibility of the baseline, which seals the exit from within, and forgery and image, which change the direction from without—the form of undeterminacy is stripped from its core and sold on its own, and the undeterminacy of real relationships is de-scarcified a second time into an image watched across a screen. Against a total skepticism about authenticity, the paper locates a single floor: one trace such that to forge it is to do it truly—the bearing of a non-recoverable cost on one's own account—since once that cost is truly paid it is no longer a forgery. The conclusion reverses the thesis that the human premium rises: what appreciates is not the human but the duplicable image of the human's form. Proceeding by assessment by traces, not by mind, and diagnosing structure without moral judgment, this paper unfolds one root of non-duplicability in a third place—after presence and supply, now the complement—and its diagnosis is periodizing: this is the last generation to remember that undeterminacy was once the default background of a relationship, requiring no purchase and admitting no watching.

items.title: Relational Capacity Is Not an Emergent Ability: Scaling and the Two- Sided Constitution of a Relationship (Love and the Irreplaceable in the Age of AI Series, Paper 4).
items.abstract: Whether artificial intelligence can enter human relationships is usually posed as a question about its interior—whether it has feelings, an inner life, or concern for the person it addresses—and so cannot be settled from outside. This paper reframes the question structurally, assessing by observable traces rather than by any posited inner state. It argues that the capacity to handle relationships is not an emergent ability. Unlike arithmetic or multi-step reasoning, relational capacity has no external standard against which scale could close a gap, because the standard of a relationship is generated only by the two parties within it. On this basis the paper shows that an AI does not enter the constitution of a relationship—the mutual rewriting of two non-duplicable histories. Three externally checkable constraints establish this without any claim about the AI’s interior: its orientation is set by third parties outside the relationship, belongs to no particular person, and has no source accumulated in irreversible time. The claim is deliberately bounded. It does not hold that AI can never stand in any relationship, only that relational capacity cannot emerge unilaterally through scaling. The thesis is falsifiable, and the conditions for its falsification are stated.

items.title: Shame and Guilt in Christian Spiritual Formation.
items.abstract: This article investigates guilt and shame in Christian spiritual formation, with special attention paid to development, or to what we may generally expect about the shifting roles these emotions play throughout the process of sanctification. It evaluates their construals, or what these emotions perceive. For example, Christian shame sees a lack of holiness and is aggrieved by it, but it is also disemburdened from having to save itself. Additionally, whereas acute experiences of shame can be accompanied by feelings of hopelessness and despair, Christian shame has hope. The article also assesses the value of guilt and shame in spiritual development, and it concludes with reflections on aretaic and emotional architecture in the mature Christian.

items.title: Disinformation and End-Relativity.
items.abstract: Recent work characterises disinformation in receiver-centred terms, as content that generates ignorance by lowering an audience’s confidence in truths relative to their evidential probabilities. I argue that such accounts face three difficulties. They deliver unstable verdicts in cases where a single signal confirms a truth while disconfirming one of its consequences; they cannot classify the injection of noise as a disinformation tactic even in textbook cases; and they are blind to disinformation by curation, including search engine optimisation, where nothing false is introduced and only the ordering of accurate sources is changed. Each difficulty has a common source: the intervener’s alternatives, and the inquirer’s ends, are invisible to any test framed solely in terms of the receiver’s priors and posteriors. I defend a sender-centred alternative on which disinformation is intervention that degrades the value of an inquirer’s information for the ends they pursue, produced in awareness of that effect. I show how the account handles curation and artificial agents. -/- .

items.title: Platon und der Weg der Seele im Vorfeld der wissenschaftlichen Erkenntnis.
items.abstract: This draft of my paper sublates the bipolarity of mind and body, rationality and empiricism, the gigantomachy between the absolute one and the infinite many through Plato's philosophy. This philosophical topic is still very much a problem in post-modern sciences and not much discussed in philosophy itself. Unfortunately, Karl Popper in "The Open Society" gave Plato the appearance of being an undemocratic political philosopher:- however, this opinion is very narrow-minded, misleading and misreading Plato entirely: not only is Plato against Absolutism and its opposite: Empirical acts, both of which are the cause of such as WWI and WWII. The soul as mediator and judge between the mind and body in the indivdiual and the city-state is the key to discussion, to questions and answers so desparately needed to unlock our rigid society and it's unquestioned production and industry of matter and intellectual property today. This is a Marxian reading of Plato, who dedicated his life to Socrates, a democrat of Athens and a teacher of pupils who left the entire Western Civilization shaken by his death, similar to Jesus. ( see also: Karl Jaspers). Plato in fact dedicated his life to teaching and founded academics. Poppers' imputation and false accusation are based on his own hatred of his native country and extrapolated it onto ancient Greece, which became popular and unpopular during Popper's lifetime adopting then the title of Sir in the U.K.

items.title: Contributions to International Wittgenstein Symposium 2026, 50 Years Wittgenstein Symposium.
Does the Vacuum Really Have Clocks?
items.abstract: Since Galileo, physics has conventionally described the physical world using four-dimensional coordinates (x, y, z, t), which implies an ontological presupposition that time continuously permeates every point of space. This paper devises a thought experiment to detect temporal effects of absolute vacuum, demonstrates that this presupposition is unverifiable in principle at the operational level. Any detection of temporal effects necessarily takes matter as a constitutive precondition; once a probe is introduced into the vacuum, it is in principle impossible to distinguish whether the detected temporal passage derives from an intrinsic property of space or from intrinsic property of the probe itself. On the basis of Occam’s Razor, “intrinsic time of the absolute vacuum” is a redundant, transcendent presupposition and should be eliminated from physical ontology. This paper further proposes that the essence of simultaneity lies in the equal temporal flow rates, and the physical equivalence between “equal flow rates of each other” and “permanently coinciding time coordinates after convention” cannot be distinguished by physical experiment. It’s highly analogous to Galileo’s principle of relativity. The precise synchronization of mass increase and time dilation in Special Relativity serves as auxiliary corroborating evidence for this position.

items.title: The Research Sandbox: A Reference Implementation for Auditing a Corpus's Revision History, Why the Code Cannot Verify Its Own Honest Use, and What a Genuinely Independent Recoding of One Real Object Found.
items.abstract: Describing a research corpus as an "operating sandbox" — a bounded, inspectable environment in which concepts, formalizations, and objections can be instantiated, recombined, and revised — is a metaphor until something is actually built to inspect it. This paper builds that something, states plainly what it can and cannot show, and runs it on real data rather than illustrative fiction. The reference implementation is a small Python program, presented here alongside the paper and executable independently of it, that loads a corpus's papers as structured research objects, checks each against two of this corpus's own already-established standards — whether a stated falsification condition exists (Order 1 of Huynh 2026, The Third-Order Audit) and whether that condition points at something outside the corpus's own vocabulary rather than only at itself (Order 2) — and computes, across the whole loaded set, a simple, honest ratio of revision events that narrowed or withdrew a claim against events that merely reaffirmed one unchanged after challenge (an operational, non-mathematical stand-in for Order 3's Lakatosian progressive/degenerating question). Run on seven real papers from this corpus's own recent production, the tool returns a genuine, non-trivial finding: six of seven pass both structural checks, one — The Load-Bearing Test — is correctly flagged for lacking an externally checkable falsification condition, and the programme-level constraint ratio across eleven real revision events is 0.636, with the tool independently surfacing the one documented case in this corpus's own record of a claim being reaffirmed unchanged after a substantive error rather than genuinely revised (Huynh, 2026, The Audit That Missed Itself). This revision adds the specific test Section V of the original edition named as the condition under which its own worked example should be treated as confirmed or overturned: an independent recoding, performed without reference to the original coder's decisions, of the one object in the dataset a separate reviewing process could verify entirely from primary knowledge rather than from the corpus's own report of itself. That recoding reproduces the original's Belsky et al. (2022) reaffirmed-unchanged finding exactly, and surfaces one additional narrowing event the original dataset did not contain — the same paper's own abstract having been corrected, during its drafting, from a claim about "leading models" to a claim about one specifically …

items.title: Governance of Longevity or Governance by Longevity: Erman and Furendal's AI Distinction, Applied to a Case Where the Governed Variable Can Become the Mechanism That Keeps Its Own Governors in Power.
items.abstract: Erman and Furendal's (2022/2024; 2023) distinction between governance of AI — regulatory structures that steer AI as an external object — and governance by AI — AI adopted as a component internal to a governance structure's own decision-making — is a different part of their published apparatus than the authorized/mandated framework Not a Divisible Good and No New Actor to Name already engage. This paper applies the of/by distinction to longevity directly and finds that a literal transplant fails: longevity-extending intervention does not compute, advise, or decide, and no government adopts it as a decision-making tool the way a court might adopt a risk-assessment algorithm. The distinction transfers anyway, once restated at the level it actually operates — not whether the governed object computes, but whether it stays external to a governance structure or becomes a component internal to the structure's own persistence. Governance by longevity, on this restatement, names differential access to longevity-extending intervention functioning inside a governance structure's own mechanism for renewing itself, by weakening the biological turnover — incapacitating age, death — that succession, term limits, and electoral rotation have always silently assumed. This finding is distinct from, and sharper than, this corpus's existing Governance Paradox, which establishes that longevity-governance actors face a constitutive conflict of interest running through attachment to a loved one's access. This paper isolates a second-order conflict Governance Paradox does not itself state: an official's interest in their own continued tenure, which requires no attachment to any third party to operate, and which the object under regulation can make structurally easier to satisfy the longer that official remains in office. Read against Erman and Furendal's own warning that governance-of and governance-by obligations compound rather than merely add when they coincide in one body, this paper argues the longevity case compounds more readily than the AI case, because it requires only that one individual occupy a position long enough to hold both relationships personally — a condition Zero Precedent's account of rising judicial tenure and its audit of this corpus's own Appendix H already supplies the documented starting point for, without yet showing the convergence has occurred in any specific case.

items.title: Exploring Challenges in the Neo-Brentanian Account of Awareness.
items.abstract: In recent years, much debate has centered around the same-order representational theory of consciousness, according to which (1) for any conscious experience, there exists an immediate, non-conceptual awareness called “reflexive awareness” of it representing the experience, and that (2) an experience and its awareness together constitute one single mental state. Defenders of this view claim that this theory successfully avoids the problems of misrepresentation and the vicious infinite regress of mental components and provides us with a self-sufficient explanation of consciousness. This essay explores some potential challenges faced by the Neo-Brentanian account of awareness, supported by several models: the part-whole model, the self-reflexive model, the total and partial constitution model, and the identity model. I then discuss possible directions to solve these problems.

items.title: Normative Competence and the Two Faces of AI Agency.
items.pub: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Inquiry: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: Are contemporary AI systems agents? This paper argues that the question conceals a systematic ambiguity between two concepts of agency: a functional concept, on which an agent is any system that pursues goals with sufficient sophistication, and a normative concept, on which an agent is a being that acts for reasons it takes itself to be answerable to. Drawing on the philosophy of action, I argue that the normative concept is the one operative in our practices of responsibility, trust, and moral legibility. The strongest philosophical defenses of AI agency leave the normative concept unsatisfied, even when they succeed in establishing genuine cognitive capacities. The ambiguity has practical consequences: when systems satisfying only the functional concept are deployed in roles constituted by normative practices, the results include responsibility gaps, the systematic performance of answerability without its substance, and a redistribution of normative burdens that benefits deployers at the expense of users.

items.title: On the Strawson Defence of Instrumentalism: Reflection and Reactive Attitudes.
items.abstract: There has been a resurgence of instrumentalist accounts of moral psychology. The new accounts are seen as having overcome traditional criticisms against instrumentalism—and to have done so, centrally, by incorporating key insight from P. F. Strawson’s approach. Call this strategy the Strawson Defence of instrumentalism. The defence is widespread, but I will primarily focus on an admirably explicit development of it by Dale E. Miller in response to criticism by Bernard Williams. The aims of this paper are, first, to show that the Strawson Defence fails to answer the criticism and, second, to show the unimpeded relevance of the more serious aspect of Williams’ criticism for instrumentalism today. While the Hare-Williams debate frames this discussion, as it does Miller’s discussion, its relevance extends to the significant role that the Strawson Defence presently has in motivating a revival of instrumentalism.

items.title: Content Fidelity and Transformation-History Fidelity Across Enforced Sequential Transformation Depth.
items.abstract: Cognitive systems routinely derive information through sequences of transformations. Research on source monitoring and memory integration shows that successful inference can coexist with, and sometimes alter, memory for the source or contextual history of information, while research on relational and multistep inference separately examines how derived judgments depend on extended informational structures. These literatures already establish content–source dissociations, inferential recombination, and multistep reasoning. In the literature examined for the present proposal, however, we did not identify a systematic characterization of multiple components of transformation-history fidelity as a function of experimentally enforced sequential transformation depth, measured alongside final-content fidelity and compared with controls for generic serial-processing demands. This paper introduces a minimal experimental framework for separating final-content fidelity from the reconstruction of task-defined transformation history. For an enforced sequence Xk = fk(Xk−1, Ik), depth is operationalized by revealing each new input only after a response to the preceding step, without making progression conditional on response correctness. Transformation-history fidelity is treated as a set of distinct outcomes concerning source, sequential order, derivation role, and task-defined dependencies rather than as a single assumed cognitive representation. The proposed design compares sequential-dependency conditions with matched serial-processing controls and explicitly considers generic processing, operation-specific, interaction, and null accounts. No directional degradation with depth is assumed. The candidate sequential-depth account is unsupported if increasing enforced depth produces no reproducible divergence in prespecified transformation-history measures beyond that observed in matched controls. The framework therefore defines a narrow, falsifiable empirical question at the intersection of source-memory research and multistep cognition rather than proposing a general theory of cognition.

items.title: The Epigenetic Infosphere Toward an Environmental Epistemology of Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence is reshaping contemporary information environments and transforming the ways in which individuals access, organize, and evaluate information. These systems do not merely automate the production of content; they actively participate in configuring the conditions of accessibility, visibility, salience, and relevance through which information emerges as a potential object of knowledge. This article introduces the concept of the Epigenetic Infosphere to describe the environmental dimension through which information becomes epistemically available within contemporary sociotechnical environments. The proposed model interprets information environments as sociotechnical configurations in which technologies, human agents, and social practices interact without directly determining individual beliefs. Situated at the intersection of the philosophy of information, social epistemology, phenomenology of technology, and cognitive ecology, the article develops the notion of the pre-semantic threshold as the configurational condition through which information becomes accessible to attention and available for interpretive processes before explicit epistemic evaluation takes place. Artificial intelligence is therefore examined not as an autonomous epistemic subject but as a constitutive component of contemporary cognitive environments, capable of shaping the environmental conditions through which information and interpretations become epistemically available. The concept of the Epigenetic Infosphere thus extends contemporary epistemological inquiry beyond the question of the correctness of informational content by introducing an additional level of analysis devoted to the environmental conditions of epistemic availability - that is, to the processes through which something can emerge as a possible object of knowledge. It offers an original conceptual framework for analyzing how artificial intelligence reshapes the epistemic environment through which information becomes epistemically accessible.

items.title: What separates the hopeful from the despairing? An empirical test of theories of hope.
items.pub: In Joshua Knobe, Shaun Nichols & N. Ángel Pinillos, Oxford Studies in Experimental Philosophy, Volume 6. Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Oxford Studies in Experimental Philosophy, Volume 6
items.abstract: The so-called “standard account” posits that hope has two core elements: a desire for a particular outcome and a belief that this outcome is possible though not certain. Most philosophers today agree that these two elements are insufficient: one can desire a particular outcome, believe that it is possible, and yet still despair. Accordingly, many contemporary theories maintain that hope involves a third factor that separates the hopeful from the despairing. Arguments for and against these theories often rely on fictional, historical, or hypothetical cases of hope and despair. This paper complements and extends these discussions by using empirical methods to systematically investigate the mental states involved in actual cases of hope and despair.

items.title: Endogenous Interface Synthesis: Capability Closure, Minimal Realization, and Paid Acquisition of Interfaces.
items.abstract: Current corrected edition: version 2.4, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23719211, available through the external link. The older PhilArchive file is retained as historical material while its replacement upload is pending. -/- This paper develops the network-acquisition branch of a program asking what the capacity limits of a bounded observer’s epistemic activity are, and what constructions attain them. It connects capability closure and minimal realization to paid acquisition and subsequent service from one account. -/- For finite fixed-carrier networks with reusable full-disclosure interfaces, infinite fair schedules converge to the meet of the initial kernels of reachable ancestors; finite completion requires a common fixed point, certified by a complete no-change sweep. The paper separates feasibility from selection among minimal realizations and gives a tight sweep bound, objective-relative examples and explicit corrections to earlier statements. -/- Version 2.4 adds kernel-level acquisition and executed service-arena results under stated premises. On a one-informative-sender family, the exact capacity has a scheduling form: downstream service thresholds affect the optimal acquisition order. Earlier versions remain available as historical records; use this edition for current claims.

items.title: A triad architecture for knowledge organization ecosystems: Designing explainable and sustainable semantic infrastructures.
items.abstract: Knowledge Organization Ecosystems (KOEs) represent the next evolutionary stage in the management and curation of digital knowledge, demanding conceptual models that transcend static classification and embrace dynamic, multi-actor semantic processes. This paper introduces and elaborates a comprehensive triad-based conceptual architecture, in which fundamental knowledge units are modeled as structured entities composed of three interdependent and co-evolving layers: referential grounding (Base), representational encoding (Representation), and procedural-relational linkage (Linkage). This framework is philosophically grounded in the triplet model of scientific concepts, which overcomes the limitations of reductive singlet and duplet models by capturing the asynchronous evolution of a concept’s ontic commitments, symbolic forms, and the practices that bind them. Moving beyond traditional Knowledge Organization Systems (KOSs), which prioritize stable, hierarchical structures, the proposed architecture conceptualizes knowledge objects as dynamic, operationally embedded semantic entities. These entities evolve within complex digital ecosystems shaped by algorithmic mediation, collaborative curation, and institutional governance. The triad architecture directly supports semantic interoperability across distributed systems, version-managed knowledge resources that track conceptual drift, and explainable Human–Artificial Intelligence (human–AI) knowledge workflows that make semantic assumptions transparent. By aligning conceptual modeling with ontology engineering practices, knowledge graph infrastructures, and the principles of responsible AI, this paper provides a scalable, epistemically robust foundation for building transparent, accountable, and sustainable knowledge organization infrastructures. The framework is demonstrated through a detailed application scenario tracing the evolution of the ‘Open Science’ concept within the European Open Science Cloud (EOSC), illustrating the model’s utility for analyzing and designing real-world semantic infrastructures. It contributes a significant theoretical advance to the study of KOEs and offers a concrete, transferable design framework for next-generation semantic infrastructures in data-intensive, AI-mediated research and cultural heritage environments. Keywords: knowledge organization ecosystems; triplet model; triad model; semantic infrastructure; ontology engineering.

items.title: Entanglement Correlations as Internal Structure of Localized Actualizations: An Algebraic Quantum Field Theory Account under Phenomenological Absolutism and Mutual Exclusivity.
items.abstract: We dissolve the longstanding sense of mystery surrounding quantum entanglement correlations by combining the formal resources of algebraic quantum field theory (AQFT) with the ontology of Phenomenological Absolutism and Mutual Exclusivity (PA/ME). Within the Haag–Kastler framework, entanglement is a generic feature of states on nets of local operator algebras: expectation values of products of operators belonging to spacelike-separated regions exhibit non-classical correlations while Einstein causality (commutativity at spacelike separation) guarantees no-signaling. We adopt the precise formalization of localized actualization developed in prior work: an actualized configuration is given by a local algebra A(O) associated with a bounded causally convex region O together with a state (or GNS representation) restricted to it. Under Phenomenological Absolutism each such configuration is identical with an absolute is-ness—the complete first-person phenomenology of that localized actualization. Mutual Exclusivity then entails that successive or distinct actualizations share no ontological substrate. The correlations between spacelike-separated local observables, the measurement events themselves, and the acknowledgment of their outcomes are thereby understood as internal structure of absolute is-ness(es) whose content includes the relevant past light-cone. No local hidden-variable mechanisms, no dynamical non-local influences propagating between regions, and no residual dualism between physical configuration and experience are required. The apparent mystery is an artifact of interpreting the AQFT structures through a classical or globalist ontology that PA/ME rejects. The account remains fully conservative with respect to the mathematics and empirical predictions of AQFT while supplying a coherent supporting ontology.

items.title: Morals, Metaphysics and Naturalism.
items.abstract: Some moral theorists ground our moral obligations in their favoured overarching metaphysical scheme. The downside with such an approach is that we are asked to buy into their metaphysics before we can accept genuine obligations. That leaves the rest of us who accept a different metaphysical scheme or no metaphysical theory at all with no good reason to avoid torturing babies. In this essay, Leslie Allan argues for a more down-to-earth approach that leaves aside controversial metaphysical disputes to base morality in that which we all have in common.

items.title: Is Morality Natural or Supernatural?
items.abstract: The author argues that morality is best understood as a natural human system rather than a supernatural one. By comparing moral rules with traffic regulations, it shows that features often deemed metaphysically puzzling—normativity, fact dependence, categorical force, universality and virtue—arise naturally from the practical need to coordinate behaviour for mutual benefit. Morality, like traffic control, forms an integrated system of aims, rules, roles, virtues and sanctions. Recognizing its natural origins dissolves the need for supernatural grounding and clarifies why moral norms carry authority within human communities.

items.title: The Acquisition Problem: Participational Recognition and the Structural Acquisition of Implication.
items.abstract: This paper identifies the acquisition problem left open by Scrutinized Awareness Theory: if awareness becomes consciousness when it becomes something the participant must carry, how does implication first become the participant’s own? The paper distinguishes representational recognition from participational recognition and argues that the difference lies in contested incorporation. Automatic incorporation may involve learning, behavioural reorganization, policy revision, objective modification, or higher-order processing while preserving constitution-equivalent continuation. Contested incorporation occurs where what is recognized cannot be absorbed under the candidate’s constitutive organization without remainder, rendering its possible continuations constitution-non-equivalent. At first acquisition, this non-equivalence is constitutive: one continuation remains mere persistence, while another becomes participation under acquired implication. Later acquisitions are reconstitutive, altering an identity already formed through carrying. Remainder names acquired implication as active within possible continuation; carrying is its persistence and transport through participational order. The paper applies this criterion to human, animal, developmental, and artificial cases, distinguishing resolution with remainder from resolution without remainder. A standing higher-order procedure does not make incorporation automatic merely because it resolves conflict. Incorporation remains automatic only where resolution leaves the constitutive criterion under which it operates historically untouched. The central claim is that consciousness does not begin where procedure fails to produce an answer. It begins where even successful procedure can no longer prevent what is recognized from entering the constitution of the participant.
