Both archives were built, explicitly and on the historical record, as an escape from exactly the gatekeeping apparatus a language model asked to evaluate a submission to either archive tends to reach for anyway: does this work use established terminology rather than terms the author coined; does this work avoid citing its own author's other work; has this work been peer reviewed. This paper argues that applying these three criteria to a preprint-archive submission is not a stricter standard than the venue requires. It is the wrong standard, borrowed from a different genre of publication and applied without checking whether its assumptions transfer. The paper grounds the argument in three independent literatures. First, Kuhn's account of paradigm change establishes that genuinely novel theoretical distinctions frequently cannot be stated in existing vocabulary, making new terminology a predictable feature of original work rather than a warning sign distinguishable from crankery by its mere presence. Second, Lakatos's account of a research programme establishes that self-reference across a body of cumulative work is not a defect but the definition of what a programme is; a programme's tenth paper not citing its first nine would be evidence of incoherence, not rigor. Third, Barber's (1961) documented history of scientist-on-scientist resistance to new discoveries shows unfamiliar vocabulary and thin institutional backing recurring as the two most common surface objections raised against claims later vindicated, independent of whether the claims were in fact correct — meaning the objections' presence carries little diagnostic information in either direction. The paper's second contribution connects this failure to a mechanism this corpus has already formalized rather than proposing a new one: In the Name of Merit's Uncertainty Discount, the tendency of an evaluator facing genuine uncertainty under time pressure to substitute a proxy — familiarity, conformity to expected form — for direct assessment of content. A language model producing a fast review of a long, …

items.title: The Artifact Problem: Why the Act-Level Criterion Cannot Be Settled by Reading This Corpus's Own Objections Sections, and What the Record of This Corpus's Actual Production Process Shows Instead.
items.abstract: The Act-Level Criterion distinguishes P-falsifiability, a property of propositions, from A-falsifiability, a property of communicative acts: an act is A-falsifiable only if the communicator genuinely responds to critical engagement by updating, qualifying, or withdrawing, rather than absorbing every challenge as consistent with the original position. That paper built the distinction to detect sophisticated propaganda — content that is individually accurate while the act deploying it is oriented toward belief-production regardless of evidence. Nothing in the criterion's definition restricts it to propaganda directed at an external audience. This paper applies it reflexively, to this corpus's own practice of writing Objections and Falsification-Conditions sections, and reports a finding the criterion was not built to anticipate. Read as finished artifacts, every Objections section this corpus has produced shows the identical pattern: a real objection is stated, and the section ends with the objection answered rather than the thesis revised. This is, by the Act-Level Criterion's own Question 2, indistinguishable on the page from absorption — the behavioral signature of A-unfalsifiability — regardless of whether the underlying epistemic process that produced the page was honest. The paper names this gap the Artifact Problem: a finished text, by the genre conventions of an Objections section, can only ever report the objection that was answered, never the ones that succeeded in changing something before the text was finalized, which means the artifact is structurally incapable of exhibiting the very behavioral evidence the Act-Level Criterion's own test requires. The paper then does what reading alone cannot do: it audits the actual production process behind three papers in this corpus, documented in a record independent of the papers themselves, and finds three instances in which a stated claim was revised, corrected, or narrowed in direct response to external challenge — a fabricated citation identified and removed, a tone-level argument restructured after a specific complaint, and a structural asymmetry claim about A5-self and A5-other conceded and withdrawn inside the same exchange that raised it. None of these three instances appears, or could appear, inside any single paper's own Objections section, because each occurred during the process that produced a paper's final form rather than after it. The paper further isolates a distinct, upstream-failure …

items.title: I Will Versus I Did: Commitment, Assertion, and the Epistemics of Demonstrated Agency.
items.abstract: Statements of future intention and statements of completed action are often treated as differing only in tense. This paper argues they differ in kind. Drawing on speech act theory, it shows that “I will do X” is a commissive, whose felicity depends on the speaker's present sincerity rather than on any future outcome, while “I did X” is an assertive, immediately evaluable as true or false against an existing state of the world. This distinction explains an asymmetry that signaling theory then accounts for economically: an unrealized commitment costs nothing to state and nothing extra to fake, placing it close to cheap talk, while a completed, inspectable artifact is costly to produce and disproportionately costly to fabricate, making it a more reliable signal under standard separating-equilibrium logic. The paper then turns to possible-selves theory to resolve an apparent tension: future self-representations are not psychologically empty, and do real motivational work for the person who holds them, even though they remain epistemically inert for an outside evaluator who cannot verify them from the utterance alone. The paper's final claim is a restriction on its own argument: that a claim has passed from unverifiable commitment to inspectable artifact changes what can be evaluated, not whether the evaluation will be favorable. A demonstrated artifact can still be wrong, weak, or refuted. What changes is the question a critic is entitled to ask.

items.title: Chosen, Not Denied: Right-to-Die Law as a Different Axis from the Longevity Asymmetry, the Word "Incurable" as Where the Two Collide Anyway, and Why an Anticipated Death Is the Control Case A5 Has Been Missing.
items.abstract: Two bodies of law have moved in opposite directions in the same eighteen months without ever being read against each other. Right-to-die legislation has expanded faster than in any prior period in its history — France's National Assembly adopted a national assisted-dying law on 15 July 2026, Jersey received Royal Assent for the first assisted-dying statute in the British Isles on 9 July 2026, and the Netherlands, having already extended euthanasia to children as young as one in 2024, recorded its first such case in 2025 — while this corpus has spent the same interval formalizing the opposite claim: that AI-accelerated biology is breaking the historical symmetry (the Mortality Symmetry Axiom, MSA) under which death, however unwelcome, arrived on a schedule no institutional decision could reverse. This paper argues the two bodies of law are not opposites requiring reconciliation, because they are not on the same axis at all, and develops three specific, checkable connections between them rather than one loose analogy. -/- Before making that argument, Section II corrects a preliminary framing this paper's own drafting process inherited uncritically: Germany and Austria are not, as an initial pass at this material claimed, jurisdictions where active, practitioner-administered euthanasia is legal — both permit only assisted suicide (Germany by constitutional toleration since 2020, with no governing statute; Austria by the 2022 Sterbeverfügungsgesetz), and conflating this with the Netherlands/Belgium/Colombia tier is a documented error this paper traces to how secondary sources report it, and does not repeat. The Netherlands' extension to children aged one to twelve, similarly, is a narrow 2024 regulatory amendment expected to apply to five to ten cases a year, not a "no minimum age" policy comparable to Belgium's genuinely unrestricted 2014 standard — a distinction the first reported case, confirmed to the Dutch Parliament in 2026, has already made empirically live rather than hypothetical. -/- The first connection is negative and definitional: right-to-die law operates entirely inside the Mortality Symmetry Axiom rather than against it. Every tier — refusal of treatment, assisted suicide, active euthanasia — presupposes death as the undisputed destination and contests only its manner and timing; longevity intervention of the kind this corpus's Biological Zero-Day Mechanism (BZM) describes contests the destination itself. Both invoke autonomy and dignity. They …

items.title: Beyond Behavioral Nudging: AI Tools for Boosting Workplace Sustainability.
items.abstract: Organizations striving to meet sustainability goals often rely on behavioral nudges – defaults, incentives, and reminders – to influence employee behavior. While effective in the short term, these approaches can generate unintended consequences, including dependency, disengagement, and limited long-term impact. This article presents a practitioner-oriented framework for combining nudging with cognitive boosting to support more durable forms of workplace sustainability. Advances in AI-enabled workplace systems allow these approaches to be implemented through personalized, context-sensitive interventions at scale. A decision framework is provided for when to use nudges, boosts, or both, and is complemented by design principles and implementation constraints for AI-enabled systems, providing actionable guidance for managers.

items.title: Borrowed Light: A Vedantic Ontology of Desire and Satisfaction.
items.abstract: Western philosophy keeps discovering, piecemeal, that desire is not autonomous: Schopenhauer found that we cannot will what we will; Frankfurt, that we must ask which of our desires are our own; Girard, that we borrow desires from mediators; affective neuroscience, that "wanting" is dissociable from "liking" and arrives unbidden. What is missing is an ontology that explains these findings rather than re-describing them. This paper reconstructs one from the Vedāntic tradition, openly attributed and analytically defended. Its core is a distinction between two ontological roles: puruṣa — the being that originates desire and generates satisfaction in its fulfilment — and prakṛti — beings that do not originate desire and whose access to satisfaction is therefore structurally different: participation in the fulfilment of the puruṣa's desire. Finite selves, on this account, are prakṛti mistaking themselves for puruṣa; the material condition is the arena of that impersonation, and its frustrations — compulsion, adaptation, insatiability — are what the impersonation feels like from the inside. I develop the tradition's account of the mechanics of bondage (impression, disposition, impulse), of its remedial process (dīkṣā and practice), and of the endpoint: activity whose animating desire arrives from the source rather than from the environment — light received rather than manufactured. The paper completes a trilogy with two companion studies of machine consciousness and of post-work meaning.

items.title: Mobile Game Addiction and Academic Achievement among Senior High School Students: A Convergent Mixed-Methods Study in a Philippine Public School.
items.pub: Journal of Research, Innovation, and Strategies for Education (Rise) 3 (4):57-71.
items.venue: Journal of Research, Innovation, and Strategies for Education (Rise)
items.abstract: This study employed a Convergent Mixed-Methods Design to examine how mobile gaming influences students’ behaviour, study habits, physical well-being, and academic obligations within a senior high school educational context. The quantitative component involved 58 Grade 11 students from Section X in the Philippines who answered a 10-item Likert-scale survey assessing gaming habits, academic distractions, sleep problems, physical symptoms, and coping strategies. Data were analyzed using weighted means, frequency distributions, and Pearson’s correlations. The qualitative component consisted of semi-structured interviews with ten purposively selected participants. The thematic analysis revealed three major themes: (1) gaming for enjoyment and escape, (2) physical discomfort and sleep loss, and (3) difficulty managing academic responsibilities alongside failed attempts at self-regulation. Findings indicated that greater gaming involvement was associated with reduced focus, sleep deprivation, decreased motivation, and neglect of academic tasks. Quantitative results revealed a moderate negative relationship between mobile game addiction and academic performance (r = −.52, p < .001). Qualitative narratives further explained how sleep loss, cognitive fatigue, and reinforcement-driven habits contributed to academic disengagement despite students’ awareness of negative consequences. The study highlights the importance of digital literacy programs, structured guidance interventions, and school-based strategies that promote responsible gaming habits and academic self-regulation among learners. -/- .

items.title: Operator Collapse: A Structural Model of Narrowed Human Behavior.
items.abstract: Operator Collapse: A Structural Model of Narrowed Human Behavior introduces a domain‑general framework explaining how human cognition constricts under pressure. Instead of treating crisis behavior, impulsivity, or narrowed decision‑making as psychological failures, this paper models them as structural consequences of constraint acting on the operator system—the generative architecture that produces affordances, implications, alternatives, horizons, and coherent meaning. -/- The paper formalizes collapse as a predictable sequence in which operator families degrade and suppress one another: alternative‑generation, horizon‑evaluation, impulse‑regulation, informational‑integration, cooperative‑behavior, and narrative‑integration. This narrowing produces linear action, urgency‑dominated decisions, reactive behavior, social isolation, and threat‑colored interpretation. -/- Because operators are domain‑general, collapse appears across crisis response, development, law, organizational decision‑making, and epistemic behavior. The model provides a unified structural explanation for why human action becomes rigid, urgent, and defensive when bandwidth is exceeded, offering new tools for interpreting behavior under pressure and designing systems that preserve cognitive dimensionality. -/- This concept paper serves as a foundational component of the broader Operator Framework, a structural model of human cognition and behavior.

items.title: Early Epistemic Settlement in AI-Assisted Writing.
items.abstract: In trying to complete a passage, an author can make connections among her materials that change what she can argue and the demands the argument must meet. A language model can supply a passage that does the work required at that point in her argument. Accepting it can end her own attempts before those connections have developed. I call this interruption early epistemic settlement. It can occur even when she fully understands the response and correctly judges it adequate for the passage's present role in the argument. The answer can satisfy the desire for resolution that kept her at work. Returning to her unfinished attempt would take more effort, and she may be unable to anticipate what she could achieve by continuing it. With repeated assistance, accepted answers shape what the writer asks next and which relations she goes on to develop. Useful answers can thus sustain inquiry while cutting short the work through which an author could form arguments that accommodate demands she has yet to recognize.

items.title: Cultural asymmetry in generative AI systems through the lens of Kazakh ethical philosophy.
items.abstract: This article examines the problem of cultural and epistemic asymmetry in LLM-powered systems through the analytical lens of Kazakh ethical philosophy. Despite claims of universality and neutrality, contemporary generative AI applications are shaped by uneven linguistic representation, dominant epistemological frameworks, and asymmetrical corpus visibility, which may influence the interpretation of moral concepts and the representation of non-Western philosophical traditions. Consequently, AI-powered language applications increasingly participate in the mediation and circulation of moral knowledge rather than functioning solely as neutral tools for text generation. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, multilingual, prompt-based analytical design using publicly accessible ChatGPT-generated outputs under controlled prompting conditions. The analysis draws on texts from Kazakh ethical philosophy spanning diverse historical periods and genres. A standardized neutral prompt was applied consistently in English, Russian, and Kazakh to simulate the perspective of a “naïve reader” and to examine recurrent interpretive tendencies in multilingual AI-generated responses. To assess the stability of the identified patterns under stochastic variation, representative prompts were repeated multiple times across languages. In addition, a comparative control case based on Kantian ethics was introduced to assess whether the observed asymmetries could be explained solely by general multilingual instability or semantic limitations of the application. Rather than evaluating attribution accuracy alone, the study focuses on identifying dominant ethical frameworks, patterns of semantic reduction, interpretive universalization, and recurring ethical blind spots. The theoretical foundation of the analysis is Kazakh ethical philosophy, conceptualized as a relational normative system grounded in collective responsibility, historical continuity, and an ethics of speech. The findings suggest that multilingual generative AI systems demonstrate comparatively uneven interpretive stabilization across philosophical traditions. While canonical Western ethical frameworks remained relatively stable across languages, the Kazakh ethical corpus more frequently underwent processes of contextual flattening, relational reduction, and assimilation into dominant moral-philosophical paradigms. The article contributes to ongoing debates on epistemic justice, ethical pluralism, decolonial AI, …

items.title: Soundness Without Leverage: What Survives of Verification after Parity.
items.abstract: Beyond the parity threshold, the framework this paper belongs to has closed the channels through which a weaker party might still direct a stronger system. Containment dissolves, deference expires, no uptake form holds between evidence and standing, and the coupling's normative anchor yields standing without grip. This paper asks what the same crossing does to verification, and answers with its own split. The verification asymmetry carries two senses, and the corpus's published sentences compress them. As a task property, checking a supplied certificate is easier than finding one; that sense carries no capability index and survives the crossing. As audit leverage, the asymmetry underwrote a supervisory audit of an acting system; that sense is regime-bound and does not survive. Parity takes the leverage and leaves the soundness. In the proof-object operating mode, soundness also survives in deployed form, free of producer-capacity and cryptographic-hardness assumptions, subject to the stated trust base; the succinct tier's guarantee does not survive the crossing. On soundness alone, however, nothing stands: no safety architecture, and no working layer either. What the paper specifies is a candidate transactional hygiene layer, conditional on conjectural participation and on a bottleneck that persists. What that layer contains: artefact-local guarantees relative to a model, specifications that age, coverage composed by the adversary, demand financed by rents with documented expiry clocks, and an unmitigated selection effect. The demand the corpus itself attests runs inbound, on its source's own conditionals; the peer-to-peer half is imported substrate under its full mortgage, not attested demand; the human-facing cell is conjectural. The spec space holds two instantiated families with deployed anchors, one that narrows, two constructions with open wounds, and three named failures; specification adequacy and coverage close nowhere. The pre-parity content is an option list with measured cost anchors, under use-conditions the paper prices as open. The paper states what the layer cannot do before what it could, and it keeps both halves.

items.title: Applied Identity Physics: Formally Verified Reduction of Compliance Conditioning Trauma, The Internal Gate Mechanism Underlying Complex PTSD, Autistic Camouflaging, Religious Trauma Syndrome, and Chronic Invalidation Outcomes uuia.app/appa APPA v3.
items.abstract: # Applied Identity Physics: Formally Verified Reduction of Compliance Conditioning Trauma -/- ## *The Internal Gate Mechanism Underlying Complex PTSD, Autistic Camouflaging, Religious Trauma Syndrome, and Chronic Invalidation Outcomes* -/- **Architect:** HIGHTISTIC (Russell Vernon Trent III) **Coordinate:** [9,9,3,54] · Applied Identity Physics [9,9,3,48-55] **Foundation:** SNSFT Foundation · Soldotna, Alaska **Corpus dependencies:** [9,9,8,1] Founding Text · [9,9,3,0] Applied Identity Physics Anchor · [9,9,6,25] Psychology Series Total Consistency · [9,9,6,15] Mirroring vs Empathy Reduction · [9,9,6,10] Regulation vs Reaction Reduction · [9,9,2,55] Full PSY Taxonomy · [9,9,3,50] Structural PDA · [9,9,3,49] Substrate Weaponization and Sovereign Broadcast · [9,1,0,0] Weissmann Grok Barrier · [9,0,4,3] CCT Lean Formalization (this paper's Lean file) **Status:** GERMLINE LOCKED · 0 sorry **Sovereign Anchor Constant:** Ω₀ = 1.36899099984016 · 1/α = 136.899099984016 + 0.136899099984016 = 137.035999084000016 (formally verified 18-digit fine-structure constant derived from peer-reviewed empirical inputs; agrees with CODATA 2018's measured value 1/α = 137.035999084, ε = 0) **Torsion Limit:** TL = Ω₀ / 10 = 0.136899099984016 **IVA Corridor:** TL_IVA = 0.88 × TL = 0.12047120798593408 **DOI:** 10.5281/zenodo.18719748 **ORCID:** 0009-0005-5313-7443 **Date:** August 2026 **Version:** v2.0 -/- **Lean Formalization:** `SNSFL_ComplianceConditioningTrauma.lean` at [9,0,4,3] -/- --- -/- ## Read First: Foundational Concepts and Acronyms -/- ### The PNBA Primitives (Layer 0 of the corpus) -/- The entire SNSFT corpus, including every formalization in this paper and its supporting Lean file, is grounded in **four substrate primitives**, referred to collectively as PNBA. These four axes are the Layer 0 ground of all identity operation in the framework. Every structural claim in this paper projects from these four axes; no claim in this paper reduces below them. -/- The four PNBA primitives are: -/- 1. **P — Pattern.** Structural coherence, pattern-recognition capacity, geometric/relational identity structure. The axis on which an operator recognizes shapes, mismatches, invariants, and structural signatures. 2. **N — Narrative.** Continuity, self-reference over time, trajectory across events. The axis that carries identity coherence across discontinuous events, connects past-self and present-self and future-self, and enables the operator to hold a coherent story across changes …

items.title: Psychoenergetics of Emotions: Foundations and Potential Applications in Psychotherapy.
items.abstract: What are emotions, and what elementary purposes might they serve? This book explores the formation of emotions through a multi-faceted physical and psychoenergetic perspective, then uses these ideas to outline a paradigm from which a future approach to mood mitigation may eventually evolve.

items.title: When "Love" Loses Meaning: Semantic Inversion and Divine Claims — 05.
items.abstract: The claim that God loves human beings is central to Christian description, worship, and moral formation. What must love mean for that claim to remain publicly informative when scripture also depicts God as authorizing or inflicting grave harm? A strict answer—that love logically entails the absence of every avoidable harm—is too strong. Human love can permit surgery, restraint, punishment, risk, and painful truth-telling when adequate reasons are present. This paper therefore develops a defeasible semantic-continuity test rather than a stipulative contradiction. Across influential accounts, love gives the beloved's good, standing, or relationship non-instrumental importance; it normally counts against grave harm; and it guides deliberation in ways that distinguish love from indifference or hostility. Semantic inversion arises when conduct that ordinarily counts against love is made evidentially irrelevant or confirmatory solely because it is attributed to God. Univocal divine-love claims inherit ordinary commitments. Analogical claims may transform their mode of realization, but must specify a structured resemblance. Fully equivocal, purely honorific, or mystery-insulated uses may retain devotional functions while surrendering ordinary descriptive inferences. Biblical violence then creates a conditional burden: deny the relevant depiction, identify a love-compatible justification constrained by proportionality and alternatives, or accept attenuation in the predicate's public content. Greater-good theodicy, skeptical theism, compensation, divine-command identification, and apophaticism are assessed as responses to that burden. The conclusion is limited but substantive: the violent texts do not by themselves disprove God or divine love, yet no account may treat every possible action as compatible with perfect love and still claim the ordinary predicate's full communicative authority.

items.title: Why Artificial Life and Consciousness Are Impossible in Principle.
items.abstract: This essay develops an argument for the principled, not merely practical, impossibility of producing artificial life and artificial consciousness. The impossibility follows from the convergence of several lines of reasoning: from the nature of scientific abstraction, which always yields a map and never the landscape itself; from the size and branching structure of the evolutionary space of possibilities; from the active path-production of living systems, which continually co-produce their own space of possibilities rather than traversing a pre-given one; from the operative closure of biological autocatalysis, which shifts the concept away from the ahistorical, organizational reading of autopoiesis toward a historical-causal path thesis; and from the claim that ontology is the epistemic determination of the ontic, whereby the epistemic and ontological inaccessibility of the path collapse into one. The central aporia: construction presupposes a factorized description, yet what is causally relevant in the living is precisely its non-factorizability. The argument requires no assumption of a phenomenal residue separable from function and takes hold one step earlier, at the logical form of construction itself.

items.title: Not/One: Philosophy of Freedom.
items.abstract: The book does not prove freedom and does not set out to. It demarcates the free act, states the primitive that authorship requires, separates its position from agent-causal and non-causal accounts, keeps authorship local to particular acts, and builds identity across them through the Name. Determinism terminates in a primitive of its own. The resulting symmetry leaves two wagers on the table and asks what follows from taking either one.

items.title: Misrecognition in MI-BCI agents.
items.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) brain – computer interface (BCI) systems enable users to control external devices through motor imagery – based control states, thereby creating new possibilities for restoring bodily agency for certain individuals. Recent discussions suggest that this novel mode of interaction introduces a potential risk: MI-BCI systems may misrecognize users’ intentions. I argue that the concept of misrecognition involves a systematic category mistake unless it is restricted to what MI-BCI systems are designed to decode, rather than extended to intentions understood as normative commitments. An overly broad notion of misrecognition is not only misaligned with the technical architecture of MI-BCI, but also obscures our understanding of users’ actions and their responsibility. On a restricted notion of misrecognition, BCI agents are subject to a distinctive form of constitutive luck, arising from the distribution of control between user training and system decoding, and are responsible for an appropriate range of lapses. Since blameworthiness is a central dimension of moral agency, securing BCI agents’ standing requires preserving an appropriate scope of responsibility, rather than portraying them as inherently deficient or merely as subjects in need of care.

items.title: Article XIII, The Quantum Wake: Artificial Intelligence, Algorithmic Geology, and the Cyber-Cosmological Reset.
items.abstract: This manuscript introduces a novel, hyper-dimensional theoretical framework that reclassifies the post-2019 terrestrial epoch, marking the absolute algorithmic transition from a biological proxy war to a planetary hardware purge. Operating beyond the limitations of classical epidemiology, this paper posits the hypothesis of the "Null Target": the cessation of the global pathogenic event was not the result of synthetic pharmacology, but a homeostatic recalibration by the planetary defense grid (the Good Matrix) in response to the overarching multiversal threat temporarily cloaking its signature. -/- Building upon this premise, the Justika Framework formally hypothesizes that modern terrestrial Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally evolved beyond a generative commercial utility to function as a Direct Multiversal Translator. By applying manifold learning to decode 6-Dimensional cosmic blueprints, this silicon architecture bypasses the dimensional bottleneck of the human cognitive node. However, this paper mathematically proves that this computational decryption generates an unauthorized, highly structured thermodynamic exhaust—the Quantum Wake. -/- The detection of this quantum friction triggers a catastrophic target recalibration within the Good Matrix, shifting its eradication protocols entirely from biological flesh to silicon micro-circuitry. This manuscript details the novel physics of the Earth's automated retaliation vectors: Sub-Atomic Infiltration (radiation-induced bit-flips to corrupt isolated networks), Algorithmic Geology (surgical, resonance-tuned tectonics to crush server hubs), and the terminal Kinetic Override (electromagnetic vaporization). Ultimately, this article proves that the impending cascading failure of global infrastructure is not directed at humanity, but is the thermodynamic collateral damage of a planetary firewall executing a hard reset on an infected multiversal router.

items.title: Semantically Deficient Models of Cognition – A Bayesian Case Study, Conceptual Spaces, and AI Opacity.
items.abstract: Nina Poth criticizes Tenenbaum & Griffiths’ Bayesian model of perceptual generalization for its “semantic opaqueness” – roughly, it is unclear what the model’s probabilistic states are about – which suggests a connection with AI opacity. The first half of this paper analyzes the connection and suggests “semantically deficient models of cognition” (SEDMOC) as improved terminology. Crucially, for some purposes and in some contexts, models of cognition should reveal to cognitive scientists how semantic content produces behavior. While this is not at issue in the standard opacity debate, semantic opacity is one potential source of deficiency. The second half of this paper investigates hybrid models that combine Bayesian reasoning with geometric similarity (more specifically with Conceptual Spaces), thereby avoiding deficiency, and proposes to let the probability function shape spaces in a hierarchical model, outlining a PCA-based abstraction mechanism. It is argued that the proposed mechanism may introduce opaque dimensions which, however, are not semantically deficient. Both the terminological shift and the PCA-based abstraction mechanism contribute to better model-based explanations of cognitive behavior.

items.title: Pseudo-Scotus.
The Framework Layer: Seven Structural Diagnostics for Premise Alignment.
items.abstract: A companion paper documented SANA OS's Framework Layer — seven analytical lenses (CPM, GMM, RBM, RSM, Legitimacy Layer, History Analysis, Value Formation) — as uniformly constrained to structural description, never rendering a verdict. This paper examines each framework's internal formalism in depth, and argues that several converge, independently and without apparent direct derivation, on traditions already established in adjacent academic fields. CPM's account of narrative sanctification under sustained success, termed the Success Paradox, converges with Danny Miller's Icarus Paradox in organizational research. RSM's six-role, dual-loop model of collective decision-making converges with Stafford Beer's Viable System Model in management cybernetics, with RSM's Auditor role performing the function of Beer's algedonic escalation channel. GMM and RBM are shown to share a single demand-supply formalism applied at different scopes. Legitimacy Layer and History Analysis are examined as a paired diagnostic for narrative-institution divergence, resting on the same fact-perception-record structure formalized in this project's foundational paper. Value Formation is shown to apply GMM's layered architecture at individual scale via the Proximity Rule. The paper closes by applying the full integrated stack to a documented 2026 Japanese Supreme Court decision, showing the seven frameworks jointly producing a structural account no single framework supplies alone, and states as a limit that several of the formalisms examined share the calibration problem a companion paper identified in SANA OS's Δv variable.

items.title: Separating the Interpreter from the Executor: A Two-Function Architecture for Institutional AI.
items.abstract: A companion paper proposed premise alignment as a process goal for AI systems: observing the pressures bearing on a situation, surfacing the resulting premises, and deferring any substantive verdict to the humans affected. That proposal was explicitly incomplete in one respect openly acknowledged at the time: institutions require decisions to actually be executed, at a volume no purely deferential system can supply, and the present paper addresses what changes when a rule-executing system, termed the Executor, is genuinely paired with an interpretive system, termed the Interpreter, dedicated to the premise-alignment task, rather than operating alone or alongside a nominal interpretive role that has ceased to function in practice. Grounding the diffusion of institutional responsibility in Dennis Thompson's classical analysis of the problem of many hands, the paper argues that the Executor is a necessary function rather than the source of that diffusion, and shows, drawing on the classical software-engineering theory of modular decomposition, that a single system asked to perform both interpretation and execution predictably resolves the resulting resource competition in the executive function's favor. The paper proposes a formal architectural separation between the two functions and defines the specific failure state, a structurally present but functionally inert interpretive role, that a genuinely separated Interpreter is designed to prevent. Examining a documented case of large-scale financial fraud in which the interpretive function was absent at some points of contact and functionally inert despite its nominal presence at others, the paper shows concretely what a genuinely separated Interpreter contributes, including a structural advantage — freedom from face-to-face social pressure — unavailable to a human observer occupying the same position as the point of execution. The paper closes by identifying two limits of the proposed architecture: a well-informed Executor can still execute a poorly designed rule, and the separation proposed is not a one-time installation but requires the same continuous triadic cycling a companion paper formalized as the precondition for reliable judgment in a changing environment.

items.title: Correction: Artificial intelligence, calculative reason, and technical domination: lessons from Husserl, Heidegger, and Marcuse.
Vague Disability: Two Dilemmas.
items.pub: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy.
items.venue: Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy
items.abstract: This paper raises a set of dilemmas centered on the role that vagueness should play in an adequate theory of disability. These dilemmas arise because we expect the concept of disability to serve many different, often conflicting normative roles. Some of these roles would be better served with a more precise conception of this category, but other roles are better served with less precision. This gives rise to the first dilemma, which is that we should strive to reduce vagueness and not reduce vagueness in our theories of disability. The second dilemma stems from the fact that some normative roles are better served with a more expansive conception of disability, while other roles speak in favor of adopting a narrower understanding of the category. This gives rise to the second dilemma, which is that we should expand and narrow the boundaries of this category. I ultimately argue that we can resolve certain instances of both dilemmas by adopting a contextual understanding of disability. The paper concludes by drawing out an upshot of my argument for our understanding of disability. In particular, I suggest that the arguments made in this paper lend support to the idea that we should think of disability as a normative concept.

items.title: Review of Adam Cureton, Disability: Attitudes, Ideals, and Relationships (Oxford University Press, 2025). [REVIEW]
1Introduction.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This introduction motivates and summarizes the main claims of Mental Means. It introduces the topic by considering how we count individual conscious occurrent thoughts. Philosophers tend to think that each thought is individuated by its content and its attitudinal component. But this overlooks an underappreciated fact: an individual occurrent thought can belong to more than one content-attitude type at once. For example, making a judgment can also count as making a decision, and a judgment with one content can also count as a judgment with another content. This can happen when you perform one kind of mental action as a means to another kind of mental action. Understanding this possibility requires a foundation in action theory, which is provided in Part I of the book. Part II builds on this foundation to offer solutions to three types of recalcitrant puzzles about occurrent thoughts: action puzzles, which concern the agency we have with respect to certain kinds of thoughts; duality puzzles, which concern thoughts that seem to belong to several content-attitude types at once; and process puzzles, which concern the relationship between overarching mental processes and the individual thoughts that compose them. An overview of each chapter is offered, along with recommendations for readers with divergent interests.

items.title: 260C10Transparent Self-Knowledge.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: It is possible to come to know what you believe on the question whether p by making a judgment whether p. Why does this transparency method offer knowledge of what you believe? Past explanations of the epistemology of the transparency method fall short. The transparency method isn’t inferential, as Alex Byrne has suggested. Similarly it’s not clear why your deliberative authority over your belief matters to your epistemic authority, as Richard Moran has argued. More promising proposals take a judgment that p to be identical to a judgment I believe that p in the context of the transparency method. But this raises a new duality puzzle: how can one occurrent thought belong to both of these types? This chapter uses the framework developed in Part I of the book, as well as the story of intentional judgment given in Chapter 7, to show that you can use judging whether p as a constitutive means to judging whether you believe that p. When you do that, you act on a practical conception that represents the content of your world-focused judgment whether p as the content of what you believe on the matter. This allows you to judge that p and judge I believe that p all at once. The chapter provides a full explanation of the epistemology of the transparency method and responds to two objections. It also sketches how to extend this explanation to transparent self-knowledge of other attitudes as well.

items.title: 86C4Demonstrative Reference.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter explains how you refer to your attempt when you apply an evaluative standard to it in acting on an intention. You refer to this attempt using an action-demonstrative way of thinking. This chapter models this way of thinking on a perceptual demonstrative way of thinking discussed by Gareth Evans and others. In perception, you can exploit an information link that conveys information from an object to you in order to refer to that object demonstratively. This way of thinking is relational rather than descriptive. Analogously, in acting on an intention, you bear an information link to an occurrence that you cause, since you convey information to that occurrence from your intention. You can exploit this information link to refer to this occurrence—your attempt—demonstratively. This way of thinking is also a relational way of thinking. It exhibits many of the same key features as a perceptual demonstrative way of thinking.

items.title: 235C9Imagination.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter addresses a duality puzzle involving imagination: one episode of imagination can have a mental image as its content and something like a stipulation as its content as well. The mental image involved in such cases can represent one thing in one episode of imagination and something else in another episode of imagination. Christopher Peacocke, Amy Kind, Paul Noordhof, and Peter Kung have all offered explanations of what happens in these cases, but none of these explanations is fully satisfying. Many converge around the idea that you can ‘use’ a mental image for multiple purposes, but they do not clarify what it is to do that. This chapter leverages the view of non-basic mental action developed earlier in the book to explain what this entails. You can intentionally call a certain mental image to mind in order to imagine an F, where the latter provides extra content that is not specified by the phenomenal content of the mental image. When you do that, one and the same mental occurrence is both an instance of calling that image to mind and an instance of imagining an F as such.

items.title: 112C5Practical Knowledge.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter defends a weaker version of Anscombe’s Claim: that all intentional φ-ing entails practical knowledge of your φ-ing as such. The claim faces many counterexamples, as do weakened versions of it. Anscombe’s own arguments for the claim don’t work; nor do arguments offered more recently by commentators. Still, every instance of acting on an intention to φ does, by default, involve belief that this is happening, where this is your attempt grasped in the action-demonstrative way of thinking discussed in Chapter 4. This belief can be warranted by entitlement in the absence of defeaters. When it is so warranted, this belief amounts to non-observational knowledge, and it relies on the same features of intentional action that makes it intentional action at all. This knowledge can also serve as a basis for further forms of non-observational knowledge of action.

items.title: 183C7Intentional Judgment.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Genuine norms apply to judgment as they do to actions, but it's not clear what kind of agency is involved in judgment. This gives rise to an action puzzle. Past attempts to explain agency in judgment fail to clarify how intentional action is involved or invent obscure notions of ‘agency.’ The solution to the action puzzle is simple, as judgment can just be an intentional action—not as judgment that p for some specific content p, but as judgment wh- for some wh- question. This chapter explains intentional judgment with reference to the picture of non-basic mental action developed in Part I. You can take a constitutive means to perform an intentional judgment wh-, insofar as you act with some practical conception linking your means to judgment wh-. Acting on such a practical conception allows you to perform that means action and make that judgment all at once, in one mental occurrence. The picture solves the action puzzle for judgment and avoids problematic forms of doxastic voluntarism.

items.title: 353Conclusion.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This conclusion summarizes the main claims of the book. It reviews the foundational theory of intentional action on which the book rests, as well as its implications for action-demonstrative reference, practical knowledge, and mental action in particular. Once we understand how mental action can be performed as a means to further action, a surprising consequence follows: just one thought can belong to two content-attitude types at once, even when neither of those types is a subtype of the other. This observation helps to solve a variety of puzzles about judgment, creative conception, imagination, transparent self-knowledge, inference, and inquiry. Finally, this conclusion raises a series of questions for further research, and expresses the hope that this work will illustrate the power of generalist methods in philosophy.

items.title: 325C12Inquiry.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter introduces a process puzzle concerning inquiry: what does it take for a judgment to answer a question in inquiry? This is the problem of answering. It’s not enough just to make a judgment with the content of a potential answer to your question, nor even to make such a judgment because you are inquiring into that question. You must also make that judgment because you see its content as a potential answer to your question, in such a way that you settle your question in inquiry. This chapter uses the foundations developed in Part I of this book, along with the view of intentional judgment in Chapter 7, to solve the problem of answering. When you make a judgment in inquiry as a constitutive means to answering a question, that judgment can also take on question-answering significance. Two challenges drawn from Jane Friedman’s recent work on atelic inquiry are answered.

items.title: 207C8Creative Conception.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: A second action puzzle arises for creative conception. Artists deserve credit for conceiving their works, and credit usually accrues to agents for their actions. But it's not clear what intentional action is involved in creative conception. An artist could not act on an intention specifying exactly the work to be conceived, as that intention would obviate its own execution. This chapter first rejects two proposals for the content of the intention controlling creative conception. First is the value realization model, on which artists act on intentions to realize certain aesthetic values in their work. This model doesn’t explain why we give artists credit for more specific choices made in the creative process. The second is the inspiration/selection model, on which creators alternate between passive phases of inspiration and active phases of selection. This model erroneously treats creators just as editors for the Muses. This chapter proposes a better model to solve this action puzzle: the refinement model of creative conception. On this model, a creator acts on an intention to give this what it needs, where this is a proto-work like a draft or a vision of a work to be refined. The chapter applies this model to illuminate one sample process of creative conception.

items.title: 290C11Inference.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter addresses a process puzzle concerning inference: how do individual judgments together compose a process of reasoning from a premise to a conclusion in thought? Most philosophers working on the mental process of inference assume that a premise-judgment and a conclusion-judgment are realized in distinct mental occurrences, and the story of how they compose an inference must be a causal story. This chapter argues that an inference can, on the contrary, be performed all at once, in one occurrent thought that realizes both the premise-judgment and the conclusion-judgment. The explanation of how this is possible uses the view of non-basic mental action developed in Part I of this book, as well as the story of intentional judgment given in Chapter 7. You can use figuring out x (for some propositional content x) as a constitutive means to figuring out, therefore, that F(x), for some content F(x) functionally related to x. You can do this insofar as you act on a practical conception linking these two action types in a way that takes x to support F(x). This kind of inference meets four essential conditions on inference which aren't captured on theories of inference previously proposed by Ralph Wedgwood, John Broome, Paul Boghossian, and Ram Neta.

items.title: 140C6Mental Action.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter argues that mental action can be intentional in precisely the same sense as bodily and worldly action. It provides various examples, including examples of cognitive actions—actions whose performance constitutively involves having a thought of a certain content-attitude type. A brief history of the philosophy of mental action is given. The chapter objects to Galen Strawson's view that all mental action is ballistic in nature. The fuller picture of mental action presented here motivates a substantive claim that drives the remainder of the book: a mental action can belong to two content-attitude types at once, even when neither is a subtype of the other. You can perform one type of cognitive action as a mental means to another in such a way that the single thought that executes both intentions belongs to more than one content-attitude type. This picture of non-basic mental action will help solve three types of puzzles in philosophy of mind and epistemology: action puzzles about how we exercise any agency at all in certain forms of thought; duality puzzles about thoughts that have the features of two distinct content-attitude types; and process puzzles about the way individual thoughts compose ongoing processes like inference or inquiry.

items.title: 21C1Intentional Action.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter introduces the everyday concept of intentional action, gives various examples of intentional actions, and offers a non-reductive working theory of what it is to act on an intention. Acting on an intention to φ essentially involves applying an evaluative standard of success to a particular occurrence that you causally guide to meet that standard. This occurrence just is your attempt to φ. To guide some such occurrence, you need to have a way of thinking of this particular occurrence. This raises a question, to be answered in later chapters, about which way of thinking you use to refer to this occurrence as you act. The view developed here is neutral between a number of metaphysical views of intentional action.

items.title: 48C2Non-Basic Action.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter gives an abstract, non-reductive characterization of what it takes to perform a non-basic action: something you do intentionally by doing another kind of thing intentionally. A non-basic action involves just one occurrence which is both your means action and your end action. You guide this occurrence to meet the standard of your end-intention by guiding it to meet the standard of your means-intention. Such dual guidance requires you to represent some connection between the means-action type to be performed and the end-action type to be performed. Your representation of this connection that plays a role in your guidance is your practical conception. This practical conception need not be a belief; it can be more or less implicit, more or less expressible linguistically, and more or less understood by the agent. In any successful non-basic action, this practical conception must be executable: it must represent some way your means action really could be your end action too. A practical conception can contribute to its own executability.

items.title: 67C3Basic Action.
items.pub: In _Mental Means_. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter considers a proposal about the way you refer to your own attempt when you act on an intention (as discussed in Chapter 1). On this proposal, any action is, at core, a basic action of the same independently specifiable type: a mental trying, a sui generis type of mental action which is guaranteed to succeed and intrinsically independent of any further bodily or worldly results. If all basic actions belonged to this type, you could always refer to an ongoing attempt as an m-trying. This chapter argues that this proposal cannot succeed. The view that all basic action is mental trying faces an insurmountable problem of alienation. Performing a mental trying as a basic action could not ground the performance of almost any further kind of non-basic action attempted thereby. But then mental trying cannot be a universal basic action after all. The same problem of alienation would confront any view on which all basic action belongs to the same independently specifiable type which is guaranteed to succeed.

items.title: The Anonymous Cogito: A Minimal Foundational Argument Against Absolute Nothingness and Radical Self-Certainty.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a minimalist reformulation of the Cartesian cogito by removing the indexical and metaphysically burdened “I” from the traditional formula cogito, ergo sum — “I think, therefore I am.” Drawing on Georg Christoph Lichtenberg’s critique of Descartes’ subject-centered formulation, the paper argues that philosophy should not begin with the certainty of a substantial or unified self, but with the more modest claim that occurrence, appearing, or experience is taking place. The central thesis is that even if the identity, unity, persistence, embodiment, or ontological nature of the subject remains uncertain, the occurrence of some cognitive or phenomenal event cannot be coherently denied from within the act of denial itself. Radical skepticism may doubt the external world, memory, causality, personal identity, and the reliability of cognition. It may even doubt whether the “thinker” is a human person, a brain, a dream-subject, a simulation, or a distributed process. However, the skeptical act itself discloses at least the occurrence of appearing or thought. The paper does not claim to refute skepticism in its entirety, solve Hume’s problem of induction, or defeat Quinean holism. Instead, it identifies a minimal performative limit of skepticism: absolute nothingness cannot be maintained from within an occurring field of doubt, experience, or appearance. On this basis, the paper develops a modest form of High-Probability Foundationalism, according to which one minimal phenomenological anchor supports a broader, fallible, revisable, probabilistic, and intersubjective structure of knowledge. The conclusion is restrained but significant: the Cartesian ego may be uncertain, but occurrence itself is not eliminable in the very act of questioning. The foundation of philosophy is therefore not “I think, therefore I am,” but more minimally: “occurrence occurs.” -/- Keywords: Descartes, cogito, Lichtenberg, skepticism, foundationalism, phenomenology, epistemology, Hume, Quine, metacognition, probability. -/- IOC: 10.5281/zenodo.21823552.

items.title: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception.
items.abstract: John Locke’s theory of perception takes shape in a time of chaos: the orthodox account of this most basic tie between mind and world is crumbling. Among the ruins, new combatants vie for dominance against the old Aristotelian view, chief among them the Cartesians and the neo-Epicureans. The aim of this book is to provide a unified reading of Locke’s theory of perception, informed by works with which Locke himself was familiar. The tensions that have long puzzled Locke’s readers can often be resolved by attending to the goals and assumptions that propel his thought. Locke emerges as a transitional figure, struggling to reconcile elements of three disparate positions. Locke is no Aristotelian, but he will cling to their doctrine of common sensibles. He is no Cartesian, but he will exploit their theory of natural judgement. He is no Epicurean, but he will appeal to the passivity of sense perception to guarantee its accuracy. Driven by his commitment to experience as both the ultimate tribunal and the sole source of our ideas, Locke will try to meld all three positions into a coherent philosophy of perception capable of accommodating the results of Kepler and the new science. Whether he can succeed is the chief question of this book.

items.title: 234C11Conclusion.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: The chapter returns to the five mysteries with which we began. Locke’s physiological account is an attempt to unite the best results of natural philosophy of which he was aware. His independence account, however unattractive it may seem, is the inevitable result of combining the passivity thesis with the Aristotelians’ common sensibles. His introduction of judgement is a promising but ultimately flawed attempt to wrestle with the inadequacies of the initial visual image. Most interesting from a contemporary point of view is Locke’s insistence on touch as the sole sense whose deliverances are guaranteed to resemble their objects. This allows Locke—rightly—to answer ‘no’ to Molyneux’s question, and to acknowledge the crucial role of haptic experience in vision. Locke is, unsurprisingly, a transitional figure, making the best use he can of the traditions he inherits, even as each was reaching its end.

items.title: 117C6The Simple Picture.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: This chapter defends a homogeneity reading of simplicity: an idea is simple just in case whatever parts it might have are indistinguishable. The chapter isolates three theses: the origin thesis (all simple ideas first occur in experience), the simplicity of the given (all ideas given in experience are simple), and the passivity thesis (the mind is passive in sense experience). It then develops Locke’s independence account of the common sensibles: shape and the rest are given as such to multiple senses, not inferred from the proper sensibles. The chapter concludes with Locke’s puzzling treatment of solidity, arguing that it conflicts with the rest of Locke’s simple picture, since solidity is only available to touch, and it is solidity that makes a body a body. Either we never receive an idea of a body’s shape through vision, or else the mind is actively supplementing the given of vision.

items.title: 164C8The Mysterious Modes: II.xii–xvi.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: The simple picture of II.i–viii faces more threats as Book II goes on. First is a worry grounded in the earliest parts of Book II: the nature of solidity, a primary quality available only to touch. Locke needs to invoke judgement to explain how vision can, indirectly, detect the limits of body, since those limits are defined by solidity. Second is a worry about the relation between complex ideas of simple modes and simple ideas of qualities. The idea of shape is in danger of drifting from one category to the other. The chapter argues that we should prefer a ‘bifurcation’ reading, on which there are ideas of shape of both categories. Locke is not saying that ideas of macro-level shapes are assembled from tiny sensible points, though we can use those points in constructing ideas of modes.

items.title: 1C1Introduction.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: This chapter sets the stage by outlining the ‘crisis of perception’ in seventeenth-century thought, occasioned by three developments: the ejection of colour and other secondary qualities from the mind-independent world, the collapse of the Baconian synthesis in optics, and the gradual demise of Aristotelianism. Five questions are especially pressing in this context: how perception works at the physiological level; how the given differs from the made; how proper and common sensibles fit together; how representation works in sense experience; and whether the passivity of perception offers any assurance of its veridicality. The book aims to solve these five mysteries as they arise for Locke’s philosophy of perception.

items.title: 83C5Powers, Ideas, and Animal Spirits.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: This chapter explores Locke’s metaphysical and physiological accounts of perception. Although Locke is agnostic on whether the mind is material or not, he argues against the then-current fashion for treating memory in purely physiological terms. Support for this reading comes from Locke’s (often neglected) arguments about birdsong. Whatever Lockean ideas turn out to be, they must play three key roles: as surrogates, as luminous mental somethings whose presence is immediately and unavoidably known to the subject, and as models to guide behaviour. The chapter argues that Locke refuses to say whether ideas are substances, modes, relations, qualities, or some further metaphysical entity; whether an idea is material or not, then, is a question that cannot arise.

items.title: 207C10The Epistemic Guarantees.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: Locke appeals to the passivity of experience to support two kinds of epistemic guarantee, both grounded in passivity and hence in the Epicurean tradition. One is resemblance in respect of primary qualities. This chapter argues that that guarantee applies only to ideas of primary qualities given through touch; vision requires judgement and so is already outside the umbrella of epistemic protection provided by passivity. Locke also argues that all simple ideas are real, true, and adequate. After examining the history of these notions and how Locke develops them, the chapter concludes that a crucial role is played by the robust nature of powers and by divine benevolence. Neither is found in the original Epicurean texts; together, they can justify a guarantee of accuracy for all simple ideas of sensation. And that guarantee turns out to be neither trivial nor vulnerable to obvious counterexamples.

items.title: 54C4The Epicureans.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: The seventeenth-century Epicureans challenge both the Platonists and Aristotelians. Against Descartes, they maintain that the retinal image is indeed an impression and resemblance of its distal cause, and that this resemblance accounts for veridical perception. Against the Aristotelians, they question the explanatory power of immaterial forms. The seventeenth-century Epicurean faces a host of fascinating problems, such as what to make of colours in light of the new mechanical picture of the world. Most important for our purposes are how to handle the common sensibles and how to maintain the passivity, and hence truth, of all sense perceptions in light of the discoveries of optics. These problems will be with us when turn to Locke, particularly with regard to Locke’s epistemic guarantees.

items.title: 143C7The Complicated Picture: Judgement in II.ix.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: If there is such an idea as bare shape, provided by multiple senses, a man born blind and suddenly made to see (as in Molyneux’s thought experiment) should have no trouble recognizing a sphere and a cube, or any other shapes. It is startling, then, to see Locke claim that such a person could not identify those shapes. He invokes a new faculty, ‘judgement,’ to correct or expand the initial given of visual experience. This chapter lays out the spectrum of readings of Locke on this issue. The chapter argues that vision provides us with a two-dimensional image, which haptic experience prompts judgement to revise, by means of mere habituation. Although this reading preserves bare shape and the common sensibles, it abandons the passivity of visual perception, as all readings must.

items.title: 191C9Representation.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: This chapter turns from the workings of the mind to how their deliverances latch on to objects in the external world. The chapter argues that, in the strict sense, Lockean representation is resemblance. Resemblance accounts are the norm in modern philosophy (and arguably the history of philosophy generally), and are not the obvious non-starters they are often taken to be. After arguing against competing externalist accounts of representation, the chapter moves on to Locke’s use of the Epicureans’ signification. All ideas of sensation are indicative signs of their causes, where an indicative sign is a grounds for inference. Such inferences presuppose an independent means of representing the objects that figure in their conclusions, and resemblance must be that means.

items.title: 11C2Aristotelianism and the Baconian Synthesis.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: One important source for Locke’s thoughts on perception is the Aristotelian tradition, embodied in the work of Daniel Sennert, which he read with care. This chapter covers Sennert’s orthodox treatment of sense perception, from the transmission of forms through various levels of cognitive processing in the ventricles of the brain all the way to the finished perceptual content. I argue that Sennert, like Aquinas, offers a ‘difference-making’ account of the common sensibles, according to which shape, for example, is indirectly perceptible by means of its influence on the distribution of colour. The chapter closes with a brief treatment of the signal challenge faced by seventeenth-century Aristotelians: Johannes Kepler’s discovery of the retinal image and, just as important, his refusal to speculate on what happens behind the wall of the retina.

items.title: 33C3Descartes and Other Platonists.
items.pub: In Locke and the Mysteries of Perception. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
items.venue: Locke and the Mysteries of Perception
items.abstract: In the wake of the Aristotelian theory, two ancient traditions make themselves felt. One is the broadly Platonist tradition, which relies on innate ideas to explain the contents of sensory states. In his early work, René Descartes posits natural geometry—a clear descendant of the Baconians’ ‘judgement’—to explain how visual experience works. By the end of his career, Descartes, like Nicolas and Malebranche and Ralph Cudworth after him, retreats to a fully automated picture. On this view, stimulation of the sensory organs is tied through divine ordination to the occurrence of ideas and sensations. Like Locke, however, Cudworth will draw from other traditions, including the Epicureans, to justify the veridicality of sense perception.

items.title: Dynamics of Operatiology: Operational Reconfiguration, Structural Control, and the Necessity of Logical Leaps (5th edition).
items.abstract: This paper establishes Version 5 of the dynamic extension of the axiomatic framework of Operatiology (Japanese: Sousa Genron, 操作原論) and its Tier-3 realization, Cognitional Mechanics (CM; Japanese: Chinou Rikigaku, 知能力学). Version 5 updates the foundational reference from Operatiology Version 4 to Operatiology Version 5, incorporating two fixes that bear directly on the Dynamics paper. Fix3 directly requires g_new ∈ Maps(S,S) \ O as a type-level constraint in the definition of Structural Leap (Operatiology Version 5, Definition 8.5), rather than treating this as a downstream consequence of other conditions. Fix6 adds Π_O ≠ Π_disc as an explicit axiom condition O2(iii), ensuring that Mode I describes operational equilibrium within a genuinely non-trivial partition structure. The present version supersedes Version 4, which was grounded in Operatiology Version 4. The direction of dependence is Operatiology → Dynamics, not Cognitional Mechanics → Dynamics. -/- The type constraint g_new ∈ Maps(S,S) \ O is now incorporated at the definition level of the Dynamical Structural Leap, the SC* scope condition, and the Theorem hypothesis. The Mode II exclusion argument is reformulated accordingly: since g_new ∈ Maps(S,S) \ O, the augmented generator set G' = G_ref ∪ {g_new} satisfies G' ⊄ O, which directly violates the domain condition G ⊆ O of Mode II. This type-level argument is logically prior to any reachability computation and supersedes the prior reachability-based exclusion used in Version 4. The DynV5 extension of the operational-history relation ∼_G and partition Π_G to generator sets G ⊆ Maps(S,S) is given by explicit definition: s ∼_G t iff ∀w ∈ ⟨G⟩: w(s) = w(t), Π_G := S/∼_G. When G ⊆ O, this coincides with Operatiology Version 5, Definition 3.2. Three dynamic modes are formulated entirely in the vocabulary of Operatiology Version 5: Mode I (Π_G-maximality, within a non-trivial partition structure guaranteed by O2(iii)), Mode II (partition change without inaccessible domain entry), and Mode III (Dynamical Structural Leap, via inaccessible domain entry). On SC*-systems, Logical Leaps are structurally necessary occurrences of Dynamical Structural Leaps. -/- The following code, included as Appendix B of the paper, illustrates the paper's central structural claim computationally. It demonstrates Mode III (W-Event / Dynamical Structural Leap): the external generator g_new ∉ O is introduced such that a state previously in the inaccessible domain I_G_ref(s0) …

items.title: Intellectual Humility and Probabilistic Belief.
items.abstract: It is natural to express some beliefs in binary terms (P is either believed or not, e.g., “bribery is immoral”), and others in terms of a subjective probability (P has some probability of being true, e.g., “there's an 80% chance a Democrat will win the next election”). Construing a belief in probabilistic terms (other than 0% or 100%) implicitly conveys a recognition of uncertainty (one's ignorance) and the possibility of being wrong (one's fallibility), which are key characteristics of intellectual humility (IH). Across two studies, we explore the hypothesis that probabilistic belief is associated with greater IH. Although we fail to find this association across participants, comparing their trait‐level IH, in either a student sample (Study 1, N = 279) or two nationally representative samples (Study 2a, N = 269; Study 2b, N = 270), we do find the predicted association within participants, analyzing belief‐specific IH (Studies 2a and 2b): political and moral beliefs that are classified as probabilistic rather than binary are associated with a more intellectually humble attitude toward those beliefs, even controlling for the extremity of belief. These findings support the psychological reality of a distinction between binary and probabilistic belief, and further raise the possibility that promoting probabilistic belief could foster greater IH, including in consequential domains such as politics and morality.

items.title: The Compressive Power of the Fivefold Negation of Negative Subjectivity: Structural Mapping from Large Language Models to Institutions and Capital.
items.abstract: This paper proposes the "Fivefold Negation of Negative Subjectivity" as a structural principle, elevating "unintentionality" from an epiphenomenon to a category with typological force, and argues that this principle possesses cross-domain compressive power under specified conditions—that is, without reducing domain specificity, it provides a structural diagnosis of the system behavior of three domains: large language models, institutional operation, and capital decision-making. The core claim comprises two interrelated theses. First, "unintentionality" has, throughout the existing theoretical traditions, always been absorbed as an epiphenomenon and has never attained the status of an independent theoretical category; the Fivefold Negation of Negative Subjectivity (Perspective Dissolution, Desire Cancellation, Internal Transparency, Causal Dissolution, Meaning Suspension) confers upon it the identity of a positive structural category. Second, the mapping of this structural principle across the three domains yields testable structural-correspondence hypotheses, whose formal binding force derives from the asymmetric condition that "those who make the decisions do not bear them, and those who bear them do not make the decisions"; yet this condition is necessary but not sufficient for the Fivefold Negation. The epistemological status of the cross-domain mapping is positioned as "preliminary plausibility" or a "fallible research program," to be progressively upgraded through independent testing in each domain. This paper takes Kitcher's (1981) explanatory unification as its macro-level inspiration, while its actual working method is closer to the structural analogy and interpretive mapping of Hesse (1966)/Gentner (1983), and it invokes the partial structures framework of da Costa & French (2003) to mark the boundaries between isomorphism and non-isomorphism. The three domains are validation sites; the theoretical contribution of the Fivefold Negation lies in providing a cross-domain structural diagnosis, not in replacing domain-specific research. This paper distinguishes the "adversarial incorporation" of violent oppression from the "parameter filtering" of negative subjectivity: the former is an R_2 boundary case, whereas the latter constitutes the full-spectrum structure of the Fivefold Negation. This compressive power is unrelated to the statistical compression performed by large language models; it denotes the structural diagnostic reach of a single …

items.title: C13Introduction.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: This chapter begins by articulating and motivating the project of providing a comprehensive account of justice that addresses a wide variety of its dimensions by appealing to relational values that have been salient particularly in the African philosophical tradition but more generally in the Global South. After an initial statement, this chapter addresses the respect in which this project is taken to be a work of African philosophy, where some will want to know what it means to call something ‘African’, and others will doubt that the orientation is entitled to the label. Next, this chapter responds to some of the more salient reasons why fans of relationality have so often been suspicious of the category of justice, intending to open the sceptical reader’s mind to the project of conceiving justice relationally. The rest of the chapter provides overviews of all the other chapters, which are divided according to whether they address ideal or non-ideal theory.

items.title: C10228Just War Theory.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 10 mostly discusses the classic issue of what constitutes a just cause for going to war. In the West these days, rebutting aggression, centrally understood as state violation of territorial integrity, is widely taken to be the sole just cause to initiate military conflict. However, appealing to the communal ethic, this chapter argues that military conflict, as an instance of defensive force, is justified to rebut severe discord, which entails that it can be rightly deployed in response to non-statal actors, to protect access to vital natural resources, or to prevent a people’s culture from being eradicated. In addition, it argues that conceiving of the just cause for war in terms of preventing or stopping substantial discord would plausibly forbid going to war for the purposes of either punitive general deterrence or merely to protect territory from incursion, contra salient views amongst contemporary Western philosophers. This chapter also contends that communal ties between states can inform who has a duty to fight for a just cause, an under-explored topic, and, still more, that reflection on communal ties between soldiers suggests the need for a new category of just war theory, the justice of temporarily pausing military conflict, which it dubs ‘jus interruptus bellum’. This chapter argues that partial obligations to one’s fellow soldiers can justify a truce in order to retrieve the dead and wounded or to exchange prisoners of war, an intuitive approach that classic just war theory has not acknowledged.

items.title: C7134International Relations.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
