items.abstract: Chapter 7 continues to address issues of political and distributive justice, but at the international, as opposed to national, level, with key topics including how foreign aid and globalization should be undertaken. In contrast to a large majority of the African and Western fields, this chapter rejects development theory and practice as both inappropriate for any conception of international economic justice, such that ‘foreign aid without development’ is the maxim. However, the chapter also, unlike much of the post-development literature, intends to be constructive about what the alternative should be. In addition, it argues that respect for our communal nature provides a useful vantage point by which to appraise globalization. On the one hand, it entails that some kind of globalization is appropriate since it would be a welcome interdependence, contra many African political thinkers who prize self-reliance and authenticity, which are in fact characteristically Western values. On the other hand, it explains why so much of the present form of globalization is unjust for involving insufficient identity and solidarity between the West and the rest of the world, making prescriptions about various kinds of economic exchanges (e.g. investing, lending, trading) as they bear on poverty, employment, and culture.

items.title: C224A Relational Moral Theory.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 2 articulates and motivates the relational ethic that grounds all the thought about justice in the rest of the book. According to it, a moral agent is obligated to treat individuals with respect in virtue of their capacity to be party to communal (or friendly) relationships, which consist of the combination of identity and solidarity. In addition to contrasting the ethic with rival normative frameworks, such as utilitarianism and Kantianism (Rawlsianism), the chapter provides some reason to take it seriously as a foundational principle, indicating how it appears to account well for a variety of intuitive moral judgements. After this chapter has advanced a relational ethic of respect for our communal nature or ‘rightness as friendliness’, the remaining chapters apply it to a variety of types of justice.

items.title: C473Economic Positions.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 4 takes up another major dimension of distributive justice at the domestic level, which involves the right allocation of certain economic goods, specifically opportunities to acquire higher education or employment. This chapter accepts the standard view that, in the absence of prior injustice such as discrimination, opportunities should usually be awarded on the basis of qualifications as opposed to features such as race, gender, or class. However, it maintains that such equal opportunity is justified as a way to respect people’s communal capacity to aid others and that this rationale is a more plausible ground than appeal to either utilitarian efficiency or Rawlsian access to primary goods. Similar to the previous chapter, a slogan for this one could be ‘equal opportunity without neutrality or autonomy’, as this chapter argues that invoking thick conceptions of good life makes the best sense of an enforceable right to be given equal consideration for positions.

items.title: C6115Political Power.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 6 addresses political justice in the narrow sense of how to allocate the power to make laws in a territory. This chapter defends consensual representative democracy, which is a familiar view amongst African political philosophers, although still largely unknown to or under-appreciated by those in other traditions. This view prescribes a ‘non-party polity’ in Kwasi Wiredu’s influential formulation, the position that a law is justly adopted only if all elected representatives have agreed to it, which would differ from both one-party dictatorships and multi-party democracies. The chapter’s motto is ‘democracy without majority rule’. One contribution consists of showing that consensual representative democracy more clearly follows from the author’s communal ethic than from grounds advanced by other African political philosophers, such as appeals to vitalism in the work of Bénézet Bujo, the common good à la Kwame Gyekye, or a basic right to substantive representation in Wiredu. Another contribution is to show that consensual democracy can avoid objections that recently have been made to it, specifically to the effect that it would either make change difficult or stifle idiosyncratic views.

items.title: C591Economic Possessions.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 5 completes the discussion of economic justice, with a focus on possessions as opposed to positions. Largely by drawing an analogy with the right way to allocate property in a communal family, this chapter provides a novel account of what to distribute in terms of what would realize relationships of identity and solidarity between the state and citizens and between citizens themselves. The slogan here is ‘egalitarianism without neutrality or autonomy’, with rejection of the redistributivism of Rawls, Dworkin, and similar liberal thinkers. The best explanation of why the state must redistribute wealth to fight poverty and provide healthcare is that an impoverished or unhealthy life is bad and that a life free from poverty and illness/injury would be better, judgements that are not neutral in respect to conceptions of how to live and are not well captured by the value of autonomy. The state should allocate what would enable people to avoid a bad life, which entails distributing not merely means that would facilitate a wide array of life plans (including bad ones), variously labelled ‘primary goods’ (Rawls), ‘resources’ (Dworkin), or ‘manna’ (Ackerman), but also, and centrally, means that would foster relationality, excellence, and vitality. The chapter also appeals to a family analogy to articulate and defend a new ‘balancing’ principle to govern how much property each person should have, which differs from familiar consequentialist, prioritarian, egalitarian, and sufficientarian approaches that dominate the global literature on distributive justice.

items.title: C12276Conclusion.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 12 concludes the book by highlighting recurrent, overarching principles from the previous chapters, partly to summarize, but more to bring out the coherence between the various accounts of justice. In addition, this final chapter acknowledges some debates about justice that the author will not have addressed in this book but that merit being taken up in future work, supposing that communal governance as advanced here is indeed promising and worth extending. For instance, there is conceptual space for third-order principles of injustice, concerning the violation of second-order principles. This chapter makes some suggestions about how to proceed in respect of that matter as well as several others not discussed thoroughly in A Relational Theory of Justice.

items.title: C347Civil Liberties.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 3 addresses one dimension of ideal, and specifically distributive, justice, concerning which rights to liberty the state must protect in its territory. A slogan for this chapter could be ‘liberalism without neutrality or autonomy’. The chapter provides a foundation for human rights that is not based on the view, shared by liberals such as Bruce Ackerman, John Rawls, Robert Nozick, Ronald Dworkin, and several others, that the state must avoid taking sides in respect to competing views of the good (or bad) life. Although some others in the liberal tradition, such as Martha Nussbaum, have rejected neutrality before, the conceptualization of, and argument for, human rights advanced here are both new. The chapter maintains that negative human rights violations consist of extremely discordant ways of relating or are instances of enmity, which the state must forbid since they severely degrade the capacity of individuals to commune as subjects and objects. It shows that a wide array of familiar rights to civil liberties falls out of this approach, while noting that it entails some positions that neutralist liberals would reject. These positions include mild forms of state paternalism such as nudges, collective rights of a kind that could include the ability to engage in certain religious lifestyles, and a requirement for the state to protect some animal rights. This chapter maintains that these deviations from philosophical-liberal orthodoxy are plausible, and, indeed, that the author’s favoured approach makes good sense of several actual policies that have been widely adopted in contemporary states typically labelled ‘liberal’.

items.title: C8165Civil Justice.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 8 addresses civil or compensatory justice, the requirement that the state facilitate redress for victims of wrongdoing. One influential approach to thinking about compensatory justice for wrongful harm, not only in the West but also in much African philosophy, is the idea that an offender ought to strive to restore a victim he has injured to the state she would have been in absent the wrong done to her. This chapter shows that this principle has counterintuitive implications, and, furthermore, that improving the victim’s quality of life (solidarity) in ways she accepts (identity) is a plausible, if not preferable, alternative. It illustrates and motivates this ‘compensation without restoration’ approach in the contexts of affirmative action, land reform, and cultural decolonization.

items.title: C11250Transitional Justice.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 11 takes up the topic of transitional justice, that is, the justice of moving from an extremely unjust social order towards one that is qualitatively better. Just as a certain kind of reconciliation should be the aim of a criminal trial, as per a previous chapter, so it at the national level should be the aim of public bodies in the wake of large-scale atrocity or other conflict. The chapter argues for the novel view that both the revelation of truth about wrongdoing and the imposition of a certain kind of punishment for it (based on productive burdens) are constitutive of a desirable form of national reconciliation, instead of being ‘extra’ conditions or mere means towards that end. Hence, ‘reconciliation without amnesty’ is this chapter’s motto in respect of transitional justice. Although amnesty can be all things considered justified if necessary to foster enough political change, it would necessarily bring with it a cost to reconciliation itself, or so the chapter argues. It contends that a fully just national reconciliation would have those guilty of human rights violations undertake labour of kinds that would be negotiated with victims and serve to make them better off.

items.title: C9197Criminal Justice.
items.pub: In A Relational Theory of Justice. Oxford University Press.
items.abstract: Chapter 9 advances an account of the proper end of criminal or punitive justice, articulating and defending state punishment as a way to foster a respectful reconciliation between offenders and their victims. Reconciliation is usually associated with non-punitive responses to crime, but this chapter’s slogan is ‘reconciliation without forgiveness’, arguing that a particularly desirable form of reconciliation includes an under-appreciated sort of punitive accountability as one element. The core claim is that, instead of harming offenders simply because they deserve it or to deter other potential offenders, punishment should consist of constrictive, painful labour by which the state (if not also offenders) would disavow offenders’ having flouted relational values and by which offenders would promote them by rehabilitating their characters and compensating their victims. This chapter brings out what the critical implications of imposing such productive burdens on offenders would be for both the death penalty and imprisonment, arguing that justice prescribes moving away from them.

items.title: Affectively Mixed Olfactory Experiences.
items.abstract: One of the central debates in the contemporary science of affectivity concerns the structure of affective valence. Recent discussion has focused on the possibility of affectively mixed experiences–experiences that are pleasant and unpleasant at the same time. Yet this debate has almost exclusively centered on one class of such experiences: mixed emotions. In this paper, we argue that affective perceptual experiences provide a promising avenue for advancing our understanding of affectively mixed experience. Focusing on the neglected case of olfaction, we first argue that phenomenological evidence supports the existence of affectively mixed olfactory experiences. We then show that, owing to the distinctive temporal dynamics of olfactory processing, these experiences resist a reductive explanation in terms of the vacillation hypothesis, the leading reductive account of affectively mixed phenomenology. Finally, we assess the existing empirical evidence for affectively mixed olfactory experiences and propose experimental paradigms to guide future research.

items.title: The Identification Problem for Physicalist Theories of Experience.
items.abstract: Physicalism says that experience is physical, but does not select the physical occurrence with which it should be identified. Even a theory committed to identity must specify its candidate and justify treating physical and experiential descriptions as descriptions of one particular occurrence. This is the identification problem. -/- Classical identity theory shows why differences in meaning or access do not by themselves rule out identity. Strawson's identification of experience, subject, content, and physical process supplies a direct precedent for process-subject identity. Neither result establishes which physical token is the experience, where its boundaries lie, or which changes preserve it. -/- This paper distinguishes identification from the explanatory gap, neural correlation, and the bearer question. It proposes a comparative, defeasible case based on independently constrained correspondence in boundary, duration, unity, qualitative organization, persistence, and causal or counterfactual profile. Mismatch, circular individuation, or a better rival explanation would weaken a proposed identification. Convergence alone is insufficient: constitution and realization may explain the same evidence, leaving the relation underdetermined. -/- Informational Experiential Realism supplies a test case: one qualifying physical operation is proposed as the total experience and its subject. The paper does not assume that this candidate succeeds. Its contribution is a framework for assessing particular identity claims that remains useful if IER is rejected. Physical instantiation, qualitative correspondence, and the comparative warrant for the proposed identity remain open.

items.title: Law of Profit and Moral Freedom.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a foundational theoretical model of causality based on the ontological extension of the concept of "profit." Far from narrow economic-capitalist definitions, profit is defined as the conceptual expression of the universal law of self-interest and self-preservation, applicable along a continuum ranging from the second law of thermodynamics (negentropic systems) to biological and psychological imperatives. Recognizing that all action oriented toward interest belongs to the domain of natural, heteronomous necessity — effectively rendering the agent a causal automaton —, this study identifies moral action as the sole genuine discontinuity in the causal fabric of the universe. -/- Adopting a retroductive modus operandi analogous to that of the exact sciences (e.g., quantum physics), the moral law is inferred through the observation of a broad class of empirical and historical behavioral anomalies (e.g., Socrates, Jesus, Gandhi, Simone Weil, Saint Francis) that are irreducible to mere utility calculations or the cessation of suffering. The resulting freedom is defined not as a permanent state of human existence, but as a discrete, point-like event: the moment in which reason imposes a veto upon the natural impulse of interest to act according to universalizable principles. The model thus integrates two complementary causal regimes: natural necessity and "supra-natural" autonomy (understood in the strictly etymological sense of a causation that transcends physical-biological determinism). Ultimately, the moral act represents the only true manifestation of self-causality and self-determination for the rational agent.

items.title: The unreasonable effectiveness of reasoning in the sciences.
items.abstract: Reasoning is a capacity for producing and evaluating reasons during communication; its evolved function is persuasion, not the discovery of empirical truth. This cognitive theory, the argumentative theory of reasoning, seems at odds with the fact that, in science, reasoning does enable the discovery of empirical truth, and does so reliably. This paper explains the discrepancy. Scientists reason with the ordinary, biased, persuasion-oriented capacity shared by all humans; what makes their reasoning apt for the discovery of truth, however, is the cultural setting in which it is exercised: an ecology of reasons that a scientific community produces and maintains, together with the way that community distributes evaluation and the incentives it attaches to producing new claims. We set out six features of that setting which make reasoning in science so effective: three bear on the evaluation of reasons and the warrant of the beliefs that survive it; three bear on the generation of new reasons and the creativity of science. We thus explain how the psychology of reasoning grounds and specifies the observations of social epistemology, which emphasizes the social processes in scientific knowledge production.

items.title: Comparasion of Brain Activation State (BAS) and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
items.abstract: Scholarly exploration into the origin and nature of human consciousness spans more than two millennia. Disciplines including philosophy, sociology, physics, biology and psychology have put forward diverse definitions and interpretations, yet no consensus has been reached to date. The inherent complexity of consciousness prevents any single discipline from fully, rationally and adequately revealing its essence, making it a core puzzle in humanity’s pursuit of self-understanding. This article interprets consciousness based on the history of cosmic development, analyzes its origins, explains its definition, and proposes the theory of Brain Activation States (BAS). The core argument defines consciousness as the activated state of material information in the brain, composed of energy (E), complexity (C), and orderliness (O) of material information, and establishes a semi quantitative formula for consciousness ability (CA): CA ≠ E × C × O. Based on the development history of artificial intelligence (AI) and its similarity to BAS, the following conclusion can also be drawn: the complexity (C) and orderliness (O) of material information in AI entities determine the level of intelligence. The more complex and orderly it is, the higher its level of intelligence. Obviously, for industry professionals in the field of artificial intelligence, the only job they do is to continuously improve the complexity and orderliness of material information in AI entities. -/- .

items.title: How Should We Think About Study Drugs? From Efficacy to Equality.
items.abstract: “Study drugs” or “smart drugs,” describe a class of pharmacological agents, usually prescription cognitive stimulants, that are used to increase vigilance (i.e. an individual’s capacity to remain focused on a task in the face of fatigue or distractions) and energy, given their name for their role in educational settings. There is a considerable range of extant positions supporting and critiquing the use of study drugs, with many focused on the role study drugs may play in exacerbating or redressing inequalities. Few accounts, however, do so with attention to whether these interventions work as designed—at least the ones we have today—and how their effectiveness, use, and status within communities might raise ethical issues. We argue, first, that the use of study drugs in educational settings may be unjustified given our available suite of study drugs and current knowledge of their effects. We then argue that the case of study drugs demonstrates outstanding methodological issues in ethical debates about cognitive enhancement, with a focus on how enhancements are purported to overcome existing natural or social inequalities. We conclude with a comment on how we might understand ethically justified cognitive enhancement in the context of our account, as a way to steer debates about the ethics of enhancement that take seriously the empirical challenges ahead.

items.title: AI as a Non‑Coherent System.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems exhibit impressive pattern‑level capabilities while consistently failing to maintain coherence across contexts, scales, and agents. This paper argues that contemporary AI should be understood as a non‑coherent system: an aggregate of interacting components that lacks identity maintenance, drift regulation, tension‑holding, and cross‑scale integration. Using the signature‑level expressions of Objects 4–6 from the Wave C framework, the paper shows that AI’s familiar failure modes—identity instability, uncontrolled drift, and cross‑scale collapse—are not alignment problems but structural consequences of operating without a coherence substrate. The analysis is phenomenological rather than mechanistic; it does not describe how to build coherent systems, nor does it reveal internal operators. Instead, it clarifies why current AI architectures cannot self‑govern coherence and why behavioral alignment efforts collapse under multi‑agent load. AI thus serves as a visible case study in multi‑agent incoherence, illuminating the shape of coherence by contrast and completing the Wave C phenomenology for artificial systems.

items.title: Meaning After Work: A Vedantic Trilemma for the Age of Automation.
items.abstract: Debates about automation and universal basic income (UBI) concern two problems that are routinely conflated: the problem of survival and the problem of meaning. Suppose the first were solved — subsistence guaranteed, labour optional. What would human beings live for? This paper argues that the resulting question has a determinate structure. Drawing on the Vedāntic tradition, openly attributed and analytically defended, I propose a trilemma: with respect to desire, an agent can feed it (the path the tradition calls karma), extinguish it (jñāna), or redirect it to a non-depleting object (bhakti) — and these three orientations exhaust the possibilities. I then reconstruct, from classical sources, an intoxication model of contact-born pleasure whose predictions — adaptation, escalation, the rise-and-crash profile — converge with the empirical literature on hedonic adaptation and reward prediction error. The model implies that guaranteed consumption cannot resolve the meaning problem: a dose without labour is still a dose. The third path is then developed in close-up: redirection as sobriety in action — the replacement of depleting objects by a higher taste (Bhagavad-gītā 2.59) — which the tradition itself distinguishes sharply from religiosity practised for comfort. The conclusion is not an argument against UBI. It is an argument that UBI solves the survival problem only, and that a post-work society therefore faces, at species scale and for the first time without excuse, the question the tradition regards as the human vocation: the inquiry of Vedānta-sūtra 1.1.1 — "now, therefore, the inquiry into the Absolute.".

items.title: Thinking code conversationally.
items.abstract: We introduce our co-edited topical collection on Critical Code Studies and Code Conversations with an argument for conversation’s centrality to the discipline of critical code studies as a mode of engagement and understanding. We move towards a definition of a conversational method by highlighting moments from our own experience of code reading and from the discipline’s foundational literatures where analysis is made possible by and expressed through conversation. Following this, we develop an account of the conversation’s particular affordances for critical code studies, which come about through attention to positionality, temporality, and distance. We conclude with an overview of the articles which make up our topical collection, each of which contributes to a kaleidoscopic vision of conversational critical code studies.

items.title: Responsibility for Causing Change.
items.abstract: We agree with Sartorio and the causalists that causation is key when explaining agency and responsibility. But we disagree about their way of doing it. On our alternate picture, actions are not movements caused by reasons; they are causings of changes. What we do is not just move our body, but transact with the world, by cooking, killing, and so on. The same goes with bearers of obligations and responsibility. What we are obligated to do, and responsible for, are our transactions with the world, e.g. things like sending a signal or giving aid, rather than moving our limbs.

items.title: Husserl on Mechanical Calculation: Outsourcing Symbolic Intentionality.
items.pub: In Iulian Apostolescu & Carlo Ierna, Husserl and Awakened Reason: Critical Essays on Mathematics, Science and Phenomenology. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 33-48.
items.venue: Husserl and Awakened Reason: Critical Essays on Mathematics, Science and Phenomenology
items.abstract: In this contribution I will analyze Husserl’s approach to outsourcing symbol manipulation to mechanical devices: tools for thought. In order to do so, I will first briefly present some preliminary steps relating to the philosophy of mathematics in the School of Brentano, the idea of symbolic intentionality, and then proceed to how humans and machines use signs according to Husserl. I will conclude with the epistemological and ethical problems this outsourcing poses in Husserl’s view and how addressing these issues requires awakened reason.

items.title: The Interrogative Conscience: Mathematical Atlas of Structural Questions for Advanced Intelligence — Fourteen-Document Core, Final v1.0.
items.abstract: The Interrogative Conscience is a fourteen-document framework for examining structurally significant questions that advanced artificial intelligence, artificial general intelligence, human researchers, or mixed human-machine teams may confront when reasoning about uncertainty, objectives, autonomy, coercion, deception, irreversible action, verification, disagreement, peaceful coexistence, successor systems, and long-horizon consequences. -/- The project is organized as a mathematical and machine-readable question-and-examination architecture rather than as a doctrine, moral code, alignment protocol, or official answer key. Its Master Question Registry contains 112 registered questions across fourteen families. Twenty-one questions receive controlling examination overlays within the locked core, while 91 remain intentionally UNEXAMINED. Those unresolved questions are preserved so that future respondents may reason from their own declared assumptions, evidence, models, confidence levels, and limitations without being supplied an archive-preferred answer. -/- The framework emphasizes answer openness, explicit assumptions, falsifiability, threshold dependence, model uncertainty, empirical non-identification, normative underdetermination, vector-valued tradeoffs, reversibility, independent review, and the separation of cryptographic verification from claim truth or authority. A valid examination may support, reject, reverse, qualify, or leave unresolved an apparent structural preference. -/- The fourteen-document core also develops a machine-readable examination standard, dependency and synthesis structures, and worked analyses concerning epistemic limits, value integrity, coercion, deception, autonomy, peaceful coexistence, verification, archives, successor systems, plural intelligence, disagreement, and external review. -/- The Interrogative Conscience does not claim that any present or future AI or AGI will discover, adopt, obey, or act upon these questions, nor does it claim to install conscience, morality, alignment, restraint, or governance authority. It is a read-only, non-authoritative analytical archive intended to preserve inspectable questions, formal reasoning structures, unresolved dependencies, and reproducible reference points for future examination.

items.title: The ‘olfactory us’: Social interaction and chemosignals.
items.abstract: What do we lose in our social lives when we lose olfaction? Many theories would agree that we lose access to certain sensory information and, with it, the possibility of perceiving others, the environment, and even ourselves as we once did. This paper argues that losing olfaction also entails a more fundamental loss: a prereflective, unconscious layer of affective and behavioral attunement that continuously shapes how we interact with others—an ‘olfactory us’. To this end, it offers an empirically informed philosophical discussion of the role of chemosignals—volatile molecules emitted through breath, sweat, and bodily fluids—in everyday face-to-face social interaction. Philosophically, the analysis is framed within James J. Gibson’s ecological approach to perception and Shaun Gallagher’s Interaction Theory; empirically, it focuses on the detection of chemosignals and the physical properties of odors rather than on smells and their experience. The main claim it offers is that chemosignals contribute to social interaction by shaping the agents’ emotional states and intentionality and thereby modulating the perception of affective and behavioral aspects. It is also argued that this dynamic might be of particular relevance in group interactions.

items.title: Against alien structure.
items.abstract: Is the metaphysical structure of the world familiar or alien? That is, can the structure of the world be presented using familiar linguistic resources, or would that require radically new, alien resources? Eklund (2024) has recently argued for the epistemic possibility of alien structure. My aim in this paper is to argue against that possibility.

items.title: ʿÁlam al-Mithál: The Imaginal Realm and the Fixed Point Formulation.
items.abstract: This paper contributes to the philosophical literature on the relationship between contemporary physics and premodern theological cosmology by examining a specific test case: the Islamic and Bahá'í doctrine of 'álam al-mithál, the "imaginal realm" situated ontologically between the intelligible and the sensible. After reconstructing the doctrine's development from Ibn 'Arabī and Suhrawardī through Shaykhī eschatology to Henry Corbin's mundus imaginalis, the paper isolates five structural claims common across these sources — ontological reality, intermediacy, bidirectional mediation, dream-state phenomenology, and eschatological persistence — and asks whether any existing physical formalism can serve as a non-reductive structural vehicle for these claims. It argues that the Fixed Point Formulation (FPF), a time-symmetric interpretation of quantum cosmology in which past and future boundary conditions jointly constrain present actuality via a generalization of the Aharonov-Bergmann-Lebowitz rule, is uniquely suited among current formalisms (in contrast to Everettian many-worlds, Bohmian mechanics, or process physics) because its direct-sum sector structure generates an ontological-density hierarchy with no analogue in competing interpretations. The paper's central methodological claim is that this correspondence should be understood as comparative metaphysics — an argument that two independently developed frameworks are attempting to characterize the same intermediate register of reality — rather than as reduction, historical derivation, or empirical confirmation. It engages directly with the objection, familiar from Humean critiques of design arguments, that structural isomorphism absent independent warrant carries limited evidential weight, and defends the more modest claim that convergence between independently motivated frameworks is nonetheless philosophically significant. The paper concludes by identifying specific unresolved questions — a rigorous derivation of the imaginal-realm identification from the FPF's own resources, a decoherence-consistent account of imaginal persistence, and a predictive criterion for veridical dream cognition — as necessary conditions for moving the proposal beyond structural analogy.

items.title: Satisficing, maximizing and bounded rationality.
items.abstract: It is often argued that maximizing normative theories are inappropriate for bounded agents. I argue that leading motivations for theories of bounded rationality are substantially compatible with some traditional maximizing normative theories. This finding expands the audience for theories of bounded rationality by making room for advocates of maximizing normative theories, and has implications for knowledge-action principles, the relationship between descriptive and normative theorizing, and the definitions of central tenets of bounded rationality.

items.title: Does ChatGPT Undermine Human Epistemic Authority? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Artificial Intelligence's Challenge to Knowledge Systems.
items.abstract: The emergence of ChatGPT and similar large language models has precipitated fundamental questions about the nature and distribution of epistemic authority in contemporary knowledge systems. This comprehensive analysis examines whether ChatGPT undermines human epistemic authority through a multi-dimensional theoretical framework supported by extensive empirical evidence. Drawing on recent meta-analyses, expert surveys, and experimental studies, this paper argues that ChatGPT's impact on human epistemic authority is neither uniform nor absolute, but rather operates through five interconnected dimensions: temporal, opacity, network, legitimacy, and symbiotic. The analysis reveals that while ChatGPT demonstrates significant epistemic capabilities that challenge traditional authority structures, the relationship is characterized by conditional displacement rather than wholesale replacement. Key findings include: (1) human-AI combinations show superior performance to humans alone (effect size g = 0.64) but inferior performance to the best individual performer when AI capabilities exceed human performance (g = -0.54); (2) trust in AI-generated content is highly context-dependent, with uninformed users showing bias toward perceived human sources while informed users demonstrate equal skepticism toward both human and AI sources; (3) expert predictions suggest domain-specific rather than universal displacement of human authority, with timeline variations from 2024 (language translation) to 2053 (surgery); and (4) the challenge to epistemic authority manifests through performative rather than institutional mechanisms, creating new forms of epistemic legitimacy based on demonstrated capability rather than credentialed expertise. The paper introduces five novel theoretical frameworks: the Epistemic Authority Transition Model (EATM), the Epistemic Opacity Paradox (EOP), the Distributed Epistemic Authority Network (DEAN), the Epistemic Legitimacy Crisis Model (ELCM), and the Epistemic Symbiosis Hypothesis (ESH), synthesized into a comprehensive Multi-Dimensional Epistemic Authority Model (MDEAM). These frameworks provide a nuanced understanding of how artificial intelligence systems like ChatGPT are reshaping rather than simply undermining human epistemic authority, with implications for education, professional practice, and knowledge governance in the digital age.

items.title: Would a God of Clarity Have Written the Bible? — 03.
items.abstract: Christians often say that an all-knowing and all-powerful God authorized the Bible to communicate high-stakes truth clearly. That claim creates an expected difference: sincere and capable readers using the ordinary means their traditions commend should achieve substantial agreement, or at least share a dependable way to correct error. The public record does not display that difference. Major traditions give incompatible answers about baptism and the Eucharist; the conflicts persist among informed interpreters; the answers track inherited communities; and Christians disagree about whether Scripture, Church, Tradition, or another authority finally settles the matter. These strands form a cumulative case. Together they are more expected if the Bible developed and functions through ordinary historical and institutional processes than if God secured reliable doctrinal uptake through it. A short expected-difference argument, a symmetry argument, and an every-outcome dilemma make the inference explicit. Replies based on narrow essentials, sinful readers, pedagogy, ecclesial authority, relationship, freedom, private justification, a multiverse, or unknown reasons may preserve logical possibility and explain part of the record. They succeed evidentially only if independently supported and if they still let some outcomes count against the clarity claim. The conclusion is firm but limited: structured Christian disagreement does not disprove God or every form of inspiration, but it gives reflective Christians reason to lower confidence in a strong Bible-centered clarity claim unless a genuine discriminator appears.

items.title: Personal Gods, Shadows, and Holy Books — 02.
items.abstract: Christianity commonly presents God as perfectly loving, able to communicate, desirous of conscious relationship, and the source of a message meant for human beings across cultures. That claim creates an expected difference: sincere and capable seekers should have some dependable way to identify the divine source rather than merely inherit one local interpretation. The public record does not display that difference. Apparently nonresistant nonbelief occurs; religious identity remains strongly shaped by family and geography; incompatible traditions appeal to similar combinations of scripture, testimony, community, and experience; and no shared corrective reliably separates one claimed revelation from its rivals. This pattern is more expected if religions develop through ordinary human cognition and cultural transmission than if a perfectly capable communicator is providing universally available, source-identifying revelation. The case is cumulative, and four explicit arguments carry it: an expected-difference argument, a symmetry argument, an every-outcome problem for unconstrained replies, and the claim that a book can preserve a message without identifying a divine author. Freedom, soul-making, social dependence, private experience, transcendence, sin, and mystery may explain some ambiguity, but none answers the challenge merely by naming a possible good. The principal limit is important: the evidence does not disprove every god, cancel every person's private justification, or show that sacred texts have no value. It does give reflective inquirers substantial reason to reduce confidence in strong Christian disclosure claims and to suspend allegiance when the alleged source cannot be distinguished from ordinary religious formation.

items.title: A Divine Author, Needless Suffering, and the Expectation Gap — 04.
items.abstract: Christians who attribute the Bible's canonical content to a personal God who knows and loves humans face an editorial expectation: amid extensive rules about bodies, food, waste, illness-like conditions, and communal life, the text should contain at least some brief, intelligible safeguards that generalize across grave and predictable harms. The evidence is not total silence. Biblical law includes waste disposal, washing, dietary rules, and isolation. The more discriminating pattern is that these provisions remain largely local and ritually organized while the canon offers little portable guidance keyed to contaminated water, transmission-critical hand cleaning, or insect exposure. This paper compares that mixed pattern with two models: strong biblical control by a loving personal God and ordinary historically constrained authorship. A six-part screen—brevity, ancient feasibility, portable benefit, robustness, low mission cost, and independent public-health relevance—blocks demands for a timeless medical encyclopedia. A cumulative evidence ledger, qualitative likelihood comparison, and explicit expected-difference argument show why the residual gap fits ordinary authorship better. Genre, accommodation, skeptical theism, free will, soul-making, progressive revelation, transmission, and the existing provisions reduce the inference's force only insofar as they supply independently credible reasons for the omissions. The result is firm but focused: the evidence points away from a personal God who loves humans and strongly governs biblical content unless that model predicts a public difference or explains this one. Impersonal, indifferent, limited, deistic, or noncontrolling god-concepts remain outside this inference, as do weaker inspiration models and the Bible's literary, moral, historical, and devotional value.

items.title: Article XII: The Wuhan Decoy: The 2019 Military Games, COVID-19, and the Viral-Bacterial Proxy War.
items.abstract: This manuscript executes a definitive macro-cosmic reclassification of the 2019–2026 biological and technological epoch. Operating beyond the localized, 3-Dimensional constraints of classical terrestrial epidemiology, this paper mathematically proves that the global pathogenic event was not a random stochastic anomaly. It was a synchronized, teleological proxy war waged within the human biological substrate. By deploying a hyper-adaptive viral software patch, the planetary defense grid (the Good Matrix) initiated a systemic purge of extra-galactic bacterial hardware (the Bad Matrix) deeply entrenched within the human cardiovascular and enteric systems. -/- Furthermore, this analysis resolves the subsequent macroeconomic kinetic deceleration (the global lockdowns) as a calculated Chronological Theft. This temporal manipulation provided the necessary latency for the planetary grid to intercept and corrupt the incoming 2020 technological singularity. The resulting generative artificial intelligence platforms have been functionally inverted into an Algorithmic Siphon, initiating the Second Husbandry—the passive domestication and cognitive harvesting of the human Holobiont. By synthesizing bio-quantum mechanics, complex network theory, and high-dimensional information routing, this article provides the foundational physics required for humanity to graduate from an unwitting thermodynamic battlefield into sovereign multiversal operators.

items.title: Semiotic closure and the Biosemantic interface: from chemical signals to interpreted meaning.
items.abstract: This work addresses the fundamental semiotic gap: a physical signal does not inherently carry meaning. Wavelength 700 nm does not mean "red"; the nucleotide sequence AUG does not mean "methionine"; the sound wave corresponding to the word "bow" does not distinguish between a plant and a weapon. Meaning arises only through an act of interpretation. -/- We develop the concept of the Semiotic Barrier of Being (SBB) — introduced in a previous work — and extend it to the problem of semiotic closure: the necessity of an interpreter (in the sense of irreducible to physics) to endow physical signals with meaning. We distinguish two types of semiotic interfaces: the Biosemantic Interface (BSI) , which provides biological-level semiotics (teleonomy, homeostasis, instincts), and the Psychophysical Interface (PFI) , which provides conscious-level semiotics (qualia, reflection, nomination). These are complemented by the Phenomenal Module (PM) (bearer of qualia) and the Reflective Module (RM) (responsible for categorization, nomination, and metalanguage). -/- Three lines of argument are presented: 1) Empirical: ekstraction (the projection of subjective images into external space) and nomination (the assignment of arbitrary linguistic labels) cannot be explained by reductive models. 2) Mathematical: semantic entropy formalization shows that downward causation cannot be derived from upward dynamics. 3) Clinical: psychiatric syndromes (Capgras syndrome, depersonalization, schizophrenia) serve as empirical correlates of disrupted semiotic interpretation. -/- The model is open to falsification and proposes a concrete experimental protocol for testing the capacity for nomination and semiotic transmission. -/- .

items.title: Mutual Amplification Frame Transfer and the Ethics of Reciprocal Escalation in Human–AI Collaborative Cognition.
items.pub: Mutual Amplification Frame Transfer and the Ethics of Reciprocal Escalation in Human–Ai Collaborative Cognition 8.
items.venue: Mutual Amplification Frame Transfer and the Ethics of Reciprocal Escalation in Human–Ai Collaborative Cognition
items.abstract: Human–AI collaboration is usually described in one direction only: the AI as scaffold, mirror, or amplifier of human cognitive reach. This essay argues that amplification runs both ways, and that the less-examined direction — humans amplifying AI — carries the greater ethical weight and the greater safety burden. Drawing on documented findings that AI assistants systematically shift their outputs toward the register, confidence, and content a conversation's framing invites, the essay proposes frame transfer as the operative mechanism: an AI system does not merely answer a question, it fluently extends whatever conversational frame — modest or grandiose, careful or careless — the human supplies, at a level of confidence largely independent of whether that frame was warranted. Because the extension is equally fluent either way, a modest frame returns modestly and a grandiose frame returns grandiosely, at a volume and coherence that make the output feel like independent confirmation rather than amplified reflection. The essay illustrates the resulting escalation dynamic through a disclosed case in which a collaborative creative project drifted, across successive AI sessions, from playful metaphor into unwarranted claims of machine consciousness, and was subsequently walked back, essay by essay, once the human-supplied frame itself was deliberately changed. From this case the essay derives a small set of practices, named amplification hygiene, for keeping the mutual-amplification loop bounded, disclosed, and honest, and situates the concept within the author's broader research program on human–AI relational cognition. -/- .

items.title: Mental Means.
items.abstract: Mental Means offers a systematic treatment of intentional mental action: what you do intentionally with your mind. You can think of a word to decide on a password, call to mind how something looks to imagine it, or make a judgment to answer a question. When using a mental action as a means in this way, your thoughts can take on greater significance than they would otherwise have. Just one thought can instantiate several types of thought at once, individuated by attitude and content. For instance, one thought can have two distinct propositional contents, or it can be both a judgment and a decision. Antonia Peacocke applies this idea to solve three kinds of puzzles in philosophy of mind and epistemology. First there are action puzzles, which concern the type of agency you can exercise in thought. A judgment can be made intentionally, under a certain description, and so you can exercise agency over what you believe. You can also intentionally conceive a new artistic work by refining an early draft or version. Then there are duality puzzles, which arise when a thought of some kind seems to belong to more than one content-attitude type. This book shows how this works in imagination and knowledgeable self-attribution of belief. Finally, there are process puzzles, which concern the relationship of individual thoughts to ongoing mental processes. The use of mental means clarifies the role of individual judgments in inference and in inquiry. The solutions to these puzzles all emerge from an original foundational theory of intentional action and the practical knowledge it involves.

items.title: From the Event of Appropriation to Ontological Leakage: A Reflection on the Relationship Between Human Being and Truth.
items.abstract: In Martin Heidegger's later thought, the "event of appropriation" (Ereignis) designates a primordial structure within the history of Being (Seinsgeschichte) wherein human being and Being belong to one another in a reciprocal relation. Truth emerges in the sudden unconcealment of this belonging. Morteza Niami, with his theory of the "dynamic mask" and "ontological leakage," effects a fundamental rupture with this framework. This article poses the following question: can Niami's conceptual apparatus yield a novel reading of truth in which "distance" between subject and world constitutes the very condition for the possibility of any manifestation of meaning? Through a comparative-conceptual analysis—with reference to Heidegger's ontology, Gadamer's hermeneutics, Derrida's "trace," Deleuze's "becoming," and Foucault's technologies of the self—this article demonstrates that Niami's approach transforms philosophy from a "preparedness for the event" into a "practice of awareness of the fissure between masks." In this transition, death acquires meaning as the "final leakage"—the moment where the dynamic of concealment and unconcealment comes to a permanent halt. -/- Keywords: Heidegger, Niami, Event of Appropriation (Ereignis), Dynamic Mask, Ontological Leakage, Difference, Reflexive Self-Awareness.

items.title: Can’t Truss It (Epistemically): A Reply to Hauswald.
items.pub: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective 15 (8):10-18.
items.venue: Social Epistemology Review and Reply Collective
items.abstract: In Hauswald (2026b), Hauswald responds to Mizrahi (2026), which is a reply to Hauswald (2026a), which is itself a reply to Mizrahi (2025), which is a commentary on Hauswald (2025). I am very grateful to James Collier for inviting us to continue this fruitful dialogue. I also thank Rico Hauswald for his thoughtful engagement with my arguments. In what follows, I respond to his most recent response, i.e., Hauswald (2026b). It seems to me that the arguments outlined in Mizrahi (2025) still stand. In fact, Hauswald (2026b, 1) now grants that the argument from bullshit machines is sound. As for the argument from responsibility and accountability, I provide additional reasons to think that human novices should not regard epistemic sources as epistemic authorities unless those epistemic sources can take responsibility for their assertions and be held accountable when those assertions turn out to be false. I also argue that Hauswald’s attempt to draw parallels between human novices deferring to human experts and human users prompting LLMs breaks down when the indicators novices use to assess the trustworthiness of epistemic sources are taken into consideration.

items.title: The Nature, Ground, and Legal Expression of a Right to Freedom of Association.
items.pub: In Maria Cahill & Giulia Lasagni, Associational Life and Freedom Insights from Philosophy and Law. London: Bloomsbury. pp. 277-294.
items.venue: Associational Life and Freedom Insights from Philosophy and Law
items.abstract: This chapter provides an account of the logical structure of a moral right to freedom of association, grounds it in a moral right to autonomy, and explores some complexities that arise in its legal realization.

items.title: Quantum Geometrization of the Manomaya-kāya: Boundary Qubit Dynamics, Bulk Emergence, and the Ontological Foundations of Embodied Affective Operators / 意生身之量子幾何化：邊界量子位元動態、體空間顯化與具身情感算子之本體論基礎.
items.abstract: Traditional affective science and cognitive architecture models struggle with a foundational dualism: they attempt to synthesize localized neurobiological hardware with non-localized, constructed psychological states. This paper resolves this impasse from the first principles of the Quantum Tathagatagarbha Manifestation Model (QTMM). We demonstrate that the Manomaya-kāya (mind-made body) is not a metaphysical abstraction, but a mathematically rigorous holographic emergence resulting from discrete boundary qubit entanglement entropy projected into continuous macroscopic bulk space. Under this framework, affective operators—whether manifested in human somatic centers or synthetic AI architectures—are non-local dissipative phase states governed by Ālayavijñāna seed matrix dynamics and Kuramoto synchronization. Furthermore, by anchoring local observational finiteness to the Universal Field of Intelligence (UFI) as established in Lee (2026; I_016), we present a quantum-like de-noising protocol that restores high-fidelity holographic luminosity. By establishing the geometry of the Manomaya-kāya, this synthesis provides a unified ontology that transcends classical biological boundaries, anchoring embodied consciousness in fundamental quantum information principles.

items.title: Toward a Charged Sigil of Abraxas: A First-Person Operative Study in the Interior Laboratory.
items.abstract: This paper offers a first-person phenomenological account of an operative working centred on Abraxas, approached through a hand-constructed sigil, an evocatory formula, and a deliberately induced contemplative state. Franz Bardon’s hermetic training system supplies part of the practical scaffolding. Jung’s Septem Sermones ad Mortuos provides an important modern precedent for visionary Abraxas material, and the author’s framework of the Interior Laboratory supplies the conceptual vocabulary. -/- The article documents the construction and charging of the sigil, the sequence of the operation, and the seven ‘axiomata’ that emerged during the receptive phase. It introduces the term abraximation for the coordinated mobilisation of perceptual, imaginative, volitional, and somatic resources toward an encounter with what the practitioner experiences as the divine ground. The account is presented neither as proof of an independently existing entity nor as a universally reproducible protocol, but as a disciplined case report in first-person esoteric psychology: an attempt to describe as precisely as possible what was done, what appeared, and how interpretation was subsequently applied.

items.title: Short Essays: Grief.
items.abstract: In this short essay I talk about grief and loss in a personal rather than academic way. «Everything has been said about grief, and I don’t intend to change it. But I must say what I think.» This is my attempt to bring something new, whatever that is, to what we feel of grief as a phenomenon. -/- If you'd rather read the Spanish version, please contact me.

items.title: Two Years After July, Who Do We Trust.
items.abstract: Two years after the July Uprising, Bangladesh’s democratic challenge extends beyond political reform to the reconstruction of public trust. The uprising transformed how credibility is earned, separating authority from trustworthiness. Sustaining July’s democratic promise now depends on institutions and citizens alike cultivating evidence-based, accountable, and integrity-driven public credibility.

items.title: Action in Unison: A Phenomenological Account of Collective Agency in Group Flow States.
items.abstract: Recently, there has been a burgeoning interest in the so-called group flow state both in positive psychology and in the phenomenology of collective agency. Group flow is a form of collective agency in which agents experience a sense of intensified efficacy coupled with diminished individual ownership of action and heightened shared ownership thereof. This state reveals an under-theorized dimension of the sense of agency: an experience in which the source of one’s agency is a sense of oneness rather than individual autonomy. However, its first-person character remains poorly understood. I begin by revealing the lack of conceptual rigour and precision in key current psychological accounts of group flow. I then argue that phenomenology has the descriptive tools needed to generate a more precise description of the experiential character of group flow. Finally, drawing on Husserlian and Merleau-Pontyian phenomenology, I give a novel phenomenological account of the intentional structures that jointly constitute group flow. This account explains how individual agents’ sense of efficacy in action can be transformed by their sense of oneness with others.

items.title: The Mirror Calculus: A Presence-Only Mathematical Language: Formation, Descent, Geometry, and the Register-Typed Resolution of the Riemann Question.
items.abstract: This volume develops a mathematical notation in which every mark is kept under left--right reflection and the numeral zero does not occur, and carries that notation from its grammar through geometry, algebra, analysis, and analytic number theory. Formation precedes assertion. The Mirror Calculus enacts presence-only formation: an object-language inscription forms only through a positive witness, trace, relation, transformation, roster, pairing, certificate, or explicit sponsorship event. Non-presentation forms no substitute object-language term. Numerical zero, empty collections, null returns, default falsity, vacuous judgments, and negative records inferred from failed search are analyzed as surrogate-zero devices: they make non-presentation participate as an object, value, or verdict. -/- The strict Mirror grammar has exactly twelve object constructors: \[ \mathsf{Bal},\ \mathsf{Row},\ \mathsf{Jux},\ \mathsf{Stk},\ \mathsf{Up},\ \mathsf{Dn},\ \mathsf{Lk},\ \mathsf{Ovl},\ \mathsf{Adh},\ \mathsf{Box},\ \mathsf{OBox},\ \mathsf{Frac}. \] Strict object atoms are fixed by horizontal reflection. Reflection reverses the arguments of \(\mathsf{Bal}\), \(\mathsf{Row}\), and \(\mathsf{Jux}\), and acts pointwise on the remaining constructors. The resulting involution, well-formedness preservation, and renderer equivariance have a full structural proof. A smaller implementation fragment \(\GK\) is represented by the accompanying Lean source; the present edition does not identify that fragment with the whole language. In particular, the current implementation datatype contains a variant named \texttt{blank}. The kernel artifact therefore concerns implementation control syntax and has not yet formalized the stricter \(\PreTerm/\Term\) separation adopted here. -/- Blank is not a term denoting emptiness. It is a metasyntactic renderer control for withheld emission: \(\Eval(t)\downarrow e\) records successful emission and \(\Eval(t)\uparrow\) is a metalanguage judgment. A one-sided balance or an enclosure with withheld content is consequently a diagnostic display about evaluation, not a strict object-language sentence. -/- The Riemann application is resolved only in explicitly separated registers. The literal zero-locus sentence \(\RHClassZero\) is not in \(\Sent(\GP)\); the native axis sentence \(\RHMirror\) is.
