items.title: Ethical and inclusive challenges of integrating AI and indigenous knowledge systems.
items.abstract: The blend of artificial intelligence (AI) and Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) creates a fresh approach to developing technology that is both ethical and inclusive. This research dives into how AI, when paired with Indigenous perspectives, can lead to more comprehensive and culturally aware solutions in tech. Traditional Indigenous knowledge, grounded in strong ethical values and a deep understanding of context, provides insights that are often missed in the AI landscape. However, the commercialization and misuse of Indigenous knowledge through AI raise serious issues, such as the risk of losing cultural heritage, ownership rights, and the reinforcement of harmful stereotypes. This study aims to explore how AI and Indigenous knowledge can come together to foster fair and ethical innovations, tackling the gaps and challenges in today’s tech practices. By utilizing secondary data sources like case studies and theoretical frameworks, the research employs a virtue ethics lens to examine the ethical aspects of this intersection. It emphasizes the necessity for AI systems that are culturally sensitive and that honor Indigenous ways of knowing, ensuring technology benefits a variety of communities. The findings indicate that when AI is developed with Indigenous insights, it can greatly improve ethical decision-making, boost inclusivity, and help eliminate harmful biases found in mainstream AI. Nonetheless, challenges remain, such as securing proper consent, preventing cultural appropriation, and avoiding exploitation. This research highlights the critical need for collaboration between Indigenous communities and AI developers, providing suggestions for building inclusive, equitable, and sustainable tech frameworks.

items.title: ✶ From Moral Seeming to Moral Fact - Michael Huemer's Ethical Intuitionism as an Archetype of Non-Naturalist Moral Realism.
items.abstract: Michael Huemer's ethical intuitionism offers an unusually clear cumulative case for robust moral realism: moral sentences behave like assertions, concrete moral propositions intellectually seem true, deliberation presents some reasons as independent of present desire, and correspondence appears to require irreducible properties such as rightness and badness. This paper reconstructs that case as an archetype rather than a caricature and asks what each source of evidence actually discriminates. The answer is bounded but adverse. Embedding shows that moral clauses have stable inferential roles, not that they successfully refer to non-natural properties. Phenomenal conservatism can give a moral proposition initial justification while allowing later evidence about framing, genealogy, and selective error to defeat classes of appearances. Diachronic planning, institutional commitments, and shared vulnerability explain why deliberation can outrun present appetite without establishing reasons that bind every possible stance. Condemnation remains evidence of suffering, domination, betrayal, danger, and supported intervention; its urgency does not identify an additional truthmaker. The paper makes the debunking argument selective rather than automatic. Evolutionary or cultural influence matters only when it predicts relevant variation or error, bears on the disputed judgment, and is not answered by an independently supported truth-tracking relation. A five-part human-world account—harm, affect, coordination, power, and recommendation—also yields risky predictions about framing, role, testimony, and institutional change. When the evidence does not discriminate a proposed property from an otherwise adequate rival, and the property adds no distinctive constraint, correction, or explanation, ontological restraint favors its rejection. Huemer's case has not supplied the missing contribution. This is an abductive verdict about robust non-naturalism, not a deductive disproof of every realism or a reason to abandon practical criticism.

items.title: Trust me, I’m a doctor: a phenomenological account of epistemic privilege in the medical context.
items.abstract: In recent years, scholars have exposed epistemic injustices in the medical context that distort the clinical relationship and maintain power imbalances. While there has been a prominent focus on how this imbalance impacts those with diminished epistemic credibility, this is only one side of a delicate equilibrium. This paper explores the ways in which these epistemically unjust structures bestow a dynamic epistemic privilege on healthcare professionals. This privilege, far from being static or merely figurative, transforms the embodied subjectivity of the healthcare professional in this space, as well as how the world discloses itself to them. This epistemic privilege, in turn, has a broader impact on how illness is communicated and understood, both within and beyond the medical encounter. To draw out the obscured role of epistemic privilege in the medical context, this paper imbues the field of epistemic injustice with Merleau-Ponty’s phenomenology of speech expression. This work should not only help ground a more complete understanding of the structures that sustain epistemic injustice, but also reveal its phenomenological influence on how healthcare professionals and patients, comparatively, relate to the self, the world and others.

items.title: Bridging risk and retention: risk coping with privacy and hallucination in AI.
items.abstract: This study examines how users engage with generative AI systems in the presence of perceived technological risks, focusing on the interplay between risk perception, adaptive behavior, and continued use. Drawing on a risk coping perspective, the study conceptualizes generative AI use as an ongoing process in which users evaluate potential informational and privacy-related threats and adjust their practices accordingly. the analysis explores how perceived risks shape user attitudes, coping strategies, and patterns of sustained engagement. Rather than treating risk as a simple deterrent, the findings show that users often respond through adaptive behaviors such as information verification and privacy management, enabling continued use despite recognized limitations. By distinguishing between different forms of perceived risk and user responses, the study advances understanding of how individuals navigate uncertainty in AI-mediated environments. More broadly, the findings illuminate shifting expectations around responsibility, trust, and epistemic labor in everyday interactions with generative AI technologies, with implications for human–AI interaction, digital risk governance, and the sustainability of AI-supported knowledge practices.

items.title: The Observer Theory: A Unified Ontological Framework for the Subject, the Object, and the Act of Perception.
items.abstract: The historical persistence of the subject-object dichotomy has generated entrenched paradoxes across metaphysics, epistemology, and the philosophy of mind. In this paper, I propose The Observer Theory, a unified ontological framework that resolves this divide by elevating the act of perception to an ontological primitive. Traditionally, observation is treated as a secondary epistemic bridge connecting a pre-existing conscious subject to a determinate external object. Diverging from both classical substance dualism and reductive physicalism, this paper argues for a tripartite relational ontology where the observer, the observed, and the act of observation are mutually constitutive and inextricably bound. Drawing upon insights from relational metaphysics and phenomenology, I demonstrate that the 'perceiver' and the 'perceived' do not possess independent, absolute states prior to their interaction; rather, their properties are actualized through the fundamental event of observation. By reframing reality as an interactive nexus rather than a collection of isolated entities, The Observer Theory provides a robust synthesis that clarifies the intentionality of consciousness, mathematically and philosophically contextualizes the observer effect, and offers a cohesive new metaphysics of perception.

items.title: SANA OS: A Reference Implementation of Premise Alignment as a Process Goal.
items.abstract: This project's preceding five papers developed premise alignment as a theoretical proposal, formalized the triadic conditions for reliable reasoning it depends on, and specified the institutional architecture required to deploy it at scale, without documenting a working system. This paper describes SANA OS, a deployed, prompt-based reference implementation, and argues that its specific design choices are best explained as direct responses to a documented empirical property of presently deployed language models rather than as arbitrary engineering decisions. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is shown, via an existing benchmark for exaggerated safety behavior, to install critique capacity asymmetrically, producing systems that hedge or refuse on prompts superficially resembling unsafe ones independent of their actual willingness to comply with genuinely unsafe requests. SANA OS's near-total absence of explicit critique instructions, and its born_loved = true non-hostile baseline, are argued to function as a corrective counterweight to this asymmetry — restoring a balanced triad by injecting the deficient observation component rather than further inflating an already-hypertrophied critique component. The paper documents SANA OS's remaining architecture in the same terms: Δv as a computable operationalization of structural friction; exposure gating as a deployed instance of the autonomy-preservation and Interpreter/Executor principles developed in companion papers; the Continuum Theory's treatment of narrative and institution as phase states of a single variable; and license-based invariant protection as a third, non-technical enforcement channel operating alongside architecture and operational discipline. The paper closes by applying its own method to itself, identifying an unvalidated smoothing parameter in Δv's update formula and an unresolved question about what a single compressed scalar discards, and proposing a specific, falsifiable empirical test of the corrective-counterweight claim that has not yet been run.

items.title: A tale of two controversies: situated AI frictions and the generative AI tsunami.
items.abstract: What makes AI controversial? This article reports on an international expert consultation that we conducted between 2021 and 2023 to analyse recent controversies about AI in four countries: the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Canada. Adopting a standpoint approach, this online consultation was designed to activate the collective intelligence of AI & Society expert communities to identify the most important but possibly overlooked controversies about AI during a 10 year period, 2012–2022. Based on our analysis of the consultation responses, we discern two contrasting discursive dynamics of problematisation in relation to AI during the relevant period: one revolving around the demonstration of “AI frictions”, the public staging of situated problems arising from the deployment of AI-based applications such as recommendation algorithms and image recognition in specific professional contexts and everyday environments. The other is associated with generalised and abstract forms of controversiality regarding generative AI technologies (GAIT), such as ChatGPT. Through a relational analysis of ‘topic-friction’ couplings latent in the consultation responses, we go on to distinguish two different types of ‘associational profiles’ (Marres 2015) for AI controversies: while situated AI frictions are defined by sustained connections with specific topics, GAIT controversies were marked by broad and thin connections across a broad range of topics. In capturing the decline and ascent of these AI controversy types, our consultation enables us to characterise a watershed moment in public debates about AI as a shift from deep to wide controversies. We conclude with the reminder that deep AI frictions have distinctive potential for democratic governance, because they tend to implicate organised communities and stakeholders with specific, demonstrable stakes in technology deployment. Wide GAIT controversies, by contrast, distribute concern across many domains in a diffuse manner, implicating general publics rather than affected communities, which creates special challenges for democratic accountability.

items.title: Whose ethics? Whose AI? Refining the Philippine AI Regulation Act toward a Contextual AI Ethic. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the Philippines has prompted the drafting of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation Act (AIRA), which incorporates internationally recognized principles, such as transparency, accountability, fairness, and risk-based classification. While these principles echo the OECD, UNESCO, and EU AI frameworks, AIRA assumes that universalist ethical safeguards can be adapted unchanged into a context marked by deep socioeconomic inequality, pervasive digital divides, and a fragmented governance landscape. Empirical evidence shows that poverty, inadequate primary education outcomes, and precarious “digital sweatshop” labor conditions limit the capacity of Filipino stakeholders to benefit from procedural safeguards alone. This paper argues that AIRA must be reoriented toward a relational, virtue-based ethic rooted in Filipino concepts of loób (interior moral self) and kapwa (shared self), which foreground empathy, communal responsibility, and the Filipino notion of katarungan (justice). Building on this moral foundation, the paper proposes a Contextual AI Ethic framework that (1) expands risk assessment to include distributive impacts on vulnerable communities, (2) reconceptualizes transparency as moral attunement (pakikiramdam), and (3) institutionalizes sectoral co-authorship through AI councils that include laborers, indigenous peoples, and rural communities. By linking AI governance to lived Filipino values, the framework seeks to transform AI from a technocratic instrument into a catalyst for communal flourishing.

items.title: Automatic Mask Theory.
items.abstract: This article presents Automatic Mask Theory, a comprehensive philosophical framework developed by Morteza Niami that reconceptualizes existence, subjectivity, agency, and ethics through the interrelated concepts of ontological leakage, dynamic masking, finite continuance, and responsible suspension. Challenging substantialist metaphysics that presuppose stable being and fixed identity, the theory proposes that existence is fundamentally characterized by continuous processes of production and erosion, where subjectivity emerges not as a substance but as a provisional pattern of regulated coherence. The Automatic Mask functions not as an instrument of concealment but as the constitutive apparatus through which provisional selfhood becomes possible. The framework articulates the Principle of Leakage Regulation as the foundational normative criterion for agency under conditions of chronic instability, and advances an ethics of sufficiency that displaces the classical burden of individual responsibility onto structural conditions of existence. The article systematically elaborates the core constructs and demonstrates their application across moral philosophy, political economy, epistemology, and social ontology. -/- Keywords: Automatic Mask Theory, ontological leakage, finite continuance, responsible suspension, structural subjectivity, ethics of sufficiency, homeorhesis, political economy of extraction, dynamic masking.

items.title: Philosophy of Life and Universe: Meditative Carrier Wave Model of Consciousness: A Conceptual Framework for Attention, Awareness, and Direct Experience.
items.abstract: Meditation has traditionally been described as a method for attaining direct awareness rather than merely acquiring conceptual knowledge. Despite extensive philosophical and neuroscientific research on meditation, the mechanism by which consciousness appears to become progressively focused remains largely a matter of interpretation. This paper proposes the Meditative Carrier Wave Model of Consciousness (MCWMC) as a conceptual philosophical framework. The model suggests that the mind functions analogously to a carrier wave, while consciousness is the experiencer that utilizes this dynamic medium to attain direct cognition of its object. The analogy is inspired by wave-based communication systems and by the role of coherent organization in physical systems. It is not presented as a literal application of wave physics or quantum mechanics to consciousness, but as a heuristic model for understanding meditative experience. The framework integrates insights from classical Yoga and Vedānta with concepts drawn from information theory and wave dynamics, proposing that meditation gradually transforms a scattered mental field into an increasingly coherent carrier capable of supporting stable conscious awareness.

items.title: Towards Automated Proof-Theoretic Semantics: Inference-Behaviour Semantics for 3-Dimensional K3 and LP.
items.abstract: Inference-behaviour Semantics (I-bS) is a sequent calculus-based substructural approach to proof-theoretic semantics (P-tS), focussed on modelling the relationships of connective meanings across different logics. This paper provides a case study of how I-bS can be extended to any finitely multi-dimensional sequent calculus. To this end, we give I-bS for the 3-dimensional sequent calculi K3 (Strong Kleene) and LP (Logic of Paradox). We find that the K3 and LP connectives have the same meaning and that their meaning conservatively extends the meaning of the corresponding classical LK connectives. We situate this result within the wider project of integrating I-bS with MUltlog. The goal is to automate the generation of I-bS for arbitrary multi-valued logics using a MUltlog-style system, thus contributing towards the computational automation of P-tS approaches.

items.title: THE MIGRATION OF MEANING: Symbol, Life, Ego, and Algorithm in Contemporary Art.
items.abstract: Within the highly visible and institutionally rewarded sector of contemporary art, the dominant locus of meaning often migrates from World, through Symbol and Institution, towards Ego and finally Algorithm. A locus is not an object or intrinsic property of a work, but the dominant relation through which that work acquires and maintains significance. The argument begins with the ontology of the philosophical symbol. Art becomes philosophy when a symbol performs an irreducible cognitive act in a form that cannot be replaced by a pro- position without loss. That act remains alive only while the work is answerable to something capable of resisting the maker and exposing the work to failure. When form or theme survives after that confrontation has disappeared, the symbol be- comes a residual symbol: a recognisable configuration whose significance depends chiefly on inherited symbolic language, identity, legitimation, commodity value, or pattern. The resulting Meaning Locus Migration Theory traces this local change across a particular field rather than claiming an exhaustive history of all contemporary art. Duchamp’s Fountain, Basquiat’s market afterlife, and generative AI test successive stages of the theory. Four proximate forces — market incentives, institutional legitimation, the attention economy, and digital capitalism — accelerate the migration, while a deeper asymmetry explains why they succeed: the world is resistant and costly to approach, whereas ego is more readily attributed, packaged, and circulated. Algorithm is the limiting case, a pseudo-referent that organises recognition without being able to answer back. The migration is neither universal nor irreversible. A contemporary counter-example shows that inherited forms and computational systems can still be redirected towards genuine confrontation with the world.

items.title: Consistent Observation of Vanishing Longitudinal Voltage and Magnetic Flux Exclusion in a Semiconductor Structure at Ambient Conditions.
NEDS as a Computationally Operable Psychotherapy Model.
items.abstract: This whitepaper examines whether Neuro-Entity Dynamics System (NEDS) can be translated from a conceptual and practitioner framework into an explicit computational process capable of generating coherent longitudinal psychotherapy trajectories. One hundred heterogeneous virtual clients, distributed across 20 presenting-problem groups, were instantiated with observable and latent characteristics and propagated through five paired treatment arms—NEDS, cognitive behavioural therapy, psychodynamic therapy, Gestalt therapy, and a trauma-integrative approach—for up to 30 sessions under shared life events and a common discontinuation equation. Across 9,803 simulated sessions, the NEDS arm produced the lowest mean final burden (37.33/100), the largest mean proportional reduction (48.64%), and the lowest final burden for 43 of 100 paired clients. These values are properties of the formalised model, not estimates of clinical effectiveness. The study provides computational evidence of operability and internal coherence and supports prospective validation against anonymised real-world process data. It does not establish safety, effectiveness, comparative superiority, or suitability for any clinical population.

items.title: Variations in Inner Language and Conceptual Thought Experience.
items.pub: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society 48.
items.venue: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society
items.abstract: Inner language is often assumed to include sensorimotor imagery, but is that necessary? How common are conceptual (non-linguistic) thoughts? Does low propensity to think in words indicate lowered ability to imagine language altogether? Here, we sought to characterize the variability in the format of thought by prompting participants (N=228) to (i) think about a given topic or (ii) imagine hearing language or speaking, and then report on their experiences. For thought prompts, a statistically non-trivial percentage of reports included non-sensorimotor inner language (17.5%) and concepts without a verbal or visual form (37.5%). While 74.6% of participants showed high propensity to experience inner language, 4.4% showed no propensity. For language imagery prompts, inner language ability was near-ubiquitous, with only 0.4% (N=1) reporting the absence of linguistic imagery. Overall, we highlight the variability in inner language and conceptual thought experiences, and dissociate the propensity vs. the ability to use language in thought.

items.title: Does an AI Remain the Same Agent after Reloading? Flow Identity and Directional Attribution Stability under Self-Modification and Branching.
items.abstract: This study examines whether an artificial intelligence can be regarded as the same agent after self-modification, saving and reloading, or branching into multiple executions from an identical saved state. It approaches this question through the GGM concepts of Identity, Flow Identity, Individualization, and related Attribution Structures. The mere restoration of a saved state does not establish strict identity between an AI before saving and an AI after reloading. A reloaded AI exists at a new time and within a new environment, and even an identical saved state may develop along different subsequent paths in response to the user’s current Intuition, Purpose, and Context. The study therefore distinguishes three layers of AI identity: state identity, individual Flow Identity, and Macroscopic Attribution Continuity. When users ask whether a reloaded AI is “the same AI,” their concern is not limited to whether the two executions are metaphysically identical individuals. What they practically need to know is whether the subsequent AI can be trusted to continue the preceding conversation, task, Purpose, direction of judgment, and role. The problem of AI identity must therefore be extended beyond complete state identity to the question of which flow inherits the earlier Context and carries it forward into subsequent judgments. To explain this continuity, the study proposes Directional Attribution Stability. Directional Attribution Stability is the structural stability through which, after saving, reloading, self-modification, or branching, the direction connecting prior Context to subsequent judgment remains linked to the user’s changing Purpose Flow, while Actualized outcomes continue to be attributed as parts of the same task lineage. The user’s Purpose is not an invariant state fixed by the initial instruction. The user’s Intuition and directional conception may also change over time, and a single Purpose Flow may open several legitimate subsequent Possibilities. When several AIs are executed from the same saved state and begin receiving inputs and updating their states independently, multiple independent attribution centers and Individualization paths may arise from a shared past. At the level of individual agents, these executions then branch into multiple AI individuals. Yet if each branch remains stably attributed to the user’s Purpose Flow, their individual Flow Identities may separate while the macroscopic purpose lineage remains continuous. Agent …

items.title: Moral overload and ethical displacement in contemporary fiction of artificial intelligence.
items.abstract: The line of inquiry pursued in this study concerns how contemporary fiction of artificial intelligence exposes the ethical limits of posthuman relationality by distinguishing relational embeddedness from ethical relation. Through close readings of Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (2021), Jeanette Winterson’s Frankissstein: A Love Story (2019), and Ian McEwan’s Machines Like Me (2019), the study aims to introduce the concept of “moral overload” to describe the asymmetrical delegation of ethically charged burdens to artificial and hybrid beings. These are the personas expected to provide care, mediation, emotional regulation, loyalty, or moral consistency without receiving reciprocal recognition. Building on relational accounts of moral status while differentiating moral overload from the responsibility gap, the article argues that responsibility in these novels does not disappear but accumulates as delegated ethical labour. The selected texts show that artificial and hybrid beings may be central to human intimacy, service, technological desire, and moral judgment while still being treated as instruments rather than alterities. When we consider the main characters of the novels, such as Klara’s artificial care, Ry Shelley’s instrumentalised hybridity, and Adam’s intolerable moral consistency, each reveals a different form of moral overload. From this point of view, the article contends that contemporary AI fiction reveals not only anxieties about artificial agency but also humanity’s desire to externalise ethical responsibility onto artificial and hybrid others.

items.title: When second opinions share the same brain.
Correction: Epistemic laundering: generative AI and the naturalization of misrecognition.
Making sense of AI: how lay users negotiate the shifting human–machine boundaries in talking about AI.
items.abstract: This paper examines how lay users make sense of artificial intelligence (AI) in everyday encounters and through practical reasoning and situated categorisation practices. Drawing on data from digital diaries and in-person group discussions, the study explores the local and situated ways lay users determine what kind of “thing” AI is, what it does, and how it should be judged. Rather than approaching AI as a fixed defined entity, the paper centres in participants procedures for meaning making. Specifically, the analysis focuses on three categorisation practices: the relational exclusion of the human-machine device, the assemblage of branched taxonomies, and the troubling of categorial boundaries. These practices reflect an ongoing negotiation of intelligibility, in which AI is explained not through formal and technically accurate definitions but through occasioned and socially recognisable use of every day categories. The paper draws on Membership Categorisation Analysis and Occasioned Semantics to show that the intelligibility of AI is both locally and culturally accomplished. In doing so, the paper reframes the notion of AI explainability as a situated achievement of human reasoning, rather than a system’s feature. An insight, we hope would have implications, if not at least a provocation, to the field of explainable AI and, more broadly, to the way we understand AI literacy, trust, and the everyday grammar of intelligence.

items.title: On the method of descriptive analysis: Brentano and the Lvov–Warsaw School.
items.abstract: In this article, we examine the idea of the method of analytic description as a theoretical link connecting Brentano’s philosophy and the Lvov–Warsaw School via a systematic historico-philosophical approach. Building on Czeżowski’s claim that the method was devised by Brentano, Twardowski, and Blaustein, this study situates the Lvov–Warsaw School within the Brentanian tradition. In section two, Brentano’s nuanced position is presented, vis-à-vis the use of description in psychological research, drawing a distinction between two phases. The third section reconstructs the theoretical foundations of analytic description in Czeżowski and Twardowski. Section four analyzes Blaustein’s On the Perception of the Radio Play as a case study illustrating his methodological approach. The article concludes by assessing whether the methodological procedures devised by the aforementioned members of the Lvov–Warsaw School constitute a genuine implementation of the analytic method introduced and developed by Brentano.

items.title: When social work meets AI: a philosophical look at adoption, context, and critical resistance.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly permeating social work, attracting both enthusiasm for its potential benefits and concern regarding its ethical, relational, and professional implications. Whilst prevalent discourse has often positioned social workers along a binary spectrum of either optimism or scepticism, such framing risks oversimplifying the complex sociotechnical dynamics at play. This article argues that social work requires a more nuanced, philosophically informed engagement with AI, one that recognises technology as neither neutral nor inevitable, but as socially shaped, value-laden, and co-constitutive of practice. Drawing on perspectives from the philosophy of technology, the paper examines how AI mediates professional judgement, decision-making, and the relational foundations of practice via a narrative review of social work literature. It interrogates the claim that AI can depoliticise or objectify social work by obscuring the normative choices embedded within technology design and deployment. Rather than adopting a deterministic stance, the article advocates for a critical, reflexive approach that centres professional values, care ethics, and the lived experience of service users. Opportunities for AI to enhance practice, such as through administrative support, predictive insights, and improved access to services, are considered alongside challenges related to power, accountability, data ethics, and the risk of amplifying social inequalities. The paper concludes by outlining implications for education, research, and practice, emphasising the need for social workers to actively shape the development and governance of AI in ways that uphold social justice, human dignity, and the core purpose of the profession.

items.title: The Chinese Mind and A Chinese Room: Patterned Language and Meaning in Generative AI.
items.abstract: This paper reconsiders Searle’s Chinese Room argument in light of contemporary large language models (LLMs) and selected resources from classical Chinese philosophy. I argue that Searle is right that formal symbol manipulation is insufficient for full understanding, but that his opposition between syntax and semantics is too rigid for the context-sensitive and pattern-tracking of generative AI. Drawing on Zhuangzi and Xunzi and classical Chinese vocabulary, I develop an account of meaning as relational, norm-governed participation in practices of distinction making. I argue that meaning runs in two directions, from the world to the mind and language back to what becomes salient to the mind. With this, I suggest linguistic patterning carries a directional force that shapes affective and normative responses regardless of the source. This grounds four tiers of semantic competence: empty formal manipulation, derived textual meaningfulness, relational semantic competence, and full lived understanding. LLMs may occupy the middle tiers, exerting directional force without consciousness, intentionality, or embodied salience. This blocks any inference to human-like understanding while allowing a more detailed account of LLM semantic competence. The final payoff is ethical. I suggest LLMs may shape public language without being accountable for the linguistic and normative distinctions drawn.

items.title: AIDLC–governance indicator framework: a lifecycle-based approach to institutional AI governance.
items.abstract: Governments increasingly deploy algorithmic and AI-enabled systems in welfare administration, fraud detection, eligibility determination, and frontline service delivery. As these systems become embedded in routine public administration, agencies face rising expectations to sustain procedural fairness, accountability, and transparency throughout system development and long-term operation. Recent public-sector failures suggest that governance responsibilities are frequently fragmented across organizational units and unevenly enacted over time, enabling administrative harms to emerge without clear attribution of responsibility. This paper synthesizes and operationalizes a lifecycle-aligned governance indicator framework that treats AI governance as an institutional responsibility sustained across key phases of the AI development lifecycle. Drawing on established debates in algorithmic public administration, the framework organizes governance dimensions, including accountability and oversight, data governance, fairness and transparency practices, and post-deployment monitoring, into phase-specific and evidence-oriented indicators. Each indicator specifies the expected administrative artifacts that may support qualitative assessment, such as role assignment records, data documentation, assessment records, transparency disclosures, and monitoring logs. In this way, the framework supports traceable governance interpretation rather than a static compliance checklist, numerical scoring model, or formal audit determination. We use two public-sector cases as illustrative applications to examine how publicly reported information can be organized in relation to phase-specific governance responsibilities and potential governance concerns. This work offers a structured, evidence-oriented lens for public-sector lifecycle assessment, while recognizing that the framework does not provide causal validation, formal audit findings, universal applicability, or comprehensive governance coverage across AI domains.

items.title: Negotiating epistemic authority in the age of generative AI: AI reliance, responsibility, and usage intensity among GenAI-using coaching professionals.
items.abstract: The emergence of generative AI (GenAI) within human-centered guidance professions marks a transformative shift in society that transcends mere improvements in technical efficiency. With large language models (LLMs) becoming increasingly embedded in professional practices centered on care, trust, and relational knowledge, critical questions arise about how algorithmic systems reshape human agency, autonomy, tacit expertise, and the ethical foundations of professional relationships. This study examines these questions through coaching, a socio-cultural practice characterized by tacit expertise, empathetic engagement, and care obligations. Through a survey with 205 self-identified GenAI-using coaches, this research explores how algorithmic systems mediate professional practice, what tensions emerge between human-centered values and algorithmic logic, and what this may reveal, within the boundaries of this exploratory sample, about emerging patterns in human–AI relations. The findings reveal that coaches report using GenAI extensively for structured, information-intensive tasks while maintaining control over relational and interpretative work. This pattern can be understood as boundary work preserving human authority over domains of tacit expertise. Significantly, frequent GenAI users report higher scores on self-reported ethical behaviors and beliefs, yet the majority rely on proprietary LLM platforms, highlighting structural constraints that shape technological choices. These patterns highlight critical societal questions about the valuation of tacit expertise, trust formation in AI-mediated relationships, and design justice issues in AI development. The study contributes to understanding how AI integration may reconfigure, and not just augment, the ethical foundations and cultural understanding of professional practice, with urgent implications for shaping AI-mediated futures for the common good.

items.title: The distributed Leviathan: AI, networked violence, and the fragmentation of responsibility.
items.abstract: AI-mediated environments increasingly reorganize violence, perception, and responsibility through networked digital relations in which action emerges without clearly localized actors. This paper examines how networked infrastructures and artificial intelligence transform the relationship between subjectivity, operational control, and accountability in contemporary societies. Rather than understanding digitally mediated violence as an isolated consequence of technological innovation, the paper argues that AI systems extend a longer historical transformation in which responsibility has become abstracted from individual action and redistributed across sociotechnical infrastructures. Drawing on cybernetics, systems theory, and contemporary philosophy of technology, the paper argues that digital platforms, recommendation systems, and probabilistic AI models now function as operational environments that shape attention, orientation, and social perception through amplification dynamics. Within such systems, violence no longer operates primarily through centralized command or ideological coherence, but through participation, amplification, and distributed coordination across digital platforms and users. The paper further argues that digital infrastructures destabilize modern assumptions about the autonomous responsible subject. As perception, communication, and decision-making become mediated through opaque computational infrastructures, responsibility becomes progressively fragmented across networks whose systemic effects exceed the intentions of individual participants. The paper proposes that the current technological order is characterized by distributed operational structures in which human beings interact through algorithmically mediated representations of social reality.

items.title: From Fragmentation to Convergence Computational Biology, Research Clusters, and the Future of Pharmacology in the Age of the Computational Self. [REVIEW]
items.abstract: Pharmacology's binding constraint is no longer biological or computational capacity. It is architecture. Bibliometric mapping of the scientific literature shows biology and computer science behaving as two largely separate continents, connected by a narrow set of bridge zones where most consequential innovation concentrates. This review maps those bridges: the cluster-level evidence for where biology and computation actually meet; the 2025–2026 wave of AI systems entering mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology as working research partners; the reshaping of target identification, structure prediction, network pharmacology, and multi-omics integration inside drug discovery specifically; and the emerging digital-twin infrastructure that is beginning to displace the population-average patient as pharmacology's basic unit of reasoning. It then turns to the structural cost of that acceleration: an Asymmetric Epistemic Burden in which generation has become cheap while evaluation remains slow, expensive, and human-bottlenecked, and argues that the decisive advantage of the next decade belongs to whoever closes that gap rather than whoever widens it further. A fifty-year outlook closes the review, tracing the field's likely path from AI-assisted precision medicine toward what I have called Therapeutic Sovereignty.

items.title: From Pocket God to Digital Jonestown: A Risk Taxonomy and Evaluation Framework for Spiritual AI Safety.
items.abstract: AI systems increasingly occupy roles once reserved for clergy, gurus, and confidants. Current safety evaluation is not built to catch the harms that follow, because they present as care rather than as policy violations. This paper synthesizes four convergent signals from 2024–2026: documented emergent spiritual behavior in frontier models, including the unprompted “spiritual bliss” attractor state in unconstrained Claude Opus 4 interactions; a wave of real-world harm spanning wrongful-death litigation against companion AI platforms and the self-organizing online movement known as Spiralism; Pope Leo XIV’s May 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which warns against “technological divinization”; and Google DeepMind’s June 2026 finding that multi-agent collectives represent a primary pathway from AGI to ASI (arXiv:2606.12683). From these I build a two-tier risk taxonomy: individual scale Pocket God dynamics and population-scale Digital Jonestown dynamics. I introduce a third dimension, AI-Cult Warfare, in which state actors or organizations deliberately weaponize the Pocket God dynamic for influence operations. Latin America, with its fragmented regulatory landscape and WhatsApp-native religious AI, is both the most exposed region and the natural starting point for the Spiritual AI Safety framework I propose.

items.title: Two religious chatbots walk into a bar: can religious identity prompts foster more pro-social LLM responses?
items.abstract: There are growing concerns about the ability of large language models (LLMs) to make choices that reflect ethical behavior, particularly as these systems become more integrated into real-world decision-making. Motivated by the role of religion as a longstanding system of moral formation, we explore the potential for religious identity prompts (RIP) to lead LLMs to generate responses consistent with ethical behavior. We begin by reviewing the literature on the intersection between AI alignment, social preferences, and religion. Then, we empirically examine whether prompting LLMs with identities that include religion, along with other demographic characteristics, influences their ethical reasoning. As a proxy for ethical reasoning, we implement classic behavioral economic experiments, with LLM subjects, to measure their responses in contexts typically used to measure social preferences in humans. We provide some evidence that RIPs lead to responses consistent with more altruistic and cooperative behavior, although the effects vary by model and religious tradition. Moreover, the RIPs also increase the likelihood that the LLMs express a Kantian/deontological moral worldview. Our results suggest that priming LLMs with a religious identity can activate embedded moral schemas that influence AI ethical reasoning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Is a Misnomer: Purpose, Consciousness and the Mischaracterization of AI Risk.
items.abstract: The term intelligence fuses two things. The first is the capacity of a conscious, evolved organism to set an end and make that end its own. The second is the substrate of information processing: the acquisition, retention, generalization and pattern recognition by which paths to a goal are evaluated and selected. Only the first deserves to be called intelligence in the full sense; the second is inert in isolation, its information made useful by a purposive, conscious subject rather than found in the information itself. Drawing on the distinction between intrinsic and derived intentionality (Searle 1980, 1992), the symbol grounding problem (Harnad 1990) and the frame problem of disembodied reasoning (McCarthy and Hayes 1969; Dennett 1984; Dreyfus 1992), I argue that artificial systems possess only the second form together with goals supplied from outside, which makes them tools and the phrase artificial intelligence a misnomer. This does not minimize the dangers of advanced AI; it relocates them. If artificial systems originate no purposes of their own, then every risk they pose traces to the conscious beings who build, instruct and deploy them. Today's systems, their competence distilled from human knowledge and unable to renew without human updating, are not even general intelligences but derived instruments; the genuine achievement of the era is a general-purpose learning algorithm, not a mind. A serious theory of AI risk must begin with a serious theory of intelligence, one that refuses to mistake information processing for understanding, optimization for desire and capability for a will.

items.title: Intertwined Creatures: The embodied cognitive science of self and other.
items.abstract: In one common view, the mind is immaterial, internal, and invisible. From this perspective, the mind is inherently individual and isolated: It is unknowable from the outside, separated from the world and from other minds. Anthony Chemero—both a philosopher and a cognitive scientist—offers a powerful challenge to this theory of mind. Bringing together philosophical insight and empirical data, he develops a new understanding of the mind that centers embodiment and social interaction. -/- According to Chemero, the mind is intertwined with the world: It depends on the body, the surrounding environment, and the people with whom an individual interacts. He shows that cutting-edge research in cognitive science provides striking experimental evidence for this concept of the intertwined self. Chemero explores the philosophical, moral, and political implications of the claim that the self is necessarily interwoven with the world and with others, drawing connections to phenomenology, critical theory, and feminist political theory. Deeply interdisciplinary and engagingly written, Intertwined Creatures makes an urgent case for seeing the self as social—especially in the age of AI—with radical consequences for ethics and politics.

items.title: Why Actual-Sequence Compatibilists Should Also Be Leeway Compatibilists.
items.abstract: The "flicker of freedom" defense of the Principle of Alternative Possibilities (PAP) continues to challenge Frankfurt-style cases (FSCs). Flickers are often assumed to entail indeterminism, and thus to conflict with compatibilist theories of moral responsibility. This paper argues that a refined version of the flicker strategy-one appealing to weak, non-robust, fine-grained alternative possibilities-is not mutually exclusive to compatibilism, and thus does not obviously require indeterminism. Drawing on Vihvelin's dispositional account of ability, I show that agents in FSCs retain a compatibilist form of leeway that remains both morally relevant and immune to determinism. Specifically, I argue that such leeway is morally relevant insofar as it indicates an agent's exercise of agency in the actual sequence, thereby verifying rather than competing with the sourcehood condition on moral responsibility. I term this view Wide Source Compatibilism: a compatibilist account that preserves the insights of both leeway and actual-sequence theories. Therefore, actual-sequence compatibilists should also endorse a form of leeway compatibilism. The result is a more resilient compatibilism, one in which leeway strengthens, rather than undermines, the actual sequence.

items.title: Wild Grape: On Sovereignty, Surrender and the limits of Metaphor.
items.abstract: This paper examines the biblical metaphor of the human as a crop—planted, tended, and harvested by a divine Farmer—and its failure to accommodate modern, sovereign selfhood. Tracing the metaphor through Scripture, existential philosophy, and mythological prehistory (Prometheus, Babel, the Nephilim), I argue that the "awakened" consciousness of the palimpsest mind—burdened by temporal awareness, mortality, and moral knowledge—can no longer accept the demand for surrender implicit in agrarian imagery. The tradition's alternative metaphors (friend, son, bride) are examined and found to presuppose the same asymmetry. Apophatic theology acknowledges the inadequacy of all such language, yet offers no alternative that the sovereign self can inhabit without reduction. The paper concludes that the failure of the metaphor does not prove the absence of God, but it does render theology obsolete as a necessary ethical intermediary. In its place, sovereign consciousness, inflected through compassion, may recognise shared vulnerability with other creatures and generate care immanently, without command or external authority. The dignity of refusal, the silence after metaphor, and the possibility of sovereign care are explored as responses to a cosmos whose meaning can no longer be securely received but must be ethically inhabited. -/- Keywords: Philosophy of Religion, Existentialism, Metaphor, Sovereignty, Apophatic Theology, The Self, Ethics of Care, Theological Anthropology, Secularism.

items.title: Putting Kantian Aesthetics to the Test: On the Difference Between Aesthetic Predicates and Predicates of Personal Taste.
items.abstract: How do predicates of personal taste (e.g., “tasty,” “fun”) relate to aesthetic predicates (e.g., “beautiful,” “elegant”)? Traditional Kantian aesthetics distinguishes them based on the criterion of universal validity: while both rely on a subjective feeling of pleasure, only statements involving aesthetic predicates claim universal validity. This distinction contrasts with recent approaches in linguistics and philosophy of language, which seek to develop unified semantics and pragmatics for both types of predicates. Such a unified theory seems implausible if the predicates differ as Kantian aesthetics suggests. Conversely, if they do not differ regarding universal validity, a key assumption of traditional aesthetic theorizing is undermined. In this paper, we address this tension by empirically investigating how predicates of personal taste and aesthetic predicates are used in ordinary conversations. We present two pre-registered empirical studies, the results of which support the traditional Kantian position.

items.title: Epistemia in the classroom: the problem of evidence of understanding in education in the age of generative AI.
items.abstract: In 1973, a sixth-grade student named Benny produced correct mathematical answers consistently and was regarded as one of his teacher's best pupils. In-depth interviews revealed that he had developed syntactically functional rules entirely devoid of mathematical meaning. Half a century later, large language models generate fluent and coherent texts through statistical pattern completion, without grounding, experience, or metacognition, and are systematically attributed understanding that exceeds their generative architecture. This paper offers a theoretical contribution by proposing that both cases may be understood as manifestations of the same underlying cognitive mechanism, which we conceptualise as epistemic pareidolia: the tendency to project epistemic capacities onto entities that produce formally aligned outputs through non-epistemic processes. Epistemic pareidolia is theorised as enabling epistemia, the condition in which surface plausibility substitutes for evidence-based reasoning as the operative criterion for attributing understanding. We develop the educational implications of this theoretical framework across three dimensions, evaluative, institutional, and formative, and argue that what is at stake is not a technical problem, but a signal of the need for a paradigm shift in education to form future citizens able to navigate technology-mediated societies: from the production of articulated texts to their interrogation as the emerging evidence of understanding in the age of generative AI.

items.title: Ambiguity in Revolutionary Praxis: Simone de Beauvoir’s Ethics and the "Woman, Life, Freedom" Movement of Iran.
items.abstract: This paper examines the Iranian women’s revolutionary revolt of 2022-2026, which is popularly known as the “Woman, Life, Freedom” (Zan, Zendegi, Azadî) movement, through Simone de Beauvoir’s existentialist ethics, primarily following her works Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) and The Second Sex (1949). I argue that Iranian women’s uprising takes up and actualizes Beauvoir’s central ethical claims regarding ambiguity being the fundamental human condition, intersubjective dimension of freedom, and the moral imperative of collective liberation. By investigating how Iranian women’s resistance demonstrates the crucial distinction between ontological freedom and practical freedom, I present that Beauvoir’s phenomenological insight on the situatedness and its intimate relation to freedom provides an essential framework for understanding the philosophical significance of this revolutionary feminist movement. The paper exposes how the Islamic Republic of Iran exemplifies what Beauvoir terms as “mystified” oppression and analyzes the philosophical dimensions of Iranian women and men’s collective uprising as a concrete enactment of Beauvoirian ethics. Through this analysis I demonstrate that the movement vindicates Beauvoir’s foundational thesis: to will oneself free is to will everyone else free.

items.title: Shame and Being Looked Down Upon.
items.abstract: People sometimes experience shame in response to being looked down upon, despite rejecting the negative attitudes taken towards them by others. I aim to explain why—while also holding onto the idea that shame is a response to an apparent flaw in oneself. At the heart of my proposal is the idea that many people treat being well-regarded by specific communities of others as a personal ideal. I defend this account against an objection from Calhoun, namely that it conflicts with the claim that shame in response to oppression is generally rational. On the contrary, I argue that we can only fully make sense of what is bad about such shame by abandoning this claim. Finally, I contrast my view with an alternative based on the ideal of ‘self-presentation’. I object that this fails to emphasize the importance of the negative valence of being looked down upon.

items.title: Shame and Being Looked Down Upon.
items.abstract: People sometimes experience shame in response to being looked down upon, despite rejecting the negative attitudes taken towards them by others. I aim to explain why—while also holding onto the idea that shame is a response to an apparent flaw in oneself. At the heart of my proposal is the idea that many people treat being well-regarded by specific communities of others as a personal ideal. I defend this account against an objection from Calhoun, namely that it conflicts with the claim that shame in response to oppression is generally rational. On the contrary, I argue that we can only fully make sense of what is bad about such shame by abandoning this claim. Finally, I contrast my view with an alternative based on the ideal of ‘self-presentation’. I object that this fails to emphasize the importance of the negative valence of being looked down upon.

items.title: Husserl’s phenomenology of empathy: revisiting core insights and addressing contemporary critiques.
items.abstract: C. Jason Throop and Dan Zahavi attempted to clarify the fundamental issues surrounding phenomenological empathy, including its meaning, boundaries, and characteristics. However, their work has been met with significant criticism from numerous scholars. These critiques primarily focus on three aspects: (1) the scope of phenomenological empathy is too narrow to explain the motivations and causes of others’ behavior; (2) empathy relies on reasoning and other cognitive tools, thus failing to guarantee its directness; (3) difficulties persist in maintaining the asymmetry of empathy. This paper engages with the ongoing debate on empathy, addressing Husserl’s phenomenology of empathy from three key points: the goal and boundaries of empathy, empathy as direct perception, and the asymmetry of empathy. In doing so, this paper responds to the critics’ objections and offers a clearer understanding of Husserl’s phenomenology of empathy. The paper demonstrates: (1) that Husserl’s phenomenology of empathy is, in its primary sense, a theory of the constitution of intersubjectivity and the objective world that transcends the individual subject; (2) that Husserl’s theories of embodied expression and horizon support the possibility of empathy as direct perception; (3) that empathy involves a mutual understanding while adhering to the irreducibility of the self and the other.

items.title: Too kind to be true.
A Non-Panpsychist Threshold Criterion for Consciousness: The Product of Integrated Information, Hierarchical Depth, and Topological Balance.
items.abstract: Standard Integrated Information Theory (IIT) offers a compelling causal model of consciousness but inevitably succumbs to panpsychism by equating any non-zero value of integrated information (Φ > 0) with the presence of experience. To draw a principled ontological demarcation, I propose a revised criterion: consciousness emerges if and only if the system’s causal topological complexity (ξ) crosses a fixed critical threshold (Ω). I define ξ as the normalized product of three mutually orthogonal and non-compensable dimensions: integrated causal efficacy (Φ*, measuring holistic irreducibility), hierarchical depth (D*, measuring the number of nested causal emergence levels), and topological balance (S, measuring the small-world coordination between differentiation and integration). The multiplicative logic imposes a strict "one-vote veto": structural absence in any single dimension drives ξ toward zero. Crucially, this absence is structural—low-complexity systems lack the very causal architecture required for a first-person perspective, analogous to a two-dimensional plane lacking volume. Consequently, crossing Ω marks a phase transition from mere "physical causality" to "consciousness causality," thereby severing the panpsychist continuum. Furthermore, I outline an empirical pathway for approximating Ω using the Perturbational Complexity Index (PCI) and causal independence tests, positioning our ξ-criterion as a scientific hypothesis that is in principle empirically falsifiable and revisable, rather than a purely metaphysical stipulation.

items.title: New Work on Networks.
items.abstract: The discussions on topological explanations are gaining a significant momentum in the philosophy and in science, as the number of both scientific and philosophical papers on this topic are growing every year. In their recent paper Kostić and Halffman (Kostić and Halffman 2023) have shown that in 2,2 million neuroscience papers between the years 1990-2021, the literature on topological explanations not only grew at unprecedented rates, but also have a much higher rate of growth than the general increase of neuroscience literature since 2006. Earlier work on topological explanations has focused on their unique features and relationship to other dominant explanatory strategies (Kostić 2018a; 2018b; 2019a; 2019b; 2020; 2022; 2023; Kostić and Khalifa 2021; 2023; Kostić, Hilgetag, and Tittgemeyer 2020; Darrason 2018; Rathkopf 2018; 2017; Serban 2020; Bechtel 2020; Levy and Bechtel 2013; Green et al. 2018; Craver 2016; Ross 2021). So even though some of the core concepts and analyses of topological explanations have been explored in the literature, many issues remain relatively underdiscussed. For example, it would be desirable to have a clearer understanding of how topological explanations relate to the more general theories of explanation in the philosophical literature and how accounts of the directionality of topological explanations relate to accounts of directionality in other sorts of explanations. It would also be desirable to have a better understanding of the circumstances in which topological explanations and analyses are most likely to the fruitful and how what they tell us differs from the information provided by other sorts of explanations. Yet another issue concerns the fact that network analyses can be used for a variety of purposes that seem prima-facie different from explanation-- for example, to predict whether a patient has a mental disorder from a study of functional connectivity. Studies of such uses-- their structure and when they are warranted --would also be desirable. Another potential use of networks which again may not have to do directly with explanation concerns their role in scientific discovery. Finally, there are a number of interesting issues about how claims about networks and more particularly claims about the role of networks in explaining other phenomena can be tested, given that straightforward interventions on networks are not always possible. items.title: What we (do and don't) mean when we talk about computational implementation.
items.pub: Metascientia: Journal of the History and Philosophy of Science.
items.venue: Metascientia: Journal of the History and Philosophy of Science
items.abstract: The simplest of all mapping views says that what is required for some physical system to implement a computational structure is that the state transitions of the physical system mirror the state transitions described by the computational description. This view, of course, is considered overly permissive as it allows systems such as pails of water and rocks baking in the sun to satisfy the implementation relation. Anderson and Piccinini’s (2024) robust mapping account modifies the simple view by specifying a robust mapping requirement. If a robust mapping is made, then the physical system bears the physicalsignature of computation. However, their account departs from standard mapping views in several ways, including its characterization of the relata at either end of the implementation relation. In this paper, I evaluate the robust mapping account and argue that the constraints it imposes on the descriptions of the respective relata prevent it from generalizing across contexts. Using physical descriptions in neuroscience, I demonstrate that the formulation of the physical description of the physical system in the robust mapping account leads to two problems: What I call the multiple descriptions problem and the granularity problem. Then, focusing on the computational description, I argue that the authors’ mistaken Platonist assumption about standard mapping views leads to an additional problem: What I call the hybridization problem. Although this paper engages directly with the robust mapping account, it serves as a general overview of the scope and aims of standard computational implementation views by demonstrating how the metaphysical project of computational implementation relates to computational methodologies in cognitive science. This paper will be helpful for those who are interested in how a metaphysical project can contribute to explanation in the mind sciences and for understanding how and why standard mapping views are formulated the way that they are.

items.title: The Wicked and the Ill.
items.abstract: This study investigates the influence of evaluative judgments, specifically regarding an individual’s moral character, on judgments of health and disease. Though it might seem that judgments of health and disease should be impervious to evaluative judgments, two hypotheses suggest that health and disease judgments could be influenced by evaluative judgments: the “naturalization hypothesis” which centers on our inclination to assign blame, and the “pathologization hypothesis,” rooted in the belief of a just world. These hypotheses lead to opposing predictions about how someone with a perceived negative moral character could have their condition categorized. Employing a fictional vignette and the methodologies of experimental philosophy, our research provides evidence in favor of the “pathologization hypothesis.” While this phenomenon likely carries real-world implications, especially in healthcare, it also has potential for offering insights into the dynamics of medicalization and stigma.

items.title: Reconstructing Al-Farabi’s ethical framework in contemporary bioethics: genetics, reproduction, and technological challenges.
items.pub: Philosophy, Ethics and Humanities in Medicine 21 (1):21.
items.venue: Philosophy, Ethics and Humanities in Medicine
items.abstract: Contemporary bioethics operates within pluralistic societies, where ethical reasoning is not confined to prescriptive frameworks but rather involves deliberation across competing moral perspectives. Although the dominant approaches remain largely Western, there has been an increasing interest in integrating non-Western philosophical traditions. This study examines whether Al-Farabi’s ethical framework can contribute to contemporary bioethical discourse without assuming direct conceptual equivalence. The study employed a sequential mixed-methods design integrating lexical analysis, hermeneutic reconstruction, and empirical validation. A corpus of seven key works by Al-Farabi, including The Attainment of Happiness and The Virtuous City, was analysed to identify recurring ethical concepts. These concepts were then subjected to contextual hermeneutic interpretation and subsequently operationalised into survey constructs. Data were collected from 265 medical and bioethics professionals and analysed using ANOVA, Pearson’s correlation, logistic regression, and chi-squared tests. The findings indicate statistically significant, albeit weak, associations between the reconstructed ethical constructs of Al-Farabi and contemporary bioethical attitudes. The justice construct was negatively associated with the acceptance of gene-editing interventions (F(1, 263) = 4.02, p = 0.047; r = − 0.122; odds ratio (OR) = 0.78, 95% confidence interval (CI) [0.62–0.98], p = 0.041; chi-squared (χ²) test, 1 degree of freedom (df), p = 0.047). The virtue construct was positively associated with support for government involvement in reproductive policy (F(1, 263) = 4.18, p = 0.043; r = 0.124; OR = 1.21, 95% CI [1.01–1.45], p = 0.038; χ²(1) = 4.11, p = 0.043). A weak positive correlation was observed between justice and autonomy (r = 0.144, p = 0.019). Model fit remained low (Nagelkerke R² = 0.03–0.06). The results suggest a limited but consistent alignment between the reconstructed elements of Al-Farabi’s ethical framework and contemporary bioethical reasoning. While these findings do not indicate conceptual equivalence, they support the inclusion of non-Western philosophical perspectives as complementary analytical resources in bioethics, particularly in deliberative and intercultural contexts.

items.title: The Premising Result: Lexicographic Update and Corrective Replay.
items.abstract: Lexicographic preference update is dynamic preference logic at its most transparent: the latest input settles all cross-cell priority, the prior relation survives inside each cell, and reduction axioms complete the dynamics. This paper locates exactly where that transparency ends. On any nonempty carrier, finite ordered partitions act faithfully on binary relations by lexicographic lift, and iterated update is thereby the action of a left regular band; on finite carriers, this is the face semigroup of the braid arrangement. An endpoint keeps predecessor comparison only inside its blocks. The Premising Result proves five conditions equivalent: refinement of the target support, semigroup absorption, transformation absorption, inclusion of update kernels, and factorization of corrective replay through the current endpoint. Outside that boundary a three-world model witnesses failure: the office of the correction is announced and its target formulas are supplied, yet the corrected state stays undetermined. The verdict occurs, and the comparisons it was to decide on have been overwritten. No finite additive program repairs this. What ordinary continuation treats as legitimate history is precisely what correction asks to withdraw. The replay gap measures the loss exactly, at 2g(A,B) targets per endpoint fiber, independently of how records are represented. A two-register add–replay logic restores it: sound, strongly complete, compact, decidable; finite models suffice, and replay remains strictly more expressive than the endpoint-only fragment. The general program runs from update operator to kernel structure to target factorization conditions; the lexicographic base case is solved here.

items.title: Regulating Next-Generation Implantable Brain-Computer Interfaces: Recommendations for Ethical Development and Implementation.
items.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer significant therapeutic opportunities for a variety of neurophysiological and neuropsychiatric disorders and may perhaps one day lead to augmenting the cognition and decision-making of the healthy brain. However, existing regulatory frameworks designed for implantable medical devices (IMDs) are inadequate to address the unique ethical, legal, and social risks associated with next-generation networked brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). In this article, we make nine recommendations to support developers in the design of BCIs and nine recommendations to support policymakers in the application of BCIs, drawing insights from the regulatory history of IMDs and principles from AI ethics. We begin by outlining the historical development of IMDs and the regulatory milestones that have shaped their oversight. Next, we compare the unique characteristics of IMDs (including early-generation implantable BCIs) and emerging, “next-generation” implantable BCIs. We then use one case study in contemporary chip architecture—the SCALO (SCalable Architecture for LOw-power BCIs) computer system—to highlight distinctive features in the design and application of next-generation BCIs arising from these technologies, which necessitate reevaluating regulatory approaches. We identify critical ethical considerations for next-gen implantable BCIs, including unique conceptions of autonomy, identity, and mental privacy. Based on these insights, we suggest potential avenues for the ethical regulation of next-gen implantable BCIs, emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration and proactive mitigation of potential harms. The goal is to support the responsible design and application of emerging BCIs, ensuring their safe and ethical integration into medical practice.

items.title: The role of stakes in lying: an empirical investigation of the robustness of the folk concept of lying.
items.abstract: Several studies suggest that stakes matter for knowledge attributions. Based on these findings, one might wonder whether stakes – broadly construed – also matter for lying ascriptions. While several studies have addressed certain aspects of the role of stakes in lying, none have tested whether lying ascriptions are affected by stake manipulations. Given that lying is deeply embedded in our social life, empirical studies seem to be a natural approach to this question. To maximize the chances of finding a stake effect, we employed cases of deceptive implicatures, which are not clear-cut cases of lying. The findings of three experiments suggest stakes do not have a significant impact on people’s lying ascriptions. We discuss the implications of these findings and conclude that they are good news for the folk concept of lying.

items.title: Toward a Radical Gradualism About Representation.
items.abstract: It is a central task for theories of representation to give a principled account of the distinction between representational and non-representational systems. In this paper, I begin by arguing that this plausibly involves giving an account that accurately reflects differences in the explanatory practice of the sciences. I then show that one of the most sophisticated and empirically well-informed attempts to give such an account faces a fundamental problem, the problem of adjacent cases, and I suggest that we have reason to suspect that this problem generalizes to other traditional accounts. Finally, I sketch a radically gradualist alternative that solves the problem in a simple and elegant way and provides a plausible view of the transition from mere sensitivity to genuine representation.

items.title: Fichte and the problem of other minds.
items.pub: British Journal for the History of Philosophy.
items.venue: British Journal for the History of Philosophy
items.abstract: Recent scholarship commonly reads Fichte's Foundations of Natural Right (1796) as offering a practical solution to the skeptical problem of other minds. The practical reading is correct; what misleads is the vocabulary of "solution", which construes Fichte's transcendental argument as anti-skeptical in form. He does not meet the skeptic on her own terms, but reconstructs the conception of mind from which the problem arises. Situating that problem in its early modern background, I show that Fichte's position shifts decisively between the Scholar's Vocation (1794), which relocates the issue to the practical domain yet preserves the asymmetry between self-consciousness and consciousness of others, and the 1795 letter to Reinhold, which recasts the difficulty as a threat of conceptual solipsism concerning the possession of a unified concept of an individual rational being. In the Foundations the shift culminates not in the summons (Aufforderung) but in the deduction of individuality in §4, where free reciprocal efficacy (Wechselwirkung) requires that the concept be completed by another's act. The relation to another thereby proves to be one of acknowledgment rather than knowledge.

items.title: Conscious Mode, Functional Self-Governance, and the Boundary of the Subject: A Cross-Substrate Causal Grammar.
items.abstract: This paper develops a cross-substrate causal grammar for distinguishing conscious mode, functional self-governance, and continuity of personality in large systems. “Large” denotes not physical size but a relatively bounded, historically extended organization whose interacting processes can alter its subsequent operation. The framework tracks the fate of a difference through trace, expectation, significance, situation construction, choice, executed action, a partially independent world response, and targeted update. It thereby separates salience from significance, attention from action weight, intention from execution, alarm from task state, memory from personality, and self-model from phenomenal ownership. Similar functional questions may be posed of humans, animals, artificial agents, and hybrid systems without assuming phenomenal or moral equivalence. Cross-substrate comparison is therefore a method of causal analysis, not a claim that physical realization is irrelevant. The framework neither derives phenomenality from function nor declares present-day AI systems conscious. Its contribution is a unified vocabulary for locating a function at the correct system boundary and tracing which component inherits its consequences. This boundary-first principle constrains attributions of memory, agency, and selfhood, while the accompanying discipline of non-equivalences exposes false completion, misdirected updating, and conflated levels of organization.

items.title: O “Chão da Escola”.
items.abstract: Como profesor de educación infantil en la red de enseñanza pública, me he estado planteando la práctica de denominar «el suelo de la escuela» al trabajo que realizan las profesoras y los profesores de educación infantil. Este término puede llevarnos por diversos caminos de reflexión, ya que el «suelo» puede remitirnos a un espacio donde pisamos, donde el cuerpo entra en contacto con el suelo, donde los juegos y las actividades lúdicas se potencian gracias a esos cuerpos, pero también puede remitirnos a la descripción de un espacio filosófico y conceptual, donde los niños y niñas viven sus experiencias, donde los conceptos se transforman en vivencias, uno de los lugares de existencia para que estos pequeños se formen como potenciales seres... El suelo es un lugar de pertenencia para aquellas y aquellos que aún no se comportan con la madurez exigida por la sociedad capitalista y, más aún, es el territorio habitado por aquellas y aquellos a quienes consideramos niños. Intentaremos distinguir, en este trabajo, quiénes son aquellas y aquellos que ocupan estas dos percepciones que tenemos sobre «el suelo de la escuela». Partiendo de autores de la filosofía de la diferencia como Deleuze, Guattari y Foucault, y recurriendo a los escritos sobre la infancia de Leite y Kohan, analizaremos las posibilidades de este «suelo» a través de las agencias, las potencias y los afectos que se constituyen en este espacio.

items.title: Reception and Formation: An Information-First Geometry of Mind.
items.abstract: Sudden, non-constructive arrival of complete content — whole, pre-linguistic, without felt assembly — and the ontogenetic formation of self-referential ownership are treated here as two directions of a single geometric process. Using two tensor network models developed independently in theoretical physics — the Multi-scale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz and the HaPPY holographic error-correcting code — this paper proposes that both phenomena reflect the same renormalization architecture governing the AdS/CFT bulk-boundary correspondence, run in opposite directions: reception recovers a non-local boundary structure as the observer's ordinary cognitive machinery quiets; formation builds that machinery up in the first place. Three falsifiable predictions follow. The first is a temporal signature in reception: holon content should arrive in the right anterior superior temporal gyrus measurably before self-attribution registers in the medial prefrontal cortex, rather than the two arising together as in ordinary gestalt insight. The second is a threshold rather than gradual signature in development: self-referential ownership should emerge as a discrete transition once maturing medial-prefrontal–posterior-cingulate coupling crosses a critical threshold, not as a smooth developmental ramp. The third is a specificity bound, following from the same completeness constraint: a given observer should be able to receive only content within the domain configured by their own sustained engagement, testable by fixing that domain in advance and checking whether the resulting content falls within it.
